5.w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is hyperthermia, fluctuating consciousness, muscle rigidity and autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia, labile blood pressure, sweating). It is rare but potentially fatal and can occur with any antipsychotic (BNF psychoses treatment summary).

n.0: Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and features clonus and hyperreflexia; he has started an antipsychotic.
n.1: Acute dystonia is a localised muscle spasm; it does not cause fever, confusion or autonomic instability.
n.3: Antimuscarinic toxicity causes dry, flushed skin rather than sweating and does not cause generalised rigidity.

5.q: Ravi, 37, is detained under section 3 in an independent hospital, with his care arranged and paid for by the NHS. In October 2026 he asks whether the hospital must act compatibly with his human rights. What is the accurate answer?
o: No, because the CQC protects his rights in an independent hospital
Yes, as the 2025 Act extended HRA duties to such providers in April 2026
Yes, once the remaining provisions of the 2025 Act are commenced
No, because the Human Rights Act binds NHS bodies, not private ones
5.w: Section 51 of the Mental Health Act 2025 (new s142C of the 1983 Act), in force from 6 April 2026 under SI 2026/385, makes private providers of care arranged under the MHA subject to the Human Rights Act 1998 in providing that care.

n.0: The CQC regulates providers but does not replace the provider's own HRA duties.
n.2: Section 51 was commenced on 6 April 2026; it does not wait for the rest of the Act.
n.3: Section 51 of the 2025 Act now extends HRA duties to private providers of MHA-arranged care.

5.q: At 21:00 Yusuf arrives to take charge of a 24-bed ward for the night. One registered nurse has phoned in sick and no replacement has been found, leaving Yusuf as the only registered nurse with three healthcare assistants. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the shift and complete an incident report at the end of the night describing it
Start the shift and allocate the medicines round to the most senior healthcare assistant
Escalate immediately to the site manager, as fewer than two registered nurses is a red flag
Ask the day staff to stay until midnight and then manage the remainder of the shift himself
5.w: NICE SG1 Box 2 lists fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift as a nursing red flag, which requires an immediate escalation response. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt action on risks to safety and effective management of staff and resources.

n.0: Reporting after the shift leaves the risk unmanaged throughout the night.
n.1: Healthcare assistants cannot be delegated tasks outside their competence, such as a full registered nurse medicines round (Code 11.1).
n.3: A short extension by tired day staff does not solve the shortfall for most of the night and bypasses escalation.

5.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
5.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

5.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
5.q: Mr Barnes, 51, has schizophrenia. He tells a nurse on the ward he has had a heavy pain in his chest for an hour. A colleague says he often complains of aches when he is anxious. What should the nurse do?
o: Offer PRN lorazepam to help him settle
Assess the pain fully, including observations and an ECG
Reassure him that his anxiety is causing the discomfort
Ask him to mention it at tomorrow's ward round
5.w: Attributing physical symptoms to mental illness (diagnostic overshadowing) contributes to the SMI mortality gap. Chest pain needs prompt physical assessment, observations and an ECG, with escalation as indicated (P2.5).

n.0: Sedation may mask a serious physical cause.
n.2: Reassurance without assessment could miss a cardiac event.
n.3: A day's delay with possible cardiac pain is unsafe.

5.q: Stanley, 80, has end-stage heart and kidney disease and full capacity. The consultant judges that CPR would not succeed and records a DNACPR decision. Stanley tells the nurse he does not accept this and wants 'everything done'. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record that CPR will be attempted because Stanley has requested it
Ask his family to confirm the decision on his behalf at the next visit
Leave the decision unexplained to avoid causing Stanley more distress
Explain the decision sensitively and offer him a second opinion
5.w: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BMA, RCUK, RCN): where CPR would not be successful, clinicians have no obligation to offer it, but the patient should be informed sensitively, and if they do not accept the decision a second opinion should be offered. Tracey [2014]: presumption of involving the patient.

n.0: Clinicians are not obliged to offer CPR that would not succeed; a patient request does not require it (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
n.1: Stanley has capacity, so his family cannot confirm or make the decision for him.
n.2: Stanley must be informed and his concerns heard (Tracey [2014]); avoiding the topic denies him the chance to seek another view.

5.q: Ellen, 29, had wheeze, hypotension and urticaria after eating a prawn curry on the ward. She improved after one dose of IM adrenaline and is now stable. The doctor plans her period of observation and later allergy referral. Which blood test should be taken to support the diagnosis?
o: Two sets of blood cultures
Mast cell tryptase level
Serum troponin level
Full blood count and film
5.w: RCUK guidance: take mast cell tryptase samples to help confirm anaphylaxis and support specialist allergy follow-up. Observation is risk-stratified, with a minimum of 6 hours in most people and 12 hours in higher-risk groups, or fast-track after 2 hours in selected cases.

n.0: Blood cultures are taken for suspected infection, not allergy.
n.2: Troponin assesses myocardial injury and does not confirm anaphylaxis.
n.3: FBC does not confirm anaphylaxis.

5.q: Mr Faris, 24, is on his first admission to an acute ward and has never taken antipsychotic medication. Despite de-escalation he is hitting out at staff, and he has refused oral medication. The team decides rapid tranquillisation is needed. Under NICE NG10, which medication should be used?
o: IV diazepam on its own
IM haloperidol on its own
IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
IM lorazepam on its own
5.w: NG10 1.4.37-1.4.38: use either IM lorazepam alone or IM haloperidol combined with IM promethazine; if there is insufficient information to guide the choice, or the person has not taken antipsychotics before, use IM lorazepam.

n.0: IV use is exceptional in NG10 and diazepam is not one of the recommended options.
n.1: NG10 pairs haloperidol with promethazine; haloperidol alone raises the risk of acute dystonia.
n.2: Haloperidol with promethazine is an NG10 option, but not for someone who is antipsychotic-naive.

5.q: Joy, 58, has negative pressure wound therapy (a vacuum dressing) on a leg wound. The pump alarms for a leak and the dressing is no longer collapsed. What should you do first?
o: Find and seal the leak, then confirm the seal
Switch the pump off and leave the dressing in situ
Increase the pressure setting on the pump
Remove the dressing and apply gauze until tomorrow
5.w: Vacuum dressings must maintain a seal to work. Check the dressing and connections for the leak, seal it per the manufacturer's instructions and confirm the dressing collapses. If therapy cannot be restored within the time stated in local policy, the dressing should be changed (Annexe B 4.6).

n.1: Leaving an inactive vacuum dressing in place risks infection and maceration.
n.2: Raising the pressure does not fix a leak and may harm the wound.
n.3: Removing it without trying to restore the seal is premature and loses therapy.

5.q: Police find Marcus, 32, on a bridge parapet in the town centre, distressed and responding to voices. They use section 136 and bring him to the health-based place of safety, arriving at 18:00. Without any extension, when does the authority to detain him end?
o: 18:00 the next day
06:00 two days later
06:00 the next day
18:00 three days later
5.w: Under section 136(2A) the permitted period is 24 hours beginning with arrival at the place of safety: 18:00 the next day. An extension of up to 12 hours is possible under section 136B. The old 72-hour limit was replaced in December 2017.

n.1: Thirty-six hours would require a 12-hour extension authorised by the examining doctor; without it the limit is 24 hours.
n.2: Twelve hours is the maximum extension under s136B, not the basic period.
n.3: Seventy-two hours was the pre-December 2017 limit and still appears in the 2015 Code, but the Act now allows 24 hours.

5.q: Asif, 55, weighs 70 kg and is nil by mouth after surgery. He needs routine IV maintenance fluids. Using NICE CG174, what is the appropriate total daily water range?
5.w: NICE CG174: 25-30 mL/kg/day. 70 kg x 25 = 1,750 mL; 70 kg x 30 = 2,100 mL. CG174 also notes that intake rarely needs to exceed 3 L/day.

n.0: 700-1,050 mL uses 10-15 mL/kg/day, below CG174 maintenance.
n.2: 3,500-4,200 mL is well above maintenance and risks overload.
n.3: 2,800-3,500 mL uses 40-50 mL/kg/day, above maintenance.

5.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
5.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

5.q: At the start of a late shift, Nurse Kim notices that her colleague smells strongly of alcohol, is slurring words and is about to start the medicines round. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Report her to the NMC and let her continue the shift
Offer to do the medicines round with her as a second checker
Stop her giving medicines and tell the nurse in charge now
Speak to her privately at the end of the shift about support
5.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but never at the expense of patient or public safety. Code standard 16 act without delay on risks to safety (16.1 raise and escalate concerns); P1.5.

n.0: Allowing her to continue exposes patients to harm; local escalation and removal from duties come first.
n.1: Supervising her still allows an impaired nurse to give medicines; patient safety must come first.
n.3: Support matters, but waiting leaves patients at immediate risk (Code 8.7).

5.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation, Lucy, a staff nurse, is tearful in the clean utility room. She is due to start the next medicines round in ten minutes. What is the most appropriate response from her colleague?
o: Tell her to go home and let the nurse in charge know later
Reassure her that she will get used to deaths over time
Advise her to take a few minutes and then start the round on time
Offer support, ask how she feels and help arrange cover if needed
5.w: Code 8.7: be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems without compromising safety. Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risk.

n.0: Sending her home without discussion or escalation leaves the ward uncovered and her unsupported.
n.1: This dismisses her distress and offers no practical support.
n.2: This overlooks whether she is safe to give medicines right now.

5.q: Ben, 34, is admitted to a medical ward after self-harm while intoxicated. He is now talking coherently. A doctor suggests waiting until his breath alcohol is zero before making any referral to liaison psychiatry. What does NICE NG225 recommend?
o: Refer if he repeats his self-harm while on the ward
Refer now, as alcohol levels should not delay the assessment
Wait until his breath alcohol reading has returned to zero
Refer once his physical treatment on the ward is complete
5.w: NICE NG225 recs 1.5.2 and 1.5.4: do not delay the psychosocial assessment until after medical treatment is completed, and do not use breath or blood alcohol levels to delay it. Rec 1.7.21: after admission for self-harm, offer referral to liaison psychiatry as soon as possible, alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting for a repeat episode ignores the need for prompt assessment after this one.
n.2: NG225 states alcohol levels should not be used to delay the assessment.
n.3: NG225 advises not to wait until medical treatment is finished.

5.q: A nurse is helping to design a local prevention strategy and wants to apply a life course approach. Which statement best reflects that approach?
o: Accept that adult health is fixed by genes, so early action changes little
Begin prevention once a long-term condition has been diagnosed in the person
Act early and at key transitions, as health is shaped across the whole of life
Focus prevention on older adults, as most long-term disease occurs in later life
5.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): a life course approach considers the critical stages, transitions and settings where large differences can be made, taking action early and appropriately across the life course and reducing health inequalities throughout life.

n.0: The approach rests on evidence that early and timely action changes lifelong outcomes.
n.1: Waiting for diagnosis misses the critical earlier stages the approach targets.
n.3: A life course approach acts at every stage, including early years, not just in later life.

5.q: Nurse Sara notices she has written the wrong blood pressure value in a patient's paper observation chart. What is the correct way to correct the entry?
o: Write the right value over the top of the wrong one
Cover the entry with correction fluid and rewrite it neatly
Tear out the page and copy the chart onto a new sheet
Strike through once, keep it legible, then sign, date and time
5.w: Code 10.3-10.4: complete records accurately without falsification, attribute entries and date and time them. Annexe A 1.8: write accurate, clear, legible records.

n.0: Overwriting makes both values illegible and unattributed.
n.1: Obscuring the original entry could be seen as falsification and makes the change untraceable (Code 10.3).
n.2: Removing pages destroys part of the record and breaches Code 10.3.

5.q: Sanjay, 50, has been detained under section 3 since 1 June and first received medication on 2 June. On 10 August he refuses it. A colleague says a SOAD is now needed because 'the rule changed to 2 months'. What is correct in October 2026?
o: A SOAD certificate is needed now, as 2 months have passed
A SOAD certificate is needed because he is refusing at any stage
No SOAD certificate is needed while he is detained under section 3
No SOAD certificate is needed until 3 months from 2 June
5.w: Section 14 of the 2025 Act, which will cut the section 58 period from 3 months to 2 months, is not in force. Under section 58 of the 1983 Act, the SOAD safeguard applies from 3 months after medication was first given (2 September). On 10 August, medication can still be given under section 63.

n.0: The 2-month rule is an uncommenced 2025 Act change.
n.1: Refusal within the first 3 months does not trigger section 58; section 63 applies.
n.2: Section 58 applies to section 3 patients after the 3-month period.

5.q: During handover, a nurse refers to a new admission as 'the schizophrenic in bed 4'. Which response from the nurse in charge best challenges stigma?
o: 'It is fine to use diagnoses as shorthand during a busy handover.'
'Call him "the psychotic patient" until the diagnosis is confirmed.'
'Say "Mr Osei, who has schizophrenia"; he is more than his diagnosis.'
'Use his bed number, to protect his confidentiality.'
5.w: Person-first language that uses the person's name and describes a condition the person has, rather than defining them by it, reduces stigma and supports dignity (Code standards 1 and 20). Defining people by diagnosis or bed number dehumanises them.

n.0: Labels defining a person by their diagnosis reinforce stigma, however busy the handover.
n.1: This replaces one diagnostic label with another and still defines him by his illness.
n.3: Referring to people by bed number depersonalises them and does not address the stigmatising language.

5.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
5.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

5.q: A unit of red cells for Hannah, 55, was removed from the blood fridge at 10:00. The transfusion was delayed while her cannula was resited and started at 10:40. By what time must the unit be completed?
o: By 14:00, 4 hours after leaving storage
By 13:00, 3 hours after leaving storage
By 14:40, 4 hours after the start
By 12:00, 2 hours after leaving storage
5.w: BSH (2017): red cells should be transfused within 4 hours of leaving temperature-controlled storage, to limit bacterial growth. The clock starts when the unit leaves the fridge, not when the infusion starts.

n.1: 3 hours is not the BSH limit; the standard is 4 hours from leaving storage.
n.2: Timing runs from removal from storage, so 14:40 is 40 minutes too late.
n.3: 2 hours is shorter than the BSH limit for red cells.

5.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation attempt on a medical ward, Sofia, the nurse in charge, arranges a short team debrief once the immediate tasks are complete. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: Identify which member of staff made an error so that it can be dealt with formally
Reflect together on what went well and what could improve, and support staff
Complete the incident report and the statutory notification to the regulator
Decide as a team what information the family should and should not be given
5.w: Team reflection and debriefing support staff wellbeing and turn experience into learning for future practice (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; Code 8 work cooperatively; human factors and just culture principles).

n.0: A debrief is a supportive learning discussion, not a disciplinary process; a blame focus discourages openness.
n.2: Reporting is a separate governance step and is not the purpose of a team debrief.
n.3: Communication with the family is guided by candour and the person's wishes, not by a team agreement to withhold information.

5.q: Ali, 66, had a colostomy formed 2 days ago. On inspection the stoma is dark purple-black and dry. It was red and moist yesterday. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply a smaller appliance to reduce swelling
Clean it with antiseptic and recheck in 24 hours
Record it as a normal post-operative change
Report it urgently to the surgical team
5.w: A healthy stoma is moist and red or pink. A dusky, purple or black stoma suggests ischaemia or necrosis and needs urgent surgical review (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: A tight appliance could worsen ischaemia.
n.1: Antiseptic does not address ischaemia, and waiting 24 hours risks necrosis progressing.
n.2: This is not a normal change; a healthy stoma stays moist and red.

5.q: Ms Kemp, 28, has bipolar disorder and could not tolerate lithium. Her psychiatrist is considering starting valproate for the first time. Under the MHRA safety measures set out in NICE CG185, what must happen before it is started?
o: Two specialists independently agree and document the need
A baseline plasma valproate level in the normal range
Her written consent and her GP's agreement to prescribe
A negative pregnancy test on the morning it is started
5.w: CG185 box 1 (MHRA): do not start valproate in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently agree and document that there is no other effective tolerated treatment, or that the reproductive risks do not apply. For women able to have children, the Pregnancy Prevention Programme is also put in place where appropriate.

n.1: Valproate levels are not measured routinely and there is no baseline level before starting.
n.2: GP agreement is not the safeguard, and CG185 says valproate should not be started in primary care for bipolar disorder.
n.3: Pregnancy testing forms part of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme but does not replace the two-specialist requirement.

5.q: Aaron, 33, has been detained under section 3 since 2 January and first received antipsychotic medication on 4 January. On 10 April he refuses it, and the approved clinician believes it is still needed. What is required to continue the medication lawfully?
o: The written consent of his nearest relative
Continue under section 63, which covers medication throughout detention
A best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act
A certificate from a second opinion appointed doctor
5.w: Section 58 applies once 3 months have passed since medication for mental disorder was first given in the current detention (4 January to 4 April). After that, a patient who refuses or lacks capacity can be given medication only if a SOAD certifies it is appropriate. Aaron refuses on 10 April, beyond 3 months.

n.0: The nearest relative has no power to consent to treatment under Part 4.
n.1: Section 63 is limited by section 58 after the 3-month period; a SOAD certificate is now required.
n.2: MCA s28 excludes Part 4 treatment for mental disorder from MCA authority.

5.q: A nurse is about to take blood for a full blood count and urea and electrolytes from Mrs Ellis, 66. She has a peripheral cannula in her left forearm with an IV infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride running. Which site is most appropriate?
o: The cannula itself, after briefly pausing the infusion
Her left antecubital fossa, above the cannula
A vein in her right arm, away from the infusion
A vein in the back of her left hand, below the cannula
5.w: Blood taken from a limb with an infusion running can be diluted or contaminated by the fluid, giving falsely altered results (for example sodium, potassium or glucose). The opposite arm should be used (Annexe B 2.2).

n.0: Sampling from an infusing cannula risks contaminated results and is not the most appropriate choice here.
n.1: Sampling above an infusion on the same arm risks contamination with the infused fluid.
n.3: The same limb is still affected by the infusion; the opposite arm is preferred.

5.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
5.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

5.q: Mr Simms, 64, has heart failure and is due for discharge. The team has drafted a plan for daily weights and fluid restriction. He says he does not own scales and finds it hard to remember fluid limits. What is the best next step?
o: Ask his neighbour to supervise his weights and fluid intake
Discharge with the plan as written, as it follows guidance
Revise the plan with him so it fits his life and resources
Tell him that he must follow the plan to avoid readmission
5.w: Code 3.3 asks nurses to act in partnership with people receiving care, and P3.4-P3.5 require shared planning and agreed goals. A plan he cannot follow will not work; adapting it (for example arranging scales and simple prompts) makes it achievable.

n.0: Involving a neighbour without his agreement is not partnership and may breach confidentiality.
n.1: Following guidance does not help if the plan is not achievable for him.
n.3: Instructing him without addressing the barriers he describes is not shared decision-making.

5.q: Hannah, 24, has type 1 diabetes and is on an orthopaedic ward. You are called because she is sweaty and confused. Airway is clear, RR 18, SpO2 97%, pulse 98, BP 118/72. She responds to voice. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give her 300 mg aspirin to chew while awaiting review
Complete a 4AT delirium screen before any other test
Request an urgent CT head scan to exclude a stroke
Check her capillary blood glucose straight away
5.w: With A, B and C stable, D includes a capillary blood glucose. In someone with diabetes who is sweaty and confused, hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L, RCUK first aid 2025) is the most likely reversible cause and must be excluded quickly.

n.0: Aspirin is for cardiac-sounding chest pain and is not indicated for confusion.
n.1: Delirium screening is relevant later; a reversible metabolic cause should be excluded first.
n.2: Imaging is not a nursing first step and would delay checking for a common reversible cause.

5.q: Nurses on a surgical ward want to check whether pain scores are reassessed within 30 minutes of giving analgesia, as their trust policy requires. They plan to review 40 recent patient records against this requirement. What type of activity is this?
o: Service evaluation, because it describes current care with no standard
Research, because it collects data from patient records
A PDSA cycle, because it tests a change to practice on a small scale
Clinical audit, because it measures care against a set standard
5.w: Clinical audit is a quality improvement cycle that measures the effectiveness of care against agreed standards and acts to bring practice in line with them (HQIP definition). Here an existing policy standard is being measured, so it is audit (P6.4, P6.7).

n.0: Service evaluation describes current care without reference to a standard; this project has a defined standard.
n.1: Research generates new knowledge, for example by testing a hypothesis; reviewing records against an existing standard is not research.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; no change is being tested here, only current practice measured.

5.q: A community nurse is learning about the NHS England Core20PLUS5 approach to reducing healthcare inequalities in adults. What does 'Core20' refer to?
o: The 20% of the population who are aged 65 and over in each region
The 20% of adults living with the highest number of long-term health conditions
The most deprived 20% of the population, by the Index of Multiple Deprivation
The 20% of local areas with the highest rates of emergency hospital admission
5.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): Core20 is the most deprived 20% of the national population as identified by the national Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD); PLUS groups are identified locally; the 5 are clinical areas of focus.

n.0: Age is not the basis of Core20; it is the most deprived fifth of the population.
n.1: Core20 is defined by deprivation, not by the number of long-term conditions a person has.
n.3: Admission rates are not the measure; Core20 uses the national Index of Multiple Deprivation.

5.q: Ms Reid, 29, has generalised anxiety disorder. Her symptoms have not improved after education and active monitoring. She has no marked functional impairment. What is the most appropriate next step under NICE CG113?
o: A low-dose antipsychotic prescribed by her GP
A 4-week course of diazepam
Guided self-help based on CBT principles
Individual high-intensity CBT
5.w: CG113 step 2: for GAD not improved after step 1, offer a low-intensity psychological intervention such as individual non-facilitated or guided self-help, or psychoeducational groups.

n.0: Antipsychotics should not be offered for GAD in primary care.
n.1: Benzodiazepines are not used for GAD except short term in a crisis.
n.3: High-intensity CBT is step 3, for marked impairment or no improvement after step 2.

5.q: Mr Evans, 76, is usually independent and has no psychiatric history. Over the last 24 hours on an older adults' ward he has started seeing insects on the walls, is unsure of the day and drifts in and out of conversation. What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Delirium, needing a 4AT and a search for a cause
Late-onset psychosis, needing an antipsychotic
Lewy body dementia, needing a memory clinic referral
Psychotic depression, needing a PHQ-9 and review
5.w: Acute onset over hours, fluctuating attention, disorientation and visual hallucinations point to delirium, which is a medical emergency. NICE CG103 recommends assessment (the 4AT is widely used) and identifying and treating underlying causes such as infection, medicines or dehydration.

n.1: Psychosis rarely starts over hours with fluctuating attention in an older person with no history; an antipsychotic would also miss the physical cause.
n.2: Dementia develops over months; this change happened over a day.
n.3: There is no low mood reported, and a fluctuating, acute picture suggests delirium.

5.q: Omar, 7, is anxious during a blood test. Which intervention is most appropriate during the procedure itself?
o: Distract him with bubbles, a game or a story
Delay the test until he is no longer anxious
Explain each step of the procedure in technical detail
Ask his parent to leave the room to reduce fuss
5.w: Annexe A 3.8: distraction and diversion strategies. Distraction reduces procedural distress; Annexe A 3.7 play supports children.

n.1: Waiting for anxiety to resolve may delay needed care.
n.2: Detailed explanation during the procedure may increase anxiety.
n.3: Parental presence usually comforts children during procedures.

5.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
5.q: Ms Okoro, 28, is due for discharge and tells her nurse she feels safest talking to her. She asks for the nurse's personal mobile number so she can text if she feels low at night. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give the number and ask her to text in emergencies
Decline kindly and agree crisis contacts for night-time
Agree to call her each evening after the nurse's shift
Give a work email address and reply when off duty
5.w: Code 20.6: clear professional boundaries. Sharing personal contact details creates dependence and an unsafe, unsupported route for crisis help. Agreeing crisis contacts in the safety plan meets the need safely.

n.0: Personal contact details blur boundaries and cannot guarantee a response in a crisis.
n.2: Personal calls after shifts cross professional boundaries.
n.3: Off-duty replies still create an informal, unsafe arrangement.

5.q: Mr Price, 52, on a mental health ward, is rigid and confused after starting an antipsychotic. His observations are: respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on air, blood pressure 150/92, pulse 118, temperature 39.3 C, and new confusion. What is his NEWS2 score and the response required?
o: 11, needing six-hourly observations
6, needing an urgent ward review
9, needing an emergency response
4, needing hourly observations
5.w: NEWS2: respiratory rate 21-24 = 2, SpO2 96% = 0, air = 0, systolic 150 = 0, pulse 111-130 = 2, new confusion = 3, temperature 39.1 or above = 2; total 9. A score of 7 or more triggers an emergency response, which on a mental health unit usually means emergency transfer to acute care (RCP NEWS2).

n.0: The total is 9, and any score of 7 or more needs an emergency response, not six-hourly observations.
n.1: The total is 9, not 6; new confusion alone scores 3.
n.3: The total is 9; a score of 4 would understate his deterioration.

5.q: Nadia is about to irrigate a large infected leg wound for Doreen, 81. Splashing of wound fluid towards her face is likely. There are no full-face visors on the ward. Which facial protection should Nadia wear?
o: A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with separate eye protection
A Type II surgical mask and her own prescription glasses
A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask without eye protection
An FFP3 respirator without separate eye protection
5.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: where splashing of blood or body fluids onto the face is anticipated and a full-face visor is not available, wear a Type IIR FRSM with eye protection. Regular corrective spectacles are not considered eye protection.

n.1: A Type II mask is not fluid resistant, and corrective spectacles do not count as eye protection.
n.2: The mask protects the nose and mouth, but the eyes remain exposed to the expected splashes.
n.3: An FFP3 respirator protects against airborne particles; it does not protect the eyes from splashes.

5.q: Ben, 29, detained under section 3, has been placed in seclusion. A nurse is observing him. According to the Mental Health Act Code of Practice, how often must a written record of his behaviour be made?
o: At least every hour
At least every 30 minutes
At least every 15 minutes
At least every 2 hours
5.w: COP15 26.118-26.123: a suitably skilled professional should be within sight and sound of the seclusion area at all times, and a record of the patient's behaviour should be made at least every 15 minutes.

n.0: Hourly is the minimum for written records in long-term segregation, not seclusion.
n.1: Thirty minutes matches low-level intermittent observation, not the seclusion record.
n.3: Two-hourly is the frequency for nursing reviews of seclusion, not the observation record.

5.q: A hospital is reviewing how it meets the Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605). Which patient's need falls within the scope of the standard?
o: A patient whose first language is Romanian
A patient who wants a copy of their clinic letter
A Deaf patient who uses British Sign Language
A patient who prefers appointments by email
5.w: Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025): covers information and communication needs relating to disability, impairment or sensory loss, through six stages: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review.

n.0: Language needs without a disability are met through interpreting services, not the AIS.
n.1: Receiving copies is an access right, not an AIS communication need.
n.3: A general preference unrelated to disability or sensory loss is outside the AIS.

5.q: A nurse is carrying out a whole-body systems assessment of Mr Burns, 80, who has been bedbound for several days. On the skin review she finds a red area over his sacrum that does not blanch with light finger pressure. What should she do?
o: Record it as a category 2 pressure ulcer and apply a dressing
Reassess it at his next weekly skin inspection
Massage the area to restore its circulation and recheck it tomorrow
Start pressure ulcer prevention and recheck the skin at least 2-hourly
5.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy to test blanching; if non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until resolved. A systems assessment includes skin (Annexe B 2.7).

n.0: Intact non-blanching erythema is a category 1 finding, not category 2, which involves partial-thickness skin loss.
n.1: Weekly review is too infrequent; CG179 requires at least 2-hourly reassessment.
n.2: Massaging pressure-damaged skin can cause further harm, and a day's delay is too long.

5.q: Before deciding to use section 136, an officer telephones the mental health crisis line and speaks to a registered nurse about Ayo, 37, who is sitting on a railway platform edge. Why does the Act require this contact?
o: The officer must consult a health professional first if practicable
The nurse then becomes responsible for arranging Ayo's transport
The nurse must authorise the detention before it becomes lawful
The call to the nurse starts the 24-hour permitted detention period
5.w: Section 136(1C) requires the constable, if practicable, to consult a registered medical practitioner, registered nurse, approved mental health professional or other prescribed person before removing or keeping someone at a place of safety. The decision remains the officer's.

n.1: Consultation does not transfer conveyance responsibility to the nurse.
n.2: The nurse advises; the decision to use section 136 remains with the constable.
n.3: The 24 hours begin on arrival at the place of safety (or the decision to keep the person there), not with the phone call.

5.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
5.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

5.q: During the breakfast round, Norma, 85, says she would like to take her tablets after she has eaten and asks the nurse to leave them on her table. Norma has capacity but no self-administration assessment has been done. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the tablets as refused and offer them at lunchtime
Return after breakfast to give them and record once taken
Leave the tablets and sign the chart as given
Leave the tablets and ask a support worker to check later
5.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-4 and 15-17: unless a self-administration risk assessment allows it, the nurse administering remains accountable and must see the dose taken; the record is completed at the time of administration (NICE SC1: record only after the dose is taken).

n.0: Norma has not refused; she asked to take them later, which can be accommodated.
n.2: Signing before the dose is taken creates an inaccurate record and the tablets may be lost or taken by others.
n.3: Delegating a check does not confirm administration and leaves medicines unattended.

5.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
5.q: Ms Bell, 33, has been on a rehabilitation ward for some weeks. She now books her own appointments, uses the ward groups well and asks the nurse for help when she needs it, becoming steadily more independent. Which Peplau phase best fits?
o: Identification
Orientation
Exploitation
Resolution
5.w: In Peplau's exploitation phase the person makes full use of the services and the relationship, moving towards independence before resolution.

n.0: Identification is when the person first starts to work on the problem with the nurse.
n.1: Orientation is the initial getting-to-know-you stage.
n.3: Resolution is the ending, when goals are met and the relationship closes.

5.q: Ana, 33, has moderate depression. During her assessment she says she feels 'there is no point any more'. The student nurse is worried about raising suicide. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask her directly whether she has thoughts of ending her life
Ask her partner privately whether she has mentioned suicide
Avoid the subject in case asking increases her risk
Wait for her to raise the topic when she feels ready
5.w: NG222: always ask people with depression directly about suicidal ideation and intent. Asking does not increase risk and allows safety planning (P3.10).

n.1: Collateral history can help but does not replace asking Ana herself.
n.2: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea or increase risk.
n.3: Waiting may miss serious risk that she is hinting at now.

5.q: Mrs Doyle, 63, is receiving 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannulae. Her observations are: respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96%, systolic BP 130, pulse 80, alert, temperature 36.8°C. Her SpO2 is scored on Scale 1. What is her NEWS2 score?
o: 1, because supplemental oxygen scores 1
3, because oxygen scores 3 on Scale 1
0, because each vital sign is in range
2, because supplemental oxygen scores 2
5.w: NEWS2 Chart 1: SpO2 96% or above on Scale 1 scores 0, but the 'air or oxygen' parameter scores 2 for any supplemental oxygen. All other values score 0, so the total is 2.

n.0: Supplemental oxygen scores 2, not 1.
n.1: Oxygen use scores 2; 3 is not a value in the air or oxygen parameter.
n.2: The use of supplemental oxygen is scored separately and adds 2 points.

5.q: Mr Kapoor, 67, has capacity and has told Hayley, his nurse, that he does not want the proposed amputation and would prefer palliative wound care. On the ward round the surgeon starts to describe the operation date without asking his views. What should Hayley do?
o: Say that Mr Kapoor has shared views about the operation and invite him to explain them
Record Mr Kapoor's wishes in his nursing notes once the ward round has finished
Wait until after the ward round and then ask Mr Kapoor whether he has changed his mind
Tell the surgeon that Mr Kapoor has asked her to cancel the operation on his behalf
5.w: Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice is heard in decisions about their care (AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4 act as an advocate for the vulnerable; Code 2.5 respect the right to refuse treatment). Inviting Mr Kapoor to speak supports his autonomy without speaking over him (MCA 2005 s1 principles).

n.1: Recording his wishes is necessary but does not ensure they are heard in the decision being made now.
n.2: Waiting allows a decision to be made without him; he has already expressed his wishes.
n.3: Hayley should not overstate or speak for him when he can speak for himself.

5.q: Philip, 66, is drowsy after surgery and has had no food for 6 days. His BMI is 23 kg/m² and he has no other refeeding risk factors. Nutrition support is planned. Under NICE CG32, what is the maximum initial intake for the first 2 days?
o: His full estimated requirements
No more than 50% of his estimated requirements
No more than 25% of his estimated requirements
No more than 10 kcal/kg/day
5.w: NICE CG32: people who have eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days should have nutrition support started at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days, before increasing if clinical and biochemical monitoring reveals no refeeding problems. The 10 kcal/kg/day limit is for those at high refeeding risk.

n.0: Full requirements after more than 5 days of little intake risk refeeding problems.
n.2: 25% is lower than the CG32 recommendation for this group.
n.3: 10 kcal/kg/day is the starting level for people at high refeeding risk, which he is not.

5.q: Hazel, 77, is incontinent of urine. On her buttocks you find diffuse, shiny red areas with superficial skin loss, not over a bony prominence, with no evidence of pressure. How should this be classified?
o: As a category 1 pressure ulcer
As moisture-associated skin damage
As a category 2 pressure ulcer
As an unstageable pressure ulcer
5.w: NHS Improvement (2018): damage caused by moisture alone is a moisture lesion (moisture-associated skin damage), not a pressure ulcer. Where pressure and moisture combine, it is classed as a pressure ulcer. CG179 advises barrier preparations for moisture lesions.

n.0: A category 1 ulcer is non-blanching erythema of intact skin caused by pressure.
n.2: A category 2 ulcer needs pressure or shear as a cause; here there is moisture alone.
n.3: Unstageable is the international label for full-thickness loss hidden by slough or eschar (recorded as Category 3 under the NWCSP 2024 tool in England); Hazel's damage is superficial and caused by moisture.

5.q: Jason, 26, attends the emergency department for the third time this year with injuries after drinking heavily. He tells the nurse that as a child he lived with domestic violence and that his father misused alcohol. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to use this information?
o: Refer him to children's social care about what happened in his childhood
Tell him his drinking is a choice that is unrelated to his childhood
Recognise that early adversity may underlie his current risks, and offer support
Treat his injuries and avoid discussing his past, as it is not relevant now
5.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): adults with 4+ ACEs were more likely to be high-risk drinkers and victims of violence. NMC P2.6: understand the importance of early years and childhood experiences on later physical, mental and behavioural health and wellbeing.

n.0: Jason is an adult; children's social care is for current concerns about children.
n.1: This is dismissive and contradicts evidence linking ACEs with high-risk drinking.
n.3: The ACE evidence links childhood adversity with health-harming behaviours, so it is relevant to his care.

5.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
5.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

5.q: Rose, 70, an inpatient on a medical ward, has new dysuria and frequency. She is alert with a NEWS2 score of 1. The doctor prescribes oral nitrofurantoin. No urine sample has been sent. What should the nurse do before giving the first dose?
o: Send a sample after 48 hours if her symptoms have not improved
Obtain a urine sample first, then give the antibiotic without delay
Give the first dose now and send a sample with her next void
Withhold the antibiotic until the urine culture result is available
5.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.27: for patients in hospital who have suspected infections, take microbiological samples before prescribing an antimicrobial and review the prescription when results are available. Collecting the sample first takes minutes and does not delay treatment.

n.0: Delaying the sample for 48 hours loses the chance to guide treatment, contrary to NG15.
n.2: A sample taken after the antibiotic may give a false negative culture, so the prescription cannot be reviewed against reliable results.
n.3: Treatment is not delayed until culture returns; the sample is taken first and the drug given promptly.

5.q: Kayla, 30, had a psychosocial assessment in an emergency department after self-harm and is discharged home. The team remains concerned about her safety. According to NICE NG225, within what time should initial aftercare be provided?
o: Within 14 days, at a routine outpatient clinic
Within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment
Within 7 days of the psychosocial assessment
Within 24 hours of arriving at the department
5.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.10.2: if there are ongoing safety concerns after self-harm, the responsible team should provide initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment.

n.0: A routine 14-day appointment is far later than NG225 recommends when safety concerns persist.
n.2: 7 days is longer than the 48-hour aftercare window in NG225.
n.3: The timing runs from the psychosocial assessment, and the interval is 48 hours.

5.q: At her booking appointment, a midwife asks Freya, 26, about her mental health. What does one of the two depression identification questions in NICE CG192 ask about?
o: Feeling down, depressed or hopeless in the last month
Feeling low on most days over the whole past year
Any past treatment for depression or anxiety
Feeling unable to cope since the pregnancy began
5.w: CG192 1.5.4: at first contact or booking and in the early postnatal period, consider asking: 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?' and 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?'.

n.1: The NICE questions cover the past month, not the past year.
n.2: Past treatment is asked about separately (CG192 1.5.9) and is not an identification question.
n.3: Coping since pregnancy is not one of the two CG192 identification questions.

6.q: Asif, 36, detained under section 2 on 1 October, asks on 18 October whether he can still apply to the tribunal, as he heard the window is now 21 days. What is the correct answer?
o: Yes, because the 2025 Act extended the window to 21 days
Yes, because section 2 patients may apply up to day 28
No, because section 2 patients must wait for a managers' referral
No, because the 14-day window under the 1983 Act has passed
6.w: Section 30(1) of the 2025 Act, which will extend the section 2 tribunal window from 14 to 21 days, is not in force. Under section 66(2) of the 1983 Act, Asif had to apply within 14 days of admission (by 14 October). He can still seek a hospital managers' hearing.

n.0: The 21-day window is an uncommenced 2025 Act change.
n.1: The window is 14 days, not the full 28 days of the section.
n.2: Section 2 patients may apply themselves within 14 days; s68 referrals concern section 3 and other longer-term patients.

6.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
6.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

6.q: Joan, 70, has suspected sepsis and a NEWS2 of 7. The doctor prescribes an initial intravenous fluid bolus. Under NICE NG253 (2025), what is the recommended initial bolus?
o: 20 mL/kg of 5% glucose over 30 minutes
250 mL isotonic crystalloid over 10-15 minutes
500 mL isotonic crystalloid over 10-15 minutes
1,000 mL isotonic crystalloid over 1 hour
6.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.5-1.8.9: give an initial bolus of 250 mL isotonic crystalloid ideally over 10-15 minutes, reassess after each bolus, and repeat up to 1,000 mL in total.

n.0: 5% glucose is not an isotonic resuscitation fluid and 20 mL/kg is not the adult sepsis bolus.
n.2: 500 mL in under 15 minutes is the general CG174 resuscitation bolus, not the NG253 sepsis bolus.
n.3: 1,000 mL is the cumulative ceiling before seeking senior advice, not the first bolus.

6.q: Ruby, 39, was detained under section 3. Her section was discharged by the tribunal, but she chose to stay on the ward informally for 3 more weeks before going home. Is she entitled to section 117 after-care?
o: No, because her section was discharged by the tribunal
Yes, because she ceased to be detained and then left hospital
Yes, for a fixed period of 6 weeks after she leaves hospital
No, because she left the hospital as an informal patient
6.w: Section 117(1) applies to qualifying patients who cease to be detained and, whether or not immediately after so ceasing, leave hospital. COP15 33.9 confirms patients who remain informally after detention ends are still entitled once they leave.

n.0: The way detention ended, including tribunal discharge, does not affect entitlement.
n.2: There is no 6-week limit; after-care lasts until both bodies agree it is no longer needed.
n.3: Leaving as an informal patient does not remove entitlement; the Act covers leaving 'whether or not immediately'.

6.q: An occupational health nurse is giving an intradermal tuberculin skin test into the inner forearm of Leila, 24. Which finding confirms that the injection has been placed correctly?
o: The fluid flows freely and leaves no mark on the skin
Blood flashback is seen in the hub of the syringe
A small pale bleb forms raising the skin at the site
A bruise appears at the site within a few minutes
6.w: Intradermal injections are given at a shallow angle of about 10-15 degrees with the bevel up, just under the epidermis; correct placement raises a small pale bleb (AnnexB.11.7). No bleb suggests a deeper, subcutaneous injection.

n.0: Free flow with no bleb suggests the fluid has gone into subcutaneous tissue.
n.1: Flashback indicates the needle is in a blood vessel, not the dermis.
n.3: Bruising suggests trauma to vessels, not correct dermal placement.

6.q: In theatre, Callum, a newly registered scrub nurse, sees the surgeon pick up the scalpel before the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist time out has been done. The team seems not to have noticed. What should Callum do?
o: Complete an incident report after the operation so the omission is recorded
Note the omission and raise it at the team debrief at the end of the list
Quietly tell the anaesthetist so that the surgeon is not challenged openly
Say clearly that the time out has not been done and ask the team to pause
6.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 (preserve safety) require nurses to intervene. Checklists work only if anyone can stop the process; speaking up clearly and directly at the moment of risk is the safest action, whatever the speaker's seniority (P6.6; P5.2).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate later, but the immediate risk must be addressed before the incision.
n.1: Raising it afterwards allows the operation to proceed without the safety check that prevents wrong site and wrong patient surgery.
n.2: An indirect approach delays action and may not stop the procedure in time.

6.q: Mrs Shah, 58, asks a practice nurse whether a herbal supplement she has bought online will help her blood pressure alongside her prescribed amlodipine. The nurse is unsure. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her that nurses cannot discuss non-prescribed products
Check a reliable source or the pharmacist before advising her
Advise her that herbal products are natural and safe to take
Advise her to stop the amlodipine while she tries the supplement
6.w: Code 6.1: information or advice must be evidence-based, including about health products; Code 18.3: check compatibility with other treatment, including over-the-counter medicines; Code 13.3 seek help when unsure.

n.0: Code 18.3 expects compatibility with other treatments, including over-the-counter products, to be checked.
n.2: This is not evidence-based and ignores possible interactions (Code 6.1, 18.3).
n.3: Stopping a prescribed medicine without review could be harmful and is outside the nurse's evidence base.

6.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
6.q: During a one-to-one session, Mr Price, 45, who has depression, asks his nurse: 'Have you ever been depressed?' What is the most therapeutic response?
o: Share her own history of depression in detail
Answer briefly and refocus on his experience
Move on to the next topic without answering
Tell him personal questions are not allowed
6.w: Self-disclosure should be limited and only used when it helps the person; the focus stays on the patient. A brief, warm acknowledgement keeps the relationship genuine while keeping the boundary (Annexe A 1.5).

n.0: Detailed disclosure shifts the focus to the nurse and burdens the patient.
n.2: Not responding can feel dismissive and harm trust.
n.3: A blunt refusal feels rejecting and can damage rapport.

6.q: During the breakfast round, Norma, 85, says she would like to take her tablets after she has eaten and asks the nurse to leave them on her table. Norma has capacity but no self-administration assessment has been done. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the tablets as refused and offer them at lunchtime
Return after breakfast to give them and record once taken
Leave the tablets and sign the chart as given
Leave the tablets and ask a support worker to check later
6.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-4 and 15-17: unless a self-administration risk assessment allows it, the nurse administering remains accountable and must see the dose taken; the record is completed at the time of administration (NICE SC1: record only after the dose is taken).

n.0: Norma has not refused; she asked to take them later, which can be accommodated.
n.2: Signing before the dose is taken creates an inaccurate record and the tablets may be lost or taken by others.
n.3: Delegating a check does not confirm administration and leaves medicines unattended.

6.q: Nadia, a ward manager, learns that a staff nurse who raised a concern about a doctor's practice is now being left out of break rotas and ignored by some colleagues. What does the Code require Nadia to do?
o: Act to protect the nurse from detriment or victimisation
Wait for the concern to be investigated before taking any action
Advise the nurse to request a transfer to another ward
Report the nurse's colleagues to the NMC straight away
6.w: Code 16.5-16.6: do not obstruct, intimidate or victimise anyone raising a concern, and protect anyone you have management responsibility for from harm, detriment, victimisation or unwarranted treatment after a concern is raised.

n.1: The victimisation is happening now; Code 16.6 requires her to act to protect the nurse.
n.2: Moving the nurse penalises the person who raised the concern; Code 16.6 requires protection from detriment.
n.3: Local management action comes first; referral may follow if misconduct is serious, but protection is the duty now.

6.q: Gary, 52, tells the nurse he is thinking of paying for a private 'full body' screening scan because 'the NHS does not screen for enough things'. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: NHS programmes are offered where benefits are judged to outweigh harms
Private screening tests are more accurate than NHS screening tests
All private screening tests are approved by the UK National Screening Committee
Each GP practice chooses which screening tests to offer its patients
6.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): the UK National Screening Committee advises the NHS on which screening programmes to offer and recommends screening only when the benefits to the group offered outweigh the harms; some commercial tests are not recommended because it is not clear that benefits outweigh harms.

n.1: There is no basis for this; some private tests are not recommended because benefits may not outweigh harms.
n.2: Some private tests are not recommended by the UK NSC.
n.3: The UK NSC advises the NHS in all four nations on which screening programmes to offer.

6.q: Sophie, 26, has panic disorder and is on an acute ward. She suddenly feels her chest tightening, is breathing fast and has tingling fingers. Her observations and a recent ECG are normal and she says it feels like her usual attacks. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Ask her to breathe in and out of a paper bag
Leave her in a quiet room to settle by herself
Stay with her and coach slow, steady breathing
Give her PRN lorazepam straight away
6.w: Having excluded a physical cause (normal observations, recent ECG, typical pattern), the priority is calm presence, slow controlled breathing and explaining that the symptoms are panic and will pass (Annexe A 3.6 CBT-informed techniques; CG113 discourages benzodiazepines for panic).

n.0: Paper-bag rebreathing is no longer recommended and can cause hypoxia.
n.1: Leaving her alone increases fear and removes support.
n.3: Benzodiazepines are not used for panic disorder and the attack can be managed without them.

6.q: Jamie, 24, has a learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. He brings a hospital passport describing how he communicates. On the ward round, staff talk to his mother and ignore Jamie. What should his nurse do?
o: Ask his mother to explain the ward round decisions to Jamie later
Allow the conversation to continue, as his mother knows him best
Share the passport details and invite staff to speak directly to Jamie
Ask the learning disability liaison nurse to attend the next ward round
6.w: Nurses advocate for people who are vulnerable or disabled and make reasonable adjustments (P7.9; Code 3.4; Equality Act 2010 s20). Using the hospital passport and speaking directly to Jamie in his preferred way respects his rights, involves him in decisions and supports any capacity assessment (MCA 2005 s1(3)).

n.0: Passing information on later excludes Jamie from the conversation about his own care.
n.1: His mother's knowledge is valuable, but Jamie must be involved directly in decisions about his care.
n.3: Liaison nurses offer valuable support, but the nurse should advocate for Jamie now rather than wait.

6.q: Pauline, 73, has an MRSA-colonised leg ulcer. The nurse removes a dressing heavily soaked with wound exudate. In an acute hospital in England, which waste stream should the used dressing go into?
o: Yellow and black striped offensive waste bag
Orange bag for infectious clinical waste
Black domestic waste bag
Purple bag for cytotoxic waste
6.w: NIPCM ch 1.9 (HTM 07-01): clinical waste that is infectious, for example from a patient known or suspected to be infected or colonised, goes in a UN-approved orange bag. Offensive (tiger) waste is for non-infectious waste containing body fluids.

n.0: Tiger bags are for offensive waste that is not infectious; this dressing is from a colonised wound.
n.2: Domestic bags are for non-healthcare general waste, not soiled dressings.
n.3: Purple is for waste contaminated with cytotoxic or cytostatic medicines.

6.q: Mr Okonjo, 74, now lacks capacity after a cardiac arrest. He has a valid and applicable advance decision refusing CPR, written and signed, witnessed and stating it applies even if his life is at risk. His daughter is distressed and demands that CPR be given if he arrests again. What should the nurse do?
o: Seek a best interests decision from the medical team
Follow the advance decision and support his daughter
Give CPR because the daughter is the next of kin
Ask the daughter to sign a form overriding the refusal
6.w: A valid and applicable advance decision has the same effect as a contemporaneous refusal (MCA 2005 s26(1)), and the s25 formalities for life-sustaining treatment are met. Relatives cannot override it. The nurse should explain this sensitively and support the daughter.

n.0: A best interests decision is not made where a valid and applicable advance decision already refuses the treatment.
n.2: Next of kin has no power to override a valid advance decision.
n.3: A relative cannot sign away a valid advance decision made by the person.

6.q: A trainee nurse asks which of the following grounds under section 62 (urgent treatment) can justify giving ECT without the usual section 58A safeguards. Which answer is correct?
o: To reduce a high risk of the patient absconding
To alleviate serious suffering by the patient
To prevent a serious deterioration in his condition
To prevent the patient behaving violently to others
6.w: Section 62(1A) restricts urgent ECT to the first two section 62 grounds: immediately necessary to save life, or (if not irreversible) to prevent a serious deterioration. Alleviating serious suffering and preventing violence or danger apply to medication under s58, not ECT.

n.0: Absconding risk is not a ground under section 62.
n.1: Alleviating serious suffering is a section 62 ground for medication, but s62(1A) excludes it for ECT.
n.3: Preventing violence or danger is a section 62 ground for medication, but not for ECT.

6.q: Rhian, 23, has severe anorexia nervosa. Her physical health is at serious risk, she refuses admission and food, and the team agree she can only be treated safely as an inpatient. What does NICE NG69 recommend?
o: Follow the Mental Health Act 1983 framework
Respect her refusal because she is an adult
Wait for her to lose capacity before acting
Ask her parents to give consent on her behalf
6.w: NG69 1.12: if physical health is at serious risk, the person does not consent and can only be treated safely as an inpatient, follow the Mental Health Act 1983. Nasogastric feeding can be treatment for the mental disorder.

n.1: The MHA allows treatment of mental disorder without consent when the criteria are met.
n.2: Delay until capacity is lost puts her life at risk and the MHA does not require incapacity.
n.3: Parents cannot consent for an adult.

6.q: Ms Rae, 38, is in crisis with suicidal thoughts after a bereavement. She has no plan, wants to stay at home with her children and her mother has moved in to help. Her community nurse believes she needs intensive support this week. Which service is most appropriate?
o: Admission to an acute ward under section 2
NHS Talking Therapies guided self-help
A routine outpatient review in four weeks
The crisis resolution and home treatment team
6.w: Crisis resolution and home treatment teams provide intensive support at home as an alternative to admission, which suits her wishes, support and level of need. This is the least restrictive option that meets her needs (MHA Code of Practice guiding principles; NICE CG178 1.4 for acute episodes).

n.0: Detention is not justified when intensive community care can meet her needs and she is engaging.
n.1: Low-intensity guided self-help is not suitable for a crisis with suicidal thoughts.
n.2: Four weeks is too long to wait when she needs intensive support this week.

6.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation, Lucy, a staff nurse, is tearful in the clean utility room. She is due to start the next medicines round in ten minutes. What is the most appropriate response from her colleague?
o: Tell her to go home and let the nurse in charge know later
Reassure her that she will get used to deaths over time
Advise her to take a few minutes and then start the round on time
Offer support, ask how she feels and help arrange cover if needed
6.w: Code 8.7: be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems without compromising safety. Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risk.

n.0: Sending her home without discussion or escalation leaves the ward uncovered and her unsupported.
n.1: This dismisses her distress and offers no practical support.
n.2: This overlooks whether she is safe to give medicines right now.

6.q: Mrs Lewis, 61, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 10 years and is admitted with a manic relapse. She says she has 'mostly' taken her tablets. What should happen first regarding her lithium?
o: Switch her to valproate as a more reliable mood stabiliser
Check her plasma lithium level to optimise treatment
Stop the lithium because it has failed to prevent relapse
Add an antidepressant to prevent a later depressive episode
6.w: CG185 1.5.8: if the person is already taking lithium, check plasma lithium levels to optimise treatment. Partial adherence is common and the level guides whether dose or adherence is the issue.

n.0: Valproate is not a first choice here and the level has not yet been checked.
n.2: One relapse does not mean lithium has failed; the level and adherence need checking first.
n.3: Adding an antidepressant during mania risks worsening the episode.

6.q: Ronald, 70, lives in England. He mentions to the nurse that he has never had abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) screening and asks whether it is too late. What is the most accurate response?
o: He is now too old to be included in AAA screening
Men over 65 who have not been screened can refer themselves
Screening after 65 is offered to men with symptoms of an aneurysm
He needs a GP referral for a hospital ultrasound scan
6.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): AAA screening is offered to men when they turn 65; men over 65 can self-refer.

n.0: Men over 65 can self-refer to the programme.
n.2: Screening is for men without symptoms; men over 65 who were not screened can self-refer, and symptoms need GP assessment.
n.3: Self-referral to the screening programme is available; a GP referral is for symptoms.

6.q: Ms Reid, 38, has a learning disability, epilepsy and type 1 diabetes. She has missed three diabetes clinic appointments, and her carer says the waiting room makes her very anxious. What is the most appropriate response by the community nurse?
o: Write to her to say that further missed appointments will be noted
Discharge her from clinic, as she has not attended three times
Ask her carer to attend the clinic in her place to collect advice
Arrange reasonable adjustments such as a first or quiet appointment
6.w: P7.5 requires responding to the challenges of person-centred care for people with complex needs, and the Equality Act 2010 s20 imposes a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Adjusting the appointment removes the barrier to her care.

n.0: A warning letter does not address the cause of her non-attendance.
n.1: Discharging her penalises her for a barrier the service can adjust, worsening inequality.
n.2: Her carer cannot receive her care or examinations for her; she needs to be seen.

6.q: Clive, 80, had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) that was still active when he died on a cardiology ward. The registered nurse has verified his expected death. Which action relating to the device is the nurse's responsibility?
o: Instigate deactivation and tell the mortuary or funeral director about the device
Record the device in the notes, as no further action is needed after death
Ask his family to inform the funeral director that a device is present
Remove the device before Clive is transferred to the mortuary
6.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the RN must instigate the process for deactivation of an implantable cardiac defibrillator where applicable, and must notify the funeral director or mortuary of any infections, radioactive implants, implantable devices and whether an ICD is still active.

n.1: An active ICD remains a hazard to people handling the body, so deactivation must be arranged.
n.2: Notifying the mortuary or funeral director is the verifying nurse's responsibility, not the family's.
n.3: Ward nurses do not remove implanted devices; the RN instigates deactivation and passes on the information.

6.q: During a late shift on an adult surgical ward, a healthcare assistant tells Ruby, the nurse in charge, that Mr Peter Grant, 70, asked for analgesia 45 minutes ago and has still not received it because both nurses in his bay are busy. What should Ruby do?
o: Complete an incident report at the end of the shift and continue with the current allocation
Record the delay in Mr Grant's notes and discuss the bay workload at the next team meeting
Arrange for Mr Grant's analgesia to be given now and escalate the red flag on staffing
Ask the healthcare assistant to tell Mr Grant that a nurse will come once the bay is quieter
6.w: NICE SG1 Safe staffing for nursing in adult inpatient wards (2014) lists a delay of more than 30 minutes in providing pain relief as a nursing red flag. A red flag should prompt an immediate escalation response by the registered nurse in charge, for example allocating additional staff (rec 1.4.3, Box 2). Mr Grant's pain is dealt with first.

n.0: Reporting is useful but does not relieve his pain or address the staffing problem now.
n.1: Documenting and deferring discussion does not meet the immediate escalation response that SG1 requires.
n.3: This prolongs his pain and treats a recognised red flag as routine.

6.q: Patricia, 73, lives in England and has had regular breast screening. She asks the practice nurse why she has not received an invitation since she turned 71. Which response is accurate?
o: Invitations stop after 70, but she can refer herself for screening
Women over 70 are invited every 5 years instead of every 3 years
Breast screening ends at 70 because no benefit remains after that age
She needs a GP referral to a breast clinic to be screened
6.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): breast screening is offered to women aged 50 to 70; women over 70 can self-refer.

n.1: Routine invitations are for women aged 50 to 70; after 70 screening is by self-referral.
n.2: Women over 70 can still self-refer; screening is available to them on request.
n.3: A breast clinic referral is for symptoms; screening after 70 is by self-referral.

6.q: A nurse joining a residential home notices that all residents are got up and dressed by 6 am to suit staff rotas, toileted at fixed times regardless of need, and given meals in the same order every day. Residents' preferences are not recorded. Which type of abuse does this most suggest?
o: Neglect and acts of omission
Organisational abuse
Psychological abuse
Physical abuse
6.w: Organisational abuse (Care Act statutory guidance para 14.17) includes poor care practice within an institution or service, for example rigid routines that serve the organisation rather than the people in its care.

n.0: Fixed toileting may neglect individual needs, but para 14.17 places neglect and poor practice arising from an institution's structure, policies and routines under organisational abuse.
n.2: Psychological abuse involves emotional harm such as threats or humiliation by an individual; the problem described is a system of care.
n.3: No physical harm or force is described.

6.q: Mr Rowe, 74, is recovering from a hip fracture. The nurse and Mr Rowe are agreeing a mobility goal. Which goal is most appropriate?
o: Improve his mobility as much as possible before discharge
Walk to the day room with his frame by Friday, as he chose
Follow the physiotherapy plan written for all hip patients
Walk 200 metres unaided by tomorrow, as set by the team
6.w: Proficiency P3.4: apply a person-centred approach to shared assessment, planning, decision making and goal setting. Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This is vague and not measurable or time-bound.
n.2: A standard plan is not a personal, shared goal.
n.3: This is set for him, not with him, and may be unrealistic.

6.q: Nadia is redressing a deep cavity wound on the sacrum of Ruth, 80. She is wearing non-sterile gloves and using ANTT, but realises she will need to touch the wound bed with her fingers to place the packing. What should she do?
o: Change to sterile gloves, as the Key-Site will be touched directly
Moisten the non-sterile gloves with sterile saline before packing
Rub alcohol handrub onto the gloves before touching the wound
Continue with the non-sterile gloves, as she cleaned her hands first
6.w: Under ANTT, if a Key-Site or Key-Part must be touched directly, sterile gloves are needed so that the hands do not contaminate it (a Surgical-ANTT approach). NIPCM ch 1.4 also requires sterile gloves for contact with a sterile site or body cavity.

n.1: Saline does not sterilise gloves; the gloves would still contaminate the wound bed.
n.2: Gloves are not decontaminated with handrub, and this does not make them sterile.
n.3: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable when Key-Sites are not touched; here she must touch the wound bed directly.

6.q: A ward manager in an English hospital is updating staff training on people who lack capacity and whose care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. A nurse asks which legal scheme is currently in force to authorise such arrangements in hospitals and care homes. What should the manager say?
o: The nurse's holding power under the Mental Health Act 1983
The Liberty Protection Safeguards under the 2019 Amendment Act
The community treatment order scheme under the Mental Health Act
The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards under the MCA 2005
