6.w: DoLS (MCA 2005 Schedules A1 and 1A) remain the scheme in force in England and Wales for hospitals and care homes. The Liberty Protection Safeguards in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 have not been implemented.

n.0: The nurse's holding power under MHA s5(4) briefly detains an informal inpatient with mental disorder; it does not authorise care arrangements under the MCA.
n.1: The LPS have not been brought into force; DoLS remain the live scheme.
n.2: Community treatment orders apply to certain detained patients leaving hospital, not to people lacking capacity in hospitals or care homes.

6.q: Krishna, 64, is a Hindu man on an acute ward. During his assessment he asks for a female nurse not to wash him and to wash with running water rather than a bowl. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Record his preferences in the care plan and arrange care to meet them
Ask his family to come in and do all his washing during visiting time
Tell him staffing makes it difficult and he will be washed by whoever is free
Explain that a bowl wash is the standard ward practice for every patient
6.w: Code 1.1, 4.1 and Annexe B 3.4: treat people as individuals and respect their cultural and religious preferences in personal care, documenting them so that care can be arranged to meet them where possible.

n.1: Families may help if they wish, but care remains the nurse's responsibility.
n.2: Dismissing his preference fails to respect his dignity and beliefs.
n.3: Standard practice should adapt to individual needs where reasonably possible.

6.q: Nurse Holly has been asked to support a doctor who will tell Mr Pearce, 61, that his biopsy shows cancer. Which preparation is most appropriate?
o: Tell Mr Pearce the result first so the doctor can focus on treatment
Arrange a private room and hand her bleep to a colleague
Ask a relative to break the news before the doctor arrives
Use the bay with curtains drawn to save time
6.w: Annexe A 2.9: engage in difficult conversations including breaking bad news. Code 1.1 dignity, 5.1 privacy and 2.6 respond compassionately to distress.

n.0: Delivering the diagnosis outside the planned conversation risks giving it without support.
n.2: Results should be given by the clinical team, with the patient's consent to involve others.
n.3: Curtains do not give privacy; a private room protects dignity and confidentiality.

6.q: Kyle, 22, has had one episode of psychosis and smokes high-strength cannabis every day. He says it helps him relax and asks whether it matters. Which response is most accurate?
o: Cannabis affects mood but is not linked with psychosis
Cannabis eases psychotic symptoms, so it can be a coping aid
Cannabis can worsen psychotic symptoms and raise relapse risk
Cannabis harms mental health when combined with alcohol
6.w: Cannabis, especially high-potency forms, is associated with developing psychosis, more severe symptoms and higher relapse rates. Honest, non-judgemental information supports harm reduction (P2.4).

n.0: There is a well-established link between cannabis and psychosis.
n.1: Any short-term relaxation is outweighed by worsening psychosis and relapse.
n.3: The psychosis risk applies to cannabis use itself, not just combined with alcohol.

6.q: A doctor is writing a rapid tranquillisation prescription for Ms Pike, 29, on an acute ward. The nurse checks that it follows NICE NG10 and BNF advice. Which prescription is correct?
o: Up to four doses in 24 hours, given at the nurse's discretion
A single dose, not repeated until its effect has been reviewed
A combined 'oral or IM' entry so either route can be used
A regular four-hourly IM dose for the next 48 hours
6.w: NG10 1.4.44: write the initial rapid tranquillisation prescription as a single dose and do not repeat it until the effect of the initial dose has been reviewed. The BNF adds that oral and IM doses should be prescribed separately.

n.0: Open-ended repeat doses risk cumulative over-sedation before the first dose's effect is reviewed.
n.2: The BNF says oral and IM drugs should be prescribed separately.
n.3: Regular IM doses are not rapid tranquillisation and risk high-dose prescribing.

6.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
6.q: Nadia, 24, is starting a dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) programme. She asks her named nurse what skills she will learn in the group. Which is one of the four DBT skills modules?
o: Distress tolerance
Cognitive restructuring
Graded activity scheduling
Exposure and response prevention
6.w: DBT (Linehan) teaches four skills modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness.

n.1: Cognitive restructuring is a core CBT technique, not a DBT module.
n.2: Activity scheduling belongs to behavioural activation for depression.
n.3: ERP is a CBT technique for OCD.

6.q: Rose, 79, rings her bell repeatedly at night. When you answer she says she is uncomfortable, cold and needs the toilet. Her pain score is 1 out of 10. What is the best approach to help her rest?
o: Meet her comfort and toileting needs and plan regular night checks
Explain that the bell is for emergencies and move it out of her reach
Give her a sedative to help her sleep without disturbing others
Close the door to her side room so that she is not disturbed
6.w: Annexe B 3.1 and 3.6: assess and meet comfort needs such as warmth, toileting and positioning, which are common barriers to sleep. Intentional rounding at intervals can reduce unmet need and calls.

n.1: Removing the call bell is unsafe and a breach of dignity and safety.
n.2: Sedation does not address her unmet needs and increases falls risk.
n.3: Closing the door does not meet her needs and reduces observation.

6.q: Chloe, 27, has been in continuous seclusion since 08:00. It is now 16:00. What review does the Mental Health Act Code of Practice require at this point?
o: A review by the CQC Mental Health Act reviewer
A further two-hourly nursing review by any nurse
A tribunal referral by the hospital managers
A prompt independent multidisciplinary review
6.w: COP15 26.141: an independent MDT review should be promptly undertaken where a patient has been secluded for 8 hours consecutively or 12 hours intermittently within 48 hours. Members should not have been involved in the incident that led to seclusion, and include an IMHA if she has one.

n.0: The CQC monitors use of the Act but does not carry out case reviews of seclusion.
n.1: Nursing reviews continue every 2 hours but must be by two registered nurses, and they do not replace the independent MDT review at 8 hours.
n.2: Seclusion does not trigger a tribunal referral.

6.q: Mia, 6, is due her annual flu vaccine at school. Her parents tell the school nurse they decline the nasal spray vaccine because it contains porcine gelatine, which conflicts with their beliefs, but they want her protected. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that children under 9 must have the nasal vaccine to be protected
Give the nasal vaccine, explaining that gelatine is an inactive ingredient
Discuss the injected inactivated flu vaccine as an alternative for Mia
Advise them that Mia can have a flu vaccine once she reaches adulthood
6.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: the live attenuated influenza vaccine (Fluenz, nasal) contains porcine gelatine; if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used (Green Book chapter 19). UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): consent must be given freely by an appropriately informed person.

n.0: The schedule states that if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used.
n.1: Giving it against the parents' refusal would be without valid consent (Green Book chapter 2).
n.3: An inactivated alternative is available now, so she need not go unprotected.

6.q: Mrs Grant, 59, has taken diazepam 10 mg daily for two years for anxiety. She tells her community nurse she is fed up with tablets and plans to stop them completely tomorrow. What should the nurse advise?
o: Support her plan to stop tomorrow, as she is motivated to do so
Swap to zopiclone, which can be stopped at any time safely
Halve the dose for three days and then stop it completely
Avoid stopping suddenly; agree a slow taper with the prescriber
6.w: MHRA (January 2026) strengthened warnings on dependence, withdrawal and tolerance with benzodiazepines and Z-drugs and advises avoiding abrupt cessation. After long-term use a gradual, supported dose reduction agreed with the prescriber reduces withdrawal risks such as rebound anxiety and seizures.

n.0: Stopping suddenly after two years risks severe withdrawal, including seizures.
n.1: Z-drugs such as zopiclone also carry dependence and withdrawal risks and should not be stopped abruptly.
n.2: A three-day taper is far too rapid after long-term use.

6.q: A nurse has completed a detailed physical assessment of Mr Rees, 75, who is admitted after a fall at home. She has recorded his observations, skin, mobility and continence. Which further area is most needed to make the assessment holistic before discharge planning?
o: A second set of skin checks by another registered nurse
His social circumstances, support at home and his own priorities
A full list of every past hospital admission he has had
A full repeat of his observations before the end of the day shift
6.w: Holistic assessment (P3.1, P3.4) combines physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs and the person's own goals. After a fall at home, his living situation, support and priorities are central to safe planning, and NICE NG249 includes a home hazard assessment.

n.0: A second skin check adds to the physical assessment already completed.
n.2: An exhaustive admission history adds little compared with his current social and support needs.
n.3: Repeat observations are part of physical monitoring, not the missing holistic domain.

6.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
6.q: A ward is introducing trauma-informed care. Which question best reflects the trauma-informed shift in how staff think about a person's distress?
o: 'Why are you behaving like this?'
'What is wrong with you?'
'What has happened to you?'
'What is your diagnosis?'
6.w: Trauma-informed practice reframes distress as an understandable response to experiences, moving from 'what is wrong with you?' to 'what has happened to you?'.

n.0: This implies blame and can increase shame.
n.1: This frames the person as defective.
n.3: Focusing on diagnosis overlooks the experiences behind distress.

6.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
6.q: Ms Obi's son, 22, has had his first admission for psychosis. At his discharge meeting she asks what she should do if things go wrong at home. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she reads about psychosis on reputable websites
Give written and verbal information, with crisis contacts
Reassure her that the team will contact her if needed
Explain that information must wait until his consent
6.w: CG178 1.1.4.1: give carers written and verbal information in an accessible format about the diagnosis and management, recovery, carer support, the role of teams and services, and how to get help in a crisis.

n.0: Websites, even reputable ones, do not give her tailored information or local crisis routes.
n.2: Waiting to be contacted leaves her without a plan in a crisis.
n.3: General and crisis information can be given to carers without breaching confidentiality.

6.q: At 08:00 nurse Ollie gives Mrs Brown, 72, her 10:00 dose of paracetamol 1 g in error, two hours early. She is alert and well, and the next dose has not yet been given. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell her, apologise, inform the prescriber and report it as an incident
Tell her and apologise, then retime later doses without reporting
Inform the prescriber and record the error in the medicines chart
Report it as an incident and tell her if harm develops later
6.w: Code 14.1-14.3: put the situation right, explain fully and promptly and apologise, then document and escalate. The NMC/GMC duty of candour guidance (Dec 2024) also covers reporting incidents and near misses.

n.1: Adjusting doses is right, but Code 14.3 also requires the event to be documented and escalated.
n.2: This omits explaining and apologising to Mrs Brown, which the professional duty requires.
n.3: Code 14 applies when an incident had the potential for harm; candour does not wait for harm to occur.

6.q: You are preparing to redress Stan's surgical wound using aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT). Which principle is central to ANTT?
o: Completing the dressing within 5 minutes
Protecting key parts and key sites from touch
Cleaning the wound with an antiseptic each time
Wearing sterile gloves for every dressing change
6.w: ANTT is based on identifying and protecting key parts (for example the inside of the dressing) and key sites (the wound) by not touching them directly or indirectly, with hand hygiene and an aseptic field. Glove choice depends on whether key parts must be touched.

n.0: Speed is not the defining principle of ANTT.
n.2: Routine antiseptic cleansing is not a principle of ANTT and can harm tissue.
n.3: Sterile gloves are needed when key parts must be touched; non-sterile gloves are used otherwise.

6.q: Ms Coe, 30, received IM lorazepam for rapid tranquillisation 30 minutes ago. She is now awake, calm and talking. She has no physical health problems, has not taken alcohol or drugs, was not restrained and received a standard dose. How often should her physical observations be done?
o: Every 4 hours for the whole of the next day
Every 15 minutes for the next 4 hours
Once, an hour after the injection was given
At least hourly until there are no concerns
6.w: NG10 1.4.45: after rapid tranquillisation, monitor side effects, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and level of consciousness at least every hour until there are no further concerns. 15-minute monitoring applies if any listed risk factor is present; none applies to Ms Coe.

n.0: Four-hourly checks are less frequent than the NG10 minimum of hourly.
n.1: 15-minute monitoring is for people who appear asleep or sedated, exceed the BNF maximum, have taken drugs or alcohol, have a physical health problem or were harmed by restraint.
n.2: A single check does not meet NG10, which requires ongoing monitoring until there are no concerns.

6.q: A community mental health nurse asks Leon, 27, "Think of a day recently when things were a little better. What was different about that day?" Which approach is the nurse using?
o: Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Motivational interviewing
Reminiscence therapy
6.w: Annexe A 3.2: solution-focused therapies. Asking about exceptions, when the problem was less present, builds on existing strengths.

n.0: CBT works on links between thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
n.2: MI explores ambivalence about change.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories to support wellbeing, mainly in older adults.

6.q: A trust that runs five mental health wards asks how it must meet section 2 of the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018. Which arrangement complies?
o: A separate responsible person, employed by the trust, for each ward
One suitably senior responsible person, employed by the trust, for all
Each of the five ward managers acting as responsible person on a rota
A CQC inspector appointed as the responsible person for the trust
6.w: Section 2 requires an organisation operating a mental health unit to appoint a responsible person, employed by it and of an appropriate level of seniority. An organisation with more than one unit must appoint a single responsible person for all its units.

n.0: Where an organisation runs more than one unit, it must appoint a single responsible person for all of them.
n.2: A rota of ward managers does not meet the requirement for one appointed, suitably senior responsible person.
n.3: The responsible person must be employed by the operating organisation, not the regulator.

6.q: At the start of an early shift, Nina, a staff nurse, is allocated four patients on a medical ward. Which patient should she see first?
o: Mr Ali, 66, whose insulin is due with breakfast in 45 minutes
Mrs Dunn, 74, whose respiratory rate is 28/min, SpO2 89% and who is newly confused
Ms Reid, 52, who reports post-operative pain of 5/10, last analgesia 3 hours ago
Mr Shaw, 59, who is to be discharged today and needs his discharge letter
6.w: Prioritisation uses an ABCDE approach and early warning scores: Mrs Dunn has a respiratory rate of 28 (scores 3), SpO2 89% (scores 3) and new confusion (scores 3) on NEWS2 (RCP 2017), indicating possible life-threatening deterioration needing immediate assessment and escalation (P5.5 lead and manage care of a group of people with prioritisation).

n.0: Time-critical insulin matters, but there are 45 minutes before it is due and he is not unwell.
n.2: Her pain needs prompt attention, possibly by another team member, but is not life-threatening.
n.3: Discharge paperwork can safely wait while a deteriorating patient is assessed.

6.q: Ms Brown, 36, has borderline personality disorder and arrives at the community mental health team in crisis after an argument with her partner, saying she cannot cope. What should the nurse do first?
o: Use her crisis plan and calm, validating open questions
Arrange an informal admission so she is kept safe
Advise her to come back to the team once she feels calmer
Ask her GP to increase her regular medication today
6.w: CG78 1.3.7.1: when a person with BPD presents in crisis, consult the crisis plan, maintain a calm, non-threatening attitude, try to understand the crisis from their view and use empathic open questioning with validating statements.

n.1: Admission is considered after alternatives such as home treatment, and risk has not yet been assessed.
n.2: Sending her away in crisis is unsafe and invalidating.
n.3: Drugs are not used for BPD symptoms; crisis sedation is short term and follows assessment.

6.q: A patient's family sends Hannah a thank-you card that names their mother and praises Hannah's care during her last days. Hannah wants to use it as practice-related feedback for revalidation. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Place a copy of the card in her revalidation portfolio
Ask her line manager to countersign the card before use
Note the content of the feedback without identifying details
Exclude it, as feedback must be formal and in writing
6.w: NMC revalidation: five pieces of practice-related feedback from any source, written or verbal, formal or informal. Keep a note of the content and how it improved practice, without recording anything that could identify another person.

n.0: The card names the patient; NMC guidance says not to record information that may identify another person.
n.1: Feedback does not need countersigning; the key requirement is to remove identifying information.
n.3: Feedback can be written or verbal, formal or informal, from patients, families or colleagues.

6.q: In October 2026 a ward induction pack states that 'therapeutic benefit' is now a statutory principle in section 118 that all decisions under the Act must follow. What correction should the practice educator make?
o: The 2025 Act principles apply to CTO patients and the Code principles to others
None; the principles were added to the Code by SI 2026/385 in April 2026
The 2025 Act principles await commencement; the 2015 Code's five principles apply
None; the 2025 Act principles came into force on Royal Assent
6.w: Sections 1-2 of the 2025 Act will put four statutory principles (choice and autonomy, least restriction, therapeutic benefit, the person as an individual) into section 118, but they are not in force in October 2026. The 2015 Code's five guiding principles still apply.

n.0: There is no split by patient group; the 2025 principles are not in force for anyone.
n.1: SI 2026/385 commenced sections 51 and 52 only.
n.3: Royal Assent commenced only technical provisions (ss53-57), not the principles.

6.q: Mr Pearce, 67, has capacity and peripheral vascular disease. After a full explanation of the risks, he declines a recommended below-knee amputation, saying he would rather take his chances. The team thinks this is an unwise choice. Which principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies most directly?
o: Making an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity
Any act done for a person must be in their best interests
The less restrictive option must be considered first
All practicable steps must be taken to help the person decide
6.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Mr Pearce has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (Code 2.5).

n.1: Best interests (s1(5)) applies to acts for people who lack capacity; Mr Pearce has capacity.
n.2: The less restrictive principle (s1(6)) applies when acting for someone who lacks capacity.
n.3: Supporting decision-making (s1(3)) has already been met by the full explanation; the issue now is respecting an unwise choice.

6.q: Jonas, 40, sees the practice nurse for a review of his depression. He says he has written goodbye letters, has saved a supply of tablets and intends to take them this weekend. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer him urgently to specialist mental health services
Start an antidepressant and review him in 2 weeks
Give him a crisis line number and book a review next week
Refer him to NHS Talking Therapies for high-intensity CBT
6.w: NG222 1.2.9: if a person with depression presents considerable immediate risk to themselves, refer them urgently to specialist mental health services. Goodbye letters, means and a timed plan indicate high immediate risk (P3.10).

n.1: Medication does not address the immediate risk and takes weeks to work.
n.2: A crisis number and a week's wait leave him unsafe this weekend.
n.3: Talking Therapies is not a crisis service.

6.q: Ms Clarke, 38, agrees to have a wound swab taken after the nurse explains why it is needed and what it involves. The swab is taken without problems. According to Code 4.2, what should the nurse also make sure of?
o: That the consent is confirmed again by the doctor
That Ms Clarke signs a consent form for the swab
That the consent obtained is documented in her record
That a second nurse witnesses Ms Clarke's agreement
6.w: Code 4.2: make sure that you get properly informed consent and document it before carrying out any action. Verbal consent is valid for a wound swab; the record should show it was obtained.

n.0: The nurse taking the swab obtains the consent; the doctor does not need to confirm it.
n.1: Written consent is not required for a routine swab; verbal consent is valid if documented.
n.3: There is no requirement for a witness to verbal consent for a routine procedure.

6.q: Agnes, 70, admitted for a planned hip replacement, asks to keep her own inhalers and eye drops in her bedside locker and use them herself, as she does at home. What should the nurse do?
o: Allow it once her daughter agrees to supervise her doses
Complete a self-administration risk assessment and record it
Decline, as nurses give all medicines on a hospital ward
Allow it, as they are her own supply brought in from home
6.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-5: organisations have a self-administration policy; a risk assessment considers risks, the person's ability and consent, decides the level of self-administration, and the outcome and the person's agreement are recorded and reassessed as necessary.

n.0: A relative's agreement does not replace the documented professional risk assessment.
n.2: RPS/RCN guidance expects patients to keep responsibility for their medicines unless a risk assessment indicates otherwise.
n.3: Ownership does not replace the risk assessment that decides whether self-administration is safe.

6.q: A new healthcare assistant starts on a psychiatric intensive care unit. Under section 5 of the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018, what training must she receive?
o: Restraint holds training, completed within her first year
None, as the section 5 duty covers registered nurses
Use of force training with de-escalation, soon after starting
Breakaway training, as she has been rostered for night shifts
6.w: Section 5 requires the responsible person to give all staff in the unit training in the appropriate use of force as soon as reasonably practicable after joining, with refresher training at regular intervals. Content includes patient involvement, avoiding discrimination, de-escalation, risks of force and the impact of trauma.

n.0: The training is much broader than restraint holds and must be given as soon as reasonably practicable, not within a year.
n.1: The duty covers all staff working in the unit, including healthcare assistants.
n.3: Training applies to all staff in the unit; shift pattern does not change the content or timing.

6.q: Toby, 17, is detained under section 3 with severe depression. He has capacity and consents to electroconvulsive therapy recommended by his team. His parents also agree. What else is legally required before ECT can be given (outside an emergency)?
o: The written consent of both of his parents
A Court of Protection order
A SOAD certificate that the treatment is appropriate
The approved clinician's certificate of his consent
6.w: Under section 58A, ECT for a patient under 18 who consents still needs a SOAD certificate confirming that he is capable of consenting and that the treatment is appropriate. For capable adults the approved clinician can certify consent instead.

n.0: Parental consent is not the s58A safeguard; for a consenting under-18 a SOAD must certify capacity and appropriateness.
n.1: The Court of Protection is not involved in Part 4 ECT for a detained patient.
n.3: Approved clinician certification is available for capable consenting adults, not under-18s.

6.q: Marcus Bell, 66, is on a surgical ward. His observations are: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on air, BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, alert, temperature 37.2°C. His NEWS2 total is 3. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Increase observations to at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat the observations in 4 hours and escalate if the total rises
Continue 4 to 6 hourly observations as the total score is below 5
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
6.w: A respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3 in a single parameter (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Chart 1). A score of 3 in any one parameter triggers a low-medium clinical risk response: minimum 1-hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team, who decide whether escalation is needed (Chart 4). Two steps: calculate the parameter score, then apply the single-parameter rule.

n.1: Four-hourly review delays recognition of deterioration when a single parameter is already scoring 3.
n.2: The aggregate of 3 is low, but a single red score of 3 overrides this and requires at least hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.3: Emergency critical care assessment is the response to an aggregate of 7 or more; this is an urgent ward-based response.

6.q: Ms Rae, 24, has a first episode of psychosis, and the team is about to start an antipsychotic. Before the first dose, the nurse joins the discussion with her. Which approach best reflects NICE CG178?
o: Let the team choose the drug so that she is not overwhelmed
Tell her side effects are rare and not worth worrying about
Advise her not to read the leaflet to avoid worrying her
Discuss which side effects she would most accept, and benefits
6.w: CG178 1.3.6.3: treat antipsychotic medication as an explicit individual therapeutic trial, discussing and recording the side effects the person is most willing to tolerate, the expected benefits and risks, and the time to change in symptoms.

n.0: Drug choice should be made with the person, based on side-effect profiles and her preferences.
n.1: Side effects are common with antipsychotics; minimising them undermines informed consent and trust.
n.2: Discouraging her from reading information undermines informed, shared decisions.

6.q: Agnes, 86, lives in a care home and has a NEWS2 of 2 with a suspected chest infection. The staff say she 'cannot have sepsis because she has no fever'. Which statement by the nurse is best?
o: Fever or hypothermia does not rule sepsis in or out
Older people with no fever are unlikely to have sepsis
Sepsis is ruled out while her NEWS2 remains below 5
A temperature above 38°C is needed before sepsis is considered
6.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.1: do not rely on fever or hypothermia alone to rule sepsis in or out. Older people may not mount a fever; NEWS2 supports, but does not replace, clinical judgement.

n.1: Older people frequently do not develop a fever, so its absence does not lower risk.
n.2: A NEWS2 below 5 means low risk, not that sepsis is excluded.
n.3: No temperature threshold is required before considering sepsis.

6.q: A company representative gives a ward manager a single-site study of 20 patients, funded by the company, with no control group, reporting that its new catheter reduces infections. The manager wants to switch at once. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Switch now, as published evidence shows a clear benefit
Appraise the study's limits and seek stronger evidence first
Reject the product, as industry-funded studies are invalid
Switch now and audit infection rates after six months
6.w: Proficiency P1.7-P1.8: critically analyse research findings and think critically when applying evidence. Code 6.1 information must be evidence-based; small uncontrolled studies sit low in evidence hierarchies.

n.0: A small, uncontrolled, industry-funded study has a high risk of bias and does not justify a change alone.
n.2: Funding source raises the risk of bias but does not automatically invalidate a study; appraisal is needed.
n.3: Auditing after a change does not replace appraising whether the evidence supports the change.

6.q: Hannah, 24, has type 1 diabetes and is on an orthopaedic ward. You are called because she is sweaty and confused. Airway is clear, RR 18, SpO2 97%, pulse 98, BP 118/72. She responds to voice. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give her 300 mg aspirin to chew while awaiting review
Complete a 4AT delirium screen before any other test
Request an urgent CT head scan to exclude a stroke
Check her capillary blood glucose straight away
6.w: With A, B and C stable, D includes a capillary blood glucose. In someone with diabetes who is sweaty and confused, hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L, RCUK first aid 2025) is the most likely reversible cause and must be excluded quickly.

n.0: Aspirin is for cardiac-sounding chest pain and is not indicated for confusion.
n.1: Delirium screening is relevant later; a reversible metabolic cause should be excluded first.
n.2: Imaging is not a nursing first step and would delay checking for a common reversible cause.

6.q: At 22:00 Sean, 36, an informal in-patient on an acute ward, suddenly packs his bag and says he will 'end it tonight'. No doctor can attend quickly. The registered mental health nurse invokes section 5(4). For how long can Sean be held under this power?
o: Up to 72 hours, or until the approved mental health professional arrives if sooner
Up to 6 hours, renewable once by a second nurse of the prescribed class
Up to 6 hours, or until a doctor or approved clinician with s5(2) power arrives if sooner
Up to 24 hours, with a possible 12-hour extension by the duty doctor
6.w: Section 5(4) allows detention for up to 6 hours or until a doctor or approved clinician able to use section 5(2) arrives, whichever is earlier. It cannot be renewed (COP15 18.25).

n.0: Seventy-two hours is the maximum for the doctor's or approved clinician's section 5(2) power, not the nurse's.
n.1: Section 5(4) cannot be renewed by any nurse (COP15 18.25, 18.38).
n.3: Twenty-four hours plus a 12-hour extension is the place of safety limit under sections 135 and 136.

6.q: Mr Gray, 70, has capacity and a physical disability. He discloses that his son pushes him when angry, but asks the nurse to do nothing. The nurse discusses the options, and there is no apparent risk to anyone else. Which of the six adult safeguarding principles requires the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk?
o: Empowerment
Protection
Accountability
Proportionality
6.w: The six principles (Care Act statutory guidance ch 14) are empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership and accountability. Proportionality means the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk presented.

n.0: Empowerment concerns person-led decisions and informed consent, not the scale of response.
n.1: Protection concerns support and representation for those in greatest need.
n.2: Accountability concerns accountability and transparency in delivering safeguarding, not the scale of the response.

6.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Stanley, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
o: Twelve-lead ECG at rest
Lying and standing BP
Peak expiratory flow
Ankle brachial pressure index
6.w: NICE NG249: the multifactorial falls assessment includes lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension, alongside medication review, cognition, continence, vision, footwear, gait and balance.

n.0: An ECG may be needed in some people but is not the standard NG249 component listed.
n.2: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not falls risk.
n.3: ABPI assesses arterial supply before leg compression, not falls.

6.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
6.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

6.q: Mr Ito, 38, has a head injury. On assessment his eyes open to pressure on the fingertip, he is talking but disorientated about time and place, and he localises to a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
6.w: GCS: eye opening to pressure = 2; confused speech = 4; localising = 5. Total 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 out of 15 (range 3-15). Any fall in GCS after head injury needs urgent escalation.

n.0: Orientated speech scores 5 and obeying commands 6; he is confused and localises.
n.1: Eye opening to speech scores 3; he opens his eyes only to pressure, which scores 2.
n.2: Inappropriate words score 3; he is talking in sentences but confused, which scores 4.

6.q: Mrs Brennan, 66, has heart failure and wants to stay well at home. Which nursing action best supports her self-management?
o: Agree a written plan with her, including when to seek help
Tell her to rest and avoid activity until her next review
Arrange for a carer to manage her medicines at home
Ask her to phone the ward whenever she feels unwell
6.w: Proficiency P4.2: work in partnership to encourage shared decision making and support people to manage their own care. Code 2.1-2.3.

n.1: This is not person-centred and may not reflect her condition or goals.
n.2: Taking over her medicines reduces self-management without a reason to do so.
n.3: This keeps her dependent and does not build her own management skills.

6.q: Tom, 19, attends with low mood. His father has schizophrenia and Tom asks whether he will develop it too. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: It is not inherited, so your risk is the same as anyone else's
Your risk is about one in two because your father has the condition
A blood test can show whether you carry the gene for schizophrenia
Your risk is raised, but most children of affected parents are unaffected
6.w: SPEC.T2 lists genomics linked to MH conditions. Schizophrenia is polygenic: a first-degree relative raises lifetime risk (to roughly 10%), and environmental stressors interact with this vulnerability (stress-vulnerability model), so most children of affected parents are not affected.

n.0: Family history is a recognised risk factor, so his risk is higher than average.
n.1: One in two greatly overstates the risk from one affected parent.
n.2: No single gene or diagnostic genetic test exists; risk is polygenic.

6.q: Mr Mann, 56, takes sertraline. Yesterday his GP added tramadol for back pain. Today he is agitated and sweating, with a tremor, jerking of his legs, brisk reflexes, diarrhoea and a temperature of 38.3 C. What is the most likely cause and response?
o: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; ask for dantrolene
Serotonin toxicity; withhold both drugs and get urgent review
A panic attack; give PRN lorazepam and reassure him
Antidepressant withdrawal; give an extra sertraline dose
6.w: Serotonin toxicity can follow within hours of adding a second serotonergic drug (tramadol has serotonergic activity). Neuromuscular excitability, autonomic signs and altered mental state are characteristic. Treatment is withdrawing the serotonergic drugs, supportive care and specialist advice (BNF).

n.0: NMS follows antipsychotics and shows slow-onset rigidity, not clonus and hyperreflexia.
n.2: Fever, clonus and hyperreflexia are physical signs of toxicity, not panic.
n.3: He has not missed doses; extra sertraline would worsen serotonin toxicity.

6.q: Samuel, 79, is in the last days of life. Yesterday a trial of subcutaneous fluids was started because he was thirsty and slightly confused. Today the nurse notes new crackles at both lung bases and increasing ankle swelling. He is more breathless. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 'as required' midazolam for breathlessness and continue the fluids
Increase the infusion rate because his thirst is still present
Continue the fluids and reassess them at tomorrow's daily review
Reduce or stop the fluids and inform the team of signs of fluid overload
6.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.4.9: for a person started on clinically assisted hydration, monitor at least every 12 hours for benefit or harm; continue if there is clinical benefit and reduce or stop it if there are signs of possible harm such as fluid overload, or if the person no longer wants it.

n.0: Sedating him without removing the cause of the overload is not appropriate; the fluids are causing harm.
n.1: Increasing fluid would worsen the overload; thirst is managed with mouth care and sips (rec 1.4.2).
n.2: NG31 rec 1.4.9 says reduce or stop clinically assisted hydration if there are signs of harm such as fluid overload.

6.q: Before a short handover, Graham, a staff nurse, needs to ask a healthcare assistant to monitor Mr Okafor, 70, who had a hypotensive episode earlier. Which instruction is clearest?
o: 'Please check Mr Okafor's BP and pulse at 14:00 and tell me at once if systolic is under 100.'
'Please keep an eye on Mr Okafor this afternoon and let me know how he gets on.'
'Please do the usual observations on everyone in bay 2, including Mr Okafor, this afternoon.'
'Please do Mr Okafor's observations when you have time and tell me if anything looks off.'
6.w: AnnexA.1.11 requires clear verbal, digital or written information and instructions when delegating or handing over. An instruction stating what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when removes ambiguity (Code 11.2; AnnexA.4.1.2).

n.1: 'Keep an eye on' does not specify what to measure, when, or what to report.
n.2: A general bay instruction does not flag Mr Okafor's specific risk or what to report.
n.3: There is no time set or threshold for reporting; 'anything off' depends on the assistant's interpretation.

6.q: Ms Jones, 24, is in a busy emergency department cubicle after cutting her forearm. The mental health liaison nurse arrives to carry out her psychosocial assessment. Ms Jones asks quietly whether a woman could do the assessment, because she does not want to talk to a man. What should happen?
o: Assess her in the cubicle with the curtain closed to avoid delay
Ask her to wait until the morning when more staff will be on duty
Arrange a private room and offer a female clinician to assess her
Explain that the clinician on duty is the one who must assess her
6.w: NICE NG225 says psychosocial assessment should take place in a private, designated area where the person cannot be overheard, with the option of a healthcare professional of the same sex when the person requests this (1.5, 1.7.15).

n.0: A curtained cubicle does not allow her to speak in confidence without being overheard.
n.1: The assessment should happen at the earliest opportunity, not be put off overnight.
n.3: NG225 provides for a same-sex assessor on request; refusing it may stop her disclosing.

6.q: Frank, 70, has a nasogastric tube. Before his morning feed you aspirate and the pH is 6.5. He takes a proton pump inhibitor. He is comfortable with normal observations. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the feed, as the pH is close to the safe range
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Use the whoosh test to confirm the tube position
Flush with 50 mL of water and start feeding
6.w: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not feed; follow local protocol, which may involve waiting and retesting, or an X-ray. CG32 rec 1.7.17 notes that pH may be invalid with acid suppression, which local protocols must address. Air auscultation (the whoosh test) is not a safe method.

n.0: Feeding with an unconfirmed tube position risks feed entering the lungs.
n.2: The whoosh test is unreliable and was removed from practice by the NPSA in 2005.
n.3: Flushing an unconfirmed tube risks fluid entering the lungs.

6.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
6.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

6.q: At 02:00 on a stand-alone mental health unit, Mr Lyle, 60, has suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome with a NEWS2 score of 8. The on-call psychiatrist is 40 minutes away and the unit has no acute medical team. What should the nurse in charge do?
o: Recheck his observations in an hour before escalating
Wait for the on-call psychiatrist to assess him first
Give oral fluids and paracetamol and review at 06:00
Arrange emergency transfer to acute care by calling 999
6.w: A NEWS2 score of 7 or more needs an emergency response with critical care competencies. On a unit without an acute medical team this means emergency transfer (999) under local policy, informing the on-call doctor in parallel (RCP NEWS2; NMC P4.10).

n.0: A score of 8 already requires an emergency response; waiting an hour delays it.
n.1: Waiting 40 minutes for a psychiatrist delays emergency care for a life-threatening condition.
n.2: Simple measures and a review hours later are unsafe for suspected NMS with a score of 8.

6.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
6.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

6.q: Anna, 31, has bipolar disorder and a relapse plan she wrote with her community nurse. Her early warning signs are sleeping less, writing through the night and becoming irritable. At a home visit she says she has slept four hours a night this week and has started a novel. What should the nurse do?
o: Recognise her early warning signs and follow the agreed relapse plan
Advise her to take extra lithium tonight to settle her sleep
Reassure her that a few short nights are common and review in a month
Advise her to stop her medication for a week to see if it is the cause
6.w: Early warning signs in a person's relapse signature allow early action. Acting on the plan agreed with Anna (for example increased contact, sleep strategies, medication review with the prescriber) respects her expertise and reduces the risk of full relapse (NICE CG185 on relapse prevention).

n.1: Changing a lithium dose needs a prescriber and level monitoring; extra doses risk toxicity.
n.2: Her own early warning signs are present; waiting a month risks a full manic relapse.
n.3: Stopping medication suddenly increases relapse risk; lithium in particular should be withdrawn gradually.

6.q: While giving a subcutaneous injection to Peter, 61, who has hepatitis C, nurse Hana sustains a needlestick injury to her finger through her glove. The needle has been used. What should Hana do immediately?
o: Let it bleed without squeezing, wash with soap and running water, then report
Squeeze the wound firmly to express blood, then apply an alcohol wipe
Suck the wound, cover it with a plaster and report it after the drug round
Scrub the wound with a nail brush and chlorhexidine, then apply a dressing
6.w: NIPCM appendix 10: allow the area to bleed but do not squeeze, do not suck, and wash with warm running water and non-antimicrobial soap. The incident is then reported urgently so that occupational health or A&E can assess the need for post-exposure management; the Sharps Regulations 2013 require all sharps injuries to be reported.

n.1: Squeezing can push contaminated material deeper into tissue; NIPCM says allow bleeding without squeezing.
n.2: Sucking the wound is specifically advised against, and reporting must be prompt so treatment is not delayed.
n.3: Scrubbing damages tissue and may increase uptake; gentle washing under running water is advised.

6.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
6.q: Chloe, 15, attends a school nursing drop-in. She is low in mood, wants to be referred for talking therapy and asks the nurse not to tell her parents. What should the nurse do first?
o: Inform her parents because she is under 16
Explain therapy must wait until she turns 16
Assess whether she understands enough to consent herself
Assess her capacity using the Mental Capacity Act test
6.w: Under 16s can consent to treatment if they are Gillick competent: they have sufficient understanding and intelligence to understand what is proposed. Confidentiality is respected unless there is a risk of serious harm.

n.0: Being under 16 does not on its own require parental involvement.
n.1: Gillick competent under 16s can consent now.
n.3: The MCA applies from age 16; for under 16s Gillick competence is used.

6.q: Two hours after IV morphine, Brian, 79, is difficult to rouse, has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 7 breaths per minute. His SpO2 is 89% on air. Naloxone is prescribed as required. What is the priority?
o: Call for help, support his breathing and give the prescribed naloxone
Recheck his observations in 15 minutes and document the findings
Sit him upright and encourage him to take deep breaths until he wakes
Withhold the next morphine dose and inform the doctor on the ward round
6.w: Opioid toxicity with respiratory depression is an emergency (P4.15): call for help, support airway and breathing with oxygen, and give naloxone, the opioid antagonist, titrating to restore adequate breathing while monitoring for recurrence. Opioids are high-risk medicines.

n.1: Delaying treatment of a respiratory rate of 7 risks respiratory arrest.
n.2: Repositioning does not reverse opioid respiratory depression in a barely rousable patient.
n.3: Withholding the next dose is needed but does not reverse the current toxicity.

6.q: A nurse on an intensive care unit in England is caring for four patients for whom organ donation after death may be possible. None has recorded a decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. Which patient is excluded from deemed consent?
o: Leah, 30, who had not discussed donation with her family
Amy, 17, a student who has lived in England all her life
Victor, 75, who completed treatment for bowel cancer last year
Paul, 60, who moved to England from Wales three years ago
6.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England: the opt-out law does not apply to people under 18, people who lack capacity to understand the arrangements for a significant period before death, visitors and people not living in England voluntarily, or people who lived in England for less than 12 months before their death.

n.0: Not having discussed donation does not exclude an adult; her family are approached about any known views.
n.2: Medical history affects suitability, not whether deemed consent applies; age 75 is not an exclusion.
n.3: He has lived in England for more than 12 months and is an adult, so he is not in an excluded group.

6.q: Ravi, 37, is detained under section 3 in an independent hospital, with his care arranged and paid for by the NHS. In October 2026 he asks whether the hospital must act compatibly with his human rights. What is the accurate answer?
o: No, because the CQC protects his rights in an independent hospital
Yes, as the 2025 Act extended HRA duties to such providers in April 2026
Yes, once the remaining provisions of the 2025 Act are commenced
No, because the Human Rights Act binds NHS bodies, not private ones
6.w: Section 51 of the Mental Health Act 2025 (new s142C of the 1983 Act), in force from 6 April 2026 under SI 2026/385, makes private providers of care arranged under the MHA subject to the Human Rights Act 1998 in providing that care.

n.0: The CQC regulates providers but does not replace the provider's own HRA duties.
n.2: Section 51 was commenced on 6 April 2026; it does not wait for the rest of the Act.
n.3: Section 51 of the 2025 Act now extends HRA duties to private providers of MHA-arranged care.

6.q: Malik, 50, has suspected sepsis with a NEWS2 of 5. How often should his NEWS2 be recalculated under NICE NG253 (2025)?
o: Hourly
Every 4-6 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 30 minutes
6.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.6.5: recalculate NEWS2 every 30 minutes for high risk, hourly for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6), every 4-6 hours for low risk.

n.1: 4-6 hourly is for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.2: 12-hourly is the general NEWS2 minimum for a score of 0, not for suspected sepsis at 5.
n.3: Every 30 minutes is for high risk (NEWS2 7 or more).

6.q: Ms Lane, 24, is about to start carbamazepine for bipolar disorder. She mentions that she takes the combined contraceptive pill and does not want to become pregnant. What should the nurse discuss with her and the prescriber?
o: Her pill will raise her carbamazepine to toxic levels
Carbamazepine can make her pill less effective
Carbamazepine increases the pill's contraceptive effect
Taking her pill at night prevents any interaction
6.w: Carbamazepine is a hepatic enzyme inducer that speeds the metabolism of hormonal contraceptives and can make the combined pill unreliable; the BNF and FSRH advise discussing a method unaffected by enzyme inducers, such as an intrauterine method. It is also teratogenic, so effective contraception matters.

n.0: The interaction runs the other way: carbamazepine reduces contraceptive hormone levels.
n.2: Enzyme induction reduces, not increases, contraceptive effect.
n.3: Changing the time of day does not prevent enzyme induction.

6.q: Darren, 35, is shouting in the ward corridor, pacing and jabbing his finger at staff about a cancelled visit. Four staff members gather round, each trying to calm him at once. According to NICE NG10, what should happen?
o: One staff member takes the lead in communicating with him
All four staff keep talking to him so he feels well supported
Security staff are called to stand beside him
Staff withdraw until he calms down on his own
6.w: NICE NG10 1.3.18: if a service user becomes agitated or angry, one staff member should take the primary role in communicating with them, assess safety, seek clarification and negotiate a non-confrontational resolution. Several people talking at once can overwhelm and provoke.

n.1: Multiple people speaking at once is confusing and can escalate agitation; NG10 recommends a single lead.
n.2: Bringing security alongside early can be perceived as threatening and is not a de-escalation technique.
n.3: Withdrawing entirely leaves an agitated person unsupported and does not use de-escalation skills.

6.q: Mr Moore, 83, has delirium. He is shouting, pulling at his cannula and swinging his arms at staff. No one has been hurt yet. What should the nurse do first?
o: Request haloperidol as the first step to calm him down quickly
Restrain his arms so the cannula is not pulled out
Ask security to stay with him until he settles down
Use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and look for causes
6.w: NICE CG103: if a person with delirium is distressed or a risk to themselves or others, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation; consider short-term haloperidol if de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate. Underlying causes such as pain, retention or hypoxia should be sought (Annexe B 1.1.5).

n.0: Medication is considered when de-escalation fails or is inappropriate, not as the first step.
n.1: Physical restraint is a last resort and may worsen agitation and delirium.
n.2: Security presence is restrictive and does not address his distress or its cause.

6.q: Noah, 23, is seen after self-harm. A colleague suggests using a risk scale to decide whether he can be discharged. Under NICE NG225, what should happen instead?
o: A person-centred psychosocial assessment and an agreed safety plan
A higher-risk score threshold before he is allowed to go home
Discharge if his risk is rated as low on the global scale
A repeat of the same scale after 24 hours of observation
6.w: NICE NG225 (2022): do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict suicide or repetition of self-harm or to decide who is discharged, and do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification. Develop a safety plan with, and agreed by, the person.

n.1: Adjusting a scale threshold still relies on a risk tool to make the decision.
n.2: Global low, medium or high stratification is specifically advised against.
n.3: Repeating the scale does not make it a valid basis for decisions.

6.q: Blood from a dislodged cannula has spilled onto the hard floor beside the bed of Thomas, 66. Spill granules are available. The nurse has put on non-sterile gloves and an apron. What should the nurse do next?
o: Cover with paper towels and apply 70% alcohol to the towels
Apply 1,000 ppm chlorine solution and mop the area straight away
Wipe it up with paper towels and clean the area with detergent
Apply chlorine-releasing granules and leave for the contact time
6.w: NIPCM appendix 9: for blood or high-risk body fluid spills apply chlorine-releasing granules (or towels soaked in 10,000 ppm available chlorine), follow the contact time (or 3 minutes), discard the waste as healthcare waste, then wash with detergent and dry.

n.0: Alcohol is not the NIPCM agent for blood spills.
n.1: 1,000 ppm is for urine, faeces or vomit spills; blood needs granules or 10,000 ppm, with contact time.
n.2: Detergent alone does not disinfect a blood spill, which may contain blood-borne viruses.

6.q: The Department of Health and Social Care opens a public consultation on changes to nurse education funding. Mariam, a staff nurse, has concerns about the effect on recruitment to her mental health service. What is the most appropriate way for her to influence the policy?
o: Post her views on social media, naming her employer and the vacancies
Respond to the consultation with evidence, directly or through her union
Ask her manager to raise it with the patients' families at visiting
Write to the NMC and ask it to block the proposed funding changes
6.w: P5.12 and P7.13 ask nurses to understand mechanisms for influencing public policy and to use political awareness. Responding to consultations with evidence, individually or through professional bodies and unions, is a legitimate and effective route, consistent with Code 20 (professionalism).

n.0: Naming her employer and service on social media risks breaching Code 20.10 and confidentiality, and is not a formal route of influence.
n.2: Involving visiting families is inappropriate and does not feed into the consultation.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not control government education funding.

6.q: On a surgical ward, Femi asks the ward manager about the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 because a new bariatric care pathway is being written. Which step do the regulations require the employer to take first?
o: Set a maximum weight that any member of staff may lift on the ward
Reduce the risk of injury to the lowest level by providing equipment
Avoid hazardous manual handling so far as is reasonably practicable
Assess the risk of injury from every manual handling task on the ward
6.w: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 set out a hierarchy for employers: avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable; assess the risk of injury from any hazardous operations that cannot be avoided; and reduce that risk to as low as reasonably practicable (HSE, Manual handling at work).

n.0: The HSE states that the law does not set specific weight limits; weight is one factor in the risk assessment.
n.1: Reducing risk is the third step, after avoidance and assessment.
n.3: Assessment is the second step and applies to hazardous handling that cannot be avoided, not to every task.

6.q: A community mental health nurse takes a call from Ms Rowe, 25, who is known to the team. She says she took 40 paracetamol tablets an hour ago after an argument, now regrets it and feels physically fine. What should the nurse advise?
o: Wait at home for a crisis team visit later this afternoon
Monitor herself at home, as she feels physically well
Book an urgent GP appointment for tomorrow morning
Go to the emergency department now, by ambulance if needed
6.w: Paracetamol overdose may cause no early symptoms while liver damage develops, and treatment depends on blood levels and timing. She needs emergency medical assessment now (NICE NG225 1.7.4; BNF/TOXBASE emergency treatment of poisoning), with psychosocial assessment alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting delays time-critical assessment and treatment for paracetamol poisoning.
n.1: Feeling well does not exclude serious paracetamol toxicity, which often has no early symptoms.
n.2: Waiting until tomorrow could miss the window for effective treatment.

6.q: At 02:00 Ryan, 22, arrives at a health-based place of safety under section 136. He is so heavily intoxicated that the doctor cannot assess him. Who can extend his detention and what is the latest time it could then end?
o: The doctor responsible for his examination, to 02:00 the day after next
The doctor responsible for his examination, to 14:00 the next day
The duty inspector, to 14:00 the next day
The AMHP, to 14:00 the next day
6.w: Section 136B allows the registered medical practitioner responsible for the examination to authorise up to 12 further hours if the person's condition makes assessment within 24 hours impracticable. 02:00 plus 24 hours plus 12 hours is 14:00 the next day.

n.0: A further 24 hours is not available; the maximum extension is 12 hours.
n.2: Police officers do not extend health-based place of safety detention; a superintendent's approval is needed only when assessment is at a police station.
n.3: The AMHP cannot authorise an extension; s136B gives the power to the examining doctor.

6.q: Eric, 58, has a PEG tube. His paracetamol oral suspension, baclofen liquid and a dispersible aspirin tablet are due at 12:00. His feed is running. How should the nurse give these medicines?
o: Give all three, then flush once with water at the end
Give each separately, flushing with water before, between and after
Add the three medicines into the feed bag to run with the feed
Mix all three in one enteral syringe and give them together
6.w: For enteral tubes, each medicine is given separately in a suitable liquid or dispersed form via an enteral syringe, with the tube flushed with water before, between and after each medicine to prevent interactions and blockage (AnnexB.11.9; RPS/RCN references the NEWT guidelines). The feed is paused while medicines are given.

n.0: Without flushing between medicines they may interact in the tube and block it.
n.2: Adding medicines to feed risks incompatibility and unpredictable dosing if the feed stops.
n.3: Mixing medicines can cause physical or chemical incompatibilities and tube blockage.

6.q: According to NICE CG32, which finding indicates that an adult is malnourished?
o: BMI under 18.5 kg/m²
BMI between 20 and 25 kg/m²
Unintentional weight loss of 3% in 6 months
Eating normally for the past 5 days
6.w: NICE CG32 defines malnutrition as BMI under 18.5 kg/m²; or unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3-6 months; or BMI under 20 kg/m² with unintentional weight loss over 5% in 3-6 months.

n.1: BMI 20-25 is within the healthy range.
n.2: 3% weight loss is below the CG32 thresholds.
n.3: Normal intake is not a malnutrition criterion.

6.q: Jamal, a first-year student nurse, is visibly upset after caring for a patient who died unexpectedly on his shift. Later that day his practice supervisor, Helen, has time to talk. What is the most helpful approach?
o: Invite him to talk through the event and reflect on his feelings and learning
Ask him to write a reflective account for his portfolio before his next shift
Reassure him that he will get used to deaths with more experience
Suggest he takes the rest of the week off and speaks to occupational health
6.w: Supervisors encourage colleagues and students to reflect on practice (AnnexA.4.1.4) and support their wellbeing. A supportive conversation that explores feelings and learning helps the student process the event, with further support offered if needed (P5.8 promote reflection).

n.1: Written reflection may help later, but setting a task first misses the need for supportive discussion now.
n.2: This dismisses his distress and does not support reflection.
n.3: Some students need time off or occupational health input, but the first step is to listen and explore with him.

6.q: Dolores, 88, is frail and drowsy after a stroke. She has a dry, coated tongue and cracked lips, takes nothing by mouth and has an unsafe swallow. Which oral care plan is most appropriate?
o: Daily chlorhexidine mouthwash rinses by mouth
Lemon and glycerine swabs every two hours
Gentle mouth care with a soft brush and lip balm
Mouth care whenever her relatives request it
6.w: People who are nil by mouth and drowsy need frequent oral assessment and gentle care with a soft toothbrush, moistening and lip care. Lemon and glycerine dry the mouth further and mouthwashes risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow (Annexe B 4.5; NICE NG31 advises frequent mouth and lip care).

n.0: Rinses she cannot spit out risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow.
n.1: Lemon and glycerine swabs dry the mucosa further and can damage teeth.
n.3: Oral care is a planned nursing intervention based on assessment, not on request.

6.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. Which is the most appropriate way to interpret this information?
o: As a possible sign of acute illness that needs assessment
As part of his learning disability needing no action
As evidence that he lacks capacity for all decisions
As a behavioural issue for the support team to manage
6.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability or dementia; rec 1.4.7 says assessment should include history from family or carers. A change from his baseline is significant.

n.1: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability (diagnostic overshadowing) risks missing illness.
n.2: Behaviour change does not establish incapacity; capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2-3).
n.3: Treating it as behaviour to manage ignores a possible physical cause.

6.q: George Hall, 80, has a NEWS2 score of 1. His nurse, Precious, feels uneasy: he is quieter than usual and has not eaten, though nothing specific is abnormal. She is unsure whether to act on this feeling. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase his observations and discuss her concern with the medical team
Ask the healthcare assistant to repeat the observations at the next round
Record her impression and continue observations at the planned frequency
Wait until his score reaches 5 so that escalation is clearly justified
6.w: NEWS2 supports, and does not replace, clinical judgement (RCP 2017; NICE NG253). For scores of 1-4 the registered nurse decides on monitoring frequency and escalation. Acting on clinical concern under uncertainty, by increasing monitoring and escalating, is safe practice (P6.11 accept and manage uncertainty; Code 13.3 ask for help).

n.1: Repeating routine observations later does not address her clinical concern now.
n.2: Recording a concern without acting on it leaves a possible deterioration unaddressed.
n.3: Waiting for a threshold ignores the nurse's assessment and may delay recognition of deterioration.

6.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
6.q: Kai, 24, has first-episode psychosis and has gained weight since starting an antipsychotic. He is worried about it and keen to change his lifestyle. What does NICE CG178 recommend his mental health provider offers?
o: Advice to stop the antipsychotic to reverse the weight gain
A repeat weight check at his annual review
A combined healthy eating and physical activity programme
Referral for bariatric surgery assessment
6.w: CG178 1.1.2.1: people with psychosis or schizophrenia, especially those taking antipsychotics, should be offered a combined healthy eating and physical activity programme by their mental healthcare provider.

n.0: Stopping without review risks relapse; any medication change is a shared decision with the prescriber.
n.1: Waiting a year allows further rapid weight gain.
n.3: Bariatric surgery is not a first response to early antipsychotic weight gain.

6.q: Thomas, 71, has advanced lung cancer and full capacity. The registrar decides that CPR would not be in his interests and plans to complete a DNACPR form. The registrar tells the nurse they will not mention it to Thomas because 'it might upset him'. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Remind the registrar that Thomas should be consulted unless it would cause him harm
Ask Thomas's wife to decide whether he should be told about the decision
Accept the plan, as DNACPR decisions are a medical matter that need no discussion
Record the DNACPR now and plan to tell Thomas at next week's ward round
6.w: R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals NHS FT [2014] EWCA Civ 822: Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions, and there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Lord Dyson MR (para 54) said doctors should be wary of being too ready to exclude patients from the process on the grounds that their involvement is likely to distress them; a belief that discussion would cause distress is unlikely to be enough unless the distress is likely to cause harm (para 56).

n.1: Thomas has capacity; his wife cannot decide what he is told about his own care.
n.2: R (Tracey) [2014] held there is a presumption the patient will be consulted, and warned against excluding patients because the discussion may distress them.
n.3: Delaying the conversation until after the decision is recorded still breaches the duty to consult him first.

7.q: A ward is running an improvement project to discharge more patients before midday. The team is already measuring the percentage of discharges before 12:00. Which additional measure would act as a balancing measure?
o: Number of patients discharged before 12:00 each day
Average time that discharge letters are completed
Number of take-home prescriptions ready the evening before
Readmission rate within 30 days of discharge
7.w: Balancing measures check whether improving one part of a system causes problems elsewhere. Rushing discharges could increase readmissions, so 30-day readmission is a balancing measure. The other options are outcome or process measures for the same aim (Model for Improvement measures: outcome, process, balancing; P6.4, P6.7). Two steps: classify each measure, then identify the one that detects unintended harm.

n.0: This is the outcome measure itself, restated as a count.
n.1: Discharge letter timing is a process measure that supports the aim, not a check for unintended harm.
n.2: Prescriptions ready in advance is a process measure on the route to earlier discharge.

7.q: Mr Simms, 64, has heart failure and is due for discharge. The team has drafted a plan for daily weights and fluid restriction. He says he does not own scales and finds it hard to remember fluid limits. What is the best next step?
o: Ask his neighbour to supervise his weights and fluid intake
Discharge with the plan as written, as it follows guidance
Revise the plan with him so it fits his life and resources
Tell him that he must follow the plan to avoid readmission
7.w: Code 3.3 asks nurses to act in partnership with people receiving care, and P3.4-P3.5 require shared planning and agreed goals. A plan he cannot follow will not work; adapting it (for example arranging scales and simple prompts) makes it achievable.

n.0: Involving a neighbour without his agreement is not partnership and may breach confidentiality.
n.1: Following guidance does not help if the plan is not achievable for him.
n.3: Instructing him without addressing the barriers he describes is not shared decision-making.

7.q: During the morning medication round, Lewis notices the sharps container on the drug trolley has reached the manufacturer's fill line. Several injections are still due. What should Lewis do with the full container?
o: Close and lock it, label it with origin and date, and replace it
Leave it open and start a second container beside it on the trolley
Press the contents down to make room for the remaining needles
Use it until it is completely full, then seal it before lunch
7.w: NIPCM ch 1.9: sharps containers must be disposed of when the manufacturer's fill line is reached, labelled with point of origin and dates of assembly and disposal, and use the temporary closure when not in use.

n.1: A full container left open is a sharps hazard; it should be locked and removed.
n.2: Pushing down sharps risks a needlestick injury and overfills the container.
n.3: Filling past the fill line risks protruding sharps and injury.

7.q: A ward manager wants to check whether patients' falls risk assessments are completed within 6 hours of admission, as the trust policy requires, by reviewing 50 sets of notes. How should this project be classified?
o: Research, which needs NHS research ethics committee review
Health surveillance, which tracks outbreaks and health threats
Service evaluation, which judges a service without a standard
Clinical audit, which measures practice against a set standard
7.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (October 2022): clinical audit answers 'Does this service reach a predetermined standard?', uses care already in use and does not require REC review.

n.0: It tests no hypothesis and seeks no generalisable knowledge; it compares practice with an existing standard.
n.1: Surveillance monitors threats to population health, not compliance with a ward policy.
n.2: Service evaluation does not measure against a predetermined standard; this project does.

7.q: Mrs Ball, 79, started sertraline three weeks ago. Her daughter reports she has become drowsy and muddled over two days. Her blood results show sodium 124 mmol/L (previously 139). What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Possible SSRI-induced hyponatraemia; inform the prescriber urgently
Expected sedation from sertraline; give the dose at night instead
Progression of dementia; continue the sertraline as prescribed
Worsening depression; ask for the sertraline dose to be increased
7.w: Hyponatraemia, usually in older people and possibly due to inappropriate ADH secretion, is associated with all antidepressants and more often with SSRIs. The BNF says to consider it in anyone who develops drowsiness, confusion or convulsions on an antidepressant.

n.1: Drowsiness with low sodium is a serious adverse effect, not expected sedation.
n.2: An acute change over two days with a falling sodium is not dementia progression.
n.3: Increasing the SSRI could worsen hyponatraemia.

7.q: Lily, 83, wears full upper and lower dentures. She asks what she should do with them at night while in hospital. What is the best advice?
o: Keep them in overnight so that her gums keep their shape
Soak them in boiling water overnight to sterilise them
Remove, clean and store them in a labelled pot overnight
Wrap them in a tissue on her bedside table overnight
7.w: Dentures should be removed and cleaned daily and generally left out overnight to rest the gums, stored in a labelled, named denture pot to prevent loss or damage (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wearing dentures overnight increases the risk of denture stomatitis and infection.
n.1: Boiling water can warp acrylic dentures.
n.3: Tissue-wrapped dentures are easily thrown away by mistake.

7.q: Kwesi, 28, has just been admitted under section 3. A student asks when section 117 after-care planning should begin. What is the most accurate answer?
o: As soon as he is admitted to hospital
On the day he is discharged from hospital
When the responsible clinician first grants section 17 leave
At his first tribunal hearing
7.w: COP15 33.10: although the duty to provide after-care begins when the patient leaves hospital, planning should start as soon as the patient is admitted, so services are identified in good time for discharge.

n.1: Planning on the day of discharge is too late; the Code says it should start on admission.
n.2: Leave is a later step; planning should already be under way from admission.
n.3: Tribunals expect after-care information, but planning should not wait for a hearing.

7.q: Beryl, 84, is admitted to an older people's ward after a fall at home. A colleague suggests completing a falls risk prediction score to decide whether she needs falls prevention. What does NICE NG249 (2025) recommend?
o: Offer an assessment if she falls again on the ward
Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and plan
Complete the prediction tool and act on a high score
Use the prediction tool weekly to monitor her risk
7.w: NICE NG249 (2025): do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Offer all hospital inpatients aged 65 and over (or 50-64 at higher risk) a comprehensive, multifactorial falls assessment and management plan.

n.0: She already qualifies for assessment as an inpatient aged 65 or over.
n.2: NG249 advises against using prediction tools to identify risk.
n.3: Repeating a prediction tool does not make it a valid basis for care.

7.q: In theatre, Callum, a newly registered scrub nurse, sees the surgeon pick up the scalpel before the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist time out has been done. The team seems not to have noticed. What should Callum do?
o: Complete an incident report after the operation so the omission is recorded
Note the omission and raise it at the team debrief at the end of the list
Quietly tell the anaesthetist so that the surgeon is not challenged openly
Say clearly that the time out has not been done and ask the team to pause
7.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 (preserve safety) require nurses to intervene. Checklists work only if anyone can stop the process; speaking up clearly and directly at the moment of risk is the safest action, whatever the speaker's seniority (P6.6; P5.2).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate later, but the immediate risk must be addressed before the incision.
n.1: Raising it afterwards allows the operation to proceed without the safety check that prevents wrong site and wrong patient surgery.
n.2: An indirect approach delays action and may not stop the procedure in time.

7.q: Two staff nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station about who should admit a new patient. Patients and visitors nearby are watching. Lorna is the nurse in charge. What should Lorna do first?
o: Admit the new patient herself so that the disagreement is no longer relevant
Calmly ask them both to step into the office and talk the issue through there
Tell both nurses firmly that they will each be reported to the ward manager
Leave them to resolve it between themselves, as they are both experienced nurses
7.w: A calm presence and moving the conflict to a private place protects patients' dignity and the team's professionalism and allows the issue to be resolved (AnnexA.4.2.3 calm presence when dealing with conflict; Code 20.1 and 20.3). The admission can then be allocated clearly.

n.0: Taking the task herself avoids the conflict without addressing it and adds to her workload.
n.2: Threatening sanctions in public escalates the conflict and does not resolve the allocation.
n.3: A public argument is affecting patients now; the nurse in charge needs to intervene.

7.q: Peter, 55, is an informal in-patient with depression. He has capacity and decides to stop his antidepressant, against advice. He is not asking to leave and shows no new risk. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the medication under section 63, as he is an in-patient
Respect his decision, explore his reasons and inform the team
