Use section 5(4) so the medication can be given
Give the medication covertly in his best interests
7.w: A capable informal patient can refuse treatment. Section 63 applies to detained patients, not informal ones. The nurse should explore reasons (for example side effects), give information, record the discussion and inform the team.

n.0: Section 63 applies to detained patients, not informal patients.
n.2: Section 5(4) is for preventing an informal patient leaving, not for imposing medication, and its criteria are not met.
n.3: Covert medication is never appropriate for a person with capacity; it may be considered only for people who lack capacity, under the MCA.

7.q: Owen, a staff nurse, realises he gave Ruth Price, 76, 10 mg of morphine instead of the prescribed 2.5 mg. She becomes drowsy with a respiratory rate of 9/min. The doctor has reviewed her and naloxone has been given. Which action best meets Owen's professional duty of candour?
o: Tell Mrs Price's daughter what happened and leave her to explain it to her mother
Ask the doctor to decide whether Mrs Price needs to be told about the overdose
Wait until the incident review is complete before telling Mrs Price what happened
Tell Mrs Price promptly what happened, apologise, and explain what is being done
7.w: Code 14.1-14.3 and the NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (2024): when something goes wrong, tell the person (or their advocate) promptly, apologise, explain what happened and the likely effects, put matters right where possible, and record and report the incident (P1.3).

n.0: Mrs Price is the person affected; information goes to her unless she lacks capacity or asks for it to be shared.
n.1: The professional duty of candour belongs to each registrant; Owen cannot pass the decision to another clinician.
n.2: Candour is prompt; waiting for a review delays information the person is entitled to now.

7.q: Ms Grey, 45, has twice taken overdoses of her prescribed antidepressant. She is now well engaged with her community nurse, and her GP plans to continue sertraline. Which prescribing approach best reflects NICE NG225?
o: Prescribe three months' supply to reduce visits to the surgery
Ask her partner to hold the tablets without discussing it with her
Agree smaller, weekly supplies with her through shared decisions
Switch her to a tricyclic antidepressant to improve her mood
7.w: NG225 1.13.1-1.13.2: consider toxicity in overdose (tricyclics are more dangerous) and use shared decision-making to discuss limiting the quantity supplied, for example weekly prescriptions, and returning unwanted medicines.

n.0: A large supply increases access to a means of overdose.
n.1: Changes should be agreed through shared decision-making, not arranged behind her back.
n.3: Tricyclic antidepressants are more toxic in overdose, which NG225 asks prescribers to take into account.

7.q: Priti, a registered nurse, delegates a simple wound dressing to Dean, a registered nursing associate who is competent in this task. Dean applies the wrong dressing type. Who is accountable for what?
o: Priti for the decision to delegate; Dean for how he carried out the dressing
Priti is accountable for the dressing, as Dean was working under her direction
The ward manager is accountable, as the allocation of staff was set by her each shift
Dean is accountable for all aspects, as he is a registered professional in his own right
7.w: The Code (standard 11) makes the registrant accountable for decisions to delegate and for confirming outcomes. Nursing associates are NMC registrants bound by the Code, so Dean is accountable for his own practice in carrying out the task (P5.4; FACTS S-CODE).

n.1: Dean is a registrant accountable for his own actions in carrying out the dressing; Priti's accountability is for the decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome.
n.2: The manager is accountable for her own decisions, but this does not remove Priti's or Dean's accountability.
n.3: Priti remains accountable for her decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome (Code 11.3).

7.q: Harold, 76, has COPD with a prescribed target of 88-92%. He is on 28% oxygen via a Venturi mask with SpO2 95%. He is alert and comfortable. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remove the mask and recheck his saturation in 4 hours
Reduce the oxygen concentration and recheck his saturation
Continue the current oxygen, as 95% is a reassuring level
Increase the oxygen to 35% to prevent a fall in saturation
7.w: BTS guideline: titrate oxygen to keep saturation within the prescribed target. Above 92% in someone at risk of hypercapnia risks CO2 retention, so step down (for example to 24%) and monitor closely. On Scale 2, 95% on oxygen also scores 2 points (RCP 2017).

n.0: Stopping oxygen abruptly without close monitoring risks rebound hypoxaemia.
n.2: 95% is above his prescribed range and risks hypercapnia.
n.3: Increasing oxygen pushes his saturation further above target.

7.q: A practice nurse is reviewing which patients might be contacted for lung cancer screening, available in some parts of England. Which person meets the age and smoking criteria?
o: Susan, 50, who currently smokes 15 cigarettes a day
Thomas, 78, who stopped smoking 30 years ago
Raj, 60, who smoked for 20 years and stopped 10 years ago
Ann, 65, a lifelong non-smoker who lives with a smoker
7.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked may be contacted by their GP or a local NHS service to take part in lung cancer screening.

n.0: Lung cancer screening is for people aged 55 to 74; Susan is under 55.
n.1: Thomas is over 74, above the age range for lung cancer screening.
n.3: Screening is for people who have ever smoked; Ann has never smoked.

7.q: A ward nurse is checking which patients qualify for an independent mental health advocate (IMHA). Which patient is a qualifying patient?
o: Sam, held under section 136 at a place of safety
Ash, held under section 4 before a second recommendation
Bo, held by a nurse under section 5(4)
Lee, detained under section 2 on an acute ward
7.w: Under sections 130A-130C qualifying patients include those liable to be detained under the Act (including section 2 and section 3), CTO and guardianship patients. Short-term powers (s4 before conversion, s5(2), s5(4), s135, s136) are excluded.

n.0: People held under section 136 are excluded from IMHA eligibility.
n.1: Section 4 patients qualify once the second recommendation converts the section; before that they are excluded.
n.2: Patients held under the section 5 holding powers are excluded.

7.q: An approved mental health professional last saw Priya, 41, in person 16 days ago. Two doctors have now recommended section 3. The AMHP asks the community nurse whether the application can be completed today without visiting Priya again. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Yes, because the 28-day limit for personal contact has not passed
Yes, because the doctors' examinations were within the last 5 days
No, because the AMHP must have seen her personally within 14 days
No, because a fresh nearest relative consultation is due every 7 days
7.w: Section 11(5) requires the applicant to have personally seen the patient within the 14 days ending with the date of the application. Sixteen days have passed, so the AMHP must see Priya again before applying, whatever the dates of the medical examinations.

n.0: There is no 28-day personal-contact window; 28 days is the maximum length of section 2 detention.
n.1: Recent medical examinations do not satisfy the separate requirement that the applicant has seen the patient within 14 days (s11(5)).
n.3: There is no 7-day rule on nearest relative consultation; the issue here is the 14-day personal-contact rule for the applicant.

7.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
7.q: Mrs Iqbal, 81, is on an older adult ward. A nurse is asked which change might indicate hypoactive delirium, which is often missed. Which is the best answer?
o: Pacing, shouting and pulling at her cannula
Low mood and early waking for several months
Withdrawal, slowed responses and reduced appetite
Memory loss that has worsened slowly over 2 years
7.w: CG103 1.3.2: be particularly vigilant for hypoactive delirium, often missed: withdrawal, slow responses, reduced mobility and movement, worsened concentration and reduced appetite.

n.0: These are features of hyperactive delirium.
n.1: Months of low mood and early waking suggest depression.
n.3: Slow decline over years suggests dementia.

7.q: Mr Moore, 83, has delirium. He is shouting, pulling at his cannula and swinging his arms at staff. No one has been hurt yet. What should the nurse do first?
o: Request haloperidol as the first step to calm him down quickly
Restrain his arms so the cannula is not pulled out
Ask security to stay with him until he settles down
Use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and look for causes
7.w: NICE CG103: if a person with delirium is distressed or a risk to themselves or others, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation; consider short-term haloperidol if de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate. Underlying causes such as pain, retention or hypoxia should be sought (Annexe B 1.1.5).

n.0: Medication is considered when de-escalation fails or is inappropriate, not as the first step.
n.1: Physical restraint is a last resort and may worsen agitation and delirium.
n.2: Security presence is restrictive and does not address his distress or its cause.

7.q: Stanley, 83, has a nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. The tube was confirmed in the stomach by X-ray yesterday and is secured at 60 cm at the nostril. He needs medicines, flushes and feeds today. Under NICE CG32, when must the tube position be confirmed?
o: Before the first feed of each day
When the person reports discomfort
After placement and before each use
After placement and then once a day
7.w: NICE CG32 rec 1.7.17: confirm the position of all nasogastric tubes after placement and before each use (each feed, flush or medicine) by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary.

n.0: A single check at the start misses later displacement from coughing, vomiting or movement.
n.1: Displacement may cause no symptoms, so checks cannot wait for discomfort.
n.3: Daily checks miss displacement between uses.

7.q: Clive, 76, has moved from hospital to a nursing home. The nurse is asked to transcribe his discharge medicines onto the home's MAR chart. The insulin entry on the discharge letter reads '10U' with a smudged figure in front of it. What should the nurse do?
o: Transcribe it as 100 units, reading the smudge as a zero
Transcribe it as 10 units, as that is the most legible figure
Contact the prescriber to clarify the dose before transcribing it
Leave the insulin off the MAR until his next GP review
7.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 31: medicines are not transcribed where details are illegible, unclear, ambiguous or incomplete, with particular care for high-risk medicines such as insulin. The abbreviation 'U' is itself a recognised cause of insulin overdose. Clarification is sought without delay.

n.0: Reading 'U' or a smudge as a zero is the classic tenfold insulin error.
n.1: Guessing at an illegible insulin dose risks a serious error.
n.3: Omitting insulin until a routine review risks hyperglycaemia; prompt clarification is needed.

7.q: Single rooms are full on a respiratory ward. Two patients with the same confirmed respiratory virus are to be cohorted in a bay. Under current NIPCM guidance, what is the minimum separation between their beds?
o: At least 0.5 metres between the bed spaces
At least 3 metres between the bed spaces
At least 2 metres between the bed spaces
At least 1 metre between the bed spaces
7.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 states cohorted infectious patients should be separated by at least 3 feet (1 metre) with the door closed. Droplet precautions use at least 1 metre; the 2 metres introduced during COVID-19 has reverted to 1 metre in all areas.

n.0: Half a metre is below the 1 metre minimum for separation in a cohort.
n.1: 3 metres exceeds the NIPCM standard; the distance given is 3 feet, which is about 1 metre.
n.2: 2 metres was a COVID-19 measure that NIPCM says has returned to 1 metre.

7.q: Ernest, 81, has Parkinson's disease with a tremor and struggles to get food to his mouth. He is eating less than half his meals. Which intervention should be tried first to help him eat?
o: Provide adapted cutlery, a plate guard and help
Give his meals later, when the ward is quieter
Refer him for insertion of a nasogastric feeding tube
Prescribe oral nutritional supplements three times a day
7.w: Annexe B 5.3: assist with eating and drinking and use feeding and drinking aids. Adapted cutlery, plate guards and non-slip mats, plus assistance (for example via a red tray system or protected mealtimes), address the cause of his poor intake.

n.1: Delaying meals does not address his difficulty and may mean food is cold.
n.2: Enteral feeding is not indicated when oral intake can be improved with help.
n.3: Supplements may follow, but his barrier is a physical one that aids can address first.

7.q: In a GP surgery waiting room, the practice nurse notices Colin, 56, coughing repeatedly into his hands. He has a fever and says he has no tissues. Other patients are seated close by. Which action best applies respiratory and cough hygiene?
o: Give tissues, a bin and a facemask, and seat him at least 1 metre from others
Ask him to cough into his hands and seat him at least 2 metres from others
Give him an FFP3 respirator to wear until he is called in for his appointment
Ask him to wait outside the building in his car until the nurse is ready to see him
7.w: NIPCM ch 1.3 and ch 2: cover the nose and mouth with a disposable tissue, dispose of it promptly and clean hands; outpatients with respiratory symptoms should be asked to wear a facemask if tolerated and be separated from others by at least 1 metre. Prioritising his appointment also helps.

n.1: Coughing into hands contaminates them; the crook of the arm is the fallback, and the NIPCM distance is 1 metre, not the pandemic-era 2 metres.
n.2: NIPCM states an FFP3 respirator must not be worn by an infectious patient, as it filters incoming rather than expelled air.
n.3: Sending a febrile patient to wait outside delays assessment and is not a standard respiratory hygiene measure.

7.q: A patient's family sends Hannah a thank-you card that names their mother and praises Hannah's care during her last days. Hannah wants to use it as practice-related feedback for revalidation. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Place a copy of the card in her revalidation portfolio
Ask her line manager to countersign the card before use
Note the content of the feedback without identifying details
Exclude it, as feedback must be formal and in writing
7.w: NMC revalidation: five pieces of practice-related feedback from any source, written or verbal, formal or informal. Keep a note of the content and how it improved practice, without recording anything that could identify another person.

n.0: The card names the patient; NMC guidance says not to record information that may identify another person.
n.1: Feedback does not need countersigning; the key requirement is to remove identifying information.
n.3: Feedback can be written or verbal, formal or informal, from patients, families or colleagues.

7.q: On a dementia ward, Mr Payne, 81, lacks capacity and needed to be briefly held by two trained staff to stop him hitting another patient. He is now calm. Besides checking him for injury, what should the nurse record about the incident?
o: The details in the incident system, rather than his care record
A brief note that restraint was needed, to avoid labelling him
The reasons for the hold, technique used, duration and his response
That he was held in his best interests, with the names of staff
7.w: Code 10.1-10.4 requires accurate, timely records that attribute, date and time entries. Any restraint must be justified as necessary and proportionate (MCA s6), so the record should show why it was used, how, for how long and its effect, supporting review and learning.

n.0: Incident reporting is appropriate, but the care record must also document what happened to him.
n.1: A minimal note fails Code 10 and prevents review of whether the restraint was justified.
n.3: Stating 'best interests' without reasons, technique and duration does not show the hold was necessary and proportionate.

7.q: A ward pharmacist explains to nursing staff how NICE judges whether a new medicine is cost-effective in its technology appraisals. Since April 2026, what is NICE's standard cost-effectiveness threshold?
o: £100,000 to £300,000 per QALY gained
£20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained
£30,000 to £50,000 per QALY gained
£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained
7.w: Following a government decision, NICE's standard threshold in technology appraisals rose from £20,000-£30,000 to £25,000-£35,000 per QALY gained from April 2026 (NICE, Changes to NICE's cost-effectiveness thresholds; P7.4 implications of current health policy).

n.0: This higher range applies to highly specialised technologies for ultra-rare diseases, not the standard threshold.
n.1: This was the threshold before April 2026.
n.2: This is not a NICE threshold range.

7.q: Ella, 14, is in school Year 9. The school nurse assesses her as Gillick competent, and Ella consents to her MenACWY vaccine. Her mother has returned a form refusing the vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the vaccine, as a parent cannot override a Gillick competent child's consent
Delay the vaccine until Ella is 16 and can legally consent for herself
Ask the head teacher to decide whether the vaccine should be given
Withhold the vaccine, because a parent's refusal takes priority under age 16
7.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): children under 16 who understand fully what is involved (Gillick competent) can give consent, ideally with parental involvement; where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent. UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: MenACWY at 14 years (school Year 9).

n.1: Gillick competent children under 16 can consent, so waiting is unnecessary.
n.2: The head teacher has no role in consent to Ella's treatment.
n.3: The Green Book states that where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent.

7.q: Mr Craig, 50, developed a tremor and stiffness after his first-generation depot antipsychotic was increased. The team decides to stop the depot. He asks whether the side effects will go away as soon as it is stopped. What should the nurse explain?
o: Side effects will be reversed at once by an antimuscarinic
Side effects may continue until the drug clears from the site
Side effects will stop within a few hours of the decision
Side effects can be ended by injecting a different depot
7.w: The BNF notes that with depot antipsychotics, side effects may persist until the drug has been cleared from its depot site, which can take weeks. This is one reason doses and changes are made carefully.

n.0: An antimuscarinic may ease parkinsonism but does not reverse the effects immediately or remove the drug.
n.2: A long-acting depot keeps releasing drug for weeks, so effects do not stop within hours.
n.3: Another depot adds more antipsychotic exposure and would not end the current effects.

7.q: A nurse on a postnatal ward is explaining immunity to a new mother. She says her baby is born with some protection against measles because of antibodies the mother made. Which type of immunity is this?
o: Population immunity from high vaccine coverage in the community
Active immunity produced by the baby's own immune system
Innate immunity from the baby's skin and mucous membranes
Passive immunity from antibodies that crossed the placenta
7.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): passive immunity is protection from antibodies transferred from immune individuals, most commonly across the placenta; it is temporary, commonly lasting a few weeks or months, and is more effective against some infections (for example tetanus and measles) than others.

n.0: Population immunity reduces exposure; it is not antibody protection inside the baby.
n.1: The baby did not make these antibodies; they were transferred from the mother, which is passive immunity.
n.2: Innate immunity is non-specific; measles-specific antibodies from the mother are passive acquired immunity.

7.q: Mrs Lewis, 61, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 10 years and is admitted with a manic relapse. She says she has 'mostly' taken her tablets. What should happen first regarding her lithium?
o: Switch her to valproate as a more reliable mood stabiliser
Check her plasma lithium level to optimise treatment
Stop the lithium because it has failed to prevent relapse
Add an antidepressant to prevent a later depressive episode
7.w: CG185 1.5.8: if the person is already taking lithium, check plasma lithium levels to optimise treatment. Partial adherence is common and the level guides whether dose or adherence is the issue.

n.0: Valproate is not a first choice here and the level has not yet been checked.
n.2: One relapse does not mean lithium has failed; the level and adherence need checking first.
n.3: Adding an antidepressant during mania risks worsening the episode.

7.q: After one patient used a phone charger cable to self-harm, a ward manager proposes removing all mobile phones and chargers from every patient on the acute ward indefinitely. What does the Mental Health Act Code of Practice advise?
o: Apply the ban to detained patients and exempt informal patients
Apply the ban to every patient, as ward safety must come first
Apply the ban until the next CQC inspection has approved it
Avoid a blanket ban; restrict on individual risk and record it
7.w: COP15 8.5-8.7 and 8.19-8.20: blanket restrictions (including banning mobile phones and chargers) should be avoided unless justified as necessary and proportionate to individually identified risks; their impact on each patient should be documented. A blanket phone ban may breach Article 8.

n.0: Restricting by legal status is still a blanket restriction without individual risk assessment.
n.1: Safety concerns must be met by individualised, proportionate measures; a blanket ban may breach Article 8.
n.2: The CQC does not approve restrictions; they must be justified individually and authorised by hospital managers (COP15 8.9).

7.q: A registered nurse is reviewing four recent deaths on a care of older people ward. All were verified, and none involved suspicious circumstances. Which death should be referred to the coroner?
o: Bill, 74, who died an expected death in a hospice from motor neurone disease
Harold, 79, who died an expected death from confirmed COVID-19
Edith, 88, who died five days after a hip fracture from a fall at home
Joan, 91, who died an expected death from heart failure under her GP
7.w: RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024), Appendix 1 (Ministry of Justice): refer to the coroner where the death may have been caused by violence, trauma or physical injury, whether intentional or otherwise, among other criteria. A notifiable disease such as COVID-19 is not a reason to refer.

n.0: An expected death from a diagnosed progressive illness is not, on these facts, reportable to the coroner.
n.1: A notifiable infectious disease such as COVID-19 is not, by itself, a reason to refer a death to the coroner.
n.3: An expected death from a known natural cause with an attending practitioner does not need coroner referral.

7.q: George, 71, has known COPD with previous hypercapnic respiratory failure. He arrives breathless with SpO2 84% on air. Blood gas results are awaited. What target saturation range is appropriate?
7.w: BTS guideline: for people with known COPD or other risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure, aim for 88-92% pending blood gas results; NEWS2 Scale 2 is then used if this target is prescribed (RCP 2017).

n.0: 85-88% leaves him below the recommended lower limit of 88%.
n.1: 92-95% overshoots the 88-92% target for people at risk of hypercapnia.
n.2: 94-98% risks worsening hypercapnia in someone with previous hypercapnic failure.

7.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
7.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

7.q: Before deciding to use section 136, an officer telephones the mental health crisis line and speaks to a registered nurse about Ayo, 37, who is sitting on a railway platform edge. Why does the Act require this contact?
o: The officer must consult a health professional first if practicable
The nurse then becomes responsible for arranging Ayo's transport
The nurse must authorise the detention before it becomes lawful
The call to the nurse starts the 24-hour permitted detention period
7.w: Section 136(1C) requires the constable, if practicable, to consult a registered medical practitioner, registered nurse, approved mental health professional or other prescribed person before removing or keeping someone at a place of safety. The decision remains the officer's.

n.1: Consultation does not transfer conveyance responsibility to the nurse.
n.2: The nurse advises; the decision to use section 136 remains with the constable.
n.3: The 24 hours begin on arrival at the place of safety (or the decision to keep the person there), not with the phone call.

7.q: Martha, 58, reads the leaflet for a newly prescribed medicine and finds it describes a different condition from hers. The pharmacist confirms the medicine is licensed in the UK but has been prescribed outside the terms of its licence. Martha asks the nurse whether this is allowed. Which reply is accurate?
o: It is a dispensing error, as the leaflet does not match her condition
It is off-label use, and the prescriber should explain it to her
It is allowed once a second doctor countersigns the prescription
It is unlicensed use, so it cannot legally be given on the ward
7.w: Off-label use means prescribing a licensed medicine outside its marketing authorisation (P4.16). It is lawful, but the prescriber takes on greater responsibility and should give the person enough information to make an informed choice. The nurse should check Martha's understanding and refer questions to the prescriber.

n.0: The pharmacist has confirmed the supply is correct; a mismatched leaflet is expected with off-label use.
n.2: Off-label prescribing does not require a second doctor's countersignature.
n.3: An unlicensed medicine has no UK licence at all; this medicine is licensed but used off-label, which is lawful.

7.q: Ollie, 15, is diagnosed with anorexia nervosa and lives with both parents, who are keen to help. Which treatment does NICE NG69 suggest considering first?
o: A group psychoeducation programme
Individual eating-disorder-focused CBT
An SSRI alongside regular dietetic advice
Anorexia-focused family therapy (FT-AN)
7.w: NG69 1.3.10: consider FT-AN for children and young people with anorexia nervosa. Individual CBT-ED or adolescent-focused psychotherapy are alternatives if FT-AN is unacceptable or ineffective.

n.0: Group psychoeducation is not a recommended treatment for anorexia in young people.
n.1: CBT-ED is an alternative for young people when FT-AN is not suitable.
n.2: NG69 1.3.24: do not offer medication as the sole treatment for anorexia nervosa.

7.q: A doctor is writing a rapid tranquillisation prescription for Ms Pike, 29, on an acute ward. The nurse checks that it follows NICE NG10 and BNF advice. Which prescription is correct?
o: Up to four doses in 24 hours, given at the nurse's discretion
A single dose, not repeated until its effect has been reviewed
A combined 'oral or IM' entry so either route can be used
A regular four-hourly IM dose for the next 48 hours
7.w: NG10 1.4.44: write the initial rapid tranquillisation prescription as a single dose and do not repeat it until the effect of the initial dose has been reviewed. The BNF adds that oral and IM doses should be prescribed separately.

n.0: Open-ended repeat doses risk cumulative over-sedation before the first dose's effect is reviewed.
n.2: The BNF says oral and IM drugs should be prescribed separately.
n.3: Regular IM doses are not rapid tranquillisation and risk high-dose prescribing.

7.q: Ms Hill, 19, is on a general medical ward after self-harm, and the mental health and ward teams agree she needs close observation tonight. The ward is short-staffed, and the nurse in charge suggests asking the hospital security officer to sit with her. What should the nurse do?
o: Agree, as the security officer is available and nearby
Ask her mother to stay overnight and observe her
Request a member of staff trained in clinical observation
Ask a first-year student nurse to observe her instead
7.w: NICE NG225 1.12.2: do not use staff who are untrained in clinical observation, such as security staff or trainees, to observe a person who has self-harmed. Observation should be by appropriately skilled and trained staff, engaging with the person (1.7.23, 1.14.4).

n.0: NG225 names security staff as unsuitable to undertake clinical observation.
n.1: Family may support her, but responsibility for clinical observation stays with trained staff.
n.3: Trainee staff are also named as unsuitable to undertake these observations.

7.q: Bernadette, 68, detained under section 3, has severe depression. She has capacity and clearly refuses electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). She is eating and drinking and is not in danger. The team believe ECT would help. What is the legal position?
o: ECT cannot be given while she has capacity and refuses
ECT can be given if her nearest relative agrees
ECT can be given under section 63 because she is detained
ECT can be given if a SOAD certifies it as appropriate
7.w: Section 58A provides that ECT cannot be given to a capable adult who refuses. The only exception is urgent treatment under section 62 to save life or prevent serious deterioration, which does not apply on these facts.

n.1: The nearest relative has no power to consent to ECT on her behalf.
n.2: ECT is governed by section 58A, so section 63 cannot authorise it.
n.3: A SOAD can certify ECT for a patient who lacks capacity, not override a capable adult's refusal.

7.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
7.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

7.q: Two nurses are at the bedside to start a red cell transfusion for Edith, 73, who is alert and orientated. Which method of patient identification meets the BSH standard for positive patient identification?
o: Ask 'Are you Edith Morris?' and then check her wristband details
Ask her to state her name and date of birth, then match wristband and unit
Check her wristband against the unit label and the bed-end name card
Confirm her identity with her daughter, then check the unit label
7.w: BSH guideline on administration of blood components (2017): positive patient identification at every stage, asking the patient to state full name and date of birth where able, and checking these against the identification band and the component label, using a structured bedside checklist (SHOT recommendation).

n.0: A closed question invites a confused or hard-of-hearing person to agree to the wrong name.
n.2: Bed-end cards are unreliable, and Edith can state her own details.
n.3: Relatives may be used when a patient cannot respond; Edith is alert and should identify herself.

7.q: During a teaching session, a practice educator lists four sources a nurse might rely on when explaining informed consent: the Mental Capacity Act 2005, the Care Act 2014, the NMC Code and Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]. A student asks which of these is case law made by the courts. Which source should the educator identify?
o: The Mental Capacity Act 2005
The NMC Code, professional standards of practice
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]
The Care Act 2014
7.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 is a Supreme Court judgment, so it is common (case) law. The two Acts are statutes made by Parliament and the Code is a set of professional standards set by the regulator.

n.0: The MCA 2005 is primary legislation (statute) passed by Parliament, not case law.
n.1: The Code is the NMC's professional standards; it is a regulatory document, not a court decision.
n.3: The Care Act 2014 is statute; its safeguarding duties come from Parliament, not a court judgment.

7.q: Maureen, 66, started ramipril for hypertension 6 weeks ago. She tells the community nurse she has had a persistent tickly dry cough since, with no fever or breathlessness. Her chest is clear. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain dry cough is a known ramipril effect and arrange a review
Advise buying a cough suppressant from the pharmacy and continue
Explain the cough is likely viral and should settle in 2 weeks
Advise her to stop the ramipril straight away and see her GP
7.w: A persistent dry cough is a recognised adverse effect of ACE inhibitors such as ramipril (P4.5, supporting people with their medication). The prescriber should review, as an alternative such as an angiotensin II receptor blocker may be considered. Stopping without review leaves blood pressure untreated.

n.1: A cough suppressant masks a drug-induced cause without a medication review.
n.2: The timing and features point to an ACE inhibitor effect, not a viral illness.
n.3: Stopping an antihypertensive without review risks uncontrolled blood pressure.

7.q: A nurse has completed a detailed physical assessment of Mr Rees, 75, who is admitted after a fall at home. She has recorded his observations, skin, mobility and continence. Which further area is most needed to make the assessment holistic before discharge planning?
o: A second set of skin checks by another registered nurse
His social circumstances, support at home and his own priorities
A full list of every past hospital admission he has had
A full repeat of his observations before the end of the day shift
7.w: Holistic assessment (P3.1, P3.4) combines physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs and the person's own goals. After a fall at home, his living situation, support and priorities are central to safe planning, and NICE NG249 includes a home hazard assessment.

n.0: A second skin check adds to the physical assessment already completed.
n.2: An exhaustive admission history adds little compared with his current social and support needs.
n.3: Repeat observations are part of physical monitoring, not the missing holistic domain.

7.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
7.q: Kara, 26, who is in DBT, tells the nurse: 'No one understands how much this hurts.' Which response best reflects DBT validation?
o: 'You need to calm down before we can talk.'
'Lots of people have it much worse than you do.'
'After all you have been through, that makes sense.'
'I know exactly how you feel, I have been there.'
7.w: Validation communicates that the person's emotions are understandable in context. It reduces emotional arousal and is a core DBT and CG78 approach (empathic, validating statements in crisis).

n.0: Demanding calm first is invalidating and may escalate her.
n.1: Comparison invalidates her experience and may increase distress.
n.3: Claiming to know exactly how she feels is presumptuous and shifts focus to the nurse.

7.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
7.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

7.q: A ward manager in an English hospital is updating staff training on people who lack capacity and whose care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. A nurse asks which legal scheme is currently in force to authorise such arrangements in hospitals and care homes. What should the manager say?
o: The nurse's holding power under the Mental Health Act 1983
The Liberty Protection Safeguards under the 2019 Amendment Act
The community treatment order scheme under the Mental Health Act
The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards under the MCA 2005
7.w: DoLS (MCA 2005 Schedules A1 and 1A) remain the scheme in force in England and Wales for hospitals and care homes. The Liberty Protection Safeguards in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 have not been implemented.

n.0: The nurse's holding power under MHA s5(4) briefly detains an informal inpatient with mental disorder; it does not authorise care arrangements under the MCA.
n.1: The LPS have not been brought into force; DoLS remain the live scheme.
n.2: Community treatment orders apply to certain detained patients leaving hospital, not to people lacking capacity in hospitals or care homes.

7.q: Charlie, a mental health nurse in England, asks in October 2026 whether the Mental Health Act 2025 has replaced the 1983 Act for detentions on his ward. Which statement is correct?
o: The 2025 Act received Royal Assent, but most provisions are not yet in force
The 2025 Act applies to new detentions; the 1983 Act applies to existing ones
The 2025 Act is still a Bill and has not yet completed its parliamentary stages
The 2025 Act is fully in force and has replaced the 1983 Act in England
7.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions (including changes to sections 3 and 4) were not in force at October 2026. The Mental Health Act 1983 as amended remains the current law for detention (BUILD-PLAN unsettled law note; P7.4 implications of current and future health policy).

n.1: There is no rule of this kind; detentions continue under the 1983 Act as amended until provisions are commenced.
n.2: The Act completed its passage and received Royal Assent in December 2025.
n.3: Most provisions of the 2025 Act await commencement, so the 1983 Act as amended still applies.

7.q: Ms Douglas, 55, has capacity. Last year she made a valid advance decision refusing antibiotics for pneumonia. Today she tells the nurse she has changed her mind and would want antibiotics if she became unwell. She does not want to put this in writing. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep following the advance decision until it is replaced
Ask her to sign a written withdrawal before it can apply
Accept the withdrawal and document it in her records
Ask two witnesses to confirm her change of mind
7.w: MCA 2005 s24(3)-(4): a person may withdraw an advance decision at any time when they have capacity, and a withdrawal need not be in writing. The nurse should record it clearly and tell the team.

n.0: Her withdrawal takes effect now; the old decision does not continue until replaced.
n.1: Withdrawal does not need to be in writing, so a signature is not required.
n.3: There is no witness requirement for withdrawing an advance decision.

7.q: A district nursing team wants to find out how patients rate their new evening visiting service, with no benchmark to compare against, by asking current patients to complete a short questionnaire. What type of project is this?
o: Qualitative research study
Clinical audit
Randomised controlled trial
Service evaluation
7.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): service evaluation asks 'What standard does this service achieve?', measures the current service without reference to a standard and does not need REC review.

n.0: It aims to judge the current service, not to generate generalisable knowledge.
n.1: Audit compares practice with a predetermined standard; here there is no standard.
n.2: There is no allocation to interventions or randomisation.

7.q: Nina, 33, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name and her pain score is 9 while she is using her phone. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
o: Accept her report of pain and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Delay analgesia until her behaviour matches her pain score
Offer paracetamol until the doctor has assessed her pain
Ask her to stop using her phone before reassessing her pain
7.w: Pain is what the person says it is; self-report is the most reliable measure. People with long-term painful conditions often know which analgesia works and may cope with distraction. Prompt analgesia is essential, and judgement based on stereotypes breaches Code 20.2 and 1.1.

n.1: Behaviour is a poor guide to pain in people with recurrent pain, and delay causes harm.
n.2: Withholding effective prescribed analgesia leaves severe pain undertreated.
n.3: Distraction is a coping strategy and does not invalidate her pain score.

7.q: A student nurse asks Eleni to explain the difference between the two duties of candour that apply in English hospitals. Which statement is correct?
o: The statutory duty applies to doctors; the professional duty applies to nurses
The statutory duty applies to individual nurses; the professional duty applies to NHS trusts
Both duties apply to individual nurses and are enforced by the CQC
Statutory duty binds registered providers; professional duty binds individual registrants
7.w: Regulation 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 places the statutory duty on registered providers (regulated by CQC). The professional duty (Code 14, NMC/GMC guidance refreshed December 2024) applies to individual registrants.

n.0: The professional duty applies to all regulated professionals including doctors; the statutory duty binds organisations.
n.1: This reverses the two duties; reg 20 binds registered providers and the Code binds individual registrants.
n.2: The CQC regulates the statutory duty on providers; the NMC oversees the professional duty on nurses.

7.q: Ms Barr, 58, takes valproate for bipolar disorder. Her psychiatrist plans to add lamotrigine for persistent depressive symptoms. Which interaction should the nurse be aware of when the lamotrigine is started?
o: Valproate lowers lamotrigine levels, so higher doses are used
Lamotrigine raises valproate levels, so valproate is halved
Lamotrigine levels must be measured weekly during titration
Valproate raises lamotrigine levels, so titration is slower
7.w: CG185 1.10.36: when starting lamotrigine be aware of its interaction with valproate and follow the SPC/BNF titration, which is slower because valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism and raises its levels (and rash risk). Lamotrigine levels are not measured routinely (1.10.38).

n.0: Valproate increases, not lowers, lamotrigine levels.
n.1: The clinically important effect is valproate raising lamotrigine levels, not the reverse.
n.2: CG185 says not to measure lamotrigine levels routinely.

7.q: Noah, 23, is seen after self-harm. A colleague suggests using a risk scale to decide whether he can be discharged. Under NICE NG225, what should happen instead?
o: A person-centred psychosocial assessment and an agreed safety plan
A higher-risk score threshold before he is allowed to go home
Discharge if his risk is rated as low on the global scale
A repeat of the same scale after 24 hours of observation
7.w: NICE NG225 (2022): do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict suicide or repetition of self-harm or to decide who is discharged, and do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification. Develop a safety plan with, and agreed by, the person.

n.1: Adjusting a scale threshold still relies on a risk tool to make the decision.
n.2: Global low, medium or high stratification is specifically advised against.
n.3: Repeating the scale does not make it a valid basis for decisions.

7.q: Jamal, a first-year student nurse, is visibly upset after caring for a patient who died unexpectedly on his shift. Later that day his practice supervisor, Helen, has time to talk. What is the most helpful approach?
o: Invite him to talk through the event and reflect on his feelings and learning
Ask him to write a reflective account for his portfolio before his next shift
Reassure him that he will get used to deaths with more experience
Suggest he takes the rest of the week off and speaks to occupational health
7.w: Supervisors encourage colleagues and students to reflect on practice (AnnexA.4.1.4) and support their wellbeing. A supportive conversation that explores feelings and learning helps the student process the event, with further support offered if needed (P5.8 promote reflection).

n.1: Written reflection may help later, but setting a task first misses the need for supportive discussion now.
n.2: This dismisses his distress and does not support reflection.
n.3: Some students need time off or occupational health input, but the first step is to listen and explore with him.

7.q: Daniel, 45, is on an intensive care unit in England after a catastrophic brain haemorrhage. Treatment is to be withdrawn. He has lived in England all his life and has not recorded a donation decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. What happens about organ donation?
o: His organs are retrieved without discussion because his consent is deemed
His family are approached to find out whether he held any views about donation
The consultant decides on donation at a best interests meeting
Donation cannot proceed because he did not register as an organ donor
7.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England (opt out from 20 May 2020): adults are considered to agree to donate unless they recorded a decision not to donate or are in an excluded group, and families are still consulted when donation is a possibility, to share any knowledge of the person's decision.

n.0: Under the opt-out law the family are still consulted when donation is possible; retrieval does not proceed without that discussion.
n.2: Donation decisions follow the deemed consent law and the person's known views, not a clinical best interests meeting.
n.3: In England, adults not in an excluded group are considered to agree unless they opted out; registration is not required.

7.q: Halfway through placement, Steph, a practice supervisor, is concerned that her third-year student repeatedly forgets to escalate abnormal observations. What should Steph record and do?
o: Write in the document that the student has an attitude problem with escalation
Raise it verbally with the student and leave any record until the final review
Keep private notes until the final interview so the student is not distracted
Record specific dated examples in the document and inform the practice assessor
7.w: Unambiguous records of performance (AnnexA.4.1.5) are factual, specific and dated, so the student knows what must improve and the practice assessor can act early with an action plan (SSSA; P5.8 documenting performance).

n.0: Vague, judgemental labels are not evidence and do not tell the student what to change.
n.1: Concerns raised verbally without a record leave no evidence for the assessor or the student's action plan.
n.2: Private notes hidden from the student remove the chance to improve and are not transparent.

7.q: Linda, 64, has IV fluids running through a volumetric infusion pump. The pump alarms 'downstream occlusion'. What should you check first?
o: The line, clamps and cannula site for a blockage
The pump's battery level and mains connection
The fluid bag for an air bubble near the top
The prescription chart for the next bag due
7.w: A downstream occlusion means resistance between the pump and the patient: check for closed clamps, kinked tubing and the cannula site (phlebitis, infiltration or a positional cannula) before restarting (Annexe B 5.9).

n.1: Battery alarms are separate from occlusion alarms.
n.2: Air at the top of the bag is above the pump and does not cause a downstream occlusion.
n.3: The prescription does not explain an occlusion alarm.

7.q: Ms Dace, 35, received IM lorazepam 45 minutes ago because of severe violence. She has had no response and remains very agitated. She regularly takes an antipsychotic, and an ECG yesterday was normal. Under NICE NG10, what should the team consider next?
o: Further IM lorazepam every 15 minutes until calm
IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
An urgent team meeting before any further medicine
IV haloperidol for a faster onset of sedation
7.w: NG10 1.4.40-1.4.41: if there is a partial response to IM lorazepam, consider a further dose; if there is no response, consider IM haloperidol with IM promethazine. An urgent team review is for when there is no response to both options (1.4.43).

n.0: A further lorazepam dose is for a partial response, and repeated 15-minute doses would risk respiratory depression.
n.2: An urgent team review is for no response to both lorazepam and haloperidol with promethazine.
n.3: IV administration is exceptional and carries more cardiac risk; NG10 next step is the IM combination.

7.q: Mr Brennan, 74, was assessed last month as lacking capacity to manage his complex investments. Today he tells the nurse he would like fish rather than chicken for lunch and wants to wear his own clothes. Which statement is correct?
o: His financial attorney should make these choices on his behalf
He lacks capacity for all decisions until a new assessment is completed
He can choose his lunch but not his clothing without an assessment
He may be able to make these decisions, as capacity is decision-specific
7.w: MCA 2005 s2(1): lack of capacity relates to a specific matter at the material time. Being unable to manage complex investments says nothing about everyday choices, which he is presumed able to make (s1(2)).

n.0: A property and financial affairs attorney has no authority over personal welfare choices such as food or clothing.
n.1: Incapacity is not global; a finding about one decision does not transfer to others.
n.2: There is no basis for treating clothing differently from food; both are everyday choices he is presumed able to make.

7.q: Mr Young, 38, has taken antipsychotics for years and needs rapid tranquillisation after de-escalation has failed. He has no known heart disease. A doctor suggests IM haloperidol with promethazine, but the nurse checks the notes first. Which finding is the main reason to use IM lorazepam instead?
o: No ECG has been done since his admission
He is younger than 40 years of age
He is detained under section 2 of the Act
He took oral lorazepam once last year
7.w: NG10 1.4.39: if there is evidence of cardiovascular disease, including a prolonged QT interval, or no ECG has been carried out, avoid IM haloperidol with IM promethazine and use IM lorazepam instead.

n.1: Age under 40 is not a reason to avoid haloperidol with promethazine; young men are more prone to dystonia, which promethazine helps prevent.
n.2: Detention status gives the legal framework; it does not decide which drug is used.
n.3: Previous lorazepam use does not rule out haloperidol with promethazine.

7.q: Joanne is the first health professional at a road traffic collision and is passing information to the ambulance control room using the M/ETHANE structure. What does the 'H' in M/ETHANE stand for?
o: Hospital
Head injuries
Hazards
Help needed
7.w: M/ETHANE (JESIP joint doctrine): Major incident declared or standby; Exact location; Type of incident; Hazards (present and potential); Access routes; Number of casualties; Emergency services present and required (P6.12).

n.0: The receiving hospital is decided by the ambulance service; it is not an M/ETHANE heading.
n.1: Injury types inform casualty numbers and severity but are not the 'H' heading.
n.3: Resources needed are reported under 'Emergency services', not 'H'.

7.q: Nurse Sara notices she has written the wrong blood pressure value in a patient's paper observation chart. What is the correct way to correct the entry?
o: Write the right value over the top of the wrong one
Cover the entry with correction fluid and rewrite it neatly
Tear out the page and copy the chart onto a new sheet
Strike through once, keep it legible, then sign, date and time
7.w: Code 10.3-10.4: complete records accurately without falsification, attribute entries and date and time them. Annexe A 1.8: write accurate, clear, legible records.

n.0: Overwriting makes both values illegible and unattributed.
n.1: Obscuring the original entry could be seen as falsification and makes the change untraceable (Code 10.3).
n.2: Removing pages destroys part of the record and breaches Code 10.3.

7.q: On an acute ward, Mr Stone, 40, is pacing and shouting that he wants to leave. He has not harmed anyone. What is the nurse's most appropriate first approach?
o: Tell him firmly to sit down and stop shouting
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and listen to him
Call security to restrain him before he leaves
Stand in the doorway to block his exit from the ward
7.w: Annexe A 3.5: de-escalation strategies and techniques. Code 13.4 personal safety; calm voice, open posture and listening come before restrictive interventions.

n.0: Commands can escalate agitation; de-escalation uses calm listening.
n.2: Restraint is a last resort; de-escalation should be tried first.
n.3: Blocking his exit increases risk and may escalate the situation.

7.q: At the 08:00 round, Pearl, 81, refuses her prescribed ramipril, saying it makes her dizzy. She has capacity and understands the reason for the tablet. How should the nurse record and act on this?
o: Record 'refused' with her reason and inform the prescriber
Leave the box blank and mention it at the handover
Record 'given', as the tablet was offered at the correct time
Leave the tablet on her locker and record it once she takes it
7.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 17: records are kept of medicines administered, withheld or declined, completed at the time or as soon as possible; the reason is recorded and the prescriber or team informed where appropriate. Dizziness may need a medication review.

n.1: A blank box is unauditable and may lead someone else to give a second dose.
n.2: Recording a refused dose as given is a false record.
n.3: She has declined it; leaving tablets unattended is unsafe and the refusal still needs recording.

7.q: You observe Jake, a first-year student nurse, using alcohol-based handrub. He applies a small amount, rubs his palms together for about 10 seconds, misses his thumbs and fingertips, and wipes the residue on his tunic. What feedback is most appropriate?
o: Apply a second dose and rub palms for a further 10 seconds
Cover all surfaces, including thumbs and fingertips, for 20 to 30 seconds until dry
Rinse the handrub off under running water after 15 seconds of firm rubbing
Rub all hand surfaces for 40 to 60 seconds, then dry them with a paper towel
7.w: The WHO handrub technique adopted in NIPCM appendix 2 covers all surfaces of the hands, including thumbs and fingertips, and takes 20 to 30 seconds, with hands left to dry naturally. 40 to 60 seconds is the duration for handwashing with soap and water.

n.0: A second dose rubbed on the palms still misses the thumbs and fingertips that he omitted.
n.2: Handrub is not rinsed off; rinsing removes the product before it has acted.
n.3: 40 to 60 seconds is the handwash duration; handrub is rubbed until dry and is not towel-dried.

7.q: Mr Evans, 76, is usually independent and has no psychiatric history. Over the last 24 hours on an older adults' ward he has started seeing insects on the walls, is unsure of the day and drifts in and out of conversation. What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Delirium, needing a 4AT and a search for a cause
Late-onset psychosis, needing an antipsychotic
Lewy body dementia, needing a memory clinic referral
Psychotic depression, needing a PHQ-9 and review
7.w: Acute onset over hours, fluctuating attention, disorientation and visual hallucinations point to delirium, which is a medical emergency. NICE CG103 recommends assessment (the 4AT is widely used) and identifying and treating underlying causes such as infection, medicines or dehydration.

n.1: Psychosis rarely starts over hours with fluctuating attention in an older person with no history; an antipsychotic would also miss the physical cause.
n.2: Dementia develops over months; this change happened over a day.
n.3: There is no low mood reported, and a fluctuating, acute picture suggests delirium.

7.q: Which finding should make a nurse consider that a person with suspected sepsis is at higher risk than their NEWS2 score suggests (NICE NG253, 2025)?
o: A pulse of 88 beats per minute
A temperature of 37.9°C
A respiratory rate of 19 per minute
A non-blanching petechial rash
7.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider higher risk than NEWS2 indicates if the person has mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue.

n.0: A pulse of 88 is within the NEWS2 0 band (51-90).
n.1: 37.9°C scores 0 on NEWS2 and is not a higher-risk feature in NG253.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 19 is within the NEWS2 0 band (12-20).

7.q: Mrs Ross, 58, takes lithium for bipolar disorder. She has had diarrhoea and vomiting for two days. At a home visit she has a coarse tremor, is unsteady when walking and her speech is slurred. Her evening lithium is due. What should the nurse do?
o: Give an anti-diarrhoeal medicine and continue her lithium
Give the dose with extra fluids and recheck her in a week
Reassure her that tremor is a common side effect of lithium
Withhold the dose and arrange an urgent level and review
7.w: Diarrhoea and vomiting cause dehydration, which raises lithium levels. Coarse tremor (a fine tremor becoming coarse), ataxia and dysarthria are signs of toxicity, which require withdrawal of treatment (BNF). She needs an urgent level and medical review.

n.0: Treating the diarrhoea alone ignores signs of lithium toxicity.
n.1: Giving more lithium when toxicity is suspected could cause seizures, arrhythmias or kidney injury.
n.2: A fine tremor is common, but a coarse tremor with ataxia and slurred speech suggests toxicity.

7.q: Mrs Bishop is angry at the nurses' station because her father's call bell went unanswered for 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her to put her complaint in writing to the manager
Explain that the ward is short-staffed with two nurses off sick
Listen, acknowledge her concern and apologise to her
Call security as she is raising her voice at staff
7.w: Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations with compassion; Code 2.6 respond compassionately and politely to distress; Code 14.2 apologise when things go wrong.

n.0: Formal routes may follow, but she first needs to be heard.
n.1: Giving reasons first can sound defensive and does not acknowledge her concern.
n.3: Raised voices about a genuine concern do not warrant security as a first step.

7.q: Hilda, 83, has end-stage pulmonary fibrosis and is in the last days of life. She says she feels breathless at rest. Her oxygen saturation is 95% on air and her chest is unchanged on examination. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
o: Use a fan and positioning, and check whether an opioid is prescribed
Arrange an arterial blood gas sample to guide oxygen therapy
Start oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula to ease her breathing
Give the 'as required' hyoscine butylbromide from her anticipatory box
7.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.16 and 1.5.17: consider non-pharmacological management of breathlessness (for example a fan), do not routinely start oxygen unless symptomatic hypoxaemia is known or suspected, and consider an opioid, a benzodiazepine or both.

n.1: An invasive test unlikely to change care should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.1.4).
n.2: With saturation of 95% she is not hypoxaemic; NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen for breathlessness.
n.3: Hyoscine butylbromide is used for secretions or bowel obstruction, not for breathlessness.

7.q: Ruth, 85, has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible but no bone, tendon or muscle is exposed. Using the international NPIAP-EPUAP classification, which category is this?
o: Category 2
Suspected deep tissue injury
Category 3
Category 4
7.w: NPIAP-EPUAP classification (used per NICE CG179): category 3 is full-thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible but bone, tendon or muscle not exposed. Category 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle; category 2 is partial-thickness loss.

n.0: Category 2 is partial-thickness loss of dermis, such as a shallow open wound or blister.
n.1: Suspected deep tissue injury is an area of purple or maroon intact skin or a blood-filled blister.
n.3: Category 4 involves exposed bone, tendon or muscle.

7.q: Nurse Kemi is asked by a colleague to countersign the controlled drugs register for a dose of subcutaneous morphine that the colleague prepared and gave while Kemi was on her break. Trust policy requires a witness for CD administration. What should Kemi do?
o: Sign it and add a note that she did not see the dose given
Sign it, as she trusts her colleague's practice and experience
Sign the stock balance but leave the witness column blank for now
Decline, and offer to witness the next dose from preparation onwards
7.w: NICE NG46 and RPS/RCN guidance: the CD administration record includes the person administering and any witness, and witnessing means observing the process. Signing for something not seen is a false record (NMC Code 10.3, records accurate). Kemi should decline and the colleague should report the gap per policy.

n.0: A witness signature with a disclaimer still misrepresents the record and breaches the witness policy.
n.1: Trust does not make a signature truthful; she did not witness the dose.
n.2: Countersigning the balance still implies checking a transaction she did not see.

7.q: Siobhan, 36, is detained under section 3. She is unmarried and has lived with her younger brother, who cares for her, for 10 years. Her mother lives in Spain and her father lives nearby. Who is her nearest relative under section 26?
o: Her mother, because she is the elder of the two parents
Her younger brother, as he lives with and cares for her
Her father, because parents rank above brothers and sisters
Whichever of her parents Siobhan chooses to nominate
7.w: Under section 26(4), a relative with whom the patient ordinarily resides or who cares for her is preferred over others. Her brother lives with and cares for her, so he is her nearest relative. Her mother is also excluded because she is not resident in the UK (s26(5)(a)).

n.0: Her mother lives abroad and is treated as dead for this purpose (s26(5)(a)); she is also displaced by the carer rule.
n.2: The list order (parents before siblings) is overridden where a relative lives with or cares for the patient (s26(4)).
n.3: Patients cannot choose their nearest relative under the 1983 Act; nomination is a 2025 Act change not in force.

7.q: Bella, 24, becomes increasingly agitated in a busy dining room. The nurse wants to help her calm down somewhere quieter. Which location does NICE NG10 advise against using routinely for de-escalation?
o: A quiet area of the ward garden
The seclusion room
Her own bedroom with staff support
A designated comfort room
7.w: NICE NG10 1.3.14 and 1.3.20: separate agitated service users from others using quiet areas, bedrooms, comfort rooms or gardens, and use a designated calming area. Do not routinely use the seclusion room for de-escalation, because the person may perceive it as threatening.

n.0: Gardens and quiet areas are suitable de-escalation spaces in NG10.
n.2: Bedrooms are listed in NG10 1.3.14 as places to aid de-escalation, ensuring staff are not isolated.
n.3: A comfort room is one of the spaces NG10 suggests for calming.

7.q: Mrs Lowe, 61, has alcohol dependence and liver impairment confirmed by her GP. She is to start assisted withdrawal. Which approach does NICE CG115 advise?
o: Chlordiazepoxide at the usual full starting dose
Diazepam at a higher dose to prevent any seizures
Clomethiazole managed by her GP at home
Lorazepam at a reduced dose with liver monitoring
7.w: CG115 1.3.5: chlordiazepoxide or diazepam are preferred generally, but with liver impairment consider a benzodiazepine needing limited liver metabolism (for example lorazepam), start at a reduced dose and monitor liver function. CG100: clomethiazole is inpatient only.

n.0: Chlordiazepoxide relies on liver metabolism and can accumulate.
n.1: Higher doses of a long-acting drug risk accumulation and oversedation.
n.2: Clomethiazole should be used in inpatient settings, not at home.

7.q: Clive, 80, had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) that was still active when he died on a cardiology ward. The registered nurse has verified his expected death. Which action relating to the device is the nurse's responsibility?
o: Instigate deactivation and tell the mortuary or funeral director about the device
Record the device in the notes, as no further action is needed after death
Ask his family to inform the funeral director that a device is present
Remove the device before Clive is transferred to the mortuary
7.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the RN must instigate the process for deactivation of an implantable cardiac defibrillator where applicable, and must notify the funeral director or mortuary of any infections, radioactive implants, implantable devices and whether an ICD is still active.

n.1: An active ICD remains a hazard to people handling the body, so deactivation must be arranged.
n.2: Notifying the mortuary or funeral director is the verifying nurse's responsibility, not the family's.
n.3: Ward nurses do not remove implanted devices; the RN instigates deactivation and passes on the information.

7.q: Nurse Ali phones a doctor about Mr Cole using SBAR. He says, "I think he may be developing sepsis." Which part of SBAR is this?
o: Assessment
Situation
Background
Recommendation
7.w: NHS England SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation): Assessment is the nurse's evaluation of the problem.

n.1: Situation states the immediate problem, for example 'his NEWS2 is 6'.
n.2: Background gives history and context.
n.3: Recommendation states what the nurse wants done.

7.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
7.q: Mia, 14, has been diagnosed with mild depression by a CAMHS practitioner. She does not want any treatment at the moment and the practitioner thinks she may recover without intervention. What does NICE NG134 recommend?
o: Starting fluoxetine at a low dose
Reassessment, normally within 2 weeks
Reassessment in about 3 months
Discharge to her GP with written advice
7.w: NG134: for children and young people with mild depression who do not want an intervention or may recover without one, arrange further assessment, normally within 2 weeks ('watchful waiting'). Antidepressants should not be used for initial treatment of mild depression.

n.0: Antidepressants are not used as initial treatment for mild depression in young people.
n.2: Three months is far longer than the 2-week reassessment NICE advises.
n.3: Discharge without follow-up misses deterioration.

7.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
7.q: Ms Fox, 22, in a DBT programme, cut her arm last night. Her wound has been treated and she is now calm. Her care plan uses DBT principles. Which approach is most appropriate now?
o: Start continuous one-to-one observation indefinitely
Avoid discussing it so as not to reinforce it
Do a chain analysis of what led to the self-harm
Stop her leave as a consequence of the incident
7.w: Step 1: deal with physical care and wait for calm. Step 2: behaviour chain analysis maps triggers, thoughts, feelings and actions to identify where skills could be used next time. Punitive responses are not part of DBT or NG225.

n.0: Indefinite observation is restrictive and not based on a current risk assessment.
n.1: Avoidance misses learning; DBT addresses self-harm directly.
n.3: Punitive restrictions damage engagement and are not therapeutic.

7.q: Ivy, 84, has dementia and becomes agitated each evening, trying to leave the ward and hitting out during personal care. Her pain has not been assessed. Which action best responds to her behaviour?
o: Ask her family to stay overnight so that staff can step back
Assess for pain and unmet needs and adapt her care around them
Keep her in a chair with a lap belt to stop her leaving
Request a prescription for regular antipsychotic medicine
7.w: Behaviour that challenges often communicates unmet need, such as pain, constipation, infection or fear. Assess pain with a behavioural observation tool where self-report is difficult (the 2018 UK guideline recommends PAINAD or Doloplus-2; Abbey is widely used) (UK guidance on pain assessment in older people, Age and Ageing 2018) and adapt care, using positive behaviour support before any restrictive or pharmacological option (Annexe A 3.5, P4.4).

n.0: Family involvement is helpful, but staff remain responsible for assessing and meeting her needs.
n.2: A lap belt is a restrictive practice and a potential deprivation of liberty, not a first response.
n.3: Antipsychotics carry significant risks in dementia and do not address the cause.

7.q: Ms Dale, 28, has attended the emergency department 12 times in three months after self-harm. At a team meeting a colleague suggests asking the police for a community protection notice to reduce her attendances. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask security to direct her to her GP the next time she attends
Offer physical treatment and withhold assessment until she engages
Support the notice, as frequent attendance blocks care for others
Arrange a multidisciplinary review with her to agree a joint plan
7.w: NICE NG225 1.7.5 says not to use aversive, punitive or criminal justice approaches such as community protection notices for frequent self-harm. For frequent episodes, 1.5.17 recommends a multidisciplinary review with the person to agree a joint plan, a care coordinator, a care plan and a safety plan.

n.0: Turning her away from the department is a punitive approach and leaves her needs unassessed.
n.1: Withholding assessment is punitive; a liaison professional should see her at every attendance (NG225 1.7.14).
n.2: NG225 specifically advises against community protection notices and other criminal justice approaches for frequent self-harm.

7.q: Mr Blake, 85, has dementia and was admitted two days ago with pneumonia. Staff describe him as 'a lovely quiet man' who sleeps most of the day, eats little and is slow to respond. His family say he is usually chatty. What should the nurse suspect?
o: Hypoactive delirium needing assessment
Expected tiredness from his pneumonia
Progression of his dementia over two days
Low mood related to being in hospital
7.w: NICE CG103 notes hypoactive delirium is easily missed. Recent changes in cognition, physical function (reduced movement, appetite, sleep) and social behaviour (withdrawal), reported by family, are indicators of delirium needing assessment with the 4AT (rec 1.3.1, 1.6.1).

n.1: Attributing a marked change from his baseline to tiredness risks missing delirium.
n.2: Dementia progresses gradually; a change over two days points to delirium.
n.3: Low mood may cause withdrawal, but slowed responses and drowsiness developing over days point to delirium first.

7.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
7.q: Mr Hart, 55, is convinced that MI5 is poisoning the ward food and refuses meals. He asks the nurse to agree that he is being targeted. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell him he will be fed by tube if he keeps refusing
Acknowledge his fear and offer sealed food items
Explain firmly why MI5 would have no reason to target him
Agree with him so that he will trust the team
7.w: Neither challenge nor collude with a delusion: acknowledge the emotion (fear), stay honest and offer practical options such as sealed or packaged food to meet nutritional needs.

n.0: Threats are coercive and damage the therapeutic relationship.
n.2: Arguing with a fixed belief tends to entrench it and harms engagement.
n.3: Agreeing colludes with the delusion and is dishonest.

7.q: At a retirement celebration on the ward, a nurse takes a team photograph. A patient sitting in a bay is visible in the background. The nurse wants to post it on her public social media account. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Post the photograph after blurring the patient's face
Post the photograph with no names or ward details
Post the photograph using strict privacy settings
Post a version without the patient, who has not consented
7.w: NMC social media guidance: do not post pictures of patients and people receiving care without their consent, regardless of whether you believe they could be identified. Code 5.1 and 20.10.

n.0: NMC guidance requires consent before posting images of patients, whether or not you believe they could be identified.
n.1: Removing names does not remove the need for the patient's consent to the image being shared.
n.2: Privacy settings do not replace consent and content can still be shared onward.

7.q: Hannah, a staff nurse, is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Derek Lowe, 58. At the bedside he tells her he is allergic to penicillin. His allergy band was missing and the chart says 'no known allergies'. No dose was given. What should Hannah do about reporting?
o: Report herself to the NMC, as she nearly gave a contraindicated drug
Record it as a near miss on the trust's patient safety reporting system
Tell the ward manager verbally, as no harm reached the patient
Correct the chart and allergy band, as no report is needed without harm
7.w: Near misses are patient safety events and must be recorded so the system can learn, whether or not harm occurred (P6.8; Code 14 and NMC/GMC candour guidance 2024, which covers reporting near misses). Local systems feed the national Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service. The chart and band must also be corrected and the prescriber informed.

n.0: Self-referral to the regulator is not the response to a near miss caught by correct checks; this is a system issue for local reporting.
n.2: Verbal reporting alone loses the learning; near misses are formally recorded on the local system.
n.3: Correcting the records is needed, but near misses are reported because they reveal weaknesses before harm occurs.

7.q: The evening before major surgery, Mrs Reid, 67, asks the nurse quietly, "Am I going to die tomorrow?" Which response is most appropriate?
o: "You'll need to ask the surgeon that question."
"Everyone feels like that the night before."
"Don't worry, the surgeons do this every day."
"What is worrying you most about tomorrow?"
7.w: Annexe A 1.5: use caring conversation techniques. Exploring the person's concern before giving information responds compassionately to distress (Code 2.6).

n.0: Redirecting her without exploring her fear misses the chance to support her now.
n.1: Generalising her feelings minimises her individual concern.
n.2: This is false reassurance that closes down her concern.

7.q: At 07:00 Nurse Joe realises he did not record that Mrs Ali, 79, had an unwitnessed fall at 02:30, though he assessed her at the time. What is the correct way to document this?
o: Ask the day nurse to record the fall at her first check
Write the entry and time it 02:30 so the record is in order
Add the fall to the handover sheet in place of the notes
Write a 07:00 entry stating it relates to the fall at 02:30
7.w: Code 10.1: complete records at the time or as soon as possible after an event, recording if notes are written some time after the event. Code 10.3 no falsification.

n.0: She did not witness the event; Code 10.4 requires entries to be attributed to the person who made them.
n.1: Back-timing misrepresents when the note was written; Code 10.1 requires late entries to be recorded as such.
n.2: Handover sheets are not the formal record; the fall must be documented in the patient's notes.

7.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
7.q: Ms Patel, 41, has severe depression with suicidal thoughts but has a supportive partner and is willing to accept daily support at home. What is the main purpose of the crisis resolution and home treatment team for her?
o: To arrange her admission to an acute ward
To give intensive home support instead of admission
To complete her discharge from mental health services
To provide weekly psychotherapy sessions
7.w: Crisis resolution and home treatment teams provide rapid assessment and intensive home-based treatment, available 24 hours, as an alternative to hospital admission where it is safe (CG178 1.4; CG78 1.4.1.1).

n.0: Their role is to avoid admission where home treatment is safe.
n.2: CRHT provides crisis care, not discharge.
n.3: Weekly therapy is not crisis care.

7.q: Holly, 20, is referred because she has become withdrawn, her college work has declined and she has had brief periods of hearing her name called. A clear diagnosis of psychosis cannot be made. Her mother asks if a low-dose antipsychotic would prevent psychosis. What should the nurse explain?
o: A low-dose antipsychotic is started to reduce the risk of transition
No treatment is offered until a diagnosis is confirmed
Individual CBT is offered; antipsychotics are not used for prevention
An antipsychotic is offered if symptoms last more than 2 weeks
