7.w: CG178 1.2.3.1-1.2.3.2: for people at increased risk of psychosis offer individual CBT with or without family intervention, and do not offer antipsychotic medication to reduce the risk of or prevent psychosis. Monitor for up to 3 years if symptoms persist.

n.0: NICE advises against antipsychotics to prevent psychosis.
n.1: She is distressed with declining function, so CBT is offered now rather than waiting.
n.3: Duration of attenuated symptoms does not change the advice against preventive antipsychotics.

7.q: A community nurse is learning about the NHS England Core20PLUS5 approach to reducing healthcare inequalities in adults. What does 'Core20' refer to?
o: The 20% of the population who are aged 65 and over in each region
The 20% of adults living with the highest number of long-term health conditions
The most deprived 20% of the population, by the Index of Multiple Deprivation
The 20% of local areas with the highest rates of emergency hospital admission
7.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): Core20 is the most deprived 20% of the national population as identified by the national Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD); PLUS groups are identified locally; the 5 are clinical areas of focus.

n.0: Age is not the basis of Core20; it is the most deprived fifth of the population.
n.1: Core20 is defined by deprivation, not by the number of long-term conditions a person has.
n.3: Admission rates are not the measure; Core20 uses the national Index of Multiple Deprivation.

7.q: Sanjay, 45, detained under section 3, is recovering from psychosis and has a job interview next week. The team worries he may relapse under stress. Which approach best reflects positive risk-taking?
o: Refuse any leave until all risk of relapse has resolved
Agree escorted leave with a nurse waiting outside the interview
Plan the leave with him, with warning signs and a contingency
Ask his employer to postpone the interview until his discharge
7.w: Positive risk-taking weighs potential benefits against harms and plans collaboratively with the person, using a contingency plan. This reflects the least restrictive and empowerment principles of the Code (COP15 ch1). The RC grants the leave under section 17.

n.0: Waiting for zero risk is unrealistic and unduly restrictive.
n.1: Escorting may be more restrictive than his risk requires and may undermine his chances.
n.3: Asking the employer to postpone breaches confidentiality and limits his recovery.

7.q: Mr Daly, 41, has panic disorder with attacks several times a week. He asks his GP practice nurse whether he can have diazepam to take when an attack starts. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange diazepam to take as needed during attacks
Explain diazepam worsens long-term outcome and discuss CBT
Suggest a sedating antihistamine at night
Suggest a low-dose antipsychotic to reduce the attacks
7.w: CG113: benzodiazepines are associated with a less good long-term outcome and should not be prescribed for panic disorder; sedating antihistamines or antipsychotics should not be prescribed either. CBT is the psychological treatment of choice.

n.0: NICE advises against benzodiazepines for panic disorder.
n.2: Sedating antihistamines should not be prescribed for panic disorder.
n.3: Antipsychotics should not be prescribed for panic disorder.

7.q: Mr Novak, 34, was in a serious car crash 4 months ago. He has flashbacks, nightmares, avoids driving and is constantly on edge. He is diagnosed with PTSD. Which treatment does NICE NG116 recommend first?
o: Non-directive supportive counselling
Regular lorazepam to reduce hyperarousal
Psychologically-focused debriefing
Individual trauma-focused CBT or EMDR
7.w: NG116 1.6.16 and 1.6.19: offer adults individual trauma-focused CBT (more than 1 month after the trauma), or EMDR for PTSD presenting more than 3 months after a non-combat trauma (1.6.19).

n.0: Non-trauma-focused counselling is not a NICE first-line treatment for PTSD.
n.1: Benzodiazepines are not a PTSD treatment and carry dependence risk.
n.2: NICE advises against debriefing to prevent or treat PTSD.

7.q: Isla, 38, an informal patient, suddenly attacks staff and another patient. As a last resort she is placed in seclusion to prevent harm to others. What must happen next?
o: Transfer her to the emergency department for review
Continue seclusion for up to 24 hours before review
Arrange a Mental Health Act assessment immediately
Ask her to sign consent to the use of seclusion
7.w: Seclusion should be used only for patients detained under the Act. If an informal patient is secluded in an emergency as a last resort, an assessment for detention under the Act should be undertaken immediately (COP15 26.106; NICE NG10 1.4.46).

n.0: Transfer to ED is not indicated; seclusion is not used in emergency departments, and the priority is MHA assessment.
n.1: There is no 24-hour period; an MHA assessment must be arranged immediately and reviews start at once.
n.3: Consent does not legitimise seclusion; the need is for a lawful framework via MHA assessment.

7.q: Lena, 41, detained under section 3, is on 5 days' overnight section 17 leave at home. Her husband rings the ward: she has stopped eating and is hearing voices telling her to harm herself. The responsible clinician decides she must return. How is the leave revoked?
o: By a magistrate's warrant under section 135(1)
By notice in writing to Lena or the person in charge of her
By an AMHP application under section 2
By a verbal instruction to her husband from the ward nurse
7.w: Section 17(4) allows the RC, where necessary for the patient's health or safety or the protection of others, to revoke leave and recall the patient by notice in writing given to the patient or the person in charge of them.

n.0: A section 135(1) warrant is for people not already liable to be detained; s135(2) may be needed only if entry to retake her is refused.
n.2: Lena is already liable to be detained under section 3, so a new section 2 application is not needed.
n.3: Revocation is the RC's power and must be in writing; a nurse's verbal instruction does not revoke leave.

7.q: Mr Patel, 39, has had low mood and poor sleep for 6 weeks. His PHQ-9 score is 11, he is working and has no thoughts of self-harm. He has no preference about treatment. Which first-line option does NICE NG222 favour?
o: Guided self-help based on CBT principles
An SSRI started at his first appointment
Referral for psychodynamic psychotherapy
Individual CBT combined with an antidepressant
7.w: NG222 1.5: for less severe depression (PHQ-9 under 16) start with the least intrusive, most effective option; guided self-help is first in the NICE table. Do not routinely offer antidepressants first line unless the person prefers.

n.1: Antidepressants are not routinely first line for less severe depression.
n.2: Psychodynamic therapy is lower in the NICE order for less severe depression.
n.3: Combined CBT and an antidepressant is the first option for more severe depression.

8.q: Raj, 52, detained under section 3, has schizophrenia and has developed cellulitis in his leg. He has capacity to decide about antibiotics, understands the risks and refuses them. A colleague says, 'He's sectioned, so we can treat him anyway.' What is the nurse's best response?
o: The Act authorises treatment of any condition while he is detained
His nearest relative can consent to the antibiotics for him
The Act does not cover unrelated physical illness, so his refusal stands
A SOAD can authorise the antibiotics because he is detained
8.w: Treatment under section 63 must be medical treatment for mental disorder (including its symptoms or manifestations). Cellulitis is unrelated to his mental disorder, so the ordinary law applies: a capable adult can refuse. The team should keep offering treatment, explain risks and record the discussion.

n.0: The Mental Health Act authorises treatment for mental disorder, not unrelated physical illness.
n.1: The nearest relative has no power to consent to treatment for an adult.
n.3: SOAD certificates relate to Part 4 treatment for mental disorder, not physical treatment.

8.q: Hannah, a registered adult nurse on a medical ward, cares for Peter, 70, an informal patient receiving treatment for a depressive illness who is trying to leave and talking about suicide. She asks whether she can use the nurse's holding power. What is the correct answer?
o: Yes, because any registered nurse can use section 5(4) on a hospital ward
No, because section 5(4) cannot be used on a general medical ward
No, because she is not a nurse of the prescribed class
Yes, if the duty psychiatrist confirms the decision by telephone
8.w: The prescribed class for section 5(4) is nurses registered on sub-parts 1 or 2 of the NMC register whose field is mental health or learning disabilities (COP15 ch18 footnote, SI 2008/1207). An adult nurse is not in that class, so she should urgently contact the doctor in charge, who may use section 5(2).

n.0: Section 5(4) is restricted to the prescribed class of mental health and learning disabilities nurses.
n.1: Section 5(4) can be used on any hospital ward for an in-patient receiving treatment for mental disorder; the bar here is her field of registration.
n.3: Telephone confirmation from a psychiatrist cannot give the power to a nurse outside the prescribed class.

8.q: Mr Fox, 48, is admitted to an acute mental health ward with depression. As part of his assessment he scores 22 on the AUDIT questionnaire and says he drinks from the morning onwards. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give brief advice on drinking and repeat the AUDIT in a year
Record hazardous drinking and address it once his mood has improved
Assess dependence and withdrawal risk and seek specialist alcohol input
Advise him to stop drinking completely from today to help his mood
8.w: An AUDIT score above 15 indicates the need for a fuller assessment (NICE CG115 1.2.2.6), and scores of 20 or more suggest possible dependence. Morning drinking suggests dependence, so withdrawal risk must be assessed (for example with CIWA-Ar) and specialist advice sought before any reduction.

n.0: Brief advice suits lower-risk drinking; a score of 22 with morning drinking needs assessment now.
n.1: Delaying assessment risks unplanned withdrawal on the ward and ignores a factor maintaining his depression.
n.3: Stopping abruptly when dependent can cause seizures or delirium tremens; withdrawal must be assessed and planned.

8.q: Nadia, 19, is waiting in the emergency department for a mental health liaison assessment and says she is leaving. The emergency medicine doctor says he will 'use a section 5(2)'. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Section 5(2) can be used for up to 6 hours in the department
Section 5(2) can be used once the liaison psychiatrist agrees
Section 5(2) cannot be used because she is not an in-patient
Section 5(2) can be used because she is on hospital premises
8.w: Section 5(2) applies to hospital in-patients. COP15 18.8 states that the power cannot be used for an out-patient attending an accident and emergency department. Other lawful options (for example the Mental Capacity Act if she lacks capacity) must be considered instead.

n.0: Six hours is the nurse's section 5(4) limit; section 5(2) lasts up to 72 hours and in any case does not apply in ED.
n.1: Agreement from a psychiatrist does not make an emergency department attender an in-patient.
n.3: Being on hospital premises is not enough; the person must be an in-patient (COP15 18.7-18.8).

8.q: Hannah, a staff nurse, is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Derek Lowe, 58. At the bedside he tells her he is allergic to penicillin. His allergy band was missing and the chart says 'no known allergies'. No dose was given. What should Hannah do about reporting?
o: Report herself to the NMC, as she nearly gave a contraindicated drug
Record it as a near miss on the trust's patient safety reporting system
Tell the ward manager verbally, as no harm reached the patient
Correct the chart and allergy band, as no report is needed without harm
8.w: Near misses are patient safety events and must be recorded so the system can learn, whether or not harm occurred (P6.8; Code 14 and NMC/GMC candour guidance 2024, which covers reporting near misses). Local systems feed the national Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service. The chart and band must also be corrected and the prescriber informed.

n.0: Self-referral to the regulator is not the response to a near miss caught by correct checks; this is a system issue for local reporting.
n.2: Verbal reporting alone loses the learning; near misses are formally recorded on the local system.
n.3: Correcting the records is needed, but near misses are reported because they reveal weaknesses before harm occurs.

8.q: Edna, 80, is admitted to a medical ward from home after a fall. She has limited mobility and a previous sacral pressure ulcer. Under NICE CG179, when should her pressure ulcer risk be assessed and documented?
o: When a skin change is first noticed
Within 72 hours of admission
At the first weekly skin review
On admission to the ward
8.w: NICE CG179 (2014): assess and document pressure ulcer risk for adults on admission to secondary care or care homes, and reassess if clinical status changes.

n.0: Waiting for skin change means prevention starts after damage has begun.
n.1: 72 hours delays prevention in someone at risk, contrary to CG179.
n.2: A weekly review would leave her unassessed during the high-risk early period.

8.q: Mrs Lowe, 90, lives in a care home in England and lacks capacity to decide where to live. The manager has concluded that her care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. What is needed to make these arrangements lawful?
o: A best interests note in her care plan by the manager
An authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
Her daughter's signed consent to the locked doors
An authorisation under the Liberty Protection Safeguards
8.w: Where a person who lacks capacity is deprived of liberty in a care home or hospital, the arrangements need authorisation under DoLS (MCA 2005 Sch A1). Article 5 of the Human Rights Act 1998 protects liberty, and DoLS supply the required safeguards.

n.0: Recording that the arrangements are in her best interests does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
n.3: The LPS are not in force, so no LPS authorisation can be given.

8.q: A community mental health nurse takes a call from Ms Rowe, 25, who is known to the team. She says she took 40 paracetamol tablets an hour ago after an argument, now regrets it and feels physically fine. What should the nurse advise?
o: Wait at home for a crisis team visit later this afternoon
Monitor herself at home, as she feels physically well
Book an urgent GP appointment for tomorrow morning
Go to the emergency department now, by ambulance if needed
8.w: Paracetamol overdose may cause no early symptoms while liver damage develops, and treatment depends on blood levels and timing. She needs emergency medical assessment now (NICE NG225 1.7.4; BNF/TOXBASE emergency treatment of poisoning), with psychosocial assessment alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting delays time-critical assessment and treatment for paracetamol poisoning.
n.1: Feeling well does not exclude serious paracetamol toxicity, which often has no early symptoms.
n.2: Waiting until tomorrow could miss the window for effective treatment.

8.q: At 23:00 the site manager asks Kwame, the nurse in charge, to transfer Mrs Lowry, 88, who has delirium, to another ward to free a bed. Kwame is concerned that a night move will worsen her delirium. Another patient in his ward is medically stable and awake. What is the best approach?
o: Refuse any transfer and tell the site manager to find a bed on another ward
Agree to the move and complete an incident report about it the next day
Explain the risk to Mrs Lowry and propose moving the stable patient instead
Agree to move Mrs Lowry, as the site manager has authority over beds
8.w: Negotiation explores both parties' needs and seeks a solution that meets them: the site manager needs a bed; Kwame needs to protect a vulnerable patient (moving people with delirium, especially at night, can worsen confusion). Offering an alternative is effective negotiation and advocacy (AnnexA.4.2.6.1; AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4).

n.0: Refusing outright without offering a solution ignores the site's legitimate need and is unlikely to resolve the problem.
n.1: Reporting afterwards does not prevent foreseeable harm that negotiation could avoid now.
n.3: Authority over beds does not remove Kwame's duty to advocate for a patient at risk of harm.

8.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
8.q: Amelia, 17, has severe anorexia nervosa and the team recommend informal admission. She has capacity and agrees to admission, but her father objects and says he will not allow it. What is the legal position?
o: Her father's objection prevents informal admission
The decision must go to the Court of Protection
Her own consent to informal admission is sufficient
Both parents must agree before she can be admitted
8.w: MHA 1983 s131(2)-(4): a 16 or 17-year-old with capacity can consent to informal admission even if a person with parental responsibility disagrees, and a capable refusal cannot be overridden by parental consent.

n.0: A parent cannot override a capable 16 or 17-year-old's consent to informal admission.
n.1: The Court of Protection is not needed where she has capacity and consents.
n.3: Parental agreement is not needed when a capable 17-year-old consents.

8.q: Siobhan, 58, two days after a laparotomy, has a NEWS2 of 9: RR 25, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 102/64, alert, temperature 38.4°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Request a ward doctor review within 4 hours and repeat the observations hourly
Recheck the observations in 30 minutes before escalating
Inform the medical team immediately and request a critical care assessment
Increase observations to 4-hourly and inform the nurse in charge
8.w: A NEWS2 of 7 or more is high clinical risk: continuous monitoring, the registered nurse immediately informs the medical team (at least specialist registrar level) and requests emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies (RCP NEWS2 2017 chart 4). Her score: RR 3, SpO2 2, pulse 2, BP 1, temperature 1 = 9.

n.0: A 4-hour review is far too slow for a high-risk score.
n.1: Delaying escalation to recheck wastes time; the score already meets the emergency threshold.
n.3: 4-hourly observations apply to a total of 1-4.

8.q: Peter, 74, has pancreatic cancer and is in the last days of life at home. He can no longer swallow tablets. Over the past 24 hours the community nurse has given three 'as required' subcutaneous doses of morphine for pain, each giving relief for a few hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue 'as required' doses and review the plan in 72 hours
Ask his wife to give oral morphine solution between visits
Discuss with the prescriber starting a continuous syringe pump
Give the next 'as required' doses by intramuscular injection
8.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.5.6: consider a syringe pump to deliver medicines for continuous symptom control if more than 2 or 3 doses of any 'as required' medicine have been given within 24 hours. Rec 1.5.5: avoid intramuscular injections.

n.0: Needing more than 2 or 3 doses in 24 hours is the NG31 trigger to consider a syringe pump; waiting 72 hours leaves pain poorly controlled.
n.1: Peter can no longer swallow safely, so the oral route is unsuitable (NG31 rec 1.5.4).
n.3: NICE NG31 rec 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life; subcutaneous or intravenous routes are used.

8.q: Mrs Rita Holmes, 87, lived alone before a fall and is now medically fit for discharge but still slow and unsteady. At the board round, a doctor suggests arranging a permanent nursing home place directly from the ward. What does current discharge guidance in England advise?
o: Discharge her home with no support and review her needs if she falls
Arrange the permanent place now, as hospital is the best place to assess needs
Discharge her for a period of recovery, then assess her long-term needs
Keep Mrs Holmes in hospital until she has fully recovered her mobility
8.w: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, not in hospital. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without an opportunity to recover first (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P4.18). Two steps: recognise she is medically fit, then apply discharge to assess.

n.0: She has clear new needs; discharge without support is unsafe.
n.1: Assessing long-term needs in hospital, before recovery, tends to overestimate need; the guidance advises against it.
n.3: Staying in hospital once medically fit risks deconditioning and delays recovery.

8.q: Beatrice, 67, has rheumatoid arthritis. She tells the nurse she would like to be more active but finds long walks painful. She enjoys swimming and used to garden. Which response best supports Beatrice to make an informed choice within the limits of her condition?
o: Explain that exercise is unsuitable for people with rheumatoid arthritis
Advise her to walk 10,000 steps a day, as recommended for everyone
Explore activities she enjoys and can manage, and agree a goal together
Give her a leaflet on exercise and ask her to decide at home
8.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.9: use appropriate communication skills and strength-based approaches to support people to make informed choices about their care within the limits of illness or disability. NICE PH49 (2014): agree goals and develop action plans with the person.

n.0: This is inaccurate and removes her choice; activity within her limits can be supported.
n.1: A fixed target ignores her pain and preferences; P2.9 asks for strength-based, person-centred support.
n.3: A leaflet alone misses the chance to build on her strengths and agree a plan with her.

8.q: Nurse Ola realises she gave Leon, 45, 10 mg of oral morphine solution instead of the prescribed 5 mg, 20 minutes ago. Leon is alert with a respiratory rate of 16 and no sedation. What should Ola do?
o: Rewrite the chart entry to 5 mg to avoid confusing the next nurse
Monitor Leon, inform the prescriber, tell Leon and report the incident
Observe Leon and report the error if he shows any signs of harm
Inform the ward manager and leave her to decide whether to tell Leon
8.w: Medication incidents are reported and reflected on (P6.8; NMC Code 19): the priority is the person's safety (monitoring sedation and respiratory rate), then informing the prescriber, being open with Leon (professional duty of candour), and reporting through the local system feeding LFPSE.

n.0: Altering the record to hide an error is dishonest and breaches the Code.
n.2: Incidents, including those without harm, are reported so that learning can occur.
n.3: The professional duty of candour is personal; Ola should be open with Leon herself.

8.q: Winston, 69, has a long-term urinary catheter. A healthcare support worker is about to empty his drainage bag into a single-use jug. There is a small risk of splashing. Which PPE is most appropriate for this task?
o: Sterile gloves and a disposable apron to protect the closed system
A disposable apron, with hand hygiene once the bag is emptied
Non-sterile gloves, a long-sleeved gown and an FFP3 respirator
Non-sterile gloves and apron, plus eye protection if splashing is likely
8.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves are worn when exposure to body fluids is anticipated, aprons protect clothing when contamination is likely, and eye or face protection is worn when splashing to the face is anticipated. Sterility is not needed to empty a drainage bag.

n.0: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures; emptying a bag via the outlet needs non-sterile gloves.
n.1: Contact with urine is anticipated, so gloves are needed as well as the apron.
n.2: Gowns are for extensive splashing and FFP3 respirators for airborne risks; neither applies to emptying a catheter bag.

8.q: Mr Hale, 45, has depression and took an overdose of paracetamol last year. His GP is choosing an antidepressant and asks the practice nurse which option carries the lowest risk in overdose. Which is most appropriate?
o: Dosulepin, as it can be started by the GP
Sertraline, as SSRIs are safer in overdose
Lofepramine, as tricyclics are safest in overdose
Amitriptyline, as it also helps his sleep
8.w: The BNF states SSRIs are better tolerated and safer in overdose than other antidepressant classes; amitriptyline and dosulepin are particularly dangerous in overdose. NICE NG225 1.13.1 asks prescribers to consider toxicity in overdose for people who have self-harmed.

n.0: Dosulepin is particularly dangerous in overdose and should be started by a specialist.
n.2: Tricyclics, including lofepramine, carry more overdose risk than SSRIs, although lofepramine is less dangerous than other tricyclics.
n.3: Amitriptyline is particularly dangerous in overdose.

8.q: Mr Kaur, 50, is reducing his sertraline with his GP's agreement. Four days after his last reduction he feels anxious and dizzy and tells the nurse he is frightened his depression is coming back. Which response best reflects NICE NG222?
o: These are common withdrawal symptoms rather than a relapse
These symptoms mean you have become addicted to sertraline
These symptoms will last for at least six months after stopping
This shows your depression has returned, so restart the full dose
8.w: NG222 1.4.19: if withdrawal symptoms occur, reassure the person that they are not having a relapse, that these symptoms are common, and that relapse does not usually happen as soon as an antidepressant is stopped or reduced.

n.1: Withdrawal symptoms do not mean addiction; they reflect the body adjusting to the change.
n.2: Withdrawal symptoms usually resolve within 1 to 2 weeks, although some last longer.
n.3: Early symptoms after a reduction are more likely withdrawal than relapse, so a full restart is not the first response.

8.q: Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool (MITT), Lucy is triaging casualties after an explosion at a shopping centre. A man with cuts to his face and arms is walking around asking for help, with no catastrophic bleeding. Which category should she assign?
o: P2
P3
P1
Dead
8.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) first checks for catastrophic bleeding (P1); if absent, anyone who is walking is categorised P3 (minor) before further physiological assessment (P6.12).

n.0: P2 is reached after the walking, breathing, voice and respiratory rate steps in a casualty who cannot walk.
n.2: P1 is for catastrophic bleeding or abnormal findings later in the algorithm; a walking casualty without catastrophic bleeding is not P1.
n.3: The man is walking and talking; 'dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened.

8.q: Mr Wood, 68, has severe depression. He has stopped eating much and tells the nurse that his insides have rotted away and that he is already dead. His mood has not improved on sertraline. What does NICE NG222 recommend?
o: Stopping the sertraline and starting an antipsychotic in its place
Group behavioural activation as the next step
Specialist referral and an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic
Doubling the sertraline dose and reviewing him in 3 months
8.w: He has depression with psychotic (nihilistic) symptoms. NG222 1.12.1-1.12.2: refer to specialist mental health services and consider combining an antidepressant with an antipsychotic such as olanzapine or quetiapine.

n.0: NICE combines the drugs rather than replacing the antidepressant.
n.1: Group therapy does not address severe psychotic depression; psychological therapy follows improvement of psychotic symptoms.
n.3: A 3-month wait is unsafe with psychotic features and poor intake.

8.q: Bella, 20, is in the third day of a refeeding plan on a specialist unit. She becomes weak and breathless and develops ankle oedema. Which action is the priority?
o: Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium urgently
Check her sodium and glucose and continue the plan
Increase her calories to speed up weight restoration
Stop feeding until her next weekly medical review
8.w: These are features of refeeding syndrome, which usually occurs in the first days of refeeding with low phosphate, potassium and magnesium. Urgent bloods and medical review guide correction (NG69 refeeding protocol referencing MEED).

n.1: Sodium and glucose miss the key electrolyte, phosphate.
n.2: Increasing calories now could worsen refeeding syndrome.
n.3: Stopping feeding for a week risks under-nutrition, which MEED also warns against.

8.q: Lewis, 30, detained under section 3, demands to go to the shop now. His section 17 leave has been suspended by his responsible clinician after a recent incident. He becomes angry. Which response by the nurse best avoids escalating this flashpoint?
o: 'That's the decision, so you'll have to wait for the ward round.'
'You know the rules. Keep shouting and you will lose more privileges.'
'I can see you're frustrated. Leave is paused; can I help another way?'
'Fine, I will walk you to the shop now if you calm down first, okay?'
8.w: Refusing a request is a known flashpoint (NICE NG10 1.3.15). The nurse should acknowledge feelings, explain clearly and respectfully, and offer realistic choices, using verbal and non-verbal skills to avoid provoking aggression (NG10 1.3.17).

n.0: A flat refusal without empathy or alternatives is dismissive and likely to provoke further anger.
n.1: Threats of sanctions are confrontational and likely to escalate; restrictive responses must never be used as punishment (NG10 1.4.6).
n.3: Taking him out would breach the RC's suspension of leave under section 17.

8.q: Mavis, 81, has died on a medical ward. Her two sons arrive an hour later and say they are unsure whether they want to see her body, as they have never seen someone who has died. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Tell them viewing is possible once she has reached the funeral director
Offer them the chance to see her and prepare them for what to expect
Advise them not to view her so they remember her as she was in life
Explain that viewing on the ward is allowed after the doctor's review
8.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): all key contacts should be offered the opportunity to view the deceased; there is evidence that, even in traumatic circumstances, key contacts found this helpful. Viewing can occur in acute hospitals, some hospices or later at the funeral directors. Prepare people sensitively for changes to the body.

n.0: Viewing can take place in hospitals and hospices, so there is no need to delay it until later.
n.2: Hospice UK guidance says all key contacts should be offered the chance to view; many find it helpful.
n.3: Viewing does not depend on a doctor's review once death has been verified.

8.q: Raymond, 74, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He usually wet shaves with a blade razor and asks for help to shave while in hospital. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply pressure to any cuts for 30 seconds afterwards
Use an electric razor to reduce the risk of bleeding
Postpone shaving until his anticoagulant is stopped
Use a new disposable blade razor and press gently
8.w: Annexe B 4.3: when assisting with shaving, consider risks such as anticoagulation. An electric razor reduces the risk of cuts and bleeding in people taking anticoagulants such as apixaban.

n.0: This responds to cuts rather than preventing them.
n.2: His anticoagulant is needed for stroke prevention and shaving is part of his personal care.
n.3: A blade razor still risks cuts that bleed more with anticoagulation.

8.q: A nurse uses the SUSS test when assessing a young person with anorexia nervosa. What does this test assess?
o: Grip strength in the person's dominant hand
Walking speed over a measured 10 metres
Muscle power sitting up and rising from a squat
Postural drop in blood pressure on standing
8.w: The Sit Up Squat Stand (SUSS) test in the MEED tool scores proximal muscle power: rising from lying to sitting and from squatting to standing. A score of 0 to 1 is a red flag.

n.0: Grip strength is used in other nutrition assessments, not SUSS.
n.1: Walking speed is not part of SUSS.
n.3: Postural blood pressure is a separate MEED item.

8.q: At her booking appointment, a midwife asks Freya, 26, about her mental health. What does one of the two depression identification questions in NICE CG192 ask about?
o: Feeling down, depressed or hopeless in the last month
Feeling low on most days over the whole past year
Any past treatment for depression or anxiety
Feeling unable to cope since the pregnancy began
8.w: CG192 1.5.4: at first contact or booking and in the early postnatal period, consider asking: 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?' and 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?'.

n.1: The NICE questions cover the past month, not the past year.
n.2: Past treatment is asked about separately (CG192 1.5.9) and is not an identification question.
n.3: Coping since pregnancy is not one of the two CG192 identification questions.

8.q: Tariq, 8, has anaphylaxis after eating peanuts at a hospital clinic. What dose of IM adrenaline should be given?
o: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL of 1 mg/mL)
500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL)
100 micrograms (0.1 mL of 1 mg/mL)
8.w: RCUK anaphylaxis doses (1 mg/mL): over 12 years 500 micrograms; 6-12 years 300 micrograms; 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms; under 6 months 100-150 micrograms.

n.0: 150 micrograms is the dose for 6 months to 6 years.
n.2: 500 micrograms is for adults and children over 12.
n.3: 100 micrograms is within the range for infants under 6 months.

8.q: Mr Novak, 48, starts telling the nurse about his worries about returning to work after a heart attack, then stops mid-sentence and looks down. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Use a gentle prompt such as "Go on" and wait
Change the subject to his discharge medicines
Summarise what he has said and close the conversation
Reassure him that everything will be fine at work
8.w: Annexe A 1.2: use prompts and positive verbal and non-verbal reinforcement. Minimal prompts and silence encourage the person to continue (Annexe A 1.1 active listening).

n.1: Moving on closes the conversation just as he is opening up.
n.2: Summarising can help, but closing now prevents him finishing his thought.
n.3: This is false reassurance that dismisses his concern.

8.q: During a morning shift, a nurse notices that Omar, 44, who is usually sociable, is sitting alone, clenching his fists, staring at another patient and muttering. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Move the other patient off the ward for the rest of the day
Increase his observation level to continuous and inform security
Approach calmly, say he seems upset and ask what is troubling him
Offer him PRN lorazepam straight away to prevent an incident
8.w: NICE NG10 1.3.13 and 1.3.17: build a close working relationship, sensitively monitor changes in mood or composure that may lead to aggression, and communicate respect and empathy. Early engagement on noticing warning signs is the first step before any restrictive measure.

n.0: Removing another patient disrupts their care and does not address Omar's distress.
n.1: Observation should be used after positive engagement fails (NG10 1.4.12); jumping to continuous observation and security is premature.
n.3: PRN medication is part of de-escalation, but the first step is to engage and understand what is wrong.

8.q: Brenda, 58, completed a bowel screening kit six months ago and the result was normal. She now tells the nurse she has had blood in her stools and looser bowel movements for four weeks. What should the nurse advise?
o: Wait for her next routine kit, due in about 18 months' time
See her GP about these symptoms now, despite the normal screen
Her normal screening result means bowel cancer can be ruled out
Request an extra screening kit to repeat the test this month
8.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): screening identifies increased risk in apparently healthy people; even with a normal result you could still develop the condition, and people with symptoms should speak to a GP. Screening tests are not 100% accurate (false negatives occur).

n.0: Symptoms need GP assessment now; screening is for people without symptoms.
n.2: A normal (screen-negative) result means low risk at the time; it does not exclude disease developing later.
n.3: Screening is not a test for symptoms; she needs clinical assessment by her GP.

8.q: Mr Kaye, 61, is on a cardiac monitor. The monitor alarms and shows a chaotic trace resembling ventricular fibrillation. The nurse looks across and sees Mr Kaye sitting up, talking and brushing his teeth. What should the nurse do first?
o: Go to him, assess him and check the electrodes and leads
Put out a cardiac arrest call and bring the defibrillator
Silence the alarm and review the monitor trace later
Give a precordial thump to restore a normal rhythm
8.w: Monitor traces must be interpreted with the patient. Movement such as tooth brushing commonly causes artefact resembling VF. The nurse should assess him directly and check electrode contact; a cardiac arrest is confirmed by assessing the patient (RCUK 2025), not by the monitor alone.

n.1: He is conscious and talking, so he is not in cardiac arrest.
n.2: Silencing without assessing the patient risks missing a genuine problem.
n.3: A precordial thump is not indicated in a conscious person and is not a response to artefact.

8.q: Siân, a nurse who has worked in England, moves to a hospital in Cardiff. She asks which body independently inspects NHS healthcare services in Wales. What is the correct answer?
o: The Nursing and Midwifery Council
Healthcare Improvement Scotland
Healthcare Inspectorate Wales
The Care Quality Commission
8.w: Health is devolved across the UK. Healthcare Inspectorate Wales inspects healthcare in Wales; the Care Quality Commission regulates in England, Healthcare Improvement Scotland in Scotland and the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority in Northern Ireland (P7.2 devolved UK differences).

n.0: The NMC regulates individual nurses, midwives and nursing associates, not services.
n.1: Healthcare Improvement Scotland covers Scotland.
n.3: The CQC regulates health and adult social care services in England only.

8.q: Valerie, 58, is choking in a hospital café. She cannot cough, speak or breathe but remains conscious. Help has been called. What should you do first?
o: Perform a blind finger sweep
Give up to 5 back blows
Start chest compressions
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts
8.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): for severe obstruction in a conscious person, give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat until relieved.

n.0: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in and are not part of the algorithm.
n.2: Chest compressions start once she becomes unconscious.
n.3: Abdominal thrusts come after 5 back blows.

8.q: Ms Coe, 30, received IM lorazepam for rapid tranquillisation 30 minutes ago. She is now awake, calm and talking. She has no physical health problems, has not taken alcohol or drugs, was not restrained and received a standard dose. How often should her physical observations be done?
o: Every 4 hours for the whole of the next day
Every 15 minutes for the next 4 hours
Once, an hour after the injection was given
At least hourly until there are no concerns
8.w: NG10 1.4.45: after rapid tranquillisation, monitor side effects, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and level of consciousness at least every hour until there are no further concerns. 15-minute monitoring applies if any listed risk factor is present; none applies to Ms Coe.

n.0: Four-hourly checks are less frequent than the NG10 minimum of hourly.
n.1: 15-minute monitoring is for people who appear asleep or sedated, exceed the BNF maximum, have taken drugs or alcohol, have a physical health problem or were harmed by restraint.
n.2: A single check does not meet NG10, which requires ongoing monitoring until there are no concerns.

8.q: A red cell transfusion for Graham, 66, started at 14:00. Baseline pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate were recorded at 13:30 and were normal. According to BSH guidance, when should the next set of observations be taken?
o: At 14:30, 30 minutes after the start
At 15:00, 1 hour after the start
At 14:15, 15 minutes after the start
At the end of the unit, within 60 minutes
8.w: BSH (2017) observations: baseline no more than 60 minutes before starting, then pulse, blood pressure and temperature 15 minutes after the start of each unit, and again no more than 60 minutes after the end. Severe reactions often occur early in the unit.

n.0: The BSH timepoint is 15 minutes, not 30.
n.1: Waiting an hour misses the early period when serious reactions usually start.
n.3: End-of-unit observations are needed, but an observation at 15 minutes comes first.

8.q: Ernest, 84, lacks capacity to decide about his medicines and actively refuses his antiepileptic. The care home manager arranges a best interests meeting about covert administration. According to NICE SC1, who should be involved?
o: The prescriber, the care home manager and the senior carer
Care staff, prescriber, pharmacist and a family member or advocate
The care home manager and the registered nurse on duty that day
The family, who make the final decision as his next of kin
8.w: NICE SC1 (1.15) and RPS/RCN 2019: covert administration follows a best interests meeting involving care home staff, the health professional prescribing, a pharmacist and a family member or advocate, with a documented management plan.

n.0: Without a pharmacist and a family member or advocate the decision lacks key input.
n.2: The prescriber and pharmacist must also be involved, as must family or an advocate.
n.3: Next of kin have no legal power to decide unless they hold a relevant LPA or are deputies; the decision is made by the team in his best interests.

8.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion with a fever of 38.4°C. The doctor requests a catheter specimen of urine (CSU) before antibiotics are started. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
o: Decontaminate hands and aspirate from the sampling port aseptically
Disconnect the bag and collect urine from the end of the catheter
Collect urine from the drainage bag outlet into a sterile pot
Replace the catheter and send a sample from the new catheter
8.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and obtain urine samples from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the drainage system closed.

n.1: Breaking the closed drainage system raises the risk of introducing infection.
n.2: Urine in the bag has stood and may be colonised, so it does not reflect bladder urine.
n.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary; changing it just to obtain a sample is not the CG139 method.

8.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
8.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

8.q: Malik, 35, has been detained under section 3 for 4 months and is ready to spend 3 weeks at home on section 17 leave before possible discharge. What must the responsible clinician do before granting this leave?
o: Obtain written consent to the leave from his nearest relative
Refer his case to the tribunal before the leave begins
Arrange a SOAD certificate to cover his medication on leave
Consider whether a community treatment order would suit him better
8.w: Section 17(2A)-(2B): longer-term leave (more than 7 consecutive days) may not be granted unless the RC first considers whether the patient should be placed on a community treatment order under section 17A instead.

n.0: The nearest relative's consent is not a legal requirement for section 17 leave.
n.1: There is no requirement to refer to a tribunal before granting leave.
n.2: A SOAD certificate depends on the 3-month rule for medication, not on granting leave; the leave rule is to consider a CTO.

8.q: Bethany, 50, is detained under section 3. Her first renewal took effect 5 months ago and the next renewal is due. If renewed, how long will the next period of detention be?
o: Two years
Six months
Three months
One year
8.w: Under section 20 of the 1983 Act a section 3 lasts up to 6 months, may be renewed for a further 6 months, and then for periods of 1 year at a time. Bethany has had the initial 6 months and one 6-month renewal, so the next renewal is for 1 year. (The 2025 Act's shorter periods are not in force.)

n.0: Renewals after the first are for 1 year at a time, not 2 years.
n.1: Six months applies to the initial period and the first renewal; she has already had both.
n.2: Three-month periods are a Mental Health Act 2025 change that is not in force.

8.q: Ms Ali, 20, has written a safety plan with her nurse. She would like her sister and her care team to have a copy, but does not want her parents, with whom she lives, to see it. What should the nurse do?
o: Share it with her parents, as they are her next of kin
Give a copy to everyone in her household to keep her safe
Share it with her sister and the professionals she agrees to
Keep it in the team's records so no family members see it
8.w: NG225 1.11.8: the safety plan is held by the person and shared with family, carers and relevant professionals as decided by the person, so that it is accessible in a crisis. Ms Ali has capacity to decide who sees it.

n.0: 'Next of kin' gives no right to see her plan; she has chosen not to share it with her parents.
n.1: Sharing with her whole household overrides her decision about her parents.
n.3: She wants her sister to have a copy, and the plan should be accessible to her supporters in a crisis.

8.q: Josh, 24, is autistic and finds busy waiting rooms overwhelming, so he has missed two outpatient appointments. Under section 20 of the Equality Act 2010, what is the clinic's duty?
o: Make adjustments if he provides a formal diagnosis letter
Offer him the same appointment process as other patients
Discharge him back to his GP after two missed appointments
Take reasonable steps to avoid his substantial disadvantage
8.w: Equality Act 2010 s20: duty to make reasonable adjustments where a provision, criterion or practice puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage. Proficiency P1.14 and P3.7.

n.0: The duty is to take reasonable steps; insisting on paperwork first delays an adjustment such as a quiet room or first appointment.
n.1: Treating him identically is what causes the disadvantage; s20 requires adjustments.
n.2: Discharging without adjustment ignores the disadvantage caused by his disability and the s20 duty.

8.q: Ravi, 55, is a day after a hernia repair. He is anxious and says he 'cannot catch his breath'. RR 26, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 128/80, alert, temperature 37.2°C. You have called for help. Which action best reflects the ABCDE approach?
o: Start oxygen, then continue to C and D while reassessing his breathing
Complete C, D and E fully before deciding whether he needs oxygen
Reassure him that anxiety is common after surgery and observe hourly
Wait for the doctor to examine him before giving any treatment
8.w: ABCDE treats each life-threatening problem as it is found and then reassesses. Hypoxaemia (93% with RR 26) is a B problem: start oxygen to a target of 94-98% (BTS; NG253 rec 1.10.1), then continue through C, D and E, re-evaluating after each intervention.

n.1: Completing the rest of the assessment first delays treatment of a breathing problem already identified.
n.2: Attributing tachypnoea and low saturation to anxiety risks missing a pulmonary embolism or other serious cause.
n.3: Nurses start initial treatment within competence while help arrives; waiting delays care (Code 15).

8.q: Liam, 33, is on a community treatment order and has been well for a year. The local authority proposes to end his section 117 after-care because he is 'stable'. What is the correct legal position?
o: After-care can end if the local authority decides he no longer needs it
After-care ends once he has had 12 months of stability
After-care can end once his CMHT care coordinator agrees
After-care cannot be ended while he remains on the CTO
8.w: Section 117(2) provides that the ICB and local authority cannot be satisfied that a community patient no longer needs after-care while he remains on a CTO (COP15 33.6). Even afterwards, both bodies must agree.

n.0: Both the ICB and the local authority must be satisfied, and neither can be while he remains on a CTO (s117(2)).
n.1: There is no automatic end after an arbitrary period (COP15 33.21).
n.2: The care coordinator's view informs the decision but cannot end after-care during a CTO.

8.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
8.q: Ms Young, 25, contacts NHS Talking Therapies with mild anxiety for 2 months. She is working and has no risk concerns. Under the stepped care model, what is she most likely to be offered first?
o: Referral to the community mental health team
Assessment for a day hospital
High-intensity individual CBT
Low-intensity guided self-help
8.w: NHS Talking Therapies uses stepped care: low-intensity interventions such as guided self-help (often with a psychological wellbeing practitioner) for milder problems, stepping up to high-intensity therapy if needed (CG113 stepped care).

n.0: CMHTs serve people with severe or complex needs.
n.1: Day hospital care is for severe illness, not mild anxiety.
n.2: High-intensity CBT is a later step for more severe or persistent problems.

8.q: Mr Ford, 61, has treatment-resistant depression and has been started on phenelzine by a specialist. He asks the nurse which foods he should avoid. Which advice is correct?
o: Mature cheese, yeast extracts and cured meats
Milk and dairy products within 2 hours of a dose
Grapefruit juice and other citrus fruit
Leafy green vegetables high in vitamin K
8.w: Monoamine-oxidase inhibitors such as phenelzine have dangerous interactions with tyramine-rich foods (for example mature cheese, yeast extracts, cured or fermented meats), which can cause a hypertensive crisis (BNF antidepressant treatment summary).

n.1: Separating dairy from doses applies to some antibiotics, not MAOIs.
n.2: Grapefruit interacts with some other medicines but is not the MAOI tyramine risk.
n.3: Vitamin K foods are relevant to warfarin, not MAOIs.

8.q: Amira, 29, is admitted to a gynaecology ward. Her notes record a history of sexual assault. When the nurse reaches to hold her hand during an examination, Amira flinches. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop, ask whether touch is acceptable and explain each step first
Ask a colleague to hold her hand in place of the nurse
Continue gently, as touch is a recognised comforting technique
Stop all communication until the examination is finished
8.w: Annexe A 1.3: use appropriate non-verbal communication, including touch, eye contact and personal space. Code 1.1 and 4.2: treat with respect and gain consent before any action.

n.1: Changing who touches her does not address whether she wants touch at all.
n.2: Comforting touch is only therapeutic when welcome; her reaction shows it is not.
n.3: Withdrawing communication leaves her anxious and unsupported.

8.q: Leon, 39, stopped smoking three months ago with support. He tells the nurse he is worried he will start again at a family wedding next month, where many guests smoke. What is the most appropriate support?
o: Help him make an 'if-then' plan for moments when he is tempted
Advise him to avoid weddings and other social events for a year
Close his episode of care, as his quit attempt is now complete
Reassure him that relapse is rare once three months have passed
8.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) recs 6 and 10: interventions should address relapse and recognise that it is common; help people maintain change by giving them well-rehearsed action plans such as 'if-then' plans, social support and feedback and monitoring for at least 1 year.

n.1: Avoiding all social contact is unrealistic and removes social support that helps people maintain change.
n.2: PH49 rec 10 recommends feedback and monitoring for at least a year to help maintain change.
n.3: PH49 recognises that relapse is common and asks for interventions to address it.

8.q: Mr Evans, 77, is being discharged home with a new leg ulcer that will need daily dressings from the district nursing team. The ward nurse hesitates to send details of his wound and medicines, worried about breaching confidentiality. Which Caldicott principle best guides her?
o: Inform patients and service users about how their information is used
Sharing for individual care matters as much as protecting confidentiality
Use the minimum necessary personal confidential data for each purpose
Access to personal confidential data should be on a strict need-to-know basis
8.w: Caldicott principle 7 (National Data Guardian, 2020): the duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty to protect patient confidentiality. Sharing with the district nurses supports his direct care.

n.0: Informing patients (principle 8) is good practice but does not resolve her concern about sharing for direct care.
n.2: Minimum necessary data (principle 3) shapes how much is shared, but the nurse's hesitation is about whether to share at all.
n.3: Need-to-know access (principle 4) limits who sees data; the district nurses clearly need to know.

8.q: Kyle, 22, has had one episode of psychosis and smokes high-strength cannabis every day. He says it helps him relax and asks whether it matters. Which response is most accurate?
o: Cannabis affects mood but is not linked with psychosis
Cannabis eases psychotic symptoms, so it can be a coping aid
Cannabis can worsen psychotic symptoms and raise relapse risk
Cannabis harms mental health when combined with alcohol
8.w: Cannabis, especially high-potency forms, is associated with developing psychosis, more severe symptoms and higher relapse rates. Honest, non-judgemental information supports harm reduction (P2.4).

n.0: There is a well-established link between cannabis and psychosis.
n.1: Any short-term relaxation is outweighed by worsening psychosis and relapse.
n.3: The psychosis risk applies to cannabis use itself, not just combined with alcohol.

8.q: At handover a colleague describes Mrs Evans, 91, who is medically fit for discharge but waiting for a care package, as 'just another bed-blocker'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Challenge the language and refocus on her needs
Laugh it off to keep handover moving quickly
Report the colleague to the NMC after the shift
Raise it at the colleague's appraisal in a few months
8.w: Code 1.1 and 1.3: treat people with respect and avoid assumptions; Code 3.4: challenge poor practice and discriminatory attitudes. Age is a protected characteristic (Equality Act 2010 s4).

n.1: Letting it pass condones an ageist label; Code 3.4 requires discriminatory attitudes to be challenged.
n.2: A first remark is best challenged directly and locally; NMC referral is for serious fitness to practise concerns.
n.3: Waiting months misses the chance to challenge it now and protect Mrs Evans's dignity.

8.q: Following a fall caused by a missed risk assessment, Mrs Doyle, 80, develops anxiety and disturbed sleep. The hospital is deciding whether this is prolonged psychological harm under the statutory duty of candour. Which threshold applies?
o: Psychological harm lasting at least 14 days in total over the admission
Psychological harm lasting at least 3 months after discharge
Psychological harm lasting, or likely to last, 28 continuous days or more
Psychological harm needing a referral to mental health services
8.w: Reg 20(7): prolonged psychological harm means psychological harm which a service user has experienced, or is likely to experience, for a continuous period of at least 28 days.

n.0: The regulation uses 28 continuous days, not 14 days.
n.1: The threshold is 28 continuous days, not three months.
n.3: Referral is not the legal test; the test is duration of at least 28 continuous days.

8.q: Kemi, 22, is restrained and secluded for long periods, sometimes without clothing, and staff mock her during restraint. Which Human Rights Act right is most clearly at risk of breach?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial and fair hearing
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 12, the right to marry and to found a family
8.w: Article 3 is an absolute right prohibiting torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. Humiliating restrictive practices such as mocking a restrained patient or unjustified removal of clothing in seclusion risk breaching it. NG10 says people in seclusion should keep their clothing.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings, not treatment during restraint.
n.1: Article 9 concerns freedom of belief, not humiliating treatment.
n.3: Article 12 concerns marriage and is not relevant here.

8.q: On a home visit, community nurse Faye watches Mrs Dobson give her husband his insulin. She injects into the same small area of his abdomen each time and Faye notices lumpy skin there. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to review the insulin dose at the next appointment
Show her how to rotate sites, observe her practice and document it
Take over all of Mr Dobson's insulin injections from now on
Leave an injection technique leaflet for Mrs Dobson to read
8.w: Nurses monitor and evaluate the quality of care delivered by lay carers (P5.7). Teaching site rotation, observing Mrs Dobson's technique and recording the plan supports safe care and independence; lumpy injection sites can alter insulin absorption.

n.0: Dose review may be needed later, but the technique problem must be addressed directly now.
n.2: Taking over removes the couple's independence when the issue can be corrected by teaching.
n.3: A leaflet without demonstration and observation does not confirm the technique has changed.

8.q: A newly qualified nurse is learning which ward medicines must be entered in the controlled drugs register. Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, which of these medicines is a Schedule 2 controlled drug?
o: Diazepam 5 mg tablets
Oxycodone 5 mg in 5 mL oral solution
Tramadol 50 mg capsules
Midazolam injection 10 mg in 2 mL
8.w: Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 (Home Office controlled drugs list), oxycodone is in Schedule 2, alongside morphine, diamorphine and fentanyl, and needs a CD register entry (NICE NG46). Midazolam and tramadol are Schedule 3; diazepam is Schedule 4 Part 1.

n.0: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 Part 1 benzodiazepine.
n.2: Tramadol is in Schedule 3.
n.3: Midazolam is a Schedule 3 controlled drug, although many hospitals record it in the register by local policy.

8.q: A nurse is about to take blood for a full blood count and urea and electrolytes from Mrs Ellis, 66. She has a peripheral cannula in her left forearm with an IV infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride running. Which site is most appropriate?
o: The cannula itself, after briefly pausing the infusion
Her left antecubital fossa, above the cannula
A vein in her right arm, away from the infusion
A vein in the back of her left hand, below the cannula
8.w: Blood taken from a limb with an infusion running can be diluted or contaminated by the fluid, giving falsely altered results (for example sodium, potassium or glucose). The opposite arm should be used (Annexe B 2.2).

n.0: Sampling from an infusing cannula risks contaminated results and is not the most appropriate choice here.
n.1: Sampling above an infusion on the same arm risks contamination with the infused fluid.
n.3: The same limb is still affected by the infusion; the opposite arm is preferred.

8.q: Ted, 67, has a PCA pump after bowel surgery. He is very drowsy, difficult to rouse, with RR 8 per minute and pinpoint pupils. His wife says he has been pressing the button for him while he slept. What is the priority?
o: Stop the PCA, support his breathing and call for urgent help
Explain to his wife that Ted must press the PCA button himself
Encourage him to take deep breaths and press the button less
Reduce the PCA bolus dose and recheck his observations in 1 hour
8.w: RR 8 scores 3 on NEWS2 and drowsiness scores 3: this is opioid toxicity. Stop the infusion, open and support the airway, give oxygen and get urgent help so that naloxone can be given as prescribed (P4.15). The PCA safety principle is that the person alone presses the button; this is addressed after the emergency.

n.1: Education is needed, but only after treating life-threatening respiratory depression.
n.2: He cannot respond reliably and needs emergency treatment, not encouragement.
n.3: Altering the dose and waiting an hour leaves respiratory depression untreated.

8.q: Laura, a staff nurse, has worried for several weeks that the night skill mix on her ward is unsafe, with frequent missed observations. She has not yet raised it with anyone. According to NMC guidance, who should she raise it with first?
o: The NMC, so that it can investigate the ward's safety
The trust chief executive, as the person accountable for staffing
The Care Quality Commission, as the regulator for the ward
Her line manager, verbally or in writing, keeping a record
8.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: stage 1 line manager (verbally or in writing, keep a record); stage 2 designated person; stage 3 higher level; stage 4 regulator or helpline. Code 16.1.

n.0: The NMC regulates individual professionals; this is a system concern for the line manager first.
n.1: A higher level in the organisation is stage 3, after the line manager and designated person.
n.2: Going to a regulator is stage 4 of the NMC guidance, used if internal routes fail or are unsuitable.

8.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
8.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

8.q: Sam, 26, has a learning disability and often hits out in the noisy dining room at mealtimes. The team wants to use positive behaviour support. What should they do first?
o: Assess what triggers the behaviour and what it achieves
Increase his sedation before every mealtime
Use restraint whenever he begins to hit out
Withdraw meals in the dining room as a planned consequence
8.w: Annexe A 3.9: positive behaviour support approaches. PBS uses functional assessment to understand behaviour and changes the environment proactively.

n.1: Medication as first response is not PBS and may cause harm.
n.2: Restraint is reactive; PBS starts with understanding the function of behaviour.
n.3: Punishment is not part of PBS and may breach his rights.

8.q: Linda, 64, has IV fluids running through a volumetric infusion pump. The pump alarms 'downstream occlusion'. What should you check first?
o: The line, clamps and cannula site for a blockage
The pump's battery level and mains connection
The fluid bag for an air bubble near the top
The prescription chart for the next bag due
8.w: A downstream occlusion means resistance between the pump and the patient: check for closed clamps, kinked tubing and the cannula site (phlebitis, infiltration or a positional cannula) before restarting (Annexe B 5.9).

n.1: Battery alarms are separate from occlusion alarms.
n.2: Air at the top of the bag is above the pump and does not cause a downstream occlusion.
n.3: The prescription does not explain an occlusion alarm.

8.q: A nursing student asks when it is lawful to restrain an adult who lacks capacity, for example by holding his hand to stop him pulling out a cannula during essential IV treatment. Which statement best describes the legal position under the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
o: It is lawful once the person has been assessed as lacking capacity
It needs a DoLS authorisation in place before any restraint
It must be necessary to prevent harm and proportionate to that harm
It is lawful once a close relative has agreed to the restraint
8.w: Under MCA 2005 s6, restraint in connection with care or treatment is permitted if the person doing it reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to the person lacking capacity, and it is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. It must also be in best interests (s1(5)) and the least restrictive option (s1(6)).

n.0: Lacking capacity is a precondition, but restraint also needs necessity and proportionality.
n.1: Brief proportionate restraint under s6 does not itself need a DoLS authorisation; DoLS concerns deprivation of liberty.
n.3: A relative's agreement does not make restraint lawful; they cannot consent for an adult without a relevant LPA.

8.q: Derek, 59, has a history of alcohol misuse. He has eaten almost nothing for 7 days and his BMI is 17.8 kg/m². Nutrition support is planned. Using NICE CG32 criteria, what is his refeeding risk and the appropriate starting approach?
o: High risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
Low risk: start at full requirements of 25-35 kcal/kg/day
Moderate risk: start at 50% of requirements without thiamin
No risk: offer normal ward meals without any monitoring
8.w: NICE CG32: high refeeding risk includes two or more of BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little or no intake for over 5 days, or alcohol misuse. Derek has three. Start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing slowly, and give thiamin and vitamin B before and during the first 10 days, with electrolyte monitoring.

n.1: Full requirements in a high-risk person can precipitate refeeding syndrome.
n.2: He meets the high-risk criteria, and thiamin is needed.
n.3: Unmonitored feeding ignores his high refeeding risk.

8.q: Ana, 33, has moderate depression. During her assessment she says she feels 'there is no point any more'. The student nurse is worried about raising suicide. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask her directly whether she has thoughts of ending her life
Ask her partner privately whether she has mentioned suicide
Avoid the subject in case asking increases her risk
Wait for her to raise the topic when she feels ready
8.w: NG222: always ask people with depression directly about suicidal ideation and intent. Asking does not increase risk and allows safety planning (P3.10).

n.1: Collateral history can help but does not replace asking Ana herself.
n.2: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea or increase risk.
n.3: Waiting may miss serious risk that she is hinting at now.

8.q: Which finding should make a nurse consider that a person with suspected sepsis is at higher risk than their NEWS2 score suggests (NICE NG253, 2025)?
o: A pulse of 88 beats per minute
A temperature of 37.9°C
A respiratory rate of 19 per minute
A non-blanching petechial rash
8.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider higher risk than NEWS2 indicates if the person has mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue.

n.0: A pulse of 88 is within the NEWS2 0 band (51-90).
n.1: 37.9°C scores 0 on NEWS2 and is not a higher-risk feature in NG253.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 19 is within the NEWS2 0 band (12-20).

8.q: Jasmine, 22, has a tonic-clonic seizure in a clinic waiting area. She is on the floor near a chair. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Restrain her limbs to prevent injury during the jerking
Give her sips of water as the jerking slows down
Place a padded object between her teeth to protect her tongue
Move objects away, cushion her head and time the seizure
8.w: Seizure first aid: keep the person safe by moving hazards, cushion the head, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, and place in the recovery position when the jerking stops. Seek emergency help for a prolonged seizure (RCUK special circumstances: treat with benzodiazepines).

n.0: Restraining limbs can cause injury to the person and the helper.
n.1: Oral fluids risk aspiration while consciousness is impaired.
n.2: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or obstruct the airway.

8.q: A ward team wants the strongest evidence on whether a new dressing reduces infection in surgical wounds. Which type of study gives the highest level of evidence for this question?
o: An expert consensus opinion paper from specialists
A single large randomised controlled trial
A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
A large prospective cohort study of patients
8.w: Oxford CEBM levels of evidence (therapy): level 1a is a systematic review of randomised controlled trials; expert opinion is level 5. Code 6.1 requires evidence-based information.

n.0: Expert opinion is the lowest level in evidence hierarchies such as the Oxford CEBM levels.
n.1: A well-designed RCT is strong evidence but ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs.
n.3: Cohort studies are observational and rank below RCTs for treatment effects.

8.q: Caroline, an off-duty theatre nurse, hears on the news that a major incident has been declared at her hospital after a building collapse. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make herself available and respond if the trust contacts her
Drive to the scene of the collapse to help the ambulance crews
Go straight to the emergency department to offer her help
Phone the theatre suite to ask whether she should come in
8.w: In a major incident, staff are called in through the trust's coordinated call-in process so that the right skills arrive at the right time and staff remain for later phases. Self-deployment to the scene or hospital can hamper command and control, and phone lines are needed for the response (P6.12).

n.1: Health staff at the scene are deployed by the ambulance service; self-deploying can add to the risk and confusion.
n.2: Self-presenting bypasses the hospital's command structure, and the trust may need her rested for later shifts.
n.3: Calling the department ties up phone lines needed for the incident response.

8.q: During a teaching session, a practice educator lists four sources a nurse might rely on when explaining informed consent: the Mental Capacity Act 2005, the Care Act 2014, the NMC Code and Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]. A student asks which of these is case law made by the courts. Which source should the educator identify?
o: The Mental Capacity Act 2005
The NMC Code, professional standards of practice
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]
The Care Act 2014
8.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 is a Supreme Court judgment, so it is common (case) law. The two Acts are statutes made by Parliament and the Code is a set of professional standards set by the regulator.

n.0: The MCA 2005 is primary legislation (statute) passed by Parliament, not case law.
n.1: The Code is the NMC's professional standards; it is a regulatory document, not a court decision.
n.3: The Care Act 2014 is statute; its safeguarding duties come from Parliament, not a court judgment.

8.q: A community nurse reviews Ms Hart, 24, who has anorexia nervosa. Which single finding is a red (high risk to life) flag on the MEED adult risk tool?
o: Heart rate of 38 beats per minute
Heart rate of 55 beats per minute
Tympanic temperature of 36.2°C
Postural heart rate rise of 15 beats per minute
8.w: MEED (RCPsych CR233) adult red flags include heart rate under 40, BMI under 13, temperature under 35.5°C, postural heart rate rise over 30, systolic BP under 90 and SUSS score 0 to 1.

n.1: A heart rate of 50 to 60 sits in the lower-risk band.
n.2: Above 36°C is low risk on the MEED tool.
n.3: A rise of 10 to 30 is amber, not red.

8.q: Ade, 42, is detained under section 3. On Monday at 10:00 his nearest relative gives the hospital managers written notice that she will discharge him. The responsible clinician believes Ade would be likely to act dangerously to himself if discharged. What should happen?
o: The AMHP can veto the discharge by applying for section 2
The RC must apply to the county court within 7 days to stop the discharge
Ade must be discharged at 10:00 on Monday
The RC can make a barring report within 72 hours, stopping the discharge
8.w: Under section 25 the nearest relative must give at least 72 hours' written notice. Within that period the RC can bar the discharge by reporting that the patient would be likely to act in a manner dangerous to himself or others. The NR then cannot order discharge again for 6 months but can apply to a tribunal.

n.0: A new section 2 would not be a lawful way to defeat an NR order; the statutory route is the RC's barring report.
n.1: No county court application is needed to bar discharge; the RC uses a barring report under s25.
n.2: The NR's order takes effect after 72 hours' notice, and can be barred by the RC within that time.

8.q: Shirley, 66, wants to eat more fruit and vegetables. She knows how to cook and is keen to change. However, her nearest shop sells no fresh food and there is no bus to the supermarket. Using the COM-B model, which component is the main barrier to her behaviour change?
o: Motivation
Health literacy
Capability
Opportunity
8.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014), glossary (COM-B, Michie et al. 2011): for behaviour change a person needs capability (physical and psychological), opportunity (physical and social) and motivation. PH49 gives the example that a healthy diet is harder in an area without shops selling fresh food and with poor transport.

n.0: She is keen to change, so motivation is not the main barrier.
n.1: Health literacy is not one of the three COM-B components, and she understands what to do.
n.2: Shirley has the knowledge and skills to cook, so physical and psychological capability are present.

8.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which national NHS service now receives the patient safety events that staff record through the trust's local reporting system in England. What is the correct answer?
o: The National Reporting and Learning System (NRLS)
The Strategic Executive Information System (StEIS)
The Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service
The MHRA Yellow Card scheme
8.w: LFPSE is the national NHS system for recording and analysing patient safety events. It replaced the NRLS, which was decommissioned on 30 June 2024; organisations record through LFPSE-compliant local systems (NHS England, LFPSE).

n.0: The NRLS was decommissioned on 30 June 2024 and replaced by LFPSE.
n.1: StEIS remains in use for specific serious incident reporting while LFPSE develops; it is not where routine safety events are recorded.
n.3: Yellow Card is the MHRA scheme for suspected adverse drug reactions and device problems, not the general patient safety event system.

8.q: Bernard, 77, is unconscious and nil by mouth. When you give mouth care, you see white patches on his tongue that can be wiped off to leave a red base. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Brush the patches off firmly with a toothbrush at each mouth care
Rinse his mouth with a large volume of water to clear the patches
Report the probable oral thrush so that treatment can be prescribed
Apply petroleum jelly inside his mouth to soothe the area
8.w: White plaques that wipe off leaving a red base suggest oral candidiasis (thrush), which needs assessment and antifungal treatment. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during oral care.

n.0: Firm brushing traumatises the mucosa and does not treat the infection.
n.1: Large-volume rinsing in an unconscious person risks aspiration.
n.3: Petroleum jelly does not treat infection and is not applied inside the mouth.

8.q: Mr Ortiz, 66, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. He is being admitted for elective surgery at an English NHS hospital. Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should the nurse do as part of the admission assessment?
o: Use written notes with him, as these work for all deaf people
Identify, record and flag his communication needs and arrange support
Ask his daughter to interpret during his stay to save time
Note his deafness in the record so staff know to speak more loudly
8.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet information and communication needs related to disability or sensory loss. For a BSL user this means arranging a qualified interpreter and flagging the need.

n.0: BSL is a distinct language; written English may not meet his needs.
n.2: Relying on a relative does not meet his needs and compromises confidentiality and accuracy.
n.3: Speaking louder does not help a profoundly deaf BSL user and does not meet the Standard.

8.q: Mrs Ivy Turner, 86, is admitted with a chest infection and has urinary incontinence at night. A colleague suggests inserting a urinary catheter so her bed stays dry. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Insert the catheter and review it after one week
Use continence pads overnight until she is discharged
Insert the catheter overnight and remove it each morning
Carry out a continence assessment and plan alternatives
8.w: Catheters carry risks of infection and loss of continence function and should not be used for staff convenience.
