o: The information relevant to the dietetic assessment
Everything except the termination of pregnancy
Her full medical history so the dietitian has the whole picture
A summary written after asking her family
9.w: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data. UK GDPR data minimisation also requires data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. Only information relevant to nutrition should be shared.

n.1: Removing one sensitive item still shares other irrelevant data; relevance, not sensitivity, decides what is sent.
n.2: Sending the full history exceeds what the dietitian needs and breaches the minimum necessary principle.
n.3: Families are not a source for a clinical referral, and involving them without consent breaches confidentiality.

9.q: Mrs Lewis, 61, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 10 years and is admitted with a manic relapse. She says she has 'mostly' taken her tablets. What should happen first regarding her lithium?
o: Switch her to valproate as a more reliable mood stabiliser
Check her plasma lithium level to optimise treatment
Stop the lithium because it has failed to prevent relapse
Add an antidepressant to prevent a later depressive episode
9.w: CG185 1.5.8: if the person is already taking lithium, check plasma lithium levels to optimise treatment. Partial adherence is common and the level guides whether dose or adherence is the issue.

n.0: Valproate is not a first choice here and the level has not yet been checked.
n.2: One relapse does not mean lithium has failed; the level and adherence need checking first.
n.3: Adding an antidepressant during mania risks worsening the episode.

9.q: Mrs Lewis, 84, has capacity and wants to return home after a fall. In a meeting her son says firmly that she must go to a care home and answers every question put to her. What is the most appropriate next step for the nurse?
o: Refer for a best interests meeting to settle the disagreement
Ask the son to put his concerns in writing for the discharge team
Speak with Mrs Lewis privately to explore her own views and wishes
Arrange a care home placement as her son holds strong views
9.w: NMC proficiency P1.9 requires decisions based on people's needs and preferences, recognising and addressing factors that may unduly influence them. Speaking with her alone lets her express her wishes freely (Code 2.3, 2.4, 4.1).

n.0: Best interests decisions apply when a person lacks capacity (MCA s4); Mrs Lewis has capacity, so the decision is hers.
n.1: This may record his concerns but leaves the undue influence unaddressed and does not establish what Mrs Lewis wants.
n.3: The son's views do not replace the decision of a person with capacity; Code 1.3 and P1.9 require decisions based on her needs and preferences.

9.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
9.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

9.q: Mrs Turner, 72, had a hip replacement two days ago. Her son tells the nurse at visiting time that his mother 'seems confused and is seeing things on the curtains', which started this afternoon. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the son to stay with her to settle her for the night
Note it and ask the night staff to see if it continues
Reassure the son that this is common after an anaesthetic
Assess her for delirium and record the reported change
9.w: NICE CG103 recs 1.3.1 and 1.5.1-1.5.2: recent changes or fluctuations (including hallucinations) may be reported by relatives and should prompt assessment with an appropriate tool; changes must be documented.

n.0: Family presence can help, but it does not replace assessment of a new change.
n.1: Deferring to night staff delays assessment of an acute change.
n.2: Dismissing a new change risks missing delirium and its cause.

9.q: A staff nurse uses a public social media profile that states she is a registered nurse at the local hospital. Which post would most clearly breach the Code?
o: Sharing the NHS flu vaccination campaign with her followers
Celebrating her own nursing graduation with a family photo
Posting a link to an NMC consultation on the Code
Urging followers, as a nurse, to vote for a political party
9.w: Code 21.5: never use your status as a registered professional to promote causes that are not related to health. Code 20.7 also cautions against expressing personal political beliefs inappropriately.

n.0: Promoting a public health message is related to health and supports Code 3.1.
n.1: A personal photo with no patient information does not breach the Code.
n.2: Sharing professional regulatory information is not a breach.

9.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
9.q: Liam, 23, has depression. After failing his driving test he tells the nurse: 'I failed that, so I am a failure at everything I do.' Which thinking error is this?
o: Personalisation
Catastrophising
Mind reading
Overgeneralising
9.w: Overgeneralisation draws a sweeping conclusion from a single event. Naming the thinking error is a CBT technique that helps the person examine and test the thought (Annexe A 3.6).

n.0: Personalisation takes responsibility for events outside one's control.
n.1: Catastrophising predicts the worst possible outcome.
n.2: Mind reading assumes knowledge of what others think.

9.q: Charlie, a mental health nurse in England, asks in October 2026 whether the Mental Health Act 2025 has replaced the 1983 Act for detentions on his ward. Which statement is correct?
o: The 2025 Act received Royal Assent, but most provisions are not yet in force
The 2025 Act applies to new detentions; the 1983 Act applies to existing ones
The 2025 Act is still a Bill and has not yet completed its parliamentary stages
The 2025 Act is fully in force and has replaced the 1983 Act in England
9.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions (including changes to sections 3 and 4) were not in force at October 2026. The Mental Health Act 1983 as amended remains the current law for detention (BUILD-PLAN unsettled law note; P7.4 implications of current and future health policy).

n.1: There is no rule of this kind; detentions continue under the 1983 Act as amended until provisions are commenced.
n.2: The Act completed its passage and received Royal Assent in December 2025.
n.3: Most provisions of the 2025 Act await commencement, so the 1983 Act as amended still applies.

9.q: Mr Ito, 38, has a head injury. On assessment his eyes open to pressure on the fingertip, he is talking but disorientated about time and place, and he localises to a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
9.w: GCS: eye opening to pressure = 2; confused speech = 4; localising = 5. Total 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 out of 15 (range 3-15). Any fall in GCS after head injury needs urgent escalation.

n.0: Orientated speech scores 5 and obeying commands 6; he is confused and localises.
n.1: Eye opening to speech scores 3; he opens his eyes only to pressure, which scores 2.
n.2: Inappropriate words score 3; he is talking in sentences but confused, which scores 4.

9.q: Mary, 74, had a hip replacement 8 hours ago. She has not passed urine since surgery, says she needs to go but cannot, and has lower abdominal discomfort. Which action is most appropriate first?
o: Restrict her fluids until she passes urine
Give her a laxative to relieve the discomfort
Insert a catheter without discussing it with her
Assess her bladder volume with a bladder scanner
9.w: Annexe B 6.4: recognise and respond to retention. A bladder scan assesses residual volume to guide whether catheterisation is needed, which is then performed with her consent and in line with local policy.

n.0: Restricting fluids does not treat retention and risks dehydration.
n.1: A laxative does not address urinary retention.
n.2: Catheterisation needs assessment and valid consent (Code 4.2).

9.q: Mr Evans, 76, is usually independent and has no psychiatric history. Over the last 24 hours on an older adults' ward he has started seeing insects on the walls, is unsure of the day and drifts in and out of conversation. What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Delirium, needing a 4AT and a search for a cause
Late-onset psychosis, needing an antipsychotic
Lewy body dementia, needing a memory clinic referral
Psychotic depression, needing a PHQ-9 and review
9.w: Acute onset over hours, fluctuating attention, disorientation and visual hallucinations point to delirium, which is a medical emergency. NICE CG103 recommends assessment (the 4AT is widely used) and identifying and treating underlying causes such as infection, medicines or dehydration.

n.1: Psychosis rarely starts over hours with fluctuating attention in an older person with no history; an antipsychotic would also miss the physical cause.
n.2: Dementia develops over months; this change happened over a day.
n.3: There is no low mood reported, and a fluctuating, acute picture suggests delirium.

9.q: Sam, 26, has a first episode of psychosis. After discussion he declines antipsychotic medication and says he wants to try talking therapy first. He is not at immediate risk. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Request a Mental Health Act assessment to start medication
Offer family intervention and CBT and review the plan in 6 months
Explain that CBT cannot start until he accepts an antipsychotic
Offer family intervention and CBT and agree a review within 1 month
9.w: CG178 1.3.4: if the person still wants psychological interventions alone, offer family intervention and CBT, agree a time (1 month or less) to review treatment options including antipsychotics, and keep monitoring symptoms and functioning.

n.0: He is not at immediate risk and is engaging; compulsion is not justified on these facts.
n.1: Six months is far longer than the 1 month or less review NICE advises.
n.2: Psychological therapy is offered even if medication is declined.

9.q: Lucy, 58, has confirmed seasonal influenza and is in a single room under droplet precautions. A nurse needs to stand beside her bed to take observations; no aerosol generating procedure is planned. What respiratory protection should the nurse wear when within 1 metre of Lucy?
o: No mask is needed for brief observations
A fluid-resistant surgical mask
A fit-tested FFP3 respirator
A Type II surgical mask
9.w: NIPCM ch 2.4: an FRSM must be worn by staff providing care within 1 metre of a patient when droplet precautions apply. FFP3 respirators are considered for airborne pathogens and for AGPs on patients with infections spread by the airborne or droplet route.

n.0: Droplet precautions require an FRSM within 1 metre, however short the contact.
n.2: An FFP3 respirator is for airborne precautions or AGPs; routine observations on a droplet-precautions patient need an FRSM.
n.3: A Type II mask is not classed as fluid resistant; droplet precautions call for an FRSM.

9.q: Marion, 85, lives in a care home and has had diarrhoea for 3 days. Staff say she has been drinking very little and seems more tired than usual. You are assessing her hydration status on admission. Which combination of findings most suggests dehydration?
o: Ankle oedema, crackles in the lungs and weight gain
Dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output and tachycardia
Moist mouth, pale dilute urine and normal skin turgor
Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and polyuria
9.w: Dehydration commonly presents with dry mucous membranes, thirst, reduced and concentrated urine, tachycardia and postural hypotension (Annexe B 5.4). CG174 indicators of fluid need include HR over 90 and systolic under 100.

n.0: Oedema, crackles and weight gain suggest fluid overload.
n.2: A moist mouth and pale dilute urine suggest adequate hydration.
n.3: Raised BP and bounding pulse do not indicate dehydration.

9.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
9.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

9.q: A ward pharmacist explains to nursing staff how NICE judges whether a new medicine is cost-effective in its technology appraisals. Since April 2026, what is NICE's standard cost-effectiveness threshold?
o: £100,000 to £300,000 per QALY gained
£20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained
£30,000 to £50,000 per QALY gained
£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained
9.w: Following a government decision, NICE's standard threshold in technology appraisals rose from £20,000-£30,000 to £25,000-£35,000 per QALY gained from April 2026 (NICE, Changes to NICE's cost-effectiveness thresholds; P7.4 implications of current health policy).

n.0: This higher range applies to highly specialised technologies for ultra-rare diseases, not the standard threshold.
n.1: This was the threshold before April 2026.
n.2: This is not a NICE threshold range.

9.q: A practice nurse needs to send a patient's wound photographs and care plan to the community nursing team. Which method is most appropriate?
o: Send them by WhatsApp to the community nurse's phone
Print them and post them by second class mail
Email them from her personal account as it is faster
Send them through an approved, secure NHS system
9.w: Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely. Code 10.5 keep records secure; Caldicott principles; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality.

n.0: Personal messaging apps are not approved secure systems for clinical data.
n.1: Post is slower and less secure than approved electronic routes.
n.2: Personal email breaches data security (Code 10.5).

9.q: Mr Dee, 47, reduced his venlafaxine dose two weeks ago. He now has severe dizziness, nausea and 'brain zaps' and has had to stop working. His mood itself has been stable. What is the most appropriate plan to discuss with his prescriber?
o: Restart the previous dose, then taper later in smaller steps
Continue the reduction, as the symptoms will pass within days
Stop the remaining dose now to get the withdrawal over with
Switch straight to a different antidepressant at full dose
9.w: NG222 1.4.21: if withdrawal symptoms are more severe, consider restarting the original antidepressant at the previous dose and then reducing more slowly with smaller decrements once symptoms have resolved.

n.1: Severe symptoms lasting two weeks and stopping him working need action, not waiting.
n.2: Stopping abruptly would make his withdrawal symptoms worse.
n.3: An abrupt switch is not the NG222 response to severe withdrawal and may add new side effects.

9.q: Mr Ellis, 55, is under the community mental health team after a suicide attempt. During his psychosocial assessment he mentions that the final hearing in his divorce is next Tuesday. Under NICE NG225, how should this be recorded in his formulation?
o: As a protective factor
As a historic factor
As a fixed static factor
As a future factor
9.w: NG225 1.5.10 asks assessors to explore historic, changeable and current, and future factors, including specific upcoming events or circumstances, plus protective factors. An upcoming court hearing is a future factor that may raise distress and should shape the plan around that date.

n.0: A stressful hearing is not protective; protective factors reduce risk, such as supportive relationships.
n.1: Historic factors are past events, such as a previous suicide attempt.
n.2: Static factors cannot change; a dated upcoming event is a future, time-specific factor.

9.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
9.q: During a motivational interviewing session, Ms Kerr, 31, says: 'Everyone keeps nagging me about my smoking.' Which response is the best reflective statement?
o: 'You sound fed up with being told what to do.'
'You really need to stop smoking for your health.'
'Why don't you just try nicotine patches?'
'Have you had a cigarette today?'
9.w: Reflective listening is a core MI skill (OARS). Reflecting her feeling reduces resistance and invites her to explore her own reasons for change, rather than triggering the 'righting reflex'.

n.1: Telling her what to do is the righting reflex and increases resistance.
n.2: Jumping to solutions skips her ambivalence and her own ideas.
n.3: A closed question does not reflect or explore her feelings.

9.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
9.q: Mrs Ray, 46, has panic disorder. She avoids the local shop because she believes that if she goes in she will panic, collapse and be humiliated. Which CBT technique is most suited to testing this belief?
o: A planned behavioural experiment to test the prediction
Avoiding the shop until her anxiety settles
Reassurance that she will not collapse in the shop
Free association about her early memories
9.w: Behavioural experiments are a CBT technique (Annexe A 3.6): the person predicts what will happen, tests it in a planned way and reviews the evidence, weakening catastrophic beliefs.

n.1: Avoidance prevents disconfirmation and keeps the fear going.
n.2: Reassurance gives short-term relief but maintains anxiety.
n.3: Free association is a psychodynamic technique, not CBT.

9.q: Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool (MITT), Lucy is triaging casualties after an explosion at a shopping centre. A man with cuts to his face and arms is walking around asking for help, with no catastrophic bleeding. Which category should she assign?
o: P2
P3
P1
Dead
9.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) first checks for catastrophic bleeding (P1); if absent, anyone who is walking is categorised P3 (minor) before further physiological assessment (P6.12).

n.0: P2 is reached after the walking, breathing, voice and respiratory rate steps in a casualty who cannot walk.
n.2: P1 is for catastrophic bleeding or abnormal findings later in the algorithm; a walking casualty without catastrophic bleeding is not P1.
n.3: The man is walking and talking; 'dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened.

9.q: On admission, Derek, 59, says he is 'allergic' to codeine. When asked, he explains that it made him nauseated and constipated, with no rash, swelling or breathing problems. How should the nurse record this?
o: Record a morphine allergy, as it is in the same group
Record a codeine allergy and apply a red allergy wristband
Record a codeine intolerance, noting nausea and constipation
Record no reaction, as nausea is not clinically relevant
9.w: Responding to adverse reactions (AnnexB.11.10) includes accurate documentation: the drug, the reaction and its nature. Nausea and constipation are predictable side effects (intolerance), not an immune allergy; labelling them as allergy can deny appropriate analgesia later.

n.0: Extending an inaccurate label to morphine compounds the error.
n.1: An allergy label for a side effect is inaccurate and may restrict future treatment.
n.3: The reaction still matters to future prescribing and should be documented.

9.q: Sophie, 26, has panic disorder and is on an acute ward. She suddenly feels her chest tightening, is breathing fast and has tingling fingers. Her observations and a recent ECG are normal and she says it feels like her usual attacks. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Ask her to breathe in and out of a paper bag
Leave her in a quiet room to settle by herself
Stay with her and coach slow, steady breathing
Give her PRN lorazepam straight away
9.w: Having excluded a physical cause (normal observations, recent ECG, typical pattern), the priority is calm presence, slow controlled breathing and explaining that the symptoms are panic and will pass (Annexe A 3.6 CBT-informed techniques; CG113 discourages benzodiazepines for panic).

n.0: Paper-bag rebreathing is no longer recommended and can cause hypoxia.
n.1: Leaving her alone increases fear and removes support.
n.3: Benzodiazepines are not used for panic disorder and the attack can be managed without them.

9.q: Ruby, 19, is restrained by trained staff after assaulting a nurse. She is taken to the floor face down. Which action is most important for the nurse coordinating the restraint?
o: Monitor her airway and breathing and move her off her front quickly
Hold her in the face-down position until rapid tranquillisation works
Apply weight across her back to keep her still until she is calm
Leave the room so that the restraining staff can work without distraction
9.w: NICE NG10: avoid taking a person to the floor; if prone restraint is needed, use it for as short a time as possible, avoid pressure on the chest, neck or abdomen, and have one staff member monitor airway, breathing and physical condition throughout.

n.1: Prolonged prone restraint increases the risk of positional asphyxia.
n.2: Pressure on the back or chest restricts breathing and has caused deaths in restraint.
n.3: A staff member must stay to monitor her airway and wellbeing throughout.

9.q: Rose, 70, an inpatient on a medical ward, has new dysuria and frequency. She is alert with a NEWS2 score of 1. The doctor prescribes oral nitrofurantoin. No urine sample has been sent. What should the nurse do before giving the first dose?
o: Send a sample after 48 hours if her symptoms have not improved
Obtain a urine sample first, then give the antibiotic without delay
Give the first dose now and send a sample with her next void
Withhold the antibiotic until the urine culture result is available
9.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.27: for patients in hospital who have suspected infections, take microbiological samples before prescribing an antimicrobial and review the prescription when results are available. Collecting the sample first takes minutes and does not delay treatment.

n.0: Delaying the sample for 48 hours loses the chance to guide treatment, contrary to NG15.
n.2: A sample taken after the antibiotic may give a false negative culture, so the prescription cannot be reviewed against reliable results.
n.3: Treatment is not delayed until culture returns; the sample is taken first and the drug given promptly.

9.q: Winifred, 86, lives alone and takes 12 regular medicines from three prescribers. She has fallen twice this month and her daughter reports increasing daytime drowsiness. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the community nurse's most appropriate action?
o: Request a structured medication review with her GP and pharmacist
Spread her doses across the day to reduce side effects
Advise her daughter to buy a pill organiser for the medicines
Stop the medicines most likely to cause drowsiness and falls
9.w: Polypharmacy with falls and drowsiness is a trigger for a structured medication review (NICE NG5 medicines optimisation; P4.15). Prescribers and pharmacists can review the indication, risks and benefits of each medicine together with Winifred.

n.1: Retiming doses without review may cause errors and does not address inappropriate medicines.
n.2: A pill organiser may help adherence but does not address why she is falling.
n.3: Stopping medicines is a prescribing decision and abrupt withdrawal can cause harm.

9.q: An approved mental health professional has serious concerns that Doreen, 79, who lives alone with severe self-neglect and possible psychosis, will not allow anyone into her flat. What is the lawful route to gain entry and, if necessary, remove her for assessment?
o: Ask her GP to complete a section 5(2) report
Ask a magistrate for a section 135(2) warrant to retake her
Apply to a magistrate for a section 135(1) warrant
Ask the police to use section 136 at her front door
9.w: Under section 135(1) a justice of the peace may, on information on oath from an AMHP, issue a warrant for a constable to enter premises, by force if needed, and remove the person to a place of safety. The constable must be accompanied by an AMHP and a registered medical practitioner (s135(4)).

n.0: Section 5(2) applies to hospital in-patients and is used by the doctor or approved clinician in charge of their treatment, not a GP at home.
n.1: Section 135(2) is for retaking a patient already liable to be detained; Doreen is not.
n.3: Section 136 cannot be used in a dwelling, including at the door of the person's own flat (s136(1A)).

9.q: Derek, 70, has COPD and has been admitted twice this winter with exacerbations. He tells the nurse that his flat is damp and that he cannot afford to heat it. Which action by the nurse best addresses the factors affecting his health?
o: Ask the prescriber to increase his inhaler dose for the winter months
Refer or signpost him to local housing and energy support services
Advise him to spend more time in bed to conserve his energy
Record the housing issue and note it is outside the nursing role
9.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.2 and P2.7: understand the wider determinants of health and explain the contribution of social influences and circumstances to health outcomes. NICE PH49 (2014): assess the context in which people live, including their physical, economic and social environment.

n.0: Medicines do not address the damp, cold housing that is affecting his health.
n.2: This does not address the housing problem and reduces his activity.
n.3: NMC P2.7 expects nurses to recognise social circumstances as influences on health and act on them.

9.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
9.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

9.q: Cyril, 82, has not opened his bowels for 6 days despite oral laxatives and is uncomfortable. The doctor has prescribed a phosphate enema, and Cyril has given consent after you explained the procedure. In what position should he be placed for administration?
o: Supine with legs raised
Right lateral with legs straight
Prone with a pillow under the hips
Left lateral with knees flexed
9.w: The left lateral position follows the anatomy of the sigmoid colon and rectum, allowing the enema to flow along the bowel by gravity (Annexe B 6.5).

n.0: Supine makes insertion and retention difficult.
n.1: Right lateral works against the anatomy of the descending and sigmoid colon.
n.2: Prone is uncomfortable and does not aid flow into the sigmoid colon.

9.q: Pharmacy has not yet collected four out-of-date diamorphine ampoules from a ward's CD cupboard. A nurse suggests destroying them in a denaturing kit with another registered nurse to tidy the cupboard before an audit. What is the correct action?
o: Destroy them in a denaturing kit with a second registered nurse
Keep them segregated and recorded until an authorised witness attends
Destroy them and record it once the ward manager has countersigned
Return them to pharmacy in the sealed internal post
9.w: NICE NG46: stock Schedule 2 controlled drugs may only be destroyed in the presence of an authorised witness (for example someone appointed by the CD accountable officer). Until then they stay in the CD cupboard, clearly segregated and recorded.

n.0: A colleague who is not an authorised witness cannot witness destruction of stock Schedule 2 CDs.
n.2: A ward manager is not an authorised witness by virtue of the role, and recording after the event does not fix this.
n.3: Internal post is not a secure, auditable transport route for Schedule 2 CDs.

9.q: Mr Fox, 48, is admitted to an acute mental health ward with depression. As part of his assessment he scores 22 on the AUDIT questionnaire and says he drinks from the morning onwards. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give brief advice on drinking and repeat the AUDIT in a year
Record hazardous drinking and address it once his mood has improved
Assess dependence and withdrawal risk and seek specialist alcohol input
Advise him to stop drinking completely from today to help his mood
9.w: An AUDIT score above 15 indicates the need for a fuller assessment (NICE CG115 1.2.2.6), and scores of 20 or more suggest possible dependence. Morning drinking suggests dependence, so withdrawal risk must be assessed (for example with CIWA-Ar) and specialist advice sought before any reduction.

n.0: Brief advice suits lower-risk drinking; a score of 22 with morning drinking needs assessment now.
n.1: Delaying assessment risks unplanned withdrawal on the ward and ignores a factor maintaining his depression.
n.3: Stopping abruptly when dependent can cause seizures or delirium tremens; withdrawal must be assessed and planned.

9.q: Kezia, a second-year adult nursing student, is ending her placement on a surgical ward. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment (SSSA), who conducts the assessment that confirms her achievement of proficiencies for this placement?
o: Her practice assessor, informed by feedback from her supervisors
Her practice supervisor, who has worked most shifts with her
Her academic assessor, who visits the ward at the end of placement
The ward manager, who signs off all students on the ward
9.w: Under the SSSA (NMC 2018), practice supervisors support and supervise and contribute feedback; the practice assessor conducts the assessment and confirms achievement of practice proficiencies, drawing on that feedback; the academic assessor works with the practice assessor on progression decisions (P5.8).

n.1: Practice supervisors contribute to assessment through feedback but do not confirm achievement of proficiencies.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement for progression with the practice assessor, but does not assess practice on the ward.
n.3: SSSA roles are defined by function, not by management position; the ward manager has no automatic assessment role.

9.q: You find Brenda, 72, unresponsive in a day room. She is not breathing normally and is making occasional gasping sounds. What does this indicate?
o: Sleep apnoea, so open her airway and observe
Cardiac arrest, so start CPR
A seizure, so protect her head
A faint, so raise her legs
9.w: RCUK 2025: if a person is unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing, assume cardiac arrest and start CPR. Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest, and brief seizure-like activity may occur at onset.

n.0: Observing an unresponsive person with abnormal breathing delays CPR.
n.2: Treating gasping as a seizure delays CPR in someone in cardiac arrest.
n.3: A faint does not cause unresponsiveness with agonal breathing.

9.q: During a home visit to Ms Dale, 29, who has schizophrenia and uses heroin, a community nurse sees used needles on a low table where her 4-year-old son is playing. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her to move the needles and take no further action
Discuss it at her next routine review in a month
Remove the immediate risk and raise a safeguarding concern
Wait for her consent before sharing any concern
9.w: NG58: ensure the safeguarding needs of people with coexisting SMI and substance misuse, their carers and wider family are met (think family). Make the child safe now, then follow local child safeguarding procedures.

n.0: A single request does not address an ongoing safeguarding risk.
n.1: A month's delay leaves the child at risk of needlestick injury and neglect.
n.3: Consent is not needed to share information to protect a child at risk of harm.

9.q: At 03:00 a nurse doing 15-minute intermittent observations sees Gary, 46, lying still in bed with his covers pulled over his head. He has been expressing suicidal thoughts. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Confirm he is breathing and lying safely, entering if unsure
Shine a torch into his face to check that he responds to light
Wait and check again at the next scheduled 15-minute time
Record 'asleep in bed' and move on to the next patient's check
9.w: Observation should confirm the person's safety, not just their presence. Staff should check for signs of breathing and a safe position, and enter the room if this cannot be confirmed. Most in-patient suicides are by hanging or strangulation, so covered heads and stillness warrant close checking.

n.1: Shining a torch in his eyes is unnecessarily intrusive when breathing can be checked by looking closely or entering quietly.
n.2: Waiting another 15 minutes when safety is unconfirmed risks missing a ligature or other harm.
n.3: Recording 'asleep' without confirming breathing and safety misses the purpose of observation.

9.q: Jim, 70, has a well-nourished diet and is at high risk of pressure ulcers. His wife asks whether he should take a nutritional supplement drink to prevent ulcers, and whether a nurse could massage his heels. According to NICE CG179, what is the best response?
o: Both are recommended to protect his skin and should be started
A supplement is recommended, but heel massage is not advised
Neither is recommended; focus on repositioning and heel offloading
Heel massage is recommended, but a supplement is not advised
9.w: NICE CG179: do not offer nutritional supplements specifically to prevent pressure ulcers in people whose intake is adequate, and do not offer skin massage or rubbing. Prevention relies on repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces and heel offloading for those at high risk.

n.0: CG179 advises against both measures in this situation.
n.1: Supplements are not recommended for prevention when intake is adequate.
n.3: Skin massage and rubbing are advised against in CG179.

9.q: Five minutes into an intravenous antibiotic infusion, Graham, 60, develops a hoarse voice, wheeze, widespread urticaria and a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the infusion, call for help and give IM adrenaline 1 mg (1 mL)
Stop the infusion, call for help and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV chlorphenamine as first-line treatment, then call for help
Slow the infusion and give an oral non-sedating antihistamine
9.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021): remove the trigger, call for help and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL into the anterolateral thigh, 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) for adults, repeating after 5 minutes if no improvement. Antihistamines are third-line and not for airway, breathing or circulation problems.

n.0: 1 mg is double the adult IM dose in the RCUK algorithm.
n.2: Chlorphenamine is not first-line for anaphylaxis, and delaying help is unsafe.
n.3: Slowing the infusion continues exposure, and antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise.

9.q: Chloe, 27, has been in continuous seclusion since 08:00. It is now 16:00. What review does the Mental Health Act Code of Practice require at this point?
o: A review by the CQC Mental Health Act reviewer
A further two-hourly nursing review by any nurse
A tribunal referral by the hospital managers
A prompt independent multidisciplinary review
9.w: COP15 26.141: an independent MDT review should be promptly undertaken where a patient has been secluded for 8 hours consecutively or 12 hours intermittently within 48 hours. Members should not have been involved in the incident that led to seclusion, and include an IMHA if she has one.

n.0: The CQC monitors use of the Act but does not carry out case reviews of seclusion.
n.1: Nursing reviews continue every 2 hours but must be by two registered nurses, and they do not replace the independent MDT review at 8 hours.
n.2: Seclusion does not trigger a tribunal referral.

9.q: Tom, 34, attends an acute medical unit with a urinary tract infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and sepsis is suspected. Under NICE NG253 (2025), within what time should broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics be given?
o: Within 3 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 6 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 4 hours of arrival in the department
9.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.3: for people at high risk (NEWS2 7 or more), give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score.

n.0: Up to 3 hours is the deferral window a clinician may use for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6).
n.2: Up to 6 hours is the deferral window for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.3: A 4-hour arrival target is not a sepsis treatment standard.

9.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
9.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

9.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
9.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

9.q: A nurse is helping to design a local prevention strategy and wants to apply a life course approach. Which statement best reflects that approach?
o: Accept that adult health is fixed by genes, so early action changes little
Begin prevention once a long-term condition has been diagnosed in the person
Act early and at key transitions, as health is shaped across the whole of life
Focus prevention on older adults, as most long-term disease occurs in later life
9.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): a life course approach considers the critical stages, transitions and settings where large differences can be made, taking action early and appropriately across the life course and reducing health inequalities throughout life.

n.0: The approach rests on evidence that early and timely action changes lifelong outcomes.
n.1: Waiting for diagnosis misses the critical earlier stages the approach targets.
n.3: A life course approach acts at every stage, including early years, not just in later life.

10.q: Four patients on an elderly care ward have laboratory-confirmed norovirus. All single rooms are occupied. The IPC team agrees a cohort bay. Which plan for the cohort is most appropriate?
o: Place them together in one bay with the door closed and dedicated equipment
Place them together with a neutropenic patient who also has diarrhoea
Place them with two patients who have diarrhoea that is not yet confirmed
Keep each in their current bay with curtains drawn and contact precautions
10.w: NIPCM ch 2.1-2.2: cohorting is considered when single rooms are short and two or more patients have the same confirmed infection; doors stay closed and reusable equipment is dedicated to the cohort area. Immunosuppressed patients and those with different or unconfirmed infections must not be mixed in.

n.1: NIPCM states patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes, such as those who are immunosuppressed, must not be cohorted with others.
n.2: Unconfirmed diarrhoea may be a different infection; cohorts are formed from patients with the same confirmed infection.
n.3: Leaving infected patients in mixed bays exposes susceptible patients; curtains do not contain norovirus.

10.q: Pharmacy has not yet collected four out-of-date diamorphine ampoules from a ward's CD cupboard. A nurse suggests destroying them in a denaturing kit with another registered nurse to tidy the cupboard before an audit. What is the correct action?
o: Destroy them in a denaturing kit with a second registered nurse
Keep them segregated and recorded until an authorised witness attends
Destroy them and record it once the ward manager has countersigned
Return them to pharmacy in the sealed internal post
10.w: NICE NG46: stock Schedule 2 controlled drugs may only be destroyed in the presence of an authorised witness (for example someone appointed by the CD accountable officer). Until then they stay in the CD cupboard, clearly segregated and recorded.

n.0: A colleague who is not an authorised witness cannot witness destruction of stock Schedule 2 CDs.
n.2: A ward manager is not an authorised witness by virtue of the role, and recording after the event does not fix this.
n.3: Internal post is not a secure, auditable transport route for Schedule 2 CDs.

10.q: A caller to a surgical ward says she is the daughter of Mrs Green, 70, who had surgery today, and asks how the operation went. The nurse cannot confirm who the caller is. What should the nurse do?
o: Check Mrs Green's wishes and agreed contacts before sharing anything
Give a brief update, as the caller knows the patient's name
Ask the caller to confirm Mrs Green's date of birth, then answer
Confirm the operation went well but give no further details
10.w: Code 5.1 requires respect for a person's right to privacy, and 5.2 that people know how and why their information is shared. The nurse should establish whether Mrs Green consents to information being given to this caller (for example agreed contacts or a password).

n.1: Knowing a patient's name does not show the caller has a right to her information.
n.2: A date of birth is easily known by others and does not establish Mrs Green's consent.
n.3: Confirming the outcome is still disclosure of confidential information without consent.

10.q: Ronald, 80, is prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch, changed every 72 hours. The new patch is due today. His previous patch is on his upper left chest. What is the correct way to apply the new patch?
o: Apply the new patch to the same area once the old one has been removed
Remove the old patch and apply the new one to a different area of skin
Apply the new patch, then remove the old one at the next 72-hour change
Apply the new patch over the old one to maintain a steady dose
10.w: For transdermal patches the old patch is removed before the new one is applied, sites are rotated to reduce skin irritation, and the patch goes on clean, dry, hairless skin (AnnexB.11.8). Leaving an old fentanyl patch in place causes opioid toxicity.

n.0: Reusing the same site raises the risk of skin irritation and altered absorption.
n.2: Leaving the old patch for another 72 hours doubles the dose for that period.
n.3: Two patches at once would double the fentanyl dose and risk respiratory depression.

10.q: At 21:00 Yusuf arrives to take charge of a 24-bed ward for the night. One registered nurse has phoned in sick and no replacement has been found, leaving Yusuf as the only registered nurse with three healthcare assistants. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the shift and complete an incident report at the end of the night describing it
Start the shift and allocate the medicines round to the most senior healthcare assistant
Escalate immediately to the site manager, as fewer than two registered nurses is a red flag
Ask the day staff to stay until midnight and then manage the remainder of the shift himself
10.w: NICE SG1 Box 2 lists fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift as a nursing red flag, which requires an immediate escalation response. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt action on risks to safety and effective management of staff and resources.

n.0: Reporting after the shift leaves the risk unmanaged throughout the night.
n.1: Healthcare assistants cannot be delegated tasks outside their competence, such as a full registered nurse medicines round (Code 11.1).
n.3: A short extension by tired day staff does not solve the shortfall for most of the night and bypasses escalation.

10.q: Mr Shaw, 58, a dependent drinker, is brought to an acute mental health unit. He is confused, unsteady on his feet and has jerky eye movements on looking sideways. He has not eaten properly for weeks. What is the priority?
o: Give chlordiazepoxide and reassess tomorrow
Give parenteral thiamine as prescribed
Give intravenous glucose before any thiamine
Give oral thiamine with his breakfast
10.w: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus suggest Wernicke's encephalopathy. CG100 1.2.1.4: offer parenteral thiamine (in the UK, Pabrinex) for suspected Wernicke's for at least 5 days unless excluded, then oral thiamine.

n.0: Withdrawal treatment does not treat thiamine deficiency.
n.2: Glucose before thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's.
n.3: Oral absorption is unreliable; suspected Wernicke's needs parenteral thiamine.

10.q: Hilda, 83, has end-stage pulmonary fibrosis and is in the last days of life. She says she feels breathless at rest. Her oxygen saturation is 95% on air and her chest is unchanged on examination. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
o: Use a fan and positioning, and check whether an opioid is prescribed
Arrange an arterial blood gas sample to guide oxygen therapy
Start oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula to ease her breathing
Give the 'as required' hyoscine butylbromide from her anticipatory box
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.16 and 1.5.17: consider non-pharmacological management of breathlessness (for example a fan), do not routinely start oxygen unless symptomatic hypoxaemia is known or suspected, and consider an opioid, a benzodiazepine or both.

n.1: An invasive test unlikely to change care should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.1.4).
n.2: With saturation of 95% she is not hypoxaemic; NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen for breathlessness.
n.3: Hyoscine butylbromide is used for secretions or bowel obstruction, not for breathlessness.

10.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

10.q: Hannah, a staff nurse, is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Derek Lowe, 58. At the bedside he tells her he is allergic to penicillin. His allergy band was missing and the chart says 'no known allergies'. No dose was given. What should Hannah do about reporting?
o: Report herself to the NMC, as she nearly gave a contraindicated drug
Record it as a near miss on the trust's patient safety reporting system
Tell the ward manager verbally, as no harm reached the patient
Correct the chart and allergy band, as no report is needed without harm
10.w: Near misses are patient safety events and must be recorded so the system can learn, whether or not harm occurred (P6.8; Code 14 and NMC/GMC candour guidance 2024, which covers reporting near misses). Local systems feed the national Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service. The chart and band must also be corrected and the prescriber informed.

n.0: Self-referral to the regulator is not the response to a near miss caught by correct checks; this is a system issue for local reporting.
n.2: Verbal reporting alone loses the learning; near misses are formally recorded on the local system.
n.3: Correcting the records is needed, but near misses are reported because they reveal weaknesses before harm occurs.

10.q: Sanjay, 50, has been detained under section 3 since 1 June and first received medication on 2 June. On 10 August he refuses it. A colleague says a SOAD is now needed because 'the rule changed to 2 months'. What is correct in October 2026?
o: A SOAD certificate is needed now, as 2 months have passed
A SOAD certificate is needed because he is refusing at any stage
No SOAD certificate is needed while he is detained under section 3
No SOAD certificate is needed until 3 months from 2 June
10.w: Section 14 of the 2025 Act, which will cut the section 58 period from 3 months to 2 months, is not in force. Under section 58 of the 1983 Act, the SOAD safeguard applies from 3 months after medication was first given (2 September). On 10 August, medication can still be given under section 63.

n.0: The 2-month rule is an uncommenced 2025 Act change.
n.1: Refusal within the first 3 months does not trigger section 58; section 63 applies.
n.2: Section 58 applies to section 3 patients after the 3-month period.

10.q: Mary, 74, had a hip replacement 8 hours ago. She has not passed urine since surgery, says she needs to go but cannot, and has lower abdominal discomfort. Which action is most appropriate first?
o: Restrict her fluids until she passes urine
Give her a laxative to relieve the discomfort
Insert a catheter without discussing it with her
Assess her bladder volume with a bladder scanner
10.w: Annexe B 6.4: recognise and respond to retention. A bladder scan assesses residual volume to guide whether catheterisation is needed, which is then performed with her consent and in line with local policy.

n.0: Restricting fluids does not treat retention and risks dehydration.
n.1: A laxative does not address urinary retention.
n.2: Catheterisation needs assessment and valid consent (Code 4.2).

10.q: Bella, 24, becomes increasingly agitated in a busy dining room. The nurse wants to help her calm down somewhere quieter. Which location does NICE NG10 advise against using routinely for de-escalation?
o: A quiet area of the ward garden
The seclusion room
Her own bedroom with staff support
A designated comfort room
10.w: NICE NG10 1.3.14 and 1.3.20: separate agitated service users from others using quiet areas, bedrooms, comfort rooms or gardens, and use a designated calming area. Do not routinely use the seclusion room for de-escalation, because the person may perceive it as threatening.

n.0: Gardens and quiet areas are suitable de-escalation spaces in NG10.
n.2: Bedrooms are listed in NG10 1.3.14 as places to aid de-escalation, ensuring staff are not isolated.
n.3: A comfort room is one of the spaces NG10 suggests for calming.

10.q: Joyce, 85, is dying in hospital and can take only sips of fluid. Her husband asks the nurse, 'If she has a drip, will it keep her alive longer? And if she doesn't, will she die sooner?' Which response is most accurate?
o: Without a drip she will die sooner from dehydration, so the team will advise starting one
It is uncertain whether a drip would lengthen her life, or whether going without would shorten it
Drips are not used at the end of life because they cause fluid overload in older people
A drip would give her several more days of life, so one is usually started at this stage
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.4.5: tell the person and those important to them that clinically assisted hydration may relieve distressing symptoms of dehydration but may cause other problems, and that it is uncertain whether giving it prolongs life or whether not giving it hastens death.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.4.5 states it is uncertain whether withholding clinically assisted hydration hastens death.
n.2: Clinically assisted hydration can be a therapeutic trial (rec 1.4.8); it is not ruled out, though overload is a risk to monitor.
n.3: NG31 rec 1.4.5 states it is uncertain whether clinically assisted hydration prolongs life or the dying process.

10.q: Sam, 34, died after an incident on a surgical ward that the trust accepts is a notifiable safety incident. Under regulation 20, who should the trust notify about the incident?
o: Sam's GP, who will discuss the incident with the family
The CQC, which notifies families on the trust's behalf
A person lawfully acting on Sam's behalf, such as next of kin
The coroner, who will then decide whether to inform the family
10.w: Reg 20(7): the relevant person is the service user or, on their death, a person lawfully acting on their behalf (also if under 16 and not competent, or 16 or over and lacking capacity).

n.0: The GP is not the relevant person; reg 20 notification goes to the person acting on Sam's behalf.
n.1: The CQC regulates compliance but does not notify relevant persons for providers.
n.3: Coroner referral is a separate duty; reg 20 requires the relevant person to be notified.

10.q: Mrs Agnes Doyle, 84, lives alone and is recovering from pneumonia on a medical ward in England. She will need help with personal care at home. Which organisation is responsible for assessing her need for care and support at home?
o: Her GP practice
The integrated care board
The local authority
The acute hospital trust
10.w: Under the Care Act 2014, local authorities assess adults who appear to need care and support and are responsible for social care (and public health) in their area. The ward nurse refers so assessment can be planned before discharge (P7.1 interagency working; FACTS S-CA, S-ICS).

n.0: The GP provides health care but does not carry out Care Act assessments.
n.1: The ICB plans and funds NHS health services, not adult social care assessments.
n.3: Hospital staff contribute to discharge planning, but the statutory needs assessment is the local authority's duty.

10.q: A ward team cannot agree whether to share a patient's HIV status with a care agency that will provide personal care at home. The patient has capacity but has not been asked yet. Who in the organisation is responsible for advising on difficult decisions about confidential information?
o: The ward matron on duty
The Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
The Data Protection Officer at the ICO
The Caldicott Guardian
10.w: The Caldicott Guardian is the senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of patient information and enabling appropriate sharing; the Caldicott principles advise involving them in difficult decisions. The first step remains asking the patient.

n.0: The matron can support the team but is not the designated lead for confidentiality decisions.
n.1: Freedom to Speak Up Guardians support staff to raise concerns; they do not advise on confidentiality decisions.
n.2: The ICO is the external regulator; it does not advise on individual sharing decisions within a trust.

10.q: During a morning shift, a nurse notices that Omar, 44, who is usually sociable, is sitting alone, clenching his fists, staring at another patient and muttering. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Move the other patient off the ward for the rest of the day
Increase his observation level to continuous and inform security
Approach calmly, say he seems upset and ask what is troubling him
Offer him PRN lorazepam straight away to prevent an incident
10.w: NICE NG10 1.3.13 and 1.3.17: build a close working relationship, sensitively monitor changes in mood or composure that may lead to aggression, and communicate respect and empathy. Early engagement on noticing warning signs is the first step before any restrictive measure.

n.0: Removing another patient disrupts their care and does not address Omar's distress.
n.1: Observation should be used after positive engagement fails (NG10 1.4.12); jumping to continuous observation and security is premature.
n.3: PRN medication is part of de-escalation, but the first step is to engage and understand what is wrong.

10.q: Blood from a dislodged cannula has spilled onto the hard floor beside the bed of Thomas, 66. Spill granules are available. The nurse has put on non-sterile gloves and an apron. What should the nurse do next?
o: Cover with paper towels and apply 70% alcohol to the towels
Apply 1,000 ppm chlorine solution and mop the area straight away
Wipe it up with paper towels and clean the area with detergent
Apply chlorine-releasing granules and leave for the contact time
10.w: NIPCM appendix 9: for blood or high-risk body fluid spills apply chlorine-releasing granules (or towels soaked in 10,000 ppm available chlorine), follow the contact time (or 3 minutes), discard the waste as healthcare waste, then wash with detergent and dry.

n.0: Alcohol is not the NIPCM agent for blood spills.
n.1: 1,000 ppm is for urine, faeces or vomit spills; blood needs granules or 10,000 ppm, with contact time.
n.2: Detergent alone does not disinfect a blood spill, which may contain blood-borne viruses.

10.q: Ada, 88, has been sleeping poorly. She dozes most of the afternoon, is woken for observations at 02:00 and 06:00, and has a NEWS2 of 0. She says she is tired all day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Review her observation times with the team to protect her sleep
Ask the doctor to prescribe a sedative for her to take at night
Wake her more often in the afternoon so that she sleeps at night
Leave her plan unchanged, as observations have to be done at night
10.w: With a NEWS2 of 0 the minimum frequency is 12-hourly (RCP 2017), so night-time waking may be avoidable. Reviewing the care plan to cluster care and protect sleep supports rest (Annexe B 3.1, 3.6).

n.1: Sedatives are not first line and increase falls risk in older people.
n.2: Repeatedly waking her during the day adds fatigue rather than addressing the night-time disturbance.
n.3: Observation timing is a clinical decision and can be reviewed when the score is 0.

10.q: Ms Field, 46, takes both an antipsychotic and an SSRI. She becomes febrile, sweaty and agitated, and the team must decide between neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin toxicity. Which finding points most towards neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
o: Lead-pipe rigidity developing over days
Onset within hours of a dose increase
Inducible clonus with brisk reflexes
Shivering with diarrhoea and dilated pupils
10.w: NMS usually develops over days with generalised 'lead-pipe' rigidity and slowed reflexes. Serotonin toxicity develops within hours of starting, increasing or combining serotonergic drugs, with neuromuscular excitability such as clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and myoclonus, plus shivering and diarrhoea (BNF antidepressant treatment summary).

n.1: Rapid onset within hours is typical of serotonin toxicity.
n.2: Clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristic of serotonin toxicity.
n.3: Shivering, diarrhoea and dilated pupils are features of serotonin toxicity.

10.q: Victor, 81, has been taking clindamycin for 5 days for cellulitis. He now has four episodes of watery diarrhoea in 12 hours and is in a four-bed bay. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop the clindamycin and keep him in the bay with curtains drawn
Isolate him, send a stool sample and ask for an antibiotic review
Give loperamide and review his bowels at the end of the day
Send a stool sample and keep him in the bay until the result returns
10.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.35 highlights the risk of selecting for C. difficile with certain antibiotics. New diarrhoea on antibiotics should prompt isolation on suspicion (NIPCM ch 2.1), a stool sample and a prescriber review of the antibiotic.

n.0: Changing antibiotics is a prescriber decision, and staying in the bay exposes other patients.
n.2: Antimotility drugs are inappropriate in suspected C. difficile and delay diagnosis.
n.3: Isolation should not wait for the result, as C. difficile spreads to others in the bay.

10.q: Grace has worked as a registered nurse in Manchester and is moving to a post in Glasgow. She asks her manager which statute governs decisions for adults who lack capacity once she is practising in Scotland, as Code 4.3 requires her to follow the law where she practises. Which statute should the manager name?
o: Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003
Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000
Mental Capacity Act 2005
10.w: Capacity law is devolved. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies in England and Wales; in Scotland decisions for adults lacking capacity fall under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000. Code 4.3 requires registrants to keep to the mental capacity law of the country in which they practise.

n.0: The 2003 Scottish Act concerns compulsory care and treatment for mental disorder, not general decisions for adults lacking capacity.
n.1: The 2019 Act amends the MCA 2005 in England and Wales to create the Liberty Protection Safeguards, which are not in force.
n.3: The MCA 2005 covers England and Wales, so it would not govern Grace's practice in Glasgow.

10.q: Nikita, 40, has been detained under section 3 for 5 months. She lacks capacity to consent to her antipsychotic. A staff nurse suggests documenting a Mental Capacity Act best interests decision instead of waiting for a SOAD visit. What should the nurse in charge explain?
o: The MCA can be used as an interim until the SOAD visits
Part 4 treatment is outside the MCA, so a SOAD is needed
The MCA can be used because she lacks capacity to consent
The MCA can be used if an IMCA has first been consulted
10.w: Section 28 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 states that the MCA does not authorise treatment for mental disorder regulated by Part 4 of the MHA. After 3 months, a detained patient who lacks capacity needs a SOAD certificate under section 58 (or s62 if urgent).

n.0: There is no interim MCA route pending a SOAD; urgent treatment uses section 62.
n.2: Lack of capacity does not bring Part 4 treatment within the MCA; s28 excludes it.
n.3: Consulting an IMCA does not overcome the s28 exclusion.

10.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
10.q: At handover a nurse wants to describe a newly admitted man in line with recovery-focused, person-first language. Which phrase is most appropriate?
o: A chronic schizophrenic
A schizophrenic young man
A schizophrenia sufferer
A man who has schizophrenia
10.w: Person-first language puts the person before the diagnosis and avoids defining them by it, reducing stigma (SPEC.T2 social stigma; Code 1.1 treat people with kindness, respect and compassion).

n.0: Labelling someone a 'chronic schizophrenic' is stigmatising and hopeless.
n.1: Using the diagnosis as an adjective defines him by the illness.
n.2: 'Sufferer' implies passivity and victimhood.

10.q: Ayesha, 19, attended an emergency department after taking an overdose. Her blood results are awaited. Before the liaison psychiatry assessment she says she is going home and stands up to leave. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess her immediate safety and mental state before she leaves
Give her a crisis line number as she walks out
Let her leave, as an adult has the right to discharge herself
Ask security to stop her leaving the department
10.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.5.14: if a person who has self-harmed wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment, assess their safety and any mental health problems before they leave. Capacity, consent and duty of care also need consideration (rec 1.7.1).

n.1: A phone number alone does not assess her safety or the medical risk of the overdose.
n.2: She may be free to leave, but NG225 requires an assessment of safety and mental state first; her overdose may also affect capacity.
n.3: Restraining her is not the first step; it may be considered only if she lacks capacity and is at serious risk.

10.q: Bill, 85, has advanced dementia and cannot describe his pain. After a fall he grimaces, groans and guards his left hip when moved. Which assessment is most appropriate?
o: A visual analogue scale explained slowly to him
A behavioural pain tool such as the Abbey pain scale
A 0-10 numerical rating scale completed by Bill himself
His daughter's estimate of his pain on a 0-10 scale
10.w: Where a person cannot reliably self-report, for example because of dementia or a learning disability, use a validated behavioural or observational pain assessment tool such as the Abbey pain scale or PAINAD (NICE NG31 principle; Annexe B 3.1).

n.0: A visual analogue scale still needs him to self-report, which he cannot reliably do.
n.2: Numerical self-report relies on abilities Bill no longer has.
n.3: Family insight is valuable, but a proxy number is not a validated assessment.

10.q: At the start of an early shift, Nina, a staff nurse, is allocated four patients on a medical ward. Which patient should she see first?
o: Mr Ali, 66, whose insulin is due with breakfast in 45 minutes
Mrs Dunn, 74, whose respiratory rate is 28/min, SpO2 89% and who is newly confused
Ms Reid, 52, who reports post-operative pain of 5/10, last analgesia 3 hours ago
Mr Shaw, 59, who is to be discharged today and needs his discharge letter
10.w: Prioritisation uses an ABCDE approach and early warning scores: Mrs Dunn has a respiratory rate of 28 (scores 3), SpO2 89% (scores 3) and new confusion (scores 3) on NEWS2 (RCP 2017), indicating possible life-threatening deterioration needing immediate assessment and escalation (P5.5 lead and manage care of a group of people with prioritisation).

n.0: Time-critical insulin matters, but there are 45 minutes before it is due and he is not unwell.
n.2: Her pain needs prompt attention, possibly by another team member, but is not life-threatening.
n.3: Discharge paperwork can safely wait while a deteriorating patient is assessed.

10.q: A ward team wants the strongest evidence on whether a new dressing reduces infection in surgical wounds. Which type of study gives the highest level of evidence for this question?
o: An expert consensus opinion paper from specialists
A single large randomised controlled trial
A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
A large prospective cohort study of patients
10.w: Oxford CEBM levels of evidence (therapy): level 1a is a systematic review of randomised controlled trials; expert opinion is level 5. Code 6.1 requires evidence-based information.

n.0: Expert opinion is the lowest level in evidence hierarchies such as the Oxford CEBM levels.
n.1: A well-designed RCT is strong evidence but ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs.
n.3: Cohort studies are observational and rank below RCTs for treatment effects.

10.q: Mrs Green, 46, has a new episode of more severe depression (PHQ-9 of 20). She has no psychotic symptoms and is willing to try either talking therapy or medication. Which option is first in the NICE NG222 list for more severe depression?
o: Counselling for 8 sessions
Guided self-help with weekly telephone support
Individual CBT combined with an antidepressant
Group exercise over 10 weeks
10.w: NG222 1.6.1, table 2: all listed treatments can be first line, matched to preference, but the first in the NICE order is a combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant.

n.0: Counselling is an option but sits lower in the NICE order for more severe depression.
n.1: Guided self-help is in the less severe depression table, not the more severe one.
n.3: Group exercise is an option but sits low in the NICE order for more severe depression.

10.q: Kwame is a practice nurse whose line manager, a non-registered practice manager, will act as his revalidation confirmer. He has written his five reflective accounts. How should he complete his reflective discussion?
o: Hold it with the practice manager during the confirmation meeting
Hold it with an NMC registrant before the confirmation meeting
Submit his five accounts to the NMC in place of a discussion
Hold it with a GP partner as part of his annual appraisal
10.w: NMC reflective discussion guidance: hold the discussion with another registered nurse, midwife or nursing associate, face to face, about your five reflective accounts. If the confirmer is not an NMC registrant, the reflective discussion must take place before the confirmation discussion.

n.0: The reflective discussion must be with an NMC registrant; a non-registrant confirmer cannot hold it.
n.2: The written accounts and the reflective discussion are separate requirements; one cannot replace the other.
n.3: A GP is registered with the GMC, not the NMC; the discussion partner must be a nurse, midwife or nursing associate.

10.q: Callum, a district nurse, mentions that his car has broken down. The son of a patient he visits offers to lend him £500 to repair it until payday. What should Callum do?
o: Accept the loan and declare it to his manager
Decline the loan and keep the relationship professional
Accept the loan and repay it in full on payday
Accept a smaller amount as a gift in place of a loan
10.w: Code 21.2: never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them. Code 21.3 requires honesty and integrity in financial dealings.

n.0: Declaring it does not make it acceptable; loans from people close to patients are prohibited by Code 21.2.
n.2: Code 21.2 says never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them, even if repaid.
n.3: A cash gift of this kind is not trivial and breaches Code 21.1.

10.q: During a ward environmental check, a nurse finds that a new wardrobe in the bedroom of Kai, 20, who has recent suicidal thoughts, has a rail that could be used as a ligature point. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Make Kai safe now (room or observation) and report it
Tell Kai not to use the rail and record that he agreed
Note the rail on the list for the next annual ligature audit
Remove the wardrobe herself using tools borrowed from estates
10.w: A newly identified ligature point is an immediate environmental risk. The nurse should mitigate it at once (for example a safer room or a change in observation) and report it through the local ligature and incident process so it can be removed. Ligature risk management is a key in-patient suicide prevention measure.

n.1: An agreement not to use the rail does not manage the risk and is not a safety measure.
n.2: Waiting for the annual audit leaves a known risk in place for a patient with suicidal thoughts.
n.3: Dismantling fittings without estates support risks injury and leaves debris; the risk should be mitigated and reported.

10.q: Ms Day, 40, has been stable on clozapine for three years. Ten days ago she stopped smoking cigarettes and switched to an e-cigarette. She now feels very drowsy, is drooling more and is unsteady on her feet. What should the nurse do?
o: Encourage her to restart cigarettes to lower her clozapine
Report a possible raised clozapine level and request testing
Ask the prescriber to increase her clozapine dose
Reassure her that e-cigarettes affect clozapine like tobacco
10.w: Tobacco smoke induces clozapine metabolism, so stopping smoking or switching to an e-cigarette can raise clozapine levels and cause toxicity. MHRA (August 2020) advises monitoring clozapine blood levels in this situation; the dose may need reducing.

n.0: Smoking cessation should be supported; the safe response is to check her level and adjust the dose.
n.2: Stopping smoking raises clozapine levels, so an increase would worsen toxicity.
n.3: E-cigarettes do not contain the tobacco smoke components that induce clozapine metabolism.

10.q: Chloe, 27, has been in continuous seclusion since 08:00. It is now 16:00. What review does the Mental Health Act Code of Practice require at this point?
o: A review by the CQC Mental Health Act reviewer
A further two-hourly nursing review by any nurse
A tribunal referral by the hospital managers
A prompt independent multidisciplinary review
10.w: COP15 26.141: an independent MDT review should be promptly undertaken where a patient has been secluded for 8 hours consecutively or 12 hours intermittently within 48 hours. Members should not have been involved in the incident that led to seclusion, and include an IMHA if she has one.

n.0: The CQC monitors use of the Act but does not carry out case reviews of seclusion.
n.1: Nursing reviews continue every 2 hours but must be by two registered nurses, and they do not replace the independent MDT review at 8 hours.
n.2: Seclusion does not trigger a tribunal referral.

10.q: Grace, 45, has schizophrenia and is showing early signs of relapse: poor sleep, suspiciousness and returning voices. She lives with a supportive partner, is not at immediate risk and wants to stay at home. Which is the most appropriate first option?
o: Referral back to the early intervention in psychosis service
Increasing her outpatient reviews to once a month
Referral to the crisis resolution and home treatment team
Informal admission to an acute inpatient ward
10.w: CG178 1.4.1: crisis resolution and home treatment teams are the first-line service for people in crisis, as an alternative to admission, where the person can be managed safely at home.

n.0: EIP is for first episode or first presentation; Grace has an established illness.
n.1: Monthly review is too slow a response to an acute relapse.
n.3: Admission is for when home treatment cannot manage the risk; here it can.

10.q: Cyril, 82, has not opened his bowels for 6 days despite oral laxatives and is uncomfortable. The doctor has prescribed a phosphate enema, and Cyril has given consent after you explained the procedure. In what position should he be placed for administration?
o: Supine with legs raised
Right lateral with legs straight
Prone with a pillow under the hips
Left lateral with knees flexed
10.w: The left lateral position follows the anatomy of the sigmoid colon and rectum, allowing the enema to flow along the bowel by gravity (Annexe B 6.5).

n.0: Supine makes insertion and retention difficult.
n.1: Right lateral works against the anatomy of the descending and sigmoid colon.
n.2: Prone is uncomfortable and does not aid flow into the sigmoid colon.

10.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
10.q: Ms Lewis, 34, has a history of sexual abuse and is admitted to a ward that searches belongings on admission. She becomes very anxious when the search is explained. Which approach is most trauma-informed?
o: Delay the search until a doctor has reviewed her
Do the search quickly so it is over for her sooner
Explain each step, offering choices and a female nurse
Search her room later while she is at a group
10.w: Trauma-informed care aims to avoid retraumatisation by promoting safety, trust, choice, collaboration and empowerment: clear explanation, gender-sensitive staffing and as much control as possible.

n.0: A medical review is not needed for the search and does not address her fear.
n.1: Speed without explanation or choice can feel like a loss of control and retraumatise her.
n.3: Searching covertly breaks trust and is not transparent.

10.q: A nurse is planning patient information for an outpatient clinic and wants to account for health literacy across the local population. Which statement about health literacy in England is supported by Public Health England evidence?
o: Up to 61% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
Health literacy is measured by a person's highest school qualification
Difficulty understanding health information mainly affects people over 80
About 10% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
10.w: NHS England, Health literacy (personalised care): a Public Health England report found that up to 61% of the English working-age population do not routinely understand the health and wellbeing information they are given. Health literacy (WHO) is the personal characteristics and social resources needed to access, understand, appraise and use information to make health decisions.

n.1: Health literacy is the ability to access, understand, appraise and use information, not a qualification level.
n.2: Low health literacy is common across working-age adults, not mainly in the oldest age groups.
n.3: The figure is far higher; PHE found up to 61% of the working-age population struggle.

10.q: Reviewing the night's charts, Nurse Hana sees that a healthcare assistant recorded hourly observations for a patient who was off the ward in theatre for three of those hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Mention it informally to the healthcare assistant next week
Amend the entries herself so the chart is accurate
Leave it, as the patient has now returned safely
Escalate it to the nurse in charge straight away
