10.w: Code 10.3: complete records without falsification, taking immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to these requirements. Code 16.1 escalate concerns.

n.0: Falsified observations are a safety concern; Code 10.3 requires immediate action.
n.1: Altering another person's entries is itself inappropriate; the concern must be escalated.
n.2: The patient's safety now does not remove the falsification; it must be acted upon.

10.q: Mr Fox, 48, is admitted to an acute mental health ward with depression. As part of his assessment he scores 22 on the AUDIT questionnaire and says he drinks from the morning onwards. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give brief advice on drinking and repeat the AUDIT in a year
Record hazardous drinking and address it once his mood has improved
Assess dependence and withdrawal risk and seek specialist alcohol input
Advise him to stop drinking completely from today to help his mood
10.w: An AUDIT score above 15 indicates the need for a fuller assessment (NICE CG115 1.2.2.6), and scores of 20 or more suggest possible dependence. Morning drinking suggests dependence, so withdrawal risk must be assessed (for example with CIWA-Ar) and specialist advice sought before any reduction.

n.0: Brief advice suits lower-risk drinking; a score of 22 with morning drinking needs assessment now.
n.1: Delaying assessment risks unplanned withdrawal on the ward and ignores a factor maintaining his depression.
n.3: Stopping abruptly when dependent can cause seizures or delirium tremens; withdrawal must be assessed and planned.

10.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
10.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

10.q: Mr Ellis, 55, is under the community mental health team after a suicide attempt. During his psychosocial assessment he mentions that the final hearing in his divorce is next Tuesday. Under NICE NG225, how should this be recorded in his formulation?
o: As a protective factor
As a historic factor
As a fixed static factor
As a future factor
10.w: NG225 1.5.10 asks assessors to explore historic, changeable and current, and future factors, including specific upcoming events or circumstances, plus protective factors. An upcoming court hearing is a future factor that may raise distress and should shape the plan around that date.

n.0: A stressful hearing is not protective; protective factors reduce risk, such as supportive relationships.
n.1: Historic factors are past events, such as a previous suicide attempt.
n.2: Static factors cannot change; a dated upcoming event is a future, time-specific factor.

10.q: Ms Sharma, 35, has taken sertraline for four months and her depression went into remission a month ago. She tells the nurse she feels well and would like to stop her tablets now. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop the tablets now, as her symptoms have resolved
Continue for at least 6 months after remission, then review
Continue for at least 2 years before any review is needed
Halve the dose now and continue it as a maintenance dose
10.w: NG222 and the BNF advise continuing antidepressant treatment for at least 6 months after remission to reduce the risk of relapse, with a shared decision and gradual tapering when stopping.

n.0: Stopping one month after remission increases relapse risk and, if abrupt, withdrawal symptoms.
n.2: Two years without review is not the standard; treatment is reviewed regularly.
n.3: NG222 advises continuing at the dose that achieved remission unless there is good reason to reduce it.

10.q: A student nurse asks how to tell delirium from dementia when an older person on the ward is confused. Which feature points most strongly to delirium?
o: A long history of difficulty with word-finding
Acute onset over hours or days with fluctuation
Confusion that is stable from day to day
Gradual memory decline over several years
10.w: NICE CG103 describes delirium indicators as recent changes or fluctuations, over hours or days, in cognition, perception, physical function or social behaviour. Dementia typically develops gradually over months to years.

n.0: Longstanding word-finding difficulty suggests an established condition rather than an acute change.
n.2: Stable confusion does not show the fluctuation characteristic of delirium.
n.3: Gradual decline over years is typical of dementia, not delirium.

10.q: Mr Green, 66, has venous leg ulcers. NICE guidance supports compression therapy, but after a full explanation he declines it because he previously found it painful. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Discharge him from the clinic as he has declined treatment
Ask the GP to prescribe stronger analgesia and apply it anyway
Apply the compression, as NICE guidance must be followed
Explore his concerns, discuss alternatives and record his choice
10.w: NICE guidance ('Your responsibility' statement, as in NG253) is not mandatory; professionals take it fully into account alongside individual needs and preferences. Code 2.5 and 4.2; P1.8 critical evidence-informed decisions.

n.0: Declining one option does not end care; alternatives and support should be explored.
n.1: Applying compression he has refused would breach his right to refuse (Code 2.5).
n.2: NICE guidance is not mandatory; it must be applied alongside the person's needs and preferences.

10.q: Mr Reid, 50, is referred to a community mental health team with low mood. The nurse is completing a biopsychosocial assessment with him. Which information belongs in the social part of the assessment?
o: His thyroid function results and current medicines
His housing, debts and close relationships
His family history of bipolar disorder
His beliefs about himself and his coping style
10.w: A biopsychosocial assessment considers biological factors (physical health, medicines, genetics), psychological factors (thoughts, beliefs, coping) and social factors (housing, money, work, relationships, support). Housing, debt and relationships are social factors (NMC P3.4).

n.0: Thyroid function and medicines are biological factors.
n.2: A family history of mental illness is a biological (genetic) vulnerability factor.
n.3: Beliefs about self and coping style are psychological factors.

10.q: Harold, 79, has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids. Overnight he becomes breathless with RR 26, SpO2 92% on air, crackles at both lung bases and new ankle swelling. His fluid balance is positive 2,300 mL over 24 hours. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase the infusion rate to correct the dehydration
Give a prescribed diuretic before informing anyone
Stop the infusion, sit him up and escalate urgently
Continue the infusion and recheck in 4 hours
10.w: Breathlessness, crackles, oedema and a large positive balance suggest fluid overload. Stop the infusion, sit him upright, give oxygen to target and escalate urgently: NEWS2 RR 26 = 3 and SpO2 92% = 2 gives at least 5 (RCP 2017). CG174 asks for fluid mismanagement to be reported as an incident.

n.0: More fluid worsens overload.
n.1: Treatment decisions need urgent medical review; giving a diuretic first delays escalation.
n.3: Continuing the infusion worsens overload and 4 hours is too long.

10.q: Agnes, 55, has received her cervical screening invitation. She tells the nurse she has heard mixed things about screening and is unsure whether to go. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that cervical screening is compulsory for women of her age group
Advise her that screening prevents every case of cervical cancer
Give balanced information on benefits and limits, and support her choice
Book her test now and explain the details at her appointment
10.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): deciding whether to have screening is a personal choice; benefits (early detection, preventing some deaths) are weighed against risks and limitations (false positives and negatives, anxiety, difficult decisions). Code 4.2: make sure informed consent is obtained.

n.0: Screening is a personal choice; NHS screening is offered, not mandated.
n.1: Screening tests are not 100% accurate; this overstates the benefit and is misleading.
n.3: Booking before she has decided bypasses informed choice.

10.q: A public health team plans to reduce average salt intake across a region by working with manufacturers to lower the salt content of bread and processed foods. Which statement best describes this strategy?
o: Secondary prevention that detects raised blood pressure at an early stage
A high-risk approach targeting people already diagnosed with hypertension
A population approach: a small benefit to each person but a large total benefit
Tertiary prevention to reduce disability in people who have had strokes
10.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the population approach recognises that society influences individual behaviour and reduces risk at population level. The prevention paradox (Rose): most people who lower their risk will not benefit directly, although the total benefit across the population is large.

n.0: No one is being tested or detected; this lowers exposure to a risk factor across the population.
n.1: The change affects everyone who buys the foods, not a selected high-risk group.
n.3: This is aimed at the whole population before disease develops, not at people with established disease.

10.q: Before lunch, Rhys, 68, who takes gliclazide and insulin, feels shaky and sweaty. His capillary blood glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. He is alert, orientated and able to swallow safely. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Give IM glucagon 1 mg and recheck in 10 minutes
Give a starchy snack and recheck his glucose in 1 hour
Give him his lunch now and recheck his glucose before the evening meal
Give 15-20 g of quick-acting carbohydrate, then recheck in 10-15 minutes
10.w: Hypoglycaemia (glucose below 4 mmol/L) in a conscious adult who can swallow is treated with 15-20 g of quick-acting carbohydrate, with glucose rechecked after 10-15 minutes and treatment repeated if still low, then a longer-acting carbohydrate (JBDS hospital hypoglycaemia guidance). Insulin and sulfonylureas are high-risk medicines (P4.15).

n.0: Glucagon is for people who cannot take oral treatment safely; Rhys can swallow.
n.1: Starchy snacks act too slowly as first-line treatment, and an hour is too long to recheck.
n.2: A meal is too slow and leaving the recheck until evening misses ongoing hypoglycaemia.

10.q: Mr Craig, 50, developed a tremor and stiffness after his first-generation depot antipsychotic was increased. The team decides to stop the depot. He asks whether the side effects will go away as soon as it is stopped. What should the nurse explain?
o: Side effects will be reversed at once by an antimuscarinic
Side effects may continue until the drug clears from the site
Side effects will stop within a few hours of the decision
Side effects can be ended by injecting a different depot
10.w: The BNF notes that with depot antipsychotics, side effects may persist until the drug has been cleared from its depot site, which can take weeks. This is one reason doses and changes are made carefully.

n.0: An antimuscarinic may ease parkinsonism but does not reverse the effects immediately or remove the drug.
n.2: A long-acting depot keeps releasing drug for weeks, so effects do not stop within hours.
n.3: Another depot adds more antipsychotic exposure and would not end the current effects.

10.q: Mr Burke, 64, has capacity and is waiting for biopsy results. His wife asks the nurse to make sure he is not told if it is cancer, as 'it would destroy him'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer the decision to the consultant to settle with his wife
Tell her that her request is unlawful and end the conversation there
Explore her worries and explain he will be asked what he wants to know
Agree, and record her request on the front of the notes
10.w: Code 2.4 respect the level of involvement a person wants; Code 5.5 share with the person the information they want or need to know. Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations.

n.0: The decision about what he is told rests with him, not with his wife and the consultant.
n.1: This dismisses her distress; her worries need exploring with compassion.
n.3: He has capacity; withholding his diagnosis at another's request breaches his right to information.

10.q: Mr Ellis, 29, developed neuroleptic malignant syndrome two days ago and his antipsychotic was stopped. His signs are improving, but his voices are returning and he is distressed. A doctor asks the nurse's view on restarting. Which plan best reflects BNF advice?
o: Restart the same dose today, as his psychosis is returning
Restart at half dose once his temperature is normal
Switch to a depot, as NMS does not occur with depot drugs
Restart after the signs fully resolve and at least 5 days off
10.w: The BNF advises stopping the antipsychotic for at least 5 days, preferably longer, and allowing the signs of NMS to resolve completely before any rechallenge, which is a specialist decision with close monitoring. His distress meanwhile needs non-antipsychotic support.

n.0: Restarting two days after NMS, before full resolution, risks recurrence.
n.1: A normal temperature does not mean NMS has fully resolved, and five days have not passed.
n.2: NMS can occur with any antipsychotic, including depot preparations.

10.q: Bernadette, 68, detained under section 3, has severe depression. She has capacity and clearly refuses electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). She is eating and drinking and is not in danger. The team believe ECT would help. What is the legal position?
o: ECT cannot be given while she has capacity and refuses
ECT can be given if her nearest relative agrees
ECT can be given under section 63 because she is detained
ECT can be given if a SOAD certifies it as appropriate
10.w: Section 58A provides that ECT cannot be given to a capable adult who refuses. The only exception is urgent treatment under section 62 to save life or prevent serious deterioration, which does not apply on these facts.

n.1: The nearest relative has no power to consent to ECT on her behalf.
n.2: ECT is governed by section 58A, so section 63 cannot authorise it.
n.3: A SOAD can certify ECT for a patient who lacks capacity, not override a capable adult's refusal.

10.q: You are performing chest compressions on Alan, 60, who has collapsed in a hospital car park. According to RCUK 2025, what compression depth and rate are correct for an adult?
o: 5-6 cm at 100-120 per minute
6-7 cm at 80-100 per minute
4-5 cm at 100-120 per minute
5-6 cm at 120-140 per minute
10.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: compress on the lower half of the sternum to a depth of at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, at 100-120 per minute, allowing full recoil.

n.1: 6-7 cm is too deep and 80-100 per minute is too slow.
n.2: 4-5 cm is too shallow for an adult.
n.3: 120-140 per minute is faster than the recommended maximum of 120.

10.q: A practice nurse is preparing a teaching session on the adult Core20PLUS5 programme. Which of the following is one of its five clinical areas?
o: Dementia diagnosis rates and post-diagnostic support
Hypertension case-finding and optimal lipid management
Rehabilitation after hip fracture in older adults
Sexual health screening for adults under 25
10.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): the five adult clinical areas are maternity, severe mental illness (annual health checks), chronic respiratory disease, early cancer diagnosis, and hypertension case-finding and optimal management with lipid optimisation.

n.0: Dementia is not one of the five adult clinical areas in Core20PLUS5.
n.2: Hip fracture rehabilitation is not one of the five adult clinical areas.
n.3: Sexual health screening is not one of the five adult clinical areas.

10.q: Mrs Abbott, 67, presses the call bell on a surgical ward with central chest tightness that started 10 minutes ago. She looks pale and clammy. After calling for help and checking her observations, which investigation should the nurse prioritise?
o: A peak flow reading to assess her breathing
A chest X-ray, requested for later in the day
A 12-lead ECG, shown promptly to the doctor
A troponin sample, sent before anything else
10.w: A 12-lead ECG should be recorded as soon as possible in suspected acute coronary syndrome and shown promptly to a doctor so ischaemia or infarction can be identified (P3.11 undertake investigations and share findings; P3.12 act promptly).

n.0: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not chest pain suggestive of a cardiac cause.
n.1: A chest X-ray does not identify acute myocardial ischaemia and should not take priority.
n.3: Troponin is useful but takes time; the ECG gives immediate information.

10.q: A charge nurse asks what a basic business case for funding two additional healthcare assistant posts should contain. Which content is most appropriate?
o: Last year's off-duty rotas to show how often extra shifts were filled
A list of the staff who support the request, with their signatures
The problem, the options considered, their costs and the expected benefits
Details of recent incidents including the patients' names and dates of birth
10.w: A business case explains why change is needed, the options (including doing nothing), costs, expected benefits to patients and the organisation, and how success will be measured (P7.12). Evidence should be anonymised to protect confidentiality (Code 5).

n.0: Past rotas may support part of the argument but are not the core content of a business case.
n.1: Support from colleagues does not show need, cost or benefit.
n.3: Identifiable patient information is not needed and would breach confidentiality; anonymised data should be used.

10.q: Leo, 12, has PTSD 4 months after a house fire. His mother asks whether medication would help. Which treatment does NICE NG116 recommend?
o: EMDR as his first treatment
An individual trauma-focused CBT intervention
Psychologically-focused debriefing at school
Sertraline with monthly review by his GP
10.w: NG116 1.6.11: offer individual trauma-focused CBT to 7 to 17 year olds presenting more than 3 months after a trauma. 1.6.14: do not offer drug treatments for PTSD in under-18s.

n.0: EMDR is considered for children only if they do not respond to or engage with trauma-focused CBT.
n.2: Debriefing is not recommended to prevent or treat PTSD.
n.3: Drug treatment is not offered for PTSD in under-18s.

10.q: Mr Shah, 47, has bipolar disorder and develops moderate depression. He is not currently taking any medicine for bipolar disorder. Which medication option does NICE CG185 recommend?
o: Mirtazapine on its own
Quetiapine on its own
Sertraline with lorazepam
Fluoxetine on its own
10.w: CG185 1.6.3: for moderate or severe bipolar depression in a person not taking a drug for bipolar disorder, offer fluoxetine combined with olanzapine, or quetiapine on its own. A psychological intervention for bipolar depression is also offered (1.6.1).

n.0: Antidepressant monotherapy risks switching into mania and is not recommended.
n.2: Neither drug addresses bipolar depression in line with CG185, and the SSRI is unprotected by an antimanic agent.
n.3: Fluoxetine is recommended combined with olanzapine, not as monotherapy.

10.q: Peggy, 90, has a hip fracture and is receiving regular analgesia. At 02:00 she is restless and calling out, her pain score using PAINAD is 7, and her bladder is distended with no urine output for 8 hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Assess for urinary retention and escalate to the medical team
Reorient her to time and place and recheck in the morning
Give a prescribed sedative to settle her for the night
Increase her analgesia without informing the medical team
10.w: Agitation and pain can result from unmet needs such as urinary retention (NICE NG31 notes a full bladder as a reversible cause of pain and agitation). Assess the cause, for example with a bladder scan, and escalate: treat the cause, not just the symptom (P4.8, Annexe B 3.1).

n.1: Reorientation does not address her pain or retention, and waiting until morning is unsafe.
n.2: Sedation masks the cause and increases falls and delirium risk.
n.3: Changing analgesia outside the prescription is not within nursing scope and misses the cause.

10.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
10.q: Mrs Ray, 46, has panic disorder. She avoids the local shop because she believes that if she goes in she will panic, collapse and be humiliated. Which CBT technique is most suited to testing this belief?
o: A planned behavioural experiment to test the prediction
Avoiding the shop until her anxiety settles
Reassurance that she will not collapse in the shop
Free association about her early memories
10.w: Behavioural experiments are a CBT technique (Annexe A 3.6): the person predicts what will happen, tests it in a planned way and reviews the evidence, weakening catastrophic beliefs.

n.1: Avoidance prevents disconfirmation and keeps the fear going.
n.2: Reassurance gives short-term relief but maintains anxiety.
n.3: Free association is a psychodynamic technique, not CBT.

10.q: Bernard, 77, is unconscious and nil by mouth. When you give mouth care, you see white patches on his tongue that can be wiped off to leave a red base. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Brush the patches off firmly with a toothbrush at each mouth care
Rinse his mouth with a large volume of water to clear the patches
Report the probable oral thrush so that treatment can be prescribed
Apply petroleum jelly inside his mouth to soothe the area
10.w: White plaques that wipe off leaving a red base suggest oral candidiasis (thrush), which needs assessment and antifungal treatment. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during oral care.

n.0: Firm brushing traumatises the mucosa and does not treat the infection.
n.1: Large-volume rinsing in an unconscious person risks aspiration.
n.3: Petroleum jelly does not treat infection and is not applied inside the mouth.

10.q: Mr Grant, 44, has bipolar disorder and alcohol dependence and is facing eviction for rent arrears. His care coordinator is reviewing his plan. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Pause his mental health care until housing is settled
Transfer the lead for his care to the alcohol service
Work with housing and alcohol services in his care plan
Leave the housing problem for him to sort out himself
10.w: NG58: the care coordinator works with other services to address social care, housing, physical and mental health needs as well as substance misuse. Do not exclude people from housing or other support because of coexisting SMI and substance misuse (P7.5 interagency working).

n.0: Pausing care leaves him unsupported at a high-risk time.
n.1: Mental health services keep a role for SMI; care is coordinated, not handed over.
n.3: Housing instability threatens his mental health and recovery and is part of coordinated care.

10.q: At 22:00 Sean, 36, an informal in-patient on an acute ward, suddenly packs his bag and says he will 'end it tonight'. No doctor can attend quickly. The registered mental health nurse invokes section 5(4). For how long can Sean be held under this power?
o: Up to 72 hours, or until the approved mental health professional arrives if sooner
Up to 6 hours, renewable once by a second nurse of the prescribed class
Up to 6 hours, or until a doctor or approved clinician with s5(2) power arrives if sooner
Up to 24 hours, with a possible 12-hour extension by the duty doctor
10.w: Section 5(4) allows detention for up to 6 hours or until a doctor or approved clinician able to use section 5(2) arrives, whichever is earlier. It cannot be renewed (COP15 18.25).

n.0: Seventy-two hours is the maximum for the doctor's or approved clinician's section 5(2) power, not the nurse's.
n.1: Section 5(4) cannot be renewed by any nurse (COP15 18.25, 18.38).
n.3: Twenty-four hours plus a 12-hour extension is the place of safety limit under sections 135 and 136.

10.q: Mrs Ahmed, 66, has capacity and care needs after a stroke. She discloses that her husband sometimes slaps her but says she does not want any action taken. Nobody else lives in the home. Following the statutory guidance, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a safeguarding referral but do not let her know it has been made
Share her disclosure with relevant professionals via the safeguarding lead
Report her husband directly to the police against her wishes
Respect her wishes, taking no further action and making no record
10.w: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.92: if an adult with capacity does not want action taken, this does not preclude sharing information with relevant professional colleagues to assess risk and check she is not being coerced. It is good practice to tell her this is being done unless that would increase the risk.

n.0: Para 14.92 says she should normally be told, unless telling her would increase the risk; nothing suggests that here.
n.2: Police involvement against her wishes is not the first step without a wider risk or public interest; colleagues should first assess the risk.
n.3: Her wishes carry great weight, but para 14.92 allows information to be shared with professional colleagues, and the disclosure must be recorded.

10.q: Zainab, a registered mental health nurse, is phoned by the consultant psychiatrist, who is off site. He tells her to 'put Mr Ali on a 5(4)' because Mr Ali is asking to go home. Zainab has just spoken to Mr Ali, who is calm and agrees to stay until the morning. What should she do?
o: Ask a second nurse to invoke section 5(4) on her behalf
Invoke section 5(4) and record that it was on the consultant's instruction
Invoke section 5(4) because the consultant has instructed it
Make her own assessment and not invoke the power on these facts
10.w: Using section 5(4) is the personal decision of the nurse, who cannot be instructed to use it by anyone else (COP15 18.27). The criteria require that the patient needs to be immediately prevented from leaving; Mr Ali has agreed to stay, so the criteria are not met.

n.0: The criteria are not met because Mr Ali agrees to stay; asking a colleague to use the power avoids the personal decision the Code requires.
n.1: Recording the instruction does not make it lawful; the nurse must personally judge that the criteria are met.
n.2: Nobody can instruct a nurse to use section 5(4); the decision is the nurse's own (COP15 18.27).

10.q: Nurse Kemi is asked by a colleague to countersign the controlled drugs register for a dose of subcutaneous morphine that the colleague prepared and gave while Kemi was on her break. Trust policy requires a witness for CD administration. What should Kemi do?
o: Sign it and add a note that she did not see the dose given
Sign it, as she trusts her colleague's practice and experience
Sign the stock balance but leave the witness column blank for now
Decline, and offer to witness the next dose from preparation onwards
10.w: NICE NG46 and RPS/RCN guidance: the CD administration record includes the person administering and any witness, and witnessing means observing the process. Signing for something not seen is a false record (NMC Code 10.3, records accurate). Kemi should decline and the colleague should report the gap per policy.

n.0: A witness signature with a disclaimer still misrepresents the record and breaches the witness policy.
n.1: Trust does not make a signature truthful; she did not witness the dose.
n.2: Countersigning the balance still implies checking a transaction she did not see.

10.q: On a ward for older people, a nurse uses old photographs, wartime songs and conversation about his working life with Mr Black, 89, who has dementia. Which therapeutic intervention is this?
o: Positive behaviour support
Distraction and diversion
Reminiscence therapy
Solution-focused therapy
10.w: Annexe A 3.3: reminiscence therapies use memories, photographs and music to support wellbeing and identity.

n.0: PBS is a framework for understanding behaviour that challenges.
n.1: Distraction redirects attention from a stressor; this is planned recall of life history.
n.3: Solution-focused work looks for exceptions and future goals.

10.q: Maureen, 87, lacks capacity and has life-threatening pneumonia. Her daughter holds a registered health and welfare lasting power of attorney (LPA). The LPA does not contain express authority over life-sustaining treatment. Her daughter says she refuses intravenous antibiotics. How should the team proceed?
o: Delay treatment until the Court of Protection has confirmed that the LPA is valid
Ask the daughter to agree as nearest relative, which overrides the terms of the LPA
Follow the daughter's refusal, as the LPA is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Decide in her best interests, consulting her daughter, who cannot refuse this treatment
10.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s9 (an LPA must be registered) and s11(7)-(8): a health and welfare attorney can give or refuse consent to treatment when the person lacks capacity, but this does not extend to life-sustaining treatment unless the LPA contains express provision. The team decide in Maureen's best interests (s4), consulting her daughter.

n.0: The registered LPA does not need court confirmation, and delaying antibiotics would put Maureen's life at risk.
n.1: There is no 'nearest relative' power under the MCA; decisions are made in Maureen's best interests.
n.2: Registration is required, but under MCA s11(8) an attorney cannot refuse life-sustaining treatment without express authority in the LPA.

10.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
10.q: Two weeks after discharge, a former patient sends a nurse a friend request on social media with a message thanking her for her care. What should the nurse do?
o: Decline the request to keep a clear boundary
Accept as he is no longer her patient
Accept it but avoid sending any messages
Report him to the police for contacting her
10.w: NMC Code 20.6: stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including former patients; 20.10: use social media responsibly. NMC social media guidance warns against relationships with service users online.

n.1: Boundaries apply to former patients as well.
n.2: Accepting still creates a personal connection that blurs boundaries.
n.3: A thank-you message is not a crime; this is disproportionate.

10.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
10.q: Mr Ford, 50, was discharged a month ago. He says he has lost touch with friends, feels isolated and that no one understands what he has been through. Which intervention most directly supports the 'connectedness' element of CHIME?
o: Giving him a leaflet on his diagnosis
Linking him with a peer support group
Increasing his antipsychotic dose
Arranging a review in 6 months
10.w: Connectedness covers peer support, relationships and being part of the community. Peers with lived experience help reduce isolation and model hope (CHIME).

n.0: Information alone does not create relationships.
n.2: Medication changes do not address social isolation.
n.3: A distant review does not build connections.

10.q: Kofi raised a patient safety concern with his manager and then with the trust's director of nursing. Three months later nothing has changed and patients remain at risk. Under NMC guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record his concerns in his reflective accounts for revalidation
Raise the concern again with his manager in writing
Contact a national newspaper to make the risk public
Raise the concern with a regulator such as the CQC
10.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance stage 4: if internal routes have not worked, raise the concern with a regulator or helpline, for example the CQC in England. Code 16.1.

n.0: Reflection does not escalate the risk to anyone able to act.
n.1: He has already used the internal stages without result; repeating stage 1 delays action.
n.2: Media disclosure is not a stage in NMC guidance and may lose legal protection.

10.q: Mr Rowe, 74, is recovering from a hip fracture. The nurse and Mr Rowe are agreeing a mobility goal. Which goal is most appropriate?
o: Improve his mobility as much as possible before discharge
Walk to the day room with his frame by Friday, as he chose
Follow the physiotherapy plan written for all hip patients
Walk 200 metres unaided by tomorrow, as set by the team
10.w: Proficiency P3.4: apply a person-centred approach to shared assessment, planning, decision making and goal setting. Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This is vague and not measurable or time-bound.
n.2: A standard plan is not a personal, shared goal.
n.3: This is set for him, not with him, and may be unrealistic.

10.q: Siobhan, 58, two days after a laparotomy, has a NEWS2 of 9: RR 25, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 102/64, alert, temperature 38.4°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Request a ward doctor review within 4 hours and repeat the observations hourly
Recheck the observations in 30 minutes before escalating
Inform the medical team immediately and request a critical care assessment
Increase observations to 4-hourly and inform the nurse in charge
10.w: A NEWS2 of 7 or more is high clinical risk: continuous monitoring, the registered nurse immediately informs the medical team (at least specialist registrar level) and requests emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies (RCP NEWS2 2017 chart 4). Her score: RR 3, SpO2 2, pulse 2, BP 1, temperature 1 = 9.

n.0: A 4-hour review is far too slow for a high-risk score.
n.1: Delaying escalation to recheck wastes time; the score already meets the emergency threshold.
n.3: 4-hourly observations apply to a total of 1-4.

10.q: Mrs Nolan, 74, has cellulitis of the leg and is otherwise well. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97%, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 84, alert, temperature 39.3°C. Using NEWS2 Chart 1, what is her temperature score and her aggregate score?
o: Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 2
Temperature scores 3, giving a NEWS2 total of 3
Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 4
Temperature scores 1, giving a NEWS2 total of 1
10.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017) Chart 1: temperature 39.1°C or above scores 2; 38.1-39.0 scores 1. All other parameters score 0 (RR 12-20, SpO2 96% or above, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert, on air), so the aggregate is 2.

n.1: No temperature band scores 3 for fever; 3 is for 35.0°C or below.
n.2: The other parameters all score 0, so the total equals the temperature score of 2.
n.3: A score of 1 applies to 38.1-39.0°C; 39.3°C is in the 39.1 or above band.

10.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
10.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

10.q: Marta, a registered nurse, asks Lewis, a healthcare assistant who is trained and assessed in clinical observations, to record observations on three stable patients in her bay. What must Marta do to delegate this task appropriately?
o: Tell Lewis which patients to observe and leave the escalation decisions to him
Explain what to report and when, check he understands and review the results
Ask Lewis to record the observations and to calculate the NEWS2 for each patient
Ask Lewis to observe the patients if he feels confident and has time this morning
10.w: Code 11.1-11.3: delegate only within the other person's competence, make sure they understand the instructions and are supervised and supported, and confirm the outcome meets the required standard. AnnexA.4.1.2 requires clear instructions and checking understanding when delegating. Marta remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for reviewing findings.

n.0: Escalation decisions require registered nurse assessment; leaving them to Lewis passes on responsibility Marta cannot delegate in this way.
n.2: Recording a score without clear thresholds for reporting and review does not meet Code 11.2-11.3.
n.3: Delegation must be clear and planned; leaving it to his confidence and time does not ensure the care is done.

10.q: Mr Mensah, 59, has Black African heritage and is recovering from pneumonia. His pulse oximeter reads 94% on air. He is a little more breathless than earlier. Which consideration is most important when interpreting this reading?
o: Oximeters underestimate saturations in people with dark skin
Oximeters can overestimate saturations in people with dark skin
His reading is within target, so his breathlessness is not significant
An SpO2 of 94% on air means oxygen therapy should be started
10.w: NICE NG253 (practical information on pulse oximeters): some oximeters underestimate or overestimate saturations, especially when borderline, and overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin. His true saturation may be lower, so the reading should be interpreted with his clinical picture and escalated if concerned.

n.0: The reported error in people with dark skin is overestimation, not underestimation.
n.2: Increasing breathlessness is significant even when the oximeter reading is within target.
n.3: 94% on air is within the 94-98% target for most adults; starting oxygen is not indicated by the number alone.

10.q: Kieran, 45, is shouting in a corridor after being told his discharge is delayed. He is pacing and red-faced but has not threatened anyone. Which approach is the best first step?
o: Call security to remove him from the ward straight away
Stand close and tell him firmly to lower his voice immediately
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and acknowledge his frustration
Walk away and leave him until he has calmed himself down
10.w: De-escalation (Annexe A 3.5; NICE NG10) is the first-line response to agitation: a calm, non-threatening stance at a safe distance, active listening and acknowledging feelings, offering choices and reducing stimulation. Restrictive options are a last resort.

n.0: Removal by security is restrictive and premature when de-escalation has not been tried.
n.1: Standing close and issuing commands can feel threatening and escalate the situation.
n.3: Leaving an agitated person unsupported misses the chance to de-escalate and to keep others safe.

10.q: Ms Hart, 44, stopped her venlafaxine suddenly three days ago because she felt better. She now feels dizzy, gets 'electric shock' sensations in her head when she moves her eyes, and is irritable and tearful. What is the most likely explanation?
o: An early relapse of her depression
Antidepressant withdrawal symptoms
A new generalised anxiety disorder
Serotonin toxicity from venlafaxine
10.w: NICE NG222 1.4.13-1.4.14: stopping abruptly, missing doses or reducing can cause withdrawal symptoms such as dizziness, electric shock sensations, irritability, anxiety and low mood, usually within a few days. Venlafaxine is particularly associated with them (1.4.18).

n.0: Relapse does not usually happen as soon as an antidepressant is stopped, and electric shock sensations point to withdrawal.
n.2: The symptoms began within days of stopping venlafaxine, which fits withdrawal.
n.3: Serotonin toxicity follows starting, increasing or combining serotonergic drugs, not stopping one.

10.q: Edward, 66, scores 3 for a respiratory rate of 26 but 0 for every other parameter, giving a NEWS2 of 3. According to NEWS2, what is the appropriate response?
o: Observe at least hourly and ask the medical team to review him
Continue 4-6 hourly observations and review at the next drug round
Observe 12-hourly and reassess if he reports feeling unwell
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
10.w: RCP NEWS2 (2017): a score of 3 in any single parameter is a low-medium clinical risk needing an urgent ward-based response, with a minimum of hourly monitoring and the registered nurse informing the medical team.

n.1: A red score of 3 in one parameter overrides the 1-4 aggregate band and needs hourly monitoring.
n.2: 12-hourly is for a score of 0 and would leave a respiratory rate of 26 unmonitored.
n.3: An emergency critical care assessment is the response to a total of 7 or more.

10.q: Aaron, 33, has been detained under section 3 since 2 January and first received antipsychotic medication on 4 January. On 10 April he refuses it, and the approved clinician believes it is still needed. What is required to continue the medication lawfully?
o: The written consent of his nearest relative
Continue under section 63, which covers medication throughout detention
A best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act
A certificate from a second opinion appointed doctor
10.w: Section 58 applies once 3 months have passed since medication for mental disorder was first given in the current detention (4 January to 4 April). After that, a patient who refuses or lacks capacity can be given medication only if a SOAD certifies it is appropriate. Aaron refuses on 10 April, beyond 3 months.

n.0: The nearest relative has no power to consent to treatment under Part 4.
n.1: Section 63 is limited by section 58 after the 3-month period; a SOAD certificate is now required.
n.2: MCA s28 excludes Part 4 treatment for mental disorder from MCA authority.

10.q: Stephen, 52, received intramuscular rapid tranquillisation on a mental health ward 10 minutes ago. He is now drowsy. Under NICE NG10, how often should his vital signs be monitored initially?
o: Once, an hour after the injection was given
Every 2 hours until he is fully awake again
Every 4 hours for the first 24 hours after the dose
At least every 15 minutes until there are no further concerns
10.w: NICE NG10 1.4.45: after rapid tranquillisation monitor side effects and vital signs at least every hour, increasing to at least every 15 minutes if the person appears asleep or sedated (as Stephen is), has had more than the BNF maximum, has used drugs or alcohol, has a physical health problem or was harmed during restraint; continue until there are no further concerns.

n.0: A single check an hour later misses the period of greatest risk.
n.1: 2-hourly observations are too infrequent after rapid tranquillisation.
n.2: 4-hourly observations miss early respiratory depression and hypotension.

10.q: During a weekly stock check, two nurses find that the oxycodone 5 mg capsule count is one lower than the balance in the controlled drugs register. They have rechecked the cupboard and the most recent entries. What should they do next?
o: Report the discrepancy to the nurse in charge and pharmacy
Wait for the next weekly check to see if the count resolves
Borrow a capsule from another ward to restore the balance
Correct the register balance to match the stock and initial it
10.w: NICE NG46: stock check SOPs include reporting and managing discrepancies between stock and records. Once rechecked, unresolved discrepancies are reported promptly to the person in charge and pharmacy (and the CD accountable officer as required) and an incident is recorded.

n.1: Delaying a week loses the trail needed to investigate a possible diversion or error.
n.2: Borrowing stock conceals the loss and creates a second unrecorded transfer.
n.3: Altering a balance to hide a discrepancy falsifies a legal record.

10.q: For a week, Sean, a staff nurse, has noticed that a colleague often takes long breaks, leaving her bay without registered nurse cover. Two call bells went unanswered yesterday. Which approach is most appropriate for Sean to take?
o: Talk to her privately, describe what he has seen and its effect on patients
Report her to the ward manager without discussing the matter with her first
Mention the long breaks during the safety huddle so the whole team is aware
Cover her bay himself during her breaks to make sure that patients are safe
10.w: Effective confrontation is private, specific and focused on behaviour and its impact on patients, inviting the other person's view and agreeing a solution. Escalation follows if the problem continues (AnnexA.4.2.4 appropriate and effective confrontation strategies; Code 8 and 16).

n.1: Escalation may be needed later, but a direct conversation is the proportionate first step.
n.2: Raising an individual's behaviour in front of the team is humiliating and may provoke defensiveness.
n.3: Covering for her hides the problem and stretches his own care.

10.q: Leah, 34, attends the emergency department after self-harm. A colleague completes a self-harm risk scale, which places her at low risk, and suggests she can be discharged on that basis. According to NICE NG225, what should happen?
o: Assess Leah's needs and agree a safety plan with her, not using the scale
Repeat the scale in four hours and discharge Leah if it is unchanged
Discharge Leah, as the scale places her in the low-risk group
Admit Leah for observation until a medium-risk score can be ruled out
10.w: NICE NG225 (2022) advises not to use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged. Care is based on a psychosocial assessment of needs and a safety plan developed with the person.

n.1: Repeating an invalid tool does not make it a valid basis for discharge.
n.2: NG225 says scales must not be used to decide discharge; a low score gives false reassurance.
n.3: NG225 advises against global low, medium or high risk stratification; admission is decided by assessed needs, not a score band.

10.q: A trust that runs five mental health wards asks how it must meet section 2 of the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018. Which arrangement complies?
o: A separate responsible person, employed by the trust, for each ward
One suitably senior responsible person, employed by the trust, for all
Each of the five ward managers acting as responsible person on a rota
A CQC inspector appointed as the responsible person for the trust
10.w: Section 2 requires an organisation operating a mental health unit to appoint a responsible person, employed by it and of an appropriate level of seniority. An organisation with more than one unit must appoint a single responsible person for all its units.

n.0: Where an organisation runs more than one unit, it must appoint a single responsible person for all of them.
n.2: A rota of ward managers does not meet the requirement for one appointed, suitably senior responsible person.
n.3: The responsible person must be employed by the operating organisation, not the regulator.

10.q: Mr Owusu, 70, has suspected sepsis from a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and the FY2 doctor has reviewed him. Under NICE NG253 (2025), which set of blood tests should the nurse make sure is taken?
o: Urea and electrolytes and FBC, with lactate if the BP falls
Venous gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, FBC and CRP
Arterial gas and troponin, then cultures after antibiotics are given
FBC, CRP and liver function tests, with cultures if fever persists
10.w: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.2-1.8.3 (high risk, NEWS2 7 or more): take a venous blood test including blood gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, full blood count and CRP (plus U&E, creatinine, liver function tests and a clotting screen), and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

n.0: Lactate is part of the initial high-risk bloods and should not depend on a further fall in BP.
n.2: NG253 specifies a venous gas with lactate and blood culture as part of the initial tests; delaying cultures is not recommended.
n.3: Cultures are part of the initial bloods and should not wait for persisting fever.

10.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
10.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

10.q: Siobhan, a registered nurse, is charged by the police with a drink-driving offence on a day off. She has not yet been to court and her line manager is unaware. According to the Code, what should Siobhan do?
o: Declare the charge at her next revalidation application
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell her employer, who will then notify the NMC for her
Tell the NMC if the court convicts her of the offence
10.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and your employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, or if you have received a conditional discharge or been found guilty of a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction). A charge is reportable before any conviction.

n.0: Revalidation is every 3 years and includes a health and character declaration, but Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as possible, not at the next renewal.
n.2: The duty is personal to the registrant and covers both the NMC and the employer; passing it to the employer does not meet it.
n.3: Code 23.2 applies at the point of charge; waiting for a conviction delays a report that is already due.

10.q: Mrs Shah, 66, lives with her husband, who is her main carer, and is due to be discharged from a mental health ward on Friday. She agrees that he can be involved. Her husband had a hip replacement during her admission. What should the nurse do?
o: Involve him, check his current needs and confirm the date early
Leave contact with her husband to the community team
Plan discharge around the support he gave her before admission
Inform her husband on Friday when she is ready to leave
10.w: NG53 1.5.22-1.5.23: recognise that carers' circumstances may have changed since admission, let carers know about discharge plans, discuss progress and readiness, and make sure they know the likely discharge date well in advance.

n.1: The inpatient team should involve carers in discharge planning, not defer it.
n.2: His hip surgery may have changed what support he can give, so the plan must reflect his current circumstances.
n.3: Telling him on the day does not allow planning; NG53 asks for the date to be known well in advance.

10.q: A community nurse reviews Ms Hart, 24, who has anorexia nervosa. Which single finding is a red (high risk to life) flag on the MEED adult risk tool?
o: Heart rate of 38 beats per minute
Heart rate of 55 beats per minute
Tympanic temperature of 36.2°C
Postural heart rate rise of 15 beats per minute
10.w: MEED (RCPsych CR233) adult red flags include heart rate under 40, BMI under 13, temperature under 35.5°C, postural heart rate rise over 30, systolic BP under 90 and SUSS score 0 to 1.

n.1: A heart rate of 50 to 60 sits in the lower-risk band.
n.2: Above 36°C is low risk on the MEED tool.
n.3: A rise of 10 to 30 is amber, not red.

10.q: Ms Lowe, 41, takes fluoxetine 20 mg daily and wants to stop after a year of being well. She has read that stopping antidepressants can be difficult. Which approach does NICE NG222 describe for her?
o: Check her fluoxetine blood level weekly during the withdrawal
Taper more slowly than for paroxetine, as fluoxetine is short-acting
Switch her to paroxetine first, as it is easier to stop
Use a period of alternate-day dosing as a dose reduction
10.w: NG222 1.4.18: fluoxetine's prolonged duration of action means that, for people taking 20 mg a day, a period of alternate-day dosing can provide a suitable reduction; higher doses need a gradual schedule.

n.0: Blood levels are not used to manage antidepressant withdrawal.
n.1: Fluoxetine is long-acting; short half-life drugs such as paroxetine need slower tapering.
n.2: Paroxetine is more likely to cause withdrawal symptoms, not less.

10.q: A newly qualified nurse is learning which ward medicines must be entered in the controlled drugs register. Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, which of these medicines is a Schedule 2 controlled drug?
o: Diazepam 5 mg tablets
Oxycodone 5 mg in 5 mL oral solution
Tramadol 50 mg capsules
Midazolam injection 10 mg in 2 mL
10.w: Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 (Home Office controlled drugs list), oxycodone is in Schedule 2, alongside morphine, diamorphine and fentanyl, and needs a CD register entry (NICE NG46). Midazolam and tramadol are Schedule 3; diazepam is Schedule 4 Part 1.

n.0: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 Part 1 benzodiazepine.
n.2: Tramadol is in Schedule 3.
n.3: Midazolam is a Schedule 3 controlled drug, although many hospitals record it in the register by local policy.

10.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
10.q: A mental health trust signs up to the Triangle of Care. A student nurse asks what the 'triangle' refers to. What is the best answer?
o: Joint working between health, housing and social care
The balance between risk, rights and recovery
Links between the GP, psychiatrist and care coordinator
A partnership of the service user, carer and professional
10.w: The Triangle of Care (Carers Trust) describes a therapeutic alliance between the service user, the carer and the professional, recognising carers as partners in care.

n.0: Interagency working matters but is not the Triangle of Care.
n.1: This is not the Triangle of Care.
n.2: This describes professional links, leaving out the service user and carer.

10.q: Lena, 41, detained under section 3, is on 5 days' overnight section 17 leave at home. Her husband rings the ward: she has stopped eating and is hearing voices telling her to harm herself. The responsible clinician decides she must return. How is the leave revoked?
o: By a magistrate's warrant under section 135(1)
By notice in writing to Lena or the person in charge of her
By an AMHP application under section 2
By a verbal instruction to her husband from the ward nurse
10.w: Section 17(4) allows the RC, where necessary for the patient's health or safety or the protection of others, to revoke leave and recall the patient by notice in writing given to the patient or the person in charge of them.

n.0: A section 135(1) warrant is for people not already liable to be detained; s135(2) may be needed only if entry to retake her is refused.
n.2: Lena is already liable to be detained under section 3, so a new section 2 application is not needed.
n.3: Revocation is the RC's power and must be in writing; a nurse's verbal instruction does not revoke leave.

10.q: A ward team wants to reduce the number of missed doses of time-critical medicines. Using the Model for Improvement, which question should they answer first?
o: Who was responsible for the missed doses last month?
What change can we make that will result in improvement?
What are we trying to accomplish?
How will we know that a change is an improvement?
10.w: The Model for Improvement (used in NHS England improvement resources) asks three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? (the aim); How will we know that a change is an improvement? (measures); What change can we make that will result in improvement? (change ideas). Changes are then tested with PDSA cycles. Setting the aim comes first (P6.4).

n.0: Improvement methods look at system causes rather than individual blame, and this is not one of the model's questions.
n.1: Change ideas are the third question, chosen once the aim and measures are agreed.
n.3: Measures are the second question; they depend on a clear aim.

10.q: Two staff nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station about who should admit a new patient. Patients and visitors nearby are watching. Lorna is the nurse in charge. What should Lorna do first?
o: Admit the new patient herself so that the disagreement is no longer relevant
Calmly ask them both to step into the office and talk the issue through there
Tell both nurses firmly that they will each be reported to the ward manager
Leave them to resolve it between themselves, as they are both experienced nurses
10.w: A calm presence and moving the conflict to a private place protects patients' dignity and the team's professionalism and allows the issue to be resolved (AnnexA.4.2.3 calm presence when dealing with conflict; Code 20.1 and 20.3). The admission can then be allocated clearly.

n.0: Taking the task herself avoids the conflict without addressing it and adds to her workload.
n.2: Threatening sanctions in public escalates the conflict and does not resolve the allocation.
n.3: A public argument is affecting patients now; the nurse in charge needs to intervene.

10.q: Mr Adeyemi, 52, has type 2 diabetes and feels he 'always gets it wrong'. Which statement by the nurse best reflects a strengths-based approach?
o: "Your HbA1c is still too high, so we need to fix your diet."
"Most people find diabetes hard. Keep trying your best."
"Let's list all the things that went wrong this month."
"You've walked every day this month. How could we build on that?"
10.w: Proficiency P2.9: use communication skills and strength-based approaches to support people to make informed choices. Code 2.2 recognise the contribution people make to their own health.

n.0: This focuses on deficits rather than his strengths.
n.1: This is generic and does not identify or use his strengths.
n.2: Focusing on failures reinforces his belief that he gets it wrong.

11.q: At the 08:00 round, Pearl, 81, refuses her prescribed ramipril, saying it makes her dizzy. She has capacity and understands the reason for the tablet. How should the nurse record and act on this?
o: Record 'refused' with her reason and inform the prescriber
Leave the box blank and mention it at the handover
Record 'given', as the tablet was offered at the correct time
Leave the tablet on her locker and record it once she takes it
11.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 17: records are kept of medicines administered, withheld or declined, completed at the time or as soon as possible; the reason is recorded and the prescriber or team informed where appropriate. Dizziness may need a medication review.

n.1: A blank box is unauditable and may lead someone else to give a second dose.
n.2: Recording a refused dose as given is a false record.
n.3: She has declined it; leaving tablets unattended is unsafe and the refusal still needs recording.

11.q: Stella, 52, is an informal patient with capacity on an acute ward whose main door is locked for the safety of other patients. She asks whether she is allowed to go out. What is the correct response?
o: No, because the ward has a locked door policy for all patients
Yes, once her consultant has given written permission to go
No, unless she signs a form agreeing to be back within an hour
Yes, she may leave when she wishes; staff will open the door
11.w: COP15 8.11: an informal patient with capacity on a locked ward must be told the locked door policy, who to speak to if they wish to leave, and must be able to leave at any time unless held under section 5 or an application for detention is made.

n.0: A locked door cannot prevent an informal patient from leaving without legal authority.
n.1: An informal patient does not need a consultant's permission to leave.
n.2: Conditions such as a return time cannot be imposed on an informal patient's right to leave.

11.q: Mr Burke, 64, has capacity and is waiting for biopsy results. His wife asks the nurse to make sure he is not told if it is cancer, as 'it would destroy him'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer the decision to the consultant to settle with his wife
Tell her that her request is unlawful and end the conversation there
Explore her worries and explain he will be asked what he wants to know
Agree, and record her request on the front of the notes
11.w: Code 2.4 respect the level of involvement a person wants; Code 5.5 share with the person the information they want or need to know. Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations.

n.0: The decision about what he is told rests with him, not with his wife and the consultant.
n.1: This dismisses her distress; her worries need exploring with compassion.
n.3: He has capacity; withholding his diagnosis at another's request breaches his right to information.

11.q: A student nurse asks Eleni to explain the difference between the two duties of candour that apply in English hospitals. Which statement is correct?
o: The statutory duty applies to doctors; the professional duty applies to nurses
The statutory duty applies to individual nurses; the professional duty applies to NHS trusts
Both duties apply to individual nurses and are enforced by the CQC
Statutory duty binds registered providers; professional duty binds individual registrants
11.w: Regulation 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 places the statutory duty on registered providers (regulated by CQC). The professional duty (Code 14, NMC/GMC guidance refreshed December 2024) applies to individual registrants.

n.0: The professional duty applies to all regulated professionals including doctors; the statutory duty binds organisations.
n.1: This reverses the two duties; reg 20 binds registered providers and the Code binds individual registrants.
n.2: The CQC regulates the statutory duty on providers; the NMC oversees the professional duty on nurses.

11.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
11.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

11.q: Mr Hale, 45, has depression and took an overdose of paracetamol last year. His GP is choosing an antidepressant and asks the practice nurse which option carries the lowest risk in overdose. Which is most appropriate?
o: Dosulepin, as it can be started by the GP
Sertraline, as SSRIs are safer in overdose
Lofepramine, as tricyclics are safest in overdose
Amitriptyline, as it also helps his sleep
11.w: The BNF states SSRIs are better tolerated and safer in overdose than other antidepressant classes; amitriptyline and dosulepin are particularly dangerous in overdose. NICE NG225 1.13.1 asks prescribers to consider toxicity in overdose for people who have self-harmed.

n.0: Dosulepin is particularly dangerous in overdose and should be started by a specialist.
n.2: Tricyclics, including lofepramine, carry more overdose risk than SSRIs, although lofepramine is less dangerous than other tricyclics.
n.3: Amitriptyline is particularly dangerous in overdose.

11.q: At the end of a shift, the nurse is evaluating Mrs Dunn's care plan for pain after a hip fracture. Which entry best documents her progress?
o: Pain management ongoing; patient seems a lot more comfortable this afternoon.
Patient complained of pain all morning but is settled now.
14:30 Pain 7/10 moving at 12:00; 3/10 at 13:00 after oxycodone. Plan continued.
Analgesia given as prescribed. Continue current plan as per care plan.
11.w: Code 10.1-10.4: complete records accurately at the time, attributing, dating and timing entries without speculation. P3.15 requires documenting progress against goals; a timed, measured pain score before and after the intervention shows whether the plan is working.

n.0: 'Seems more comfortable' gives no measurement and is open to interpretation.
n.1: 'Complained' is judgemental, and the entry gives no times, scores or interventions.
n.3: This records an action but not its effect, so progress cannot be evaluated.

11.q: Mr Ray, 31, has taken clozapine for six months and is otherwise well. He is embarrassed that he wakes with a wet pillow from drooling at night and asks whether something is wrong. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Explain it is a common effect and discuss treatment options
Withhold his clozapine until the drooling stops
Explain this means his clozapine dose is too low
Report it to the team as an early sign of agranulocytosis
11.w: Hypersalivation is a very common clozapine side effect, often worse at night. It can be managed with practical measures and, if needed, medicine such as hyoscine hydrobromide prescribed off-label (BNF). Discussing it supports adherence.

n.1: Stopping clozapine for a common side effect risks relapse and, after 48 hours, re-titration.
n.2: Hypersalivation does not indicate a low dose.
n.3: Hypersalivation is not a sign of agranulocytosis, which presents with infection symptoms.

11.q: Mr Reid, 50, is referred to a community mental health team with low mood. The nurse is completing a biopsychosocial assessment with him. Which information belongs in the social part of the assessment?
o: His thyroid function results and current medicines
His housing, debts and close relationships
His family history of bipolar disorder
His beliefs about himself and his coping style
11.w: A biopsychosocial assessment considers biological factors (physical health, medicines, genetics), psychological factors (thoughts, beliefs, coping) and social factors (housing, money, work, relationships, support). Housing, debt and relationships are social factors (NMC P3.4).

n.0: Thyroid function and medicines are biological factors.
n.2: A family history of mental illness is a biological (genetic) vulnerability factor.
n.3: Beliefs about self and coping style are psychological factors.

11.q: Nora, 80, is dying from heart failure in a nursing home. Tonight she has become restless, keeps pulling at her sheets and is groaning. She last passed urine 10 hours ago and her lower abdomen looks swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe an antipsychotic for terminal delirium
Ask a relative to sit with her and see whether she settles overnight
Give the prescribed 'as required' midazolam to settle her agitation
Assess her for urinary retention and pain before giving sedation
11.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.11 and 1.5.23: agitation in isolation is sometimes associated with unrelieved pain or a full bladder or rectum; treat reversible causes of pain such as urinary retention before considering benzodiazepines or antipsychotics.

n.0: An antipsychotic is considered for delirium only after reversible causes such as urinary retention are explored (recs 1.5.25 and 1.5.27).
n.1: Company can help, but it leaves a likely full bladder untreated; reversible causes should be assessed first.
n.2: Sedation first would mask a reversible cause; NG31 rec 1.5.23 says agitation may reflect a full bladder or unrelieved pain.

11.q: Jade believes her ward manager is altering staffing records to hide unfilled shifts. She does not feel able to raise this with the manager herself. What is the most appropriate step?
o: Raise it with the manager's own staff at the next team meeting
Raise it with the designated person named in the trust's policy
Post her concerns on a professional social media group
Wait until she has more evidence before telling anyone
11.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: if you cannot raise the concern with your line manager, stage 2 is the designated person in your organisation (for example a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian). Code 16.1.

n.0: Discussing it with peers does not escalate it to someone able to act.
n.2: Public posting bypasses proper channels and risks confidentiality; NMC guidance uses internal and regulatory routes.
n.3: Code standard 16 requires her to act without delay; she does not need proof to raise a concern.

11.q: Darren, 35, is shouting in the ward corridor, pacing and jabbing his finger at staff about a cancelled visit. Four staff members gather round, each trying to calm him at once. According to NICE NG10, what should happen?
o: One staff member takes the lead in communicating with him
All four staff keep talking to him so he feels well supported
Security staff are called to stand beside him
Staff withdraw until he calms down on his own
11.w: NICE NG10 1.3.18: if a service user becomes agitated or angry, one staff member should take the primary role in communicating with them, assess safety, seek clarification and negotiate a non-confrontational resolution. Several people talking at once can overwhelm and provoke.

n.1: Multiple people speaking at once is confusing and can escalate agitation; NG10 recommends a single lead.
n.2: Bringing security alongside early can be perceived as threatening and is not a de-escalation technique.
n.3: Withdrawing entirely leaves an agitated person unsupported and does not use de-escalation skills.

11.q: Ms Douglas, 55, has capacity. Last year she made a valid advance decision refusing antibiotics for pneumonia. Today she tells the nurse she has changed her mind and would want antibiotics if she became unwell. She does not want to put this in writing. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep following the advance decision until it is replaced
Ask her to sign a written withdrawal before it can apply
Accept the withdrawal and document it in her records
Ask two witnesses to confirm her change of mind
11.w: MCA 2005 s24(3)-(4): a person may withdraw an advance decision at any time when they have capacity, and a withdrawal need not be in writing. The nurse should record it clearly and tell the team.

n.0: Her withdrawal takes effect now; the old decision does not continue until replaced.
n.1: Withdrawal does not need to be in writing, so a signature is not required.
n.3: There is no witness requirement for withdrawing an advance decision.

11.q: Mrs Hill, 72, started haloperidol six weeks ago for late-onset psychosis. Staff notice that she now shuffles when she walks, has a tremor in her right hand, is slow to start moving and has fallen once. What should the nurse do?
o: Record tardive dyskinesia and continue the current dose
Refer her to a neurologist for new Parkinson's disease
Report possible parkinsonism so her antipsychotic is reviewed
Give PRN procyclidine and continue the haloperidol unchanged
11.w: Drug-induced parkinsonism (bradykinesia, tremor, rigidity) appears gradually, is more common in older women and increases falls risk. The BNF advises reviewing treatment to reduce exposure to high-dose, high-potency antipsychotics when parkinsonism is identified.

n.0: Tardive dyskinesia is orofacial involuntary movement after long-term use, not shuffling and tremor at six weeks.
n.1: The timing after starting haloperidol makes a drug cause likely; the first step is a medication review.
n.3: Adding an antimuscarinic in an older person without reviewing the cause adds confusion and falls risk.

11.q: Sam, 26, has a first episode of psychosis. After discussion he declines antipsychotic medication and says he wants to try talking therapy first. He is not at immediate risk. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Request a Mental Health Act assessment to start medication
Offer family intervention and CBT and review the plan in 6 months
Explain that CBT cannot start until he accepts an antipsychotic
Offer family intervention and CBT and agree a review within 1 month
11.w: CG178 1.3.4: if the person still wants psychological interventions alone, offer family intervention and CBT, agree a time (1 month or less) to review treatment options including antipsychotics, and keep monitoring symptoms and functioning.

n.0: He is not at immediate risk and is engaging; compulsion is not justified on these facts.
n.1: Six months is far longer than the 1 month or less review NICE advises.
n.2: Psychological therapy is offered even if medication is declined.

11.q: Mrs Kaur, 55, has GAD that has not improved with guided self-help. She prefers to try medication. Which drug does NICE CG113 suggest considering first?
o: Pregabalin
Quetiapine
Sertraline
Diazepam
11.w: CG113 1.2.23: if a person with GAD chooses drug treatment, offer an SSRI and consider sertraline first because it is the most cost-effective.

n.0: CG113 1.2.25: pregabalin is considered if SSRIs and SNRIs cannot be tolerated.
n.1: Antipsychotics are not offered for GAD in primary care.
n.3: Benzodiazepines are reserved for short-term crisis use.

11.q: Jake, 19, is brought to his GP practice by his mother. For three weeks he has been hearing voices commenting on him, believes he is being followed and has stopped going to college. He has no previous contact with mental health services. What should the practice nurse advise the GP to do?
o: Start a low-dose antipsychotic today and review him in four weeks
Refer him without delay to the early intervention in psychosis service
Review him in three months to see whether the symptoms settle
Refer him to NHS Talking Therapies for a course of individual CBT
11.w: NICE CG178 says early intervention in psychosis (EIP) services should be open to everyone with a first episode of psychosis and should assess people without delay. Antipsychotics should not be started in primary care for a first presentation unless in consultation with a consultant psychiatrist (CG178 1.3.2.1).

n.0: CG178 advises against starting antipsychotics for first-presentation psychosis in primary care without a consultant psychiatrist.
n.2: Delay prolongs untreated psychosis; CG178 requires assessment without delay.
n.3: Talking Therapies treats common mental health problems; first-episode psychosis needs specialist EIP care including CBT for psychosis.

11.q: Olivia, 23, has a learning disability and is anxious about her admission. During a ward round several staff discuss her care at the bedside using medical terms, talking over her. Which action best role-models person-centred care?
o: Continue the round and explain the plan to her carer afterwards
Speak to her directly in plain language and include her in the discussion
Give her a leaflet about her condition after the ward round finishes
Ask the team to discuss her care at the nurses' station instead
11.w: P4.1 asks nurses to role-model person-centred care. Code 2.1-2.3 and 7.1-7.3: work in partnership, encourage people to be involved in decisions, and use terms people can understand, making reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: Talking to her carer instead excludes her from decisions about her own care.
n.2: A leaflet afterwards does not involve her in the discussion and may not be accessible.
n.3: Moving the discussion away removes her from decisions that concern her.

11.q: An approved mental health professional is assessing Mo, 38, for section 2. Mo's wife, his nearest relative, says she does not want him detained. What should the community nurse understand about her view?
o: It prevents the section 2 application in the same way as section 3
It allows the AMHP to delay the decision by up to 14 days
It requires a tribunal decision before the application
It must be considered, but it does not prevent a section 2 application
11.w: For section 2 the AMHP must take practicable steps to inform the nearest relative (s11(3)), but the NR has no power to block it. The objection bar in section 11(4) applies to section 3 and guardianship. The NR can later order discharge under section 23, subject to the RC's barring report (s25).

n.0: The statutory objection bar applies to section 3 and guardianship, not to section 2.
n.1: There is no 14-day delay power; 14 days is the period within which the applicant must have seen the patient and the s2 tribunal window.
n.2: No tribunal decision is needed before an application; tribunals review detention after it begins.

11.q: A red cell transfusion for Graham, 66, started at 14:00. Baseline pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate were recorded at 13:30 and were normal. According to BSH guidance, when should the next set of observations be taken?
o: At 14:30, 30 minutes after the start
At 15:00, 1 hour after the start
At 14:15, 15 minutes after the start
At the end of the unit, within 60 minutes
11.w: BSH (2017) observations: baseline no more than 60 minutes before starting, then pulse, blood pressure and temperature 15 minutes after the start of each unit, and again no more than 60 minutes after the end. Severe reactions often occur early in the unit.

n.0: The BSH timepoint is 15 minutes, not 30.
n.1: Waiting an hour misses the early period when serious reactions usually start.
n.3: End-of-unit observations are needed, but an observation at 15 minutes comes first.

11.q: Mrs Harper, 58, is choosing between two treatment options for her knee. She asks the nurse what she would do. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to decide by tomorrow morning
Tell her which of the two options the nurse would personally choose
Advise her to follow whatever the consultant recommends
Explore what matters to her and each option's risks and benefits
