11.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire [2015] UKSC 11: patients must be made aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions; P4.2 shared decision making.

n.0: Written information alone, with a deadline, does not support shared decision making.
n.1: Personal preference replaces her own values and undermines shared decision making.
n.2: This removes her from the decision instead of supporting an informed choice.

11.q: A nurse on an intensive care unit in England is caring for four patients for whom organ donation after death may be possible. None has recorded a decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. Which patient is excluded from deemed consent?
o: Leah, 30, who had not discussed donation with her family
Amy, 17, a student who has lived in England all her life
Victor, 75, who completed treatment for bowel cancer last year
Paul, 60, who moved to England from Wales three years ago
11.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England: the opt-out law does not apply to people under 18, people who lack capacity to understand the arrangements for a significant period before death, visitors and people not living in England voluntarily, or people who lived in England for less than 12 months before their death.

n.0: Not having discussed donation does not exclude an adult; her family are approached about any known views.
n.2: Medical history affects suitability, not whether deemed consent applies; age 75 is not an exclusion.
n.3: He has lived in England for more than 12 months and is an adult, so he is not in an excluded group.

11.q: Ivy, 84, now has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to decide where she lives or how she is cared for. Some years ago, with capacity, she wrote a signed letter saying she would like to be cared for at home and prefers baths to showers. How should staff treat this letter?
o: As having no weight now that she lacks capacity to confirm her wishes
As a legally binding instruction that must be followed in the same way as an ADRT
As a statement of her wishes that must be considered in best interests decisions
As binding once her GP has countersigned it and placed it in her record
11.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6)(a): in deciding best interests, consider so far as reasonably ascertainable the person's past and present wishes and feelings, in particular any relevant written statement made when they had capacity. An advance statement of this kind is considered but is not legally binding, unlike a valid and applicable ADRT (ss24-26).

n.0: MCA s4(6)(a) requires decision makers to consider past wishes, in particular relevant written statements made with capacity.
n.1: A statement of wishes and preferences is not legally binding; only a valid, applicable ADRT binds staff to a refusal of treatment.
n.3: A GP signature does not convert a statement of wishes into a binding document.

11.q: Mrs Nolan, 74, has cellulitis of the leg and is otherwise well. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97%, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 84, alert, temperature 39.3°C. Using NEWS2 Chart 1, what is her temperature score and her aggregate score?
o: Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 2
Temperature scores 3, giving a NEWS2 total of 3
Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 4
Temperature scores 1, giving a NEWS2 total of 1
11.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017) Chart 1: temperature 39.1°C or above scores 2; 38.1-39.0 scores 1. All other parameters score 0 (RR 12-20, SpO2 96% or above, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert, on air), so the aggregate is 2.

n.1: No temperature band scores 3 for fever; 3 is for 35.0°C or below.
n.2: The other parameters all score 0, so the total equals the temperature score of 2.
n.3: A score of 1 applies to 38.1-39.0°C; 39.3°C is in the 39.1 or above band.

11.q: Eileen, 76, is prescribed morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously. The ward stocks morphine sulfate 10 mg in 1 mL ampoules. A second nurse witnesses throughout. Which controlled drugs register entry correctly records the dose and the remainder?
o: 2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.4 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.6 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) returned to the CD cupboard
2.5 mg (2.5 mL) given; ampoule recorded as used with no remainder
11.w: Volume = 2.5 / 10 x 1 = 0.25 mL, leaving 7.5 mg (0.75 mL). NICE NG46: for CDs left over after administration, record the amount disposed of and the signatures of the person disposing and any witness. Opened ampoules are not returned to stock.

n.1: 0.4 mL contains 4 mg, so the volume is wrong for a 2.5 mg dose.
n.2: Opened ampoules cannot be returned to stock; the remainder is disposed of and recorded.
n.3: 2.5 mL exceeds the 1 mL ampoule and would be a tenfold miscalculation.

11.q: A ward nurse is referring Mr Kaur, 70, to the community dietitian after finding he has lost 8% of his body weight in 3 months. Which action best supports a safe referral?
o: Ask his GP to make the referral so that it is from a doctor
Send the referral and let the dietitian explain it when they contact him
Send his entire hospital record so that the dietitian has all details
Explain the referral to him and include the reason, urgency and key findings
11.w: P3.16: know when and how to refer safely. The person should understand and agree to the referral (Code 4.2), and the referral should give the reason, urgency and relevant findings, sharing the minimum necessary information (Caldicott principle 3).

n.0: Nurses can refer directly to a dietitian; routing via the GP adds delay.
n.1: He should know about and agree to the referral before it is sent.
n.2: Sending the whole record exceeds the minimum necessary information for the purpose.

11.q: You see a colleague give an intramuscular injection to Lily, 34, then carefully recap the needle with both hands to carry it to the sharps container at the nurses' station. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she carries used sharps in a clean kidney dish to the sharps bin
Advise her to take a sharps container to the point of use and not recap
Advise her to use the one-handed scoop method when recapping needles
Suggest she removes the needle from the syringe before carrying it
11.w: The Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 and NIPCM ch 1.10: needles must not be resheathed or disassembled, sharps are discarded at the point of use by the person who generated them, and the needle and syringe go in the container as one unit.

n.0: Carrying used sharps to a distant bin still exposes staff; disposal should be at the point of use.
n.2: NIPCM does not recommend recapping by any method; the container should be at the point of use.
n.3: Needles and syringes are disposed of as one unit; removing the needle is a common cause of injury.

11.q: Nina, 33, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name and her pain score is 9 while she is using her phone. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
o: Accept her report of pain and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Delay analgesia until her behaviour matches her pain score
Offer paracetamol until the doctor has assessed her pain
Ask her to stop using her phone before reassessing her pain
11.w: Pain is what the person says it is; self-report is the most reliable measure. People with long-term painful conditions often know which analgesia works and may cope with distraction. Prompt analgesia is essential, and judgement based on stereotypes breaches Code 20.2 and 1.1.

n.1: Behaviour is a poor guide to pain in people with recurrent pain, and delay causes harm.
n.2: Withholding effective prescribed analgesia leaves severe pain undertreated.
n.3: Distraction is a coping strategy and does not invalidate her pain score.

11.q: Winifred, 86, lives alone and takes 12 regular medicines from three prescribers. She has fallen twice this month and her daughter reports increasing daytime drowsiness. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the community nurse's most appropriate action?
o: Request a structured medication review with her GP and pharmacist
Spread her doses across the day to reduce side effects
Advise her daughter to buy a pill organiser for the medicines
Stop the medicines most likely to cause drowsiness and falls
11.w: Polypharmacy with falls and drowsiness is a trigger for a structured medication review (NICE NG5 medicines optimisation; P4.15). Prescribers and pharmacists can review the indication, risks and benefits of each medicine together with Winifred.

n.1: Retiming doses without review may cause errors and does not address inappropriate medicines.
n.2: A pill organiser may help adherence but does not address why she is falling.
n.3: Stopping medicines is a prescribing decision and abrupt withdrawal can cause harm.

11.q: An approved mental health professional consults Liam's nearest relative, his father, about an application for section 3. His father objects in writing. What is the legal effect?
o: The father's objection delays the application for 72 hours
The AMHP cannot make the section 3 application while the objection stands
The objection means Liam must be detained under section 2 instead
The AMHP may proceed if both doctors record that the objection is unreasonable
11.w: Section 11(4) provides that an AMHP may not make a section 3 application if the nearest relative has notified the AMHP or the local authority that they object. The route is an application to the county court to displace the nearest relative (s29).

n.0: There is no 72-hour delay rule; the objection bars the application. Seventy-two hours relates to the NR's discharge notice under s25.
n.2: Section 2 may be used where its own criteria are met, but the objection does not require it; that would need clinical justification, not a workaround.
n.3: Doctors cannot override the objection; displacement of an unreasonable nearest relative is a matter for the county court under section 29.

11.q: Nurse Ella is discharging Mr Kerr, 70, with a leg wound to the district nursing team. Which referral content is most useful?
o: The wound plan, next dressing date, allergies and ward contact
A request for the team to phone the ward for details
A brief note saying that a leg wound needs regular care at home
A copy of the full nursing notes for the whole admission
11.w: Annexe A 1.9: share written reports clearly. Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care; Code 10.2 identify risks so colleagues have the information they need.

n.1: This delays care and relies on verbal handover.
n.2: This lacks the detail needed for safe continuity.
n.3: Bulk notes bury the key information the team needs.

11.q: Mr Stone, 35, has self-harmed three times this year. After his psychosocial assessment, the community team plans his treatment. Which psychological intervention does NICE NG225 recommend for adults who self-harm?
o: Single-session psychological debriefing after each new episode
Dialectical behaviour therapy adapted for adolescents
Psychodynamic psychotherapy lasting at least 12 months
A structured CBT-informed intervention, usually 4 to 10 sessions
11.w: NG225 1.11.3: offer a structured, person-centred, CBT-informed psychological intervention (for example CBT or problem-solving therapy) tailored for adults who self-harm, starting as soon as possible and typically lasting 4 to 10 sessions.

n.0: Debriefing after each episode is not a recommended self-harm treatment.
n.1: DBT-A is considered for young people with significant emotional dysregulation and frequent self-harm, not adults.
n.2: Long-term psychodynamic therapy is not the intervention NG225 recommends for self-harm.

11.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
11.q: Ms Clarke, 45, still hears voices at times but works part time, has friends and says her life feels meaningful. A student says she cannot be 'in recovery' while she has symptoms. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Recovery means the full and lasting removal of all symptoms
Recovery is measured mainly by how rarely she is admitted
Recovery means a hopeful, satisfying life even with symptoms
Recovery begins once she has stopped all medication
11.w: Personal recovery is a unique process of living a satisfying, hopeful and contributing life, even with ongoing symptoms; it differs from clinical recovery (symptom remission).

n.0: This describes clinical recovery, not personal recovery.
n.1: Admission rates are a service measure, not the person's recovery.
n.3: Recovery does not depend on stopping medication.

11.q: At a team meeting, a district nursing team leader explains the integrated care partnership (ICP) in her area. Which statement about the ICP is correct?
o: It inspects and rates the quality of local health services
It is the NHS body that commissions hospital and GP services
It is a joint committee that develops the integrated care strategy
It employs the community nurses who work in the local area
11.w: The ICP is a joint committee run by the NHS organisations and upper-tier local authorities in each ICS, with wider partners such as the voluntary sector. It must develop a long-term integrated care strategy to improve health, care and wellbeing (NHS England, What is integrated care?; P7.1).

n.0: Inspection and rating are carried out by the Care Quality Commission in England.
n.1: Planning NHS services and managing the budget is the role of the integrated care board.
n.3: Community nurses are employed by provider organisations, not by the ICP.

11.q: Elif, a ward manager, is preparing a business case for an additional registered nurse on night shifts. Which evidence would most strengthen her case?
o: Comments from staff that the ward has felt busier over recent months
The staffing levels of a similar ward in a neighbouring hospital trust
Red flag reports, acuity data and safe nursing indicators, linked to costs
The number of complaints she has personally received about night care
11.w: A basic business case sets out the problem with objective evidence, the options and their costs and benefits (P7.12 develop a basic business case using finance, resources and safe staffing). NICE SG1 recommends recording red flag events and safe nursing indicators so they can inform establishment reviews.

n.0: Staff impressions are useful context but are subjective and not linked to patient need or cost.
n.1: Another ward's staffing does not show this ward's patients' needs.
n.3: Complaint numbers are a partial measure and do not demonstrate the staffing requirement or its cost.

11.q: Ms Ruiz, 59, has hepatic encephalopathy. She is drowsy and confused in the evenings but alert and orientated most mornings. A non-urgent decision is needed about whether she wants to join a clinical trial. When is it most appropriate to assess her capacity for this decision?
o: In the evening, so the assessment reflects her worst state
In the morning, when she is usually at her most alert
After discharge, once her condition has fully resolved
At any time, since capacity is a fixed state
11.w: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific (MCA 2005 s2(1), 'at the material time'), and s1(3) requires all practicable steps to help the person decide. Choosing the time when she is most alert supports her to make the decision herself.

n.0: Assessing at her worst ignores the duty to take practicable steps to help her decide.
n.2: Delaying until full recovery is unnecessary when she has lucid periods now in which she may be able to decide.
n.3: Capacity can fluctuate; s2(2) recognises that an impairment may be temporary.

11.q: Derek, 70, has COPD and has been admitted twice this winter with exacerbations. He tells the nurse that his flat is damp and that he cannot afford to heat it. Which action by the nurse best addresses the factors affecting his health?
o: Ask the prescriber to increase his inhaler dose for the winter months
Refer or signpost him to local housing and energy support services
Advise him to spend more time in bed to conserve his energy
Record the housing issue and note it is outside the nursing role
11.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.2 and P2.7: understand the wider determinants of health and explain the contribution of social influences and circumstances to health outcomes. NICE PH49 (2014): assess the context in which people live, including their physical, economic and social environment.

n.0: Medicines do not address the damp, cold housing that is affecting his health.
n.2: This does not address the housing problem and reduces his activity.
n.3: NMC P2.7 expects nurses to recognise social circumstances as influences on health and act on them.

11.q: Mr Rees, 66, takes valproate. At a home visit his wife says he has been bruising easily for a week, and the nurse notices his eyes look yellow. He feels tired and off his food. What should the nurse do?
o: Seek urgent medical review for possible liver or blood toxicity
Advise more vitamin K foods and review him in a month
Advise him to drink more fluids to help clear the jaundice
Reassure them that bruising is a common harmless effect
11.w: CG185 1.10.30: advise people taking valproate and carers to recognise signs of blood and liver disorders and seek immediate medical help; stop valproate immediately if abnormal liver function or blood dyscrasia is detected. Jaundice and bruising need urgent assessment.

n.1: Dietary advice and a month's delay could allow serious liver failure or bleeding to progress.
n.2: Fluids do not treat liver injury, and the cause needs urgent investigation.
n.3: Bruising with jaundice and malaise suggests serious toxicity, not a harmless effect.

11.q: Ruth is running late at the end of a shift and plans to email herself her patients' details so she can finish the care plans at home on her personal laptop. What should she do?
o: Print the details and complete the plans at home that night
Email the details to herself and delete them afterwards
Finish the care plans on the trust system before leaving
Email the details to herself with the names removed
11.w: Code 10.5: take all steps to make sure records are kept securely; Caldicott principle 6 comply with the law; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality principle. Annexe A 1.10 share digital information safely.

n.0: Taking paper records home risks loss and breaches confidentiality (Code 5, 10.5).
n.1: Sending patient data to personal email breaches secure storage requirements, even if later deleted.
n.3: Pseudonymised clinical details on a personal device remain a security risk and are not trust records (Code 10.5).

11.q: Mrs Hughes, 72, has severe depression. For 4 days she has taken almost no food or fluid, her urine output has fallen and she is becoming weaker. Two antidepressants have not helped. Which treatment should be considered?
o: Electroconvulsive therapy, as a rapid response is needed
Adding lithium augmentation and reviewing in 4 weeks
Referral for individual high-intensity CBT
Switching to an antidepressant from another class
11.w: NG222 1.13.1: consider ECT for severe depression when a rapid response is needed, for example when the depression is life-threatening because the person is not eating or drinking. Consent and MHA s58A safeguards apply.

n.1: Lithium augmentation also takes weeks; a rapid response is needed.
n.2: CBT is too slow and she is too unwell to engage.
n.3: Another antidepressant would take weeks to work; her condition is life-threatening now.

11.q: Mrs Oyelaran, 79, is being discharged to a care home. Her son repeatedly tells staff in front of her that she 'has to go' and answers questions for her. When asked, Mrs Oyelaran looks at her son and says, 'I suppose so.' What should the nurse do first?
o: Refer her for an assessment of her mental capacity
Ask her son to sign the agreement on his mother's behalf
Record that she has agreed to the move to the care home
Speak with Mrs Oyelaran alone to explore her own wishes
11.w: Valid consent must be given voluntarily, free from pressure by others. The nurse should first speak with Mrs Oyelaran privately to establish her own view. Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)), so concern about influence is not a reason to question capacity.

n.0: There is nothing to suggest an impairment of mind or brain; pressure from a relative raises a question of voluntariness, not capacity.
n.1: A son has no authority to consent for an adult unless he holds a relevant LPA or deputyship; nothing suggests this.
n.2: Her hesitant answer under pressure may not be voluntary; recording it as agreement could be invalid.

11.q: Marta works as an NHS ward nurse and plans to start offering cosmetic injections at a private clinic at weekends. Her NHS employer's indemnity covers her NHS work. What does the Code require before she starts the private work?
o: Confirmation from the clinic that her NHS indemnity extends to it
An appropriate indemnity arrangement that covers the private practice
Written approval of the private work from her NHS ward manager
A note of the private work in her next revalidation application
11.w: Code 12.1: make sure you have an appropriate indemnity arrangement in place relevant to your scope of practice. Professional indemnity is also a revalidation declaration.

n.0: Her NHS indemnity covers NHS work; the clinic cannot extend it, so she needs separate appropriate cover.
n.2: Employer approval may be needed under her contract, but the Code requirement is indemnity cover relevant to her scope of practice.
n.3: Recording it later does not meet Code 12.1, which requires cover to be in place before she practises.

11.q: Eileen, 78, is admitted to a medical ward with a chest infection. Under NICE CG32, when should she be screened for malnutrition while she is an inpatient?
o: Weekly, starting on day 7 of her stay
On admission and at discharge
On admission and weekly thereafter
On admission and when she loses weight
11.w: NICE CG32 (updated 2017): screen all hospital inpatients on admission and weekly thereafter; outpatients at their first clinic appointment; care home residents on admission and when there is clinical concern.

n.0: Waiting until day 7 delays identifying those already malnourished.
n.1: Screening only at admission and discharge misses deterioration during the stay.
n.3: Waiting for weight loss means malnutrition is found late.

11.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
11.q: Mrs Hale, 37, has social anxiety. She says: 'When I speak in meetings, everyone thinks I am stupid.' No one has said this to her. Which thinking error does this show?
o: Emotional reasoning
Black-and-white thinking
Mind reading
Overgeneralisation
11.w: Mind reading is assuming you know what others are thinking, usually negatively, without evidence. In CBT the person is helped to look for evidence for and against the thought.

n.0: Emotional reasoning treats feelings as facts ('I feel stupid, so I am').
n.1: Black-and-white thinking sees things in extremes.
n.3: Overgeneralisation draws broad conclusions from one event.

11.q: At the start of an early shift, Nina, a staff nurse, is allocated four patients on a medical ward. Which patient should she see first?
o: Mr Ali, 66, whose insulin is due with breakfast in 45 minutes
Mrs Dunn, 74, whose respiratory rate is 28/min, SpO2 89% and who is newly confused
Ms Reid, 52, who reports post-operative pain of 5/10, last analgesia 3 hours ago
Mr Shaw, 59, who is to be discharged today and needs his discharge letter
11.w: Prioritisation uses an ABCDE approach and early warning scores: Mrs Dunn has a respiratory rate of 28 (scores 3), SpO2 89% (scores 3) and new confusion (scores 3) on NEWS2 (RCP 2017), indicating possible life-threatening deterioration needing immediate assessment and escalation (P5.5 lead and manage care of a group of people with prioritisation).

n.0: Time-critical insulin matters, but there are 45 minutes before it is due and he is not unwell.
n.2: Her pain needs prompt attention, possibly by another team member, but is not life-threatening.
n.3: Discharge paperwork can safely wait while a deteriorating patient is assessed.

11.q: Daniel, 52, is on a surgical ward breathing room air. His observations are: RR 18, SpO2 97%, BP 124/78, pulse 86, alert, temperature 37.4°C. His NEWS2 is 0. What is the minimum frequency of his observations under NEWS2?
o: Hourly
12-hourly
Every 30 minutes
4-6 hourly
11.w: RCP NEWS2 (2017) chart 4: an aggregate score of 0 requires a minimum of 12-hourly monitoring.

n.0: Hourly is the minimum for a single parameter scoring 3 or a total of 5 or more.
n.2: Every 30 minutes is not a NEWS2 chart 4 frequency; it is the NG253 recalculation interval for high sepsis risk.
n.3: 4-6 hourly is the minimum for a total score of 1-4.

11.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse finds a printed handover sheet listing patients' names, diagnoses and resuscitation status left on a table in the staff canteen. Which UK GDPR principle has most directly been breached?
o: Accuracy (keeping data up to date)
Storage limitation (retention periods)
Purpose limitation (use for stated purposes)
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
11.w: UK GDPR Article 5 requires personal data to be processed securely, protecting against unauthorised access (integrity and confidentiality). Code 10.5 also requires records to be kept securely.

n.0: Nothing suggests the content is inaccurate; the problem is security.
n.1: Storage limitation concerns keeping data no longer than necessary, not leaving it unsecured.
n.2: Purpose limitation concerns using data for the purpose it was collected; handover is a legitimate purpose.

11.q: A school nurse is teaching staff about adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), using the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh ACE study. Which experience is counted as an ACE in that study?
o: Living with a household member who served a prison sentence
Being born early and spending time in a neonatal unit
Moving house and changing school during the primary years
Having a parent who regularly worked night shifts
11.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): the nine ACEs were verbal, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up in a household with parental separation, domestic violence, mental illness, alcohol abuse, drug use or incarceration.

n.1: Prematurity is not one of the nine ACEs measured.
n.2: Moving house is not one of the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh study.
n.3: Parental shift work is not one of the nine ACEs measured.

11.q: On discharge, several patients offer gifts to the ward team. According to the Code, which gift would it be acceptable to accept, subject to local policy?
o: A £50 gift voucher for the nurse who cared for her
A £100 cheque for the nurse's personal use
A designer handbag for the nurse in charge
A box of chocolates for the whole team to share
11.w: Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality, as accepting them could be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment.

n.0: A voucher of this value is not trivial; Code 21.1 says refuse all but the most trivial gifts.
n.1: Money for personal use is not a trivial gift and may be seen as an inducement.
n.2: An expensive gift could be seen as seeking preferential treatment and breaches Code 21.1.

11.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. Which is the most appropriate way to interpret this information?
o: As a possible sign of acute illness that needs assessment
As part of his learning disability needing no action
As evidence that he lacks capacity for all decisions
As a behavioural issue for the support team to manage
11.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability or dementia; rec 1.4.7 says assessment should include history from family or carers. A change from his baseline is significant.

n.1: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability (diagnostic overshadowing) risks missing illness.
n.2: Behaviour change does not establish incapacity; capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2-3).
n.3: Treating it as behaviour to manage ignores a possible physical cause.

11.q: Bella, 24, becomes increasingly agitated in a busy dining room. The nurse wants to help her calm down somewhere quieter. Which location does NICE NG10 advise against using routinely for de-escalation?
o: A quiet area of the ward garden
The seclusion room
Her own bedroom with staff support
A designated comfort room
11.w: NICE NG10 1.3.14 and 1.3.20: separate agitated service users from others using quiet areas, bedrooms, comfort rooms or gardens, and use a designated calming area. Do not routinely use the seclusion room for de-escalation, because the person may perceive it as threatening.

n.0: Gardens and quiet areas are suitable de-escalation spaces in NG10.
n.2: Bedrooms are listed in NG10 1.3.14 as places to aid de-escalation, ensuring staff are not isolated.
n.3: A comfort room is one of the spaces NG10 suggests for calming.

11.q: You are preparing to redress Stan's surgical wound using aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT). Which principle is central to ANTT?
o: Completing the dressing within 5 minutes
Protecting key parts and key sites from touch
Cleaning the wound with an antiseptic each time
Wearing sterile gloves for every dressing change
11.w: ANTT is based on identifying and protecting key parts (for example the inside of the dressing) and key sites (the wound) by not touching them directly or indirectly, with hand hygiene and an aseptic field. Glove choice depends on whether key parts must be touched.

n.0: Speed is not the defining principle of ANTT.
n.2: Routine antiseptic cleansing is not a principle of ANTT and can harm tissue.
n.3: Sterile gloves are needed when key parts must be touched; non-sterile gloves are used otherwise.

11.q: Yusuf, 50, is prescribed co-amoxiclav 1.2 g by slow intravenous injection over 3 to 4 minutes via his peripheral cannula. The second check is complete. The ward is busy and his maintenance fluids are running. How should the nurse give the dose?
o: Add it to the maintenance fluid bag and let it run in with the fluids
Flush to confirm patency, give over 3 to 4 minutes, then flush again
Give it by rapid push over 30 seconds, then flush with saline
Give it without a flush, as the cannula was used this morning
11.w: Safe IV administration via a vascular access device (AnnexB.11.9; NICE CG139 flushing with 0.9% sodium chloride): check patency and the site with a flush, give the drug at the prescribed rate, observe for reactions, then flush to clear the line.

n.0: Adding drugs to a bag changes the prescribed route and rate and risks incompatibility.
n.2: Giving faster than prescribed risks adverse reactions and does not follow the prescription.
n.3: Patency must be checked before each use; a morning flush does not confirm current patency.

11.q: Ali, 52, has had anaphylaxis. Despite two appropriate doses of IM adrenaline, his breathing and circulation have not improved. How is this situation described in RCUK guidance?
o: Refractory anaphylaxis
Biphasic anaphylaxis
Recurrent anaphylaxis
Delayed anaphylaxis
11.w: RCUK (2021): refractory anaphylaxis is no improvement in respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms despite two appropriate doses of IM adrenaline; it needs expert help and a low-dose adrenaline infusion.

n.1: Biphasic anaphylaxis is a recurrence of symptoms after initial resolution.
n.2: Recurrent describes repeated episodes over time, not treatment failure.
n.3: Delayed anaphylaxis describes reactions starting some time after exposure, not failure to respond.

11.q: Mr Bell, 48, has taken clozapine for two years. He tells the nurse he has not opened his bowels for four days and his stomach feels bloated and uncomfortable. His evening clozapine is due in an hour. What should the nurse do?
o: Give his clozapine and advise a high-fibre diet
Offer an antimuscarinic medicine for his cramps
Explain that constipation is expected and will pass
Seek medical review before his next clozapine dose
11.w: MHRA (October 2017): clozapine can cause potentially fatal intestinal obstruction, faecal impaction and paralytic ileus. Patients and carers should seek medical advice before taking the next dose if constipation develops; constipation must be recognised and actively treated.

n.0: Giving the dose without medical review ignores MHRA advice, and diet alone may not treat impaction.
n.1: Antimuscarinic drugs slow the gut further and increase the risk of obstruction.
n.2: Constipation on clozapine can progress to ileus and must be treated, not dismissed.

11.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
11.q: Ms Obi's son, 22, has had his first admission for psychosis. At his discharge meeting she asks what she should do if things go wrong at home. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she reads about psychosis on reputable websites
Give written and verbal information, with crisis contacts
Reassure her that the team will contact her if needed
Explain that information must wait until his consent
11.w: CG178 1.1.4.1: give carers written and verbal information in an accessible format about the diagnosis and management, recovery, carer support, the role of teams and services, and how to get help in a crisis.

n.0: Websites, even reputable ones, do not give her tailored information or local crisis routes.
n.2: Waiting to be contacted leaves her without a plan in a crisis.
n.3: General and crisis information can be given to carers without breaching confidentiality.

11.q: Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool (MITT), Lucy is triaging casualties after an explosion at a shopping centre. A man with cuts to his face and arms is walking around asking for help, with no catastrophic bleeding. Which category should she assign?
o: P2
P3
P1
Dead
11.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) first checks for catastrophic bleeding (P1); if absent, anyone who is walking is categorised P3 (minor) before further physiological assessment (P6.12).

n.0: P2 is reached after the walking, breathing, voice and respiratory rate steps in a casualty who cannot walk.
n.2: P1 is for catastrophic bleeding or abnormal findings later in the algorithm; a walking casualty without catastrophic bleeding is not P1.
n.3: The man is walking and talking; 'dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened.

11.q: During a morning shift, a nurse notices that Omar, 44, who is usually sociable, is sitting alone, clenching his fists, staring at another patient and muttering. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Move the other patient off the ward for the rest of the day
Increase his observation level to continuous and inform security
Approach calmly, say he seems upset and ask what is troubling him
Offer him PRN lorazepam straight away to prevent an incident
11.w: NICE NG10 1.3.13 and 1.3.17: build a close working relationship, sensitively monitor changes in mood or composure that may lead to aggression, and communicate respect and empathy. Early engagement on noticing warning signs is the first step before any restrictive measure.

n.0: Removing another patient disrupts their care and does not address Omar's distress.
n.1: Observation should be used after positive engagement fails (NG10 1.4.12); jumping to continuous observation and security is premature.
n.3: PRN medication is part of de-escalation, but the first step is to engage and understand what is wrong.

11.q: Kemi, 22, is restrained and secluded for long periods, sometimes without clothing, and staff mock her during restraint. Which Human Rights Act right is most clearly at risk of breach?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial and fair hearing
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 12, the right to marry and to found a family
11.w: Article 3 is an absolute right prohibiting torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. Humiliating restrictive practices such as mocking a restrained patient or unjustified removal of clothing in seclusion risk breaching it. NG10 says people in seclusion should keep their clothing.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings, not treatment during restraint.
n.1: Article 9 concerns freedom of belief, not humiliating treatment.
n.3: Article 12 concerns marriage and is not relevant here.

11.q: Kwesi, 28, has just been admitted under section 3. A student asks when section 117 after-care planning should begin. What is the most accurate answer?
o: As soon as he is admitted to hospital
On the day he is discharged from hospital
When the responsible clinician first grants section 17 leave
At his first tribunal hearing
11.w: COP15 33.10: although the duty to provide after-care begins when the patient leaves hospital, planning should start as soon as the patient is admitted, so services are identified in good time for discharge.

n.1: Planning on the day of discharge is too late; the Code says it should start on admission.
n.2: Leave is a later step; planning should already be under way from admission.
n.3: Tribunals expect after-care information, but planning should not wait for a hearing.

11.q: Mr Okonjo, 74, now lacks capacity after a cardiac arrest. He has a valid and applicable advance decision refusing CPR, written and signed, witnessed and stating it applies even if his life is at risk. His daughter is distressed and demands that CPR be given if he arrests again. What should the nurse do?
o: Seek a best interests decision from the medical team
Follow the advance decision and support his daughter
Give CPR because the daughter is the next of kin
Ask the daughter to sign a form overriding the refusal
11.w: A valid and applicable advance decision has the same effect as a contemporaneous refusal (MCA 2005 s26(1)), and the s25 formalities for life-sustaining treatment are met. Relatives cannot override it. The nurse should explain this sensitively and support the daughter.

n.0: A best interests decision is not made where a valid and applicable advance decision already refuses the treatment.
n.2: Next of kin has no power to override a valid advance decision.
n.3: A relative cannot sign away a valid advance decision made by the person.

11.q: Lucy, 31, detained under section 3, has read that patients can now choose a 'nominated person' instead of a nearest relative. She wants her best friend to take that role today. What should the nurse explain?
o: She can nominate her friend, but the AMHP must approve the choice
Nominated persons are not yet in force; section 26 decides her nearest relative
She can nominate her friend in writing to the hospital managers now
The nominated person scheme applies to informal patients but not to detained patients
11.w: Sections 24-28 and Schedule 2 of the Mental Health Act 2025 will replace the nearest relative with a nominated person chosen by the patient, but they are not in force in October 2026. The nearest relative is still identified under section 26 of the 1983 Act.

n.0: No AMHP approval process exists because the scheme is not in force.
n.2: The nomination scheme has not been commenced, so a written nomination has no legal effect yet.
n.3: The scheme is not in force for any patient, informal or detained.

11.q: Mrs Lewis, 61, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 10 years and is admitted with a manic relapse. She says she has 'mostly' taken her tablets. What should happen first regarding her lithium?
o: Switch her to valproate as a more reliable mood stabiliser
Check her plasma lithium level to optimise treatment
Stop the lithium because it has failed to prevent relapse
Add an antidepressant to prevent a later depressive episode
11.w: CG185 1.5.8: if the person is already taking lithium, check plasma lithium levels to optimise treatment. Partial adherence is common and the level guides whether dose or adherence is the issue.

n.0: Valproate is not a first choice here and the level has not yet been checked.
n.2: One relapse does not mean lithium has failed; the level and adherence need checking first.
n.3: Adding an antidepressant during mania risks worsening the episode.

11.q: Gemma, 30, is depressed with suicidal thoughts. She has capacity, agrees she needs hospital care and is willing to be admitted. A junior doctor suggests section 2 'to be safe'. What is the most appropriate course?
o: Admit under section 2 because of the suicide risk
Admit informally and review if her consent changes
Admit under section 4 pending a second recommendation
Admit under section 3 so treatment can be given
11.w: Under the least restrictive principle (COP15 chapter 1 and chapter 14) informal admission should be considered first where a person with capacity consents. Detention criteria require that detention is necessary; a consenting capable person can usually be admitted informally.

n.0: Risk alone does not justify detention if a capable person consents; the least restrictive option is informal admission.
n.2: Section 4 is for urgent necessity with one doctor available; it is not a precaution for a consenting patient.
n.3: Section 3 requires that treatment cannot be provided unless she is detained, which is not met when she consents.

11.q: Simon, 38, has anaphylaxis after an iodinated contrast injection in the radiology department. The nurse opens the emergency drug box, which contains several adrenaline preparations. Which preparation should be drawn up for his intramuscular injection?
o: 5 mg/mL (1 in 200)
10 micrograms/mL (1 in 100,000)
100 micrograms/mL (1 in 10,000)
11.w: RCUK: IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis uses the 1 mg/mL (1 in 1,000) preparation, for example 0.5 mL = 500 micrograms in an adult.

n.0: 5 mg/mL is not a standard adrenaline preparation for anaphylaxis.
n.1: 1 in 100,000 is a dilution used by specialists for IV infusion, not IM.
n.2: 1 in 10,000 is the IV preparation used in cardiac arrest, not for IM anaphylaxis treatment.

11.q: A ward pharmacist explains to nursing staff how NICE judges whether a new medicine is cost-effective in its technology appraisals. Since April 2026, what is NICE's standard cost-effectiveness threshold?
o: £100,000 to £300,000 per QALY gained
£20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained
£30,000 to £50,000 per QALY gained
£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained
11.w: Following a government decision, NICE's standard threshold in technology appraisals rose from £20,000-£30,000 to £25,000-£35,000 per QALY gained from April 2026 (NICE, Changes to NICE's cost-effectiveness thresholds; P7.4 implications of current health policy).

n.0: This higher range applies to highly specialised technologies for ultra-rare diseases, not the standard threshold.
n.1: This was the threshold before April 2026.
n.2: This is not a NICE threshold range.

11.q: Kayleigh, 27, detained under section 2, refuses her prescribed oral antipsychotic on day 5 of admission. She is distressed and responding to voices. Under which provision can the medication be given without her consent?
o: Section 57, with her nearest relative's agreement
Section 63, by or under the direction of the approved clinician
Section 5 of the Mental Capacity Act, in her best interests
Section 58, after a SOAD has certified it
11.w: Section 63 allows medical treatment for mental disorder (other than treatments under s57, s58 and s58A) to be given to a detained patient without consent by or under the direction of the approved clinician in charge. In the first 3 months of medication, the s58 safeguard does not yet apply.

n.0: Section 57 covers psychosurgery and surgical hormone implants, and the nearest relative has no consent role.
n.2: MCA s28 prevents the MCA from authorising treatment for mental disorder regulated by Part 4 of the MHA.
n.3: The section 58 SOAD safeguard applies only once 3 months have passed since medication was first given in the current period of detention.

11.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
11.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

11.q: Ellen, 29, had wheeze, hypotension and urticaria after eating a prawn curry on the ward. She improved after one dose of IM adrenaline and is now stable. The doctor plans her period of observation and later allergy referral. Which blood test should be taken to support the diagnosis?
o: Two sets of blood cultures
Mast cell tryptase level
Serum troponin level
Full blood count and film
11.w: RCUK guidance: take mast cell tryptase samples to help confirm anaphylaxis and support specialist allergy follow-up. Observation is risk-stratified, with a minimum of 6 hours in most people and 12 hours in higher-risk groups, or fast-track after 2 hours in selected cases.

n.0: Blood cultures are taken for suspected infection, not allergy.
n.2: Troponin assesses myocardial injury and does not confirm anaphylaxis.
n.3: FBC does not confirm anaphylaxis.

11.q: Two hours after IV morphine, Brian, 79, is difficult to rouse, has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 7 breaths per minute. His SpO2 is 89% on air. Naloxone is prescribed as required. What is the priority?
o: Call for help, support his breathing and give the prescribed naloxone
Recheck his observations in 15 minutes and document the findings
Sit him upright and encourage him to take deep breaths until he wakes
Withhold the next morphine dose and inform the doctor on the ward round
11.w: Opioid toxicity with respiratory depression is an emergency (P4.15): call for help, support airway and breathing with oxygen, and give naloxone, the opioid antagonist, titrating to restore adequate breathing while monitoring for recurrence. Opioids are high-risk medicines.

n.1: Delaying treatment of a respiratory rate of 7 risks respiratory arrest.
n.2: Repositioning does not reverse opioid respiratory depression in a barely rousable patient.
n.3: Withholding the next dose is needed but does not reverse the current toxicity.

11.q: Mr Nash, 38, takes clozapine 400 mg daily. He returns from a weekend at his sister's and says he forgot his tablets and has not taken any for three days. He asks for his usual dose now. What should the nurse do?
o: Give half the dose today and full dose tomorrow
Withhold it and ask the prescriber about re-titration
Give a double dose to make up the missed days
Give his usual 400 mg dose as prescribed for today
11.w: The BNF says that if clozapine is restarted after an interval of more than 48 hours it should begin again at 12.5 mg once or twice on the first day and be re-titrated, because tolerance to its cardiovascular and respiratory effects is lost.

n.0: Half the usual dose is far above the 12.5 mg restart dose after a 48-hour gap.
n.2: Doubling doses greatly increases the risk of toxicity.
n.3: After more than 48 hours off, a full dose risks severe hypotension, collapse and respiratory or cardiac arrest.

11.q: Owen, a staff nurse, realises he gave Ruth Price, 76, 10 mg of morphine instead of the prescribed 2.5 mg. She becomes drowsy with a respiratory rate of 9/min. The doctor has reviewed her and naloxone has been given. Which action best meets Owen's professional duty of candour?
o: Tell Mrs Price's daughter what happened and leave her to explain it to her mother
Ask the doctor to decide whether Mrs Price needs to be told about the overdose
Wait until the incident review is complete before telling Mrs Price what happened
Tell Mrs Price promptly what happened, apologise, and explain what is being done
11.w: Code 14.1-14.3 and the NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (2024): when something goes wrong, tell the person (or their advocate) promptly, apologise, explain what happened and the likely effects, put matters right where possible, and record and report the incident (P1.3).

n.0: Mrs Price is the person affected; information goes to her unless she lacks capacity or asks for it to be shared.
n.1: The professional duty of candour belongs to each registrant; Owen cannot pass the decision to another clinician.
n.2: Candour is prompt; waiting for a review delays information the person is entitled to now.

11.q: Lucy, 58, has confirmed seasonal influenza and is in a single room under droplet precautions. A nurse needs to stand beside her bed to take observations; no aerosol generating procedure is planned. What respiratory protection should the nurse wear when within 1 metre of Lucy?
o: No mask is needed for brief observations
A fluid-resistant surgical mask
A fit-tested FFP3 respirator
A Type II surgical mask
11.w: NIPCM ch 2.4: an FRSM must be worn by staff providing care within 1 metre of a patient when droplet precautions apply. FFP3 respirators are considered for airborne pathogens and for AGPs on patients with infections spread by the airborne or droplet route.

n.0: Droplet precautions require an FRSM within 1 metre, however short the contact.
n.2: An FFP3 respirator is for airborne precautions or AGPs; routine observations on a droplet-precautions patient need an FRSM.
n.3: A Type II mask is not classed as fluid resistant; droplet precautions call for an FRSM.

11.q: On a home visit, community nurse Faye watches Mrs Dobson give her husband his insulin. She injects into the same small area of his abdomen each time and Faye notices lumpy skin there. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to review the insulin dose at the next appointment
Show her how to rotate sites, observe her practice and document it
Take over all of Mr Dobson's insulin injections from now on
Leave an injection technique leaflet for Mrs Dobson to read
11.w: Nurses monitor and evaluate the quality of care delivered by lay carers (P5.7). Teaching site rotation, observing Mrs Dobson's technique and recording the plan supports safe care and independence; lumpy injection sites can alter insulin absorption.

n.0: Dose review may be needed later, but the technique problem must be addressed directly now.
n.2: Taking over removes the couple's independence when the issue can be corrected by teaching.
n.3: A leaflet without demonstration and observation does not confirm the technique has changed.

11.q: Kezia, a second-year adult nursing student, is ending her placement on a surgical ward. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment (SSSA), who conducts the assessment that confirms her achievement of proficiencies for this placement?
o: Her practice assessor, informed by feedback from her supervisors
Her practice supervisor, who has worked most shifts with her
Her academic assessor, who visits the ward at the end of placement
The ward manager, who signs off all students on the ward
11.w: Under the SSSA (NMC 2018), practice supervisors support and supervise and contribute feedback; the practice assessor conducts the assessment and confirms achievement of practice proficiencies, drawing on that feedback; the academic assessor works with the practice assessor on progression decisions (P5.8).

n.1: Practice supervisors contribute to assessment through feedback but do not confirm achievement of proficiencies.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement for progression with the practice assessor, but does not assess practice on the ward.
n.3: SSSA roles are defined by function, not by management position; the ward manager has no automatic assessment role.

11.q: Mrs Shaw, 70, is weighed as 48 kg and measured as 1.62 m tall on admission. She says her clothes have been getting looser. What is her BMI to one decimal place, and how is it interpreted under NICE CG32?
o: 18.3 kg/m²; this meets the NICE criteria for malnutrition
29.6 kg/m²; this is within the overweight range
18.3 kg/m²; this is within the healthy weight range
20.1 kg/m²; this places her at moderate risk of malnutrition
11.w: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²: 48 ÷ (1.62 × 1.62) = 48 ÷ 2.6244 = 18.29, so 18.3 kg/m². NICE CG32 defines malnutrition as including a BMI under 18.5 kg/m², so she meets the criteria and needs nutrition support planning.

n.1: 29.6 results from dividing weight by height in metres once rather than by height squared.
n.2: The value is correct, but a BMI under 18.5 meets the CG32 definition of malnutrition, not healthy weight.
n.3: 20.1 is a miscalculation; the correct value is 18.3 kg/m².

11.q: In October 2026 a ward induction pack states that 'therapeutic benefit' is now a statutory principle in section 118 that all decisions under the Act must follow. What correction should the practice educator make?
o: The 2025 Act principles apply to CTO patients and the Code principles to others
None; the principles were added to the Code by SI 2026/385 in April 2026
The 2025 Act principles await commencement; the 2015 Code's five principles apply
None; the 2025 Act principles came into force on Royal Assent
11.w: Sections 1-2 of the 2025 Act will put four statutory principles (choice and autonomy, least restriction, therapeutic benefit, the person as an individual) into section 118, but they are not in force in October 2026. The 2015 Code's five guiding principles still apply.

n.0: There is no split by patient group; the 2025 principles are not in force for anyone.
n.1: SI 2026/385 commenced sections 51 and 52 only.
n.3: Royal Assent commenced only technical provisions (ss53-57), not the principles.

11.q: During a ward teaching session on transmission-based precautions, a student nurse asks which route of transmission is responsible for most cross-infection in care settings, including spread via equipment and the patient's surroundings. Which answer is correct?
o: Airborne transmission via aerosols
Droplet transmission over short distances
Blood-borne transmission via sharps injuries
Contact transmission, direct or indirect
11.w: NIPCM ch 2 defines contact precautions as preventing spread by direct contact with the patient or indirectly from the immediate care environment, including care equipment, and states this is the most common route of cross-infection transmission.

n.0: Airborne spread applies to a smaller group of organisms such as measles and TB.
n.1: Droplet spread is important for respiratory pathogens but NIPCM names contact as the most common route.
n.2: Sharps injuries carry blood-borne virus risk to staff, but are not the main route of cross-infection between patients.

11.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
11.q: Ryan, 19, has early psychosis and smokes cannabis daily. He sees no problem with it and says it helps him relax. Which approach by the nurse is most consistent with motivational interviewing?
o: Give him a step-by-step plan to stop smoking it this week
Warn him he will be discharged unless he stops
Leave the subject until he raises it himself
With permission, explore its pros and cons for him
11.w: Step 1: he is in precontemplation. Step 2: MI raises awareness with permission, explores what he values and dislikes about cannabis (decisional balance) and draws out ambivalence, rather than pushing action.

n.0: An action plan does not fit his stage and is likely to be rejected.
n.1: Threats provoke resistance and exclusion is not appropriate (NG58).
n.2: Avoidance misses the chance to raise awareness of a serious risk.

11.q: Ms Ahmed, 36, has worried about everything for eight months and scores 13 on the GAD-7 questionnaire at her first appointment with a mental health nurse. How should the nurse interpret the score?
o: As minimal anxiety, as clinical concern starts at a score of 15
As a confirmed diagnosis of GAD, so an SSRI should be started
As a low suicide risk, as anxiety scores predict suicidal acts
As a probable anxiety disorder, needing a full clinical assessment
11.w: A GAD-7 score of 10 or more suggests a probable anxiety disorder, but rating scales are aids to assessment: they support, and do not replace, a clinical assessment and diagnosis, and they do not predict suicide (NICE CG113; NG225 1.6).

n.0: A score of 13 is above the usual threshold of 10 for a probable anxiety disorder.
n.1: A screening score does not make a diagnosis or decide treatment; CG113 also offers psychological interventions before drugs.
n.2: Scales do not predict suicide; NG225 advises against using tools to predict suicide.

11.q: Tom, 19, attends with low mood. His father has schizophrenia and Tom asks whether he will develop it too. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: It is not inherited, so your risk is the same as anyone else's
Your risk is about one in two because your father has the condition
A blood test can show whether you carry the gene for schizophrenia
Your risk is raised, but most children of affected parents are unaffected
11.w: SPEC.T2 lists genomics linked to MH conditions. Schizophrenia is polygenic: a first-degree relative raises lifetime risk (to roughly 10%), and environmental stressors interact with this vulnerability (stress-vulnerability model), so most children of affected parents are not affected.

n.0: Family history is a recognised risk factor, so his risk is higher than average.
n.1: One in two greatly overstates the risk from one affected parent.
n.2: No single gene or diagnostic genetic test exists; risk is polygenic.

11.q: Nadia, a staff nurse, reports that she gave an evening dose of a medicine to the wrong patient after two patients with similar names were moved into adjacent beds. The patient is unharmed. Which response from the ward manager best reflects a just culture?
o: Remove Nadia from medicine rounds until she has completed a formal assessment
Ask Nadia to apologise to the team for the extra work the incident has created
Record a formal warning on Nadia's file because she did not check identity
Thank Nadia for reporting, support her and review the system factors involved
11.w: A just culture treats honest error as an opportunity to learn, supports the person involved and looks at system contributors (here, similar names placed side by side). This encourages reporting, which PSIRF and Code 14 and 16 depend on (P5.2; P6.6). Reckless conduct is handled differently.

n.0: Removing her from duties for an honest error with clear system causes discourages reporting; support and reflection are more proportionate.
n.1: Asking her to apologise to colleagues shames her and adds nothing to learning.
n.2: Formal sanctions for unintentional error undermine reporting and ignore the system factors.

11.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
11.q: Mrs Green's son, 19, has just been diagnosed with schizophrenia. She is his main carer and feels out of her depth. What does NICE CG178 recommend for her?
o: Advice to arrange supported housing for her son
A carer-focused education and support programme
Referral to her GP for an antidepressant
Waiting until her son's family therapy starts
11.w: CG178 1.1.4.4: offer a carer-focused education and support programme, which may be part of family intervention, as early as possible to all carers, with a positive message about recovery.

n.0: Moving her son out does not meet her own support needs.
n.2: She needs support and information, not presumed medication.
n.3: NICE says to offer support as early as possible.

11.q: Ben, 34, is admitted to a medical ward after self-harm while intoxicated. He is now talking coherently. A doctor suggests waiting until his breath alcohol is zero before making any referral to liaison psychiatry. What does NICE NG225 recommend?
o: Refer if he repeats his self-harm while on the ward
Refer now, as alcohol levels should not delay the assessment
Wait until his breath alcohol reading has returned to zero
Refer once his physical treatment on the ward is complete
11.w: NICE NG225 recs 1.5.2 and 1.5.4: do not delay the psychosocial assessment until after medical treatment is completed, and do not use breath or blood alcohol levels to delay it. Rec 1.7.21: after admission for self-harm, offer referral to liaison psychiatry as soon as possible, alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting for a repeat episode ignores the need for prompt assessment after this one.
n.2: NG225 states alcohol levels should not be used to delay the assessment.
n.3: NG225 advises not to wait until medical treatment is finished.

11.q: Linda, 64, has IV fluids running through a volumetric infusion pump. The pump alarms 'downstream occlusion'. What should you check first?
o: The line, clamps and cannula site for a blockage
The pump's battery level and mains connection
The fluid bag for an air bubble near the top
The prescription chart for the next bag due
11.w: A downstream occlusion means resistance between the pump and the patient: check for closed clamps, kinked tubing and the cannula site (phlebitis, infiltration or a positional cannula) before restarting (Annexe B 5.9).

n.1: Battery alarms are separate from occlusion alarms.
n.2: Air at the top of the bag is above the pump and does not cause a downstream occlusion.
n.3: The prescription does not explain an occlusion alarm.

11.q: Beryl, 84, is admitted to an older people's ward after a fall at home. A colleague suggests completing a falls risk prediction score to decide whether she needs falls prevention. What does NICE NG249 (2025) recommend?
o: Offer an assessment if she falls again on the ward
Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and plan
Complete the prediction tool and act on a high score
Use the prediction tool weekly to monitor her risk
11.w: NICE NG249 (2025): do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Offer all hospital inpatients aged 65 and over (or 50-64 at higher risk) a comprehensive, multifactorial falls assessment and management plan.

n.0: She already qualifies for assessment as an inpatient aged 65 or over.
n.2: NG249 advises against using prediction tools to identify risk.
n.3: Repeating a prediction tool does not make it a valid basis for care.

11.q: Mr Owusu, 81, says he 'came over funny' before his fall at home. The nurse needs to understand what happened. Which response best clarifies his account?
o: "So you fainted, then. How long were you unconscious?"
"What did 'came over funny' feel like for you?"
"Lots of older people feel funny. Let's move on."
"Did you trip on something on the floor?"
11.w: Annexe A 1.6: use clarification techniques; P1.11 communicate effectively with people at all stages of life. Code 7.4 keep misunderstanding to a minimum.

n.0: This assumes a faint and leads him to a particular answer.
n.2: This dismisses an important symptom and stops clarification.
n.3: This closed question narrows to one cause before his experience is understood.

11.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
11.q: During family work for Ben, 25, who has schizophrenia, the therapist notes that his father is often critical and hostile and his mother is very over-involved. Why is this important to address?
o: It is linked with better adherence to medication
High expressed emotion is linked with relapse
It shows that the parents caused his schizophrenia
It means the family should not be involved in his care
11.w: High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement) in families predicts relapse in schizophrenia. Family intervention reduces it and lowers relapse rates (CG178 family intervention).

n.0: High expressed emotion is linked with relapse, not better outcomes.
n.2: Family attitudes do not cause schizophrenia; this belief adds blame.
n.3: The aim is to support and involve the family, not exclude them.

11.q: Marion, 56, says she drinks four 250 mL glasses of wine a week. The wine is 12% alcohol by volume. One UK unit is 10 mL of pure alcohol. How many units does Marion drink each week?
o: 12 units
30 units
3 units
8 units
11.w: Working: 250 mL x 12% = 30 mL pure alcohol per glass; 30 mL / 10 mL = 3 units per glass; 3 x 4 glasses = 12 units a week, within the UK Chief Medical Officers' low risk drinking guidelines (2016) limit of 14 units a week.

n.1: This treats the 30 mL of pure alcohol in one glass as units; 30 mL is 3 units.
n.2: Three units is the amount in one 250 mL glass at 12%, not the weekly total of four glasses.
n.3: This undercounts; each glass contains 3 units, so four glasses contain 12.

11.q: Hugh, 70, has had a stroke and cannot bear weight. He needs to be moved from bed to chair. Which approach is safest?
o: Lift him under the arms with two staff members
Use a drag lift with one person on each side
Use a hoist with an assessed sling
Ask him to stand and pivot using a frame
11.w: Annexe B 7.2-7.3: use moving and handling equipment for people with impaired mobility. A person who cannot bear weight needs a hoist with a correctly sized and assessed sling, operated by trained staff per the handling plan. Underarm drag lifts injure patients and staff.

n.0: Lifting under the arms is a drag lift, which risks shoulder injury to him and back injury to staff.
n.1: A drag lift is an unsafe technique and not part of contemporary practice.
n.3: He cannot bear weight, so a standing pivot transfer is unsafe.

11.q: Ana, 33, has moderate depression. During her assessment she says she feels 'there is no point any more'. The student nurse is worried about raising suicide. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask her directly whether she has thoughts of ending her life
Ask her partner privately whether she has mentioned suicide
Avoid the subject in case asking increases her risk
Wait for her to raise the topic when she feels ready
11.w: NG222: always ask people with depression directly about suicidal ideation and intent. Asking does not increase risk and allows safety planning (P3.10).

n.1: Collateral history can help but does not replace asking Ana herself.
n.2: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea or increase risk.
n.3: Waiting may miss serious risk that she is hinting at now.

11.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
11.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

11.q: Code standard 19.2 asks nurses to take account of current evidence and knowledge about human factors. During preceptorship, Jade is asked which definition of human factors the Code refers to. Which is correct?
o: The physical and mental health conditions that may affect a registrant's fitness to practise safely
The personal values and beliefs that staff bring to their work and that can influence patient care
The study of individual mistakes so that staff responsible for errors can be identified and retrained
Environmental, organisational and job factors, and individual characteristics that affect behaviour at work
11.w: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety (P5.2).

n.0: Health and fitness to practise is covered by Code 20.9 and NMC processes, not by the definition of human factors.
n.1: Personal beliefs are addressed by Code 20.7; the human factors definition is wider and centres on work systems.
n.2: Human factors looks at how systems shape performance, not at singling out individuals for blame or retraining.

11.q: A ward team wants the strongest evidence on whether a new dressing reduces infection in surgical wounds. Which type of study gives the highest level of evidence for this question?
o: An expert consensus opinion paper from specialists
A single large randomised controlled trial
A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
A large prospective cohort study of patients
11.w: Oxford CEBM levels of evidence (therapy): level 1a is a systematic review of randomised controlled trials; expert opinion is level 5. Code 6.1 requires evidence-based information.

n.0: Expert opinion is the lowest level in evidence hierarchies such as the Oxford CEBM levels.
n.1: A well-designed RCT is strong evidence but ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs.
n.3: Cohort studies are observational and rank below RCTs for treatment effects.

11.q: Mr Peter Clarke, 73, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. He can wash his face and upper body himself, although it takes him 20 minutes. A healthcare assistant suggests washing him to save time. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Agree for weekdays and let Mr Clarke wash himself at weekends when it is quieter
Ask the occupational therapist to decide whether Mr Clarke should wash himself
Agree, as it reduces the risk that Mr Clarke becomes tired before therapy
Encourage Mr Clarke to wash what he can, with prompts and help where needed
11.w: Nurses support people to maintain independence and avoid unnecessary interventions (P7.8). Doing for a person what they can do for themselves reduces function and dignity; rehabilitation depends on practice with support where needed (Code 1.2 fundamentals of care; Code 2).

n.0: Inconsistent practice slows recovery and is driven by staff convenience.
n.1: The occupational therapist may advise, but supporting independence in daily care is part of the nurse's role now.
n.2: Fatigue can be managed through planning; removing the activity undermines his rehabilitation.

11.q: During a home visit to Ms Dale, 29, who has schizophrenia and uses heroin, a community nurse sees used needles on a low table where her 4-year-old son is playing. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her to move the needles and take no further action
Discuss it at her next routine review in a month
Remove the immediate risk and raise a safeguarding concern
Wait for her consent before sharing any concern
11.w: NG58: ensure the safeguarding needs of people with coexisting SMI and substance misuse, their carers and wider family are met (think family). Make the child safe now, then follow local child safeguarding procedures.

n.0: A single request does not address an ongoing safeguarding risk.
n.1: A month's delay leaves the child at risk of needlestick injury and neglect.
n.3: Consent is not needed to share information to protect a child at risk of harm.

11.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
11.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

11.q: Lorraine, 59, has had type 2 diabetes for six years and has no visual symptoms. Which of the following is an example of secondary prevention for her?
o: Annual diabetic eye screening to detect early retinopathy
Rehabilitation and mobility aids after a below-knee amputation
A structured education course to prevent diabetes developing
A low-vision service after she has lost sight in one eye
11.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: secondary prevention detects early departures from health so treatment can begin. NHS screening: diabetic eye screening is offered from age 12 to all people with diabetes to check for early signs of diabetic retinopathy.

n.1: This reduces long-term disability from an established complication, which is tertiary prevention.
n.2: Lorraine already has diabetes; preventing its onset in people at risk would be primary prevention.
n.3: Support after sight loss limits disability from established disease, which is tertiary prevention.

11.q: Ruth, 63, has cellulitis and suspected sepsis. Her NEWS2 is 6, made up of RR 3 and three single points, and her worsening is thought to be due to the infection. Under NICE NG253 (2025), how should she be managed?
o: As high risk, with IV antibiotics within 1 hour
As very low risk, with standard observation frequency
As medium risk, with antibiotics deferred up to 3 hours
As low risk, with review by a registered practitioner in 1 hour
11.w: NG253: for a NEWS2 of 5-6 that includes a single parameter scoring 3, if this is likely to be due to the infection, manage as high risk. High risk means IV antibiotics within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score.

n.1: Very low risk applies to a NEWS2 of 0.
n.2: Medium-risk deferral does not apply where a single 3 is likely caused by the infection.
n.3: Low-risk management applies to NEWS2 1-4, not 6.

11.q: Mr Hart, 44, has taken clozapine for eight months. Today's result from the monitoring service shows white cell count 3.4 x 10^9/L and neutrophils 1.3 x 10^9/L. He feels well. His morning dose is due. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the dose and repeat the blood test in a week
Withhold the dose and inform the prescriber urgently
Give the dose, as his white cell count is above 3.0
Halve the dose until his neutrophil count recovers
11.w: BNF: if the leucocyte count falls below 3000/mm3 (3.0 x 10^9/L) or the absolute neutrophil count below 1500/mm3 (1.5 x 10^9/L), clozapine must be stopped permanently and the person referred to a haematologist. His neutrophils are 1.3 x 10^9/L, below the threshold.

n.0: Continuing clozapine with neutrophils below the threshold risks agranulocytosis.
n.2: The neutrophil count is below 1.5 x 10^9/L, which requires stopping even though the white cell count is above 3.0.
n.3: Dose reduction is not the response; the BNF requires clozapine to be stopped.

12.q: Mr Faris, 24, is on his first admission to an acute ward and has never taken antipsychotic medication. Despite de-escalation he is hitting out at staff, and he has refused oral medication. The team decides rapid tranquillisation is needed. Under NICE NG10, which medication should be used?
o: IV diazepam on its own
IM haloperidol on its own
IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
IM lorazepam on its own
12.w: NG10 1.4.37-1.4.38: use either IM lorazepam alone or IM haloperidol combined with IM promethazine; if there is insufficient information to guide the choice, or the person has not taken antipsychotics before, use IM lorazepam.

n.0: IV use is exceptional in NG10 and diazepam is not one of the recommended options.
n.1: NG10 pairs haloperidol with promethazine; haloperidol alone raises the risk of acute dystonia.
n.2: Haloperidol with promethazine is an NG10 option, but not for someone who is antipsychotic-naive.

12.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
12.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

12.q: A ward nurse is checking which patients qualify for an independent mental health advocate (IMHA). Which patient is a qualifying patient?
o: Sam, held under section 136 at a place of safety
Ash, held under section 4 before a second recommendation
Bo, held by a nurse under section 5(4)
Lee, detained under section 2 on an acute ward
12.w: Under sections 130A-130C qualifying patients include those liable to be detained under the Act (including section 2 and section 3), CTO and guardianship patients. Short-term powers (s4 before conversion, s5(2), s5(4), s135, s136) are excluded.

n.0: People held under section 136 are excluded from IMHA eligibility.
n.1: Section 4 patients qualify once the second recommendation converts the section; before that they are excluded.
n.2: Patients held under the section 5 holding powers are excluded.

12.q: During equality training, a healthcare assistant asks which personal characteristic is protected under section 4 of the Equality Act 2010. Which of these is a protected characteristic?
o: Pregnancy and maternity
Body weight or size
Socioeconomic background
Caring responsibilities
12.w: Equality Act 2010 s4 lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.

n.1: Weight is not a protected characteristic, although a related condition may amount to a disability.
n.2: Socioeconomic background is not one of the nine protected characteristics in s4.
n.3: Being a carer is not itself a listed characteristic in s4.

12.q: Ruby, 39, was detained under section 3. Her section was discharged by the tribunal, but she chose to stay on the ward informally for 3 more weeks before going home. Is she entitled to section 117 after-care?
