o: No, because her section was discharged by the tribunal
Yes, because she ceased to be detained and then left hospital
Yes, for a fixed period of 6 weeks after she leaves hospital
No, because she left the hospital as an informal patient
12.w: Section 117(1) applies to qualifying patients who cease to be detained and, whether or not immediately after so ceasing, leave hospital. COP15 33.9 confirms patients who remain informally after detention ends are still entitled once they leave.

n.0: The way detention ended, including tribunal discharge, does not affect entitlement.
n.2: There is no 6-week limit; after-care lasts until both bodies agree it is no longer needed.
n.3: Leaving as an informal patient does not remove entitlement; the Act covers leaving 'whether or not immediately'.

12.q: Rose, 79, rings her bell repeatedly at night. When you answer she says she is uncomfortable, cold and needs the toilet. Her pain score is 1 out of 10. What is the best approach to help her rest?
o: Meet her comfort and toileting needs and plan regular night checks
Explain that the bell is for emergencies and move it out of her reach
Give her a sedative to help her sleep without disturbing others
Close the door to her side room so that she is not disturbed
12.w: Annexe B 3.1 and 3.6: assess and meet comfort needs such as warmth, toileting and positioning, which are common barriers to sleep. Intentional rounding at intervals can reduce unmet need and calls.

n.1: Removing the call bell is unsafe and a breach of dignity and safety.
n.2: Sedation does not address her unmet needs and increases falls risk.
n.3: Closing the door does not meet her needs and reduces observation.

12.q: Deborah, 46, received IM adrenaline 500 micrograms for anaphylaxis 5 minutes ago. She remains wheezy with BP 84/52 mmHg. What should happen next?
o: Wait a further 15 minutes before repeating adrenaline
Give chlorphenamine IV and wait for it to take effect
Sit her upright with her legs lowered to ease breathing
Give a second IM adrenaline dose and an IV crystalloid bolus
12.w: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and give an IV crystalloid bolus (adults 500-1,000 mL) for circulatory problems, with high-flow oxygen and monitoring.

n.0: RCUK advises a repeat dose after 5 minutes, not 15.
n.1: Antihistamines are not used to treat ABC problems in anaphylaxis.
n.2: With hypotension she should lie flat with or without legs raised; sitting with legs down worsens circulation.

12.q: At a serious incident review after Michael, 29, a detained patient, took his life on the ward, the panel discusses which Human Rights Act 1998 Article places a positive duty on the hospital to take reasonable steps to protect patients from a real and immediate risk of suicide. Which Article is it?
o: Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 8, right to respect for private and family life
Article 2, right to life
Article 5, right to liberty and security
12.w: Article 2 (right to life) includes a positive operational duty on the state, including NHS hospitals, to take reasonable steps to protect a person in its care, such as a detained patient, from a real and immediate risk to life that it knows or ought to know about.

n.0: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, not the duty to protect life.
n.1: Article 8 protects privacy and family life; protecting life is Article 2.
n.3: Article 5 protects liberty and governs lawful detention, not protection from suicide.

12.q: Mr Obi, 27, stopped his olanzapine a month ago because he gained a lot of weight and felt 'flat'. He tells his care coordinator he will not take it again. He is well at present. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explore his concerns and review options with the prescriber
Explain that he will be detained if he refuses to take it
Ask his mother to mix crushed tablets into his meals
Arrange a depot injection so that doses cannot be missed
12.w: Shared decision-making explores the person's experience, priorities and the side effects they are willing to tolerate, and reviews alternatives with the prescriber (NICE CG178 1.3.6.3; NG5 medicines optimisation; NMC Annexe A 3.1 motivational approaches).

n.1: Threatening detention is coercive and does not reflect the legal criteria or partnership working.
n.2: Covert administration to a person with capacity is unlawful and a breach of trust.
n.3: Imposing a depot without his agreement ignores his concerns and preferences.

12.q: A nurse audits mental health detentions in her trust and finds that Black patients are detained at much higher rates than White patients. Which NHS England framework is designed to help trusts address this inequality?
o: The Workforce Race Equality Standard (WRES)
The Triangle of Care for carers and families
The Patient and Carer Race Equality Framework
The Community Mental Health Framework (2019)
12.w: The Patient and Carer Race Equality Framework (PCREF) is NHS England's anti-racism framework for mental health providers, aimed at improving racial equity in access, experience and outcomes, including use of the Mental Health Act, where Black people are consistently over-represented.

n.0: The Workforce Race Equality Standard concerns staff, not patients and carers; PCREF is the patient-focused framework.
n.1: The Triangle of Care is a carers' partnership framework, not a race equality framework.
n.3: The Community Mental Health Framework reshapes community services; it is not the race equality framework.

12.q: Mr Shaw, 50, has been well on lithium for four years and, after discussion with his psychiatrist, has decided to stop it. He asks the nurse how this will be done. Which plan reflects NICE CG185?
o: Halve the dose for 1 week and then stop it completely
Reduce gradually over at least 4 weeks and watch for relapse
Stop over 3 days to limit time at a sub-therapeutic level
Stop it now and check his serum level after 3 months
12.w: CG185 1.10.25-1.10.26: stop lithium gradually over at least 4 weeks, preferably up to 3 months, and monitor for early signs of mania or depression during the reduction and for 3 months after stopping, because abrupt withdrawal increases relapse risk.

n.0: Halving the dose for 1 week and then stopping is a 1-week taper, well short of the minimum 4 weeks in CG185 1.10.25.
n.2: Stopping over 3 days is close to abrupt withdrawal and raises the risk of manic relapse.
n.3: Abrupt stopping risks relapse, and a level after stopping serves no purpose.

12.q: Nurse Ali phones a doctor about Mr Cole using SBAR. He says, "I think he may be developing sepsis." Which part of SBAR is this?
o: Assessment
Situation
Background
Recommendation
12.w: NHS England SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation): Assessment is the nurse's evaluation of the problem.

n.1: Situation states the immediate problem, for example 'his NEWS2 is 6'.
n.2: Background gives history and context.
n.3: Recommendation states what the nurse wants done.

12.q: A nurse is carrying out a whole-body systems assessment of Mr Burns, 80, who has been bedbound for several days. On the skin review she finds a red area over his sacrum that does not blanch with light finger pressure. What should she do?
o: Record it as a category 2 pressure ulcer and apply a dressing
Reassess it at his next weekly skin inspection
Massage the area to restore its circulation and recheck it tomorrow
Start pressure ulcer prevention and recheck the skin at least 2-hourly
12.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy to test blanching; if non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until resolved. A systems assessment includes skin (Annexe B 2.7).

n.0: Intact non-blanching erythema is a category 1 finding, not category 2, which involves partial-thickness skin loss.
n.1: Weekly review is too infrequent; CG179 requires at least 2-hourly reassessment.
n.2: Massaging pressure-damaged skin can cause further harm, and a day's delay is too long.

12.q: A patient's family sends Hannah a thank-you card that names their mother and praises Hannah's care during her last days. Hannah wants to use it as practice-related feedback for revalidation. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Place a copy of the card in her revalidation portfolio
Ask her line manager to countersign the card before use
Note the content of the feedback without identifying details
Exclude it, as feedback must be formal and in writing
12.w: NMC revalidation: five pieces of practice-related feedback from any source, written or verbal, formal or informal. Keep a note of the content and how it improved practice, without recording anything that could identify another person.

n.0: The card names the patient; NMC guidance says not to record information that may identify another person.
n.1: Feedback does not need countersigning; the key requirement is to remove identifying information.
n.3: Feedback can be written or verbal, formal or informal, from patients, families or colleagues.

12.q: Raymond, 82, has a DNACPR decision recorded after a discussion with him. Overnight he develops a temperature of 39.1°C, a heart rate of 118 and new confusion, giving a NEWS2 of 7. A colleague says there is 'no point escalating because he is DNACPR'. What should the nurse do?
o: Phone his family first to ask whether he should be treated for infection
Withhold escalation because the DNACPR shows he is not for active treatment
Escalate urgently for sepsis review, as the DNACPR decision covers CPR
Start the end of life care plan, as the DNACPR shows he is now dying
12.w: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BMA, RCUK, RCN, 3rd edition): a decision not to attempt CPR applies only to CPR and not to any other treatment. A NEWS2 of 7 needs an emergency response (RCP 2017) and possible sepsis is managed under NICE NG253 (2025).

n.0: Raymond's deterioration needs urgent escalation now; his family do not decide his treatment and delay risks harm.
n.1: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other appropriate treatment continues (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
n.3: A DNACPR decision does not mean a person is dying; recognising dying is a separate assessment (NICE NG31).

12.q: Ade, 42, is detained under section 3. On Monday at 10:00 his nearest relative gives the hospital managers written notice that she will discharge him. The responsible clinician believes Ade would be likely to act dangerously to himself if discharged. What should happen?
o: The AMHP can veto the discharge by applying for section 2
The RC must apply to the county court within 7 days to stop the discharge
Ade must be discharged at 10:00 on Monday
The RC can make a barring report within 72 hours, stopping the discharge
12.w: Under section 25 the nearest relative must give at least 72 hours' written notice. Within that period the RC can bar the discharge by reporting that the patient would be likely to act in a manner dangerous to himself or others. The NR then cannot order discharge again for 6 months but can apply to a tribunal.

n.0: A new section 2 would not be a lawful way to defeat an NR order; the statutory route is the RC's barring report.
n.1: No county court application is needed to bar discharge; the RC uses a barring report under s25.
n.2: The NR's order takes effect after 72 hours' notice, and can be barred by the RC within that time.

12.q: Nurse Ella is discharging Mr Kerr, 70, with a leg wound to the district nursing team. Which referral content is most useful?
o: The wound plan, next dressing date, allergies and ward contact
A request for the team to phone the ward for details
A brief note saying that a leg wound needs regular care at home
A copy of the full nursing notes for the whole admission
12.w: Annexe A 1.9: share written reports clearly. Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care; Code 10.2 identify risks so colleagues have the information they need.

n.1: This delays care and relies on verbal handover.
n.2: This lacks the detail needed for safe continuity.
n.3: Bulk notes bury the key information the team needs.

12.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
12.q: Mr Shah, 29, has bipolar disorder. He says: 'People like me are mad. No one will employ me, so there is no point applying for jobs.' What is he describing?
o: Public stigma
Stigma by association
Structural stigma
Self-stigma
12.w: Self-stigma (internalised stigma) is when a person accepts negative stereotypes about mental illness and applies them to themselves, lowering self-esteem and leading to the 'why try' effect.

n.0: Public stigma is the negative attitudes held by others in society.
n.1: Stigma by association affects family and carers.
n.2: Structural stigma is in policies and institutions.

12.q: Mo, 45, previously detained under section 3, has been well for 2 years and is discharged from the community mental health team to his GP. He still lives in supported accommodation arranged under section 117. What should happen to his after-care?
o: It transfers to his GP, who decides whether it should continue
It continues while he needs services related to his disorder
It ends on his discharge from the community mental health team
It ends now that 2 years have passed without any readmission
12.w: COP15 33.20-33.21: after-care continues until both the ICB and local authority are satisfied it is no longer needed. It should not be withdrawn solely because the person is discharged from specialist services or an arbitrary period has passed. Suitable alternative accommodation must be in place before withdrawal.

n.0: The GP does not hold the s117 duty; it remains with the ICB and local authority.
n.2: Discharge from specialist services is listed in COP15 33.21 as an improper sole reason to end after-care.
n.3: An arbitrary period passing is also not a valid sole reason (COP15 33.21).

12.q: Mrs Agnes Doyle, 84, lives alone and is recovering from pneumonia on a medical ward in England. She will need help with personal care at home. Which organisation is responsible for assessing her need for care and support at home?
o: Her GP practice
The integrated care board
The local authority
The acute hospital trust
12.w: Under the Care Act 2014, local authorities assess adults who appear to need care and support and are responsible for social care (and public health) in their area. The ward nurse refers so assessment can be planned before discharge (P7.1 interagency working; FACTS S-CA, S-ICS).

n.0: The GP provides health care but does not carry out Care Act assessments.
n.1: The ICB plans and funds NHS health services, not adult social care assessments.
n.3: Hospital staff contribute to discharge planning, but the statutory needs assessment is the local authority's duty.

12.q: Ana, 33, has moderate depression. During her assessment she says she feels 'there is no point any more'. The student nurse is worried about raising suicide. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask her directly whether she has thoughts of ending her life
Ask her partner privately whether she has mentioned suicide
Avoid the subject in case asking increases her risk
Wait for her to raise the topic when she feels ready
12.w: NG222: always ask people with depression directly about suicidal ideation and intent. Asking does not increase risk and allows safety planning (P3.10).

n.1: Collateral history can help but does not replace asking Ana herself.
n.2: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea or increase risk.
n.3: Waiting may miss serious risk that she is hinting at now.

12.q: At 16:30 the laboratory phones the ward with a potassium result of 6.9 mmol/L for Mr Hayes, 74, who has chronic kidney disease. He feels 'a bit weak' but is otherwise as before. The doctor who requested the test has gone home. What should the nurse do?
o: Escalate to the on-call doctor now and document the result
Recheck his observations in 4 hours and escalate if they change
Record the result for the day team to review in the morning
Ask the laboratory to send the result to his GP for review
12.w: NMC proficiency P3.12 requires nurses to interpret results and act promptly, escalating when required. A potassium of 6.9 mmol/L is markedly raised and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, so the on-call doctor must be told now and the communication documented (Code 10).

n.1: Normal-looking observations do not exclude the risk of arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia.
n.2: Waiting until morning leaves a dangerous result untreated for hours.
n.3: The GP is not responsible for an inpatient's urgent results.

12.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
12.q: A student nurse asks what makes cognitive behavioural therapy different from other talking therapies. Which description is most accurate?
o: It offers unstructured, open-ended time to talk
It focuses mainly on improving relationships with other people
It links current thoughts, feelings, behaviour and body sensations
It explores unconscious conflicts from early childhood years
12.w: CBT is structured, time-limited and collaborative, focuses on current problems and how thoughts, emotions, behaviour and physical sensations interact, and uses homework to practise new skills.

n.0: CBT is structured and goal-focused, not open-ended.
n.1: This describes interpersonal therapy.
n.3: This describes psychodynamic therapy.

12.q: Which communication tool is widely used in UK healthcare to structure an urgent telephone escalation to a doctor about a deteriorating person?
o: SOAP: subjective, objective, assessment, plan
PDSA: plan, do, study, act
SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, timed
SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation
12.w: SBAR is the standard structured tool used across the NHS for escalation, giving the listener the situation, relevant background, the nurse's assessment and a clear recommendation or request (Annexe A 4.2.6.2 appropriate escalation).

n.0: SOAP is a format for documenting a clinical encounter, not for escalation calls.
n.1: PDSA is the Model for Improvement cycle used in quality improvement.
n.2: SMART describes how to write goals or objectives.

12.q: Ruby, 19, is restrained by trained staff after assaulting a nurse. She is taken to the floor face down. Which action is most important for the nurse coordinating the restraint?
o: Monitor her airway and breathing and move her off her front quickly
Hold her in the face-down position until rapid tranquillisation works
Apply weight across her back to keep her still until she is calm
Leave the room so that the restraining staff can work without distraction
12.w: NICE NG10: avoid taking a person to the floor; if prone restraint is needed, use it for as short a time as possible, avoid pressure on the chest, neck or abdomen, and have one staff member monitor airway, breathing and physical condition throughout.

n.1: Prolonged prone restraint increases the risk of positional asphyxia.
n.2: Pressure on the back or chest restricts breathing and has caused deaths in restraint.
n.3: A staff member must stay to monitor her airway and wellbeing throughout.

12.q: A practice nurse is checking her understanding of vaccine types before a childhood immunisation clinic. Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
o: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23)
Inactivated poliomyelitis vaccine (IPV)
Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine
Tetanus vaccine containing inactivated toxin
12.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): live attenuated vaccines include yellow fever, measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) and BCG; the weakened organism replicates in the recipient. IPV contains inactivated virus, tetanus and diphtheria vaccines contain toxoids, and pneumococcal vaccine contains capsular polysaccharide.

n.0: PPV23 contains capsular polysaccharide, not a live organism.
n.1: IPV contains inactivated virus, which cannot cause the disease.
n.3: Tetanus vaccine contains an inactivated toxin (toxoid), not a live organism.

12.q: A ward team cannot agree whether to share a patient's HIV status with a care agency that will provide personal care at home. The patient has capacity but has not been asked yet. Who in the organisation is responsible for advising on difficult decisions about confidential information?
o: The ward matron on duty
The Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
The Data Protection Officer at the ICO
The Caldicott Guardian
12.w: The Caldicott Guardian is the senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of patient information and enabling appropriate sharing; the Caldicott principles advise involving them in difficult decisions. The first step remains asking the patient.

n.0: The matron can support the team but is not the designated lead for confidentiality decisions.
n.1: Freedom to Speak Up Guardians support staff to raise concerns; they do not advise on confidentiality decisions.
n.2: The ICO is the external regulator; it does not advise on individual sharing decisions within a trust.

12.q: Ida, 79, is being fed through a nasogastric tube. During the feed she starts coughing, becomes breathless and her SpO2 falls from 96% to 89%. What should the nurse do first?
o: Slow the feed rate and recheck her saturation
Flush the tube with water to clear any blockage
Stop the feed, sit her up and call for urgent help
Check the tube length mark and continue feeding
12.w: Sudden coughing, breathlessness and desaturation during a feed suggest aspiration or tube misplacement. Stop the feed, sit her upright, give oxygen and get urgent help (Annexe B 5.7; misplaced tubes are a Never Event).

n.0: Continuing a slower feed risks further aspiration.
n.1: Flushing adds more fluid to a possibly misplaced tube.
n.3: Continuing feeding is unsafe until the cause is established.

12.q: Mrs Webb, 72, takes ibuprofen for arthritis. She vomits a moderate amount of dark brown material that looks like coffee grounds. Her pulse is 108 and her blood pressure is lower than earlier. What should the nurse do?
o: Send a stool sample to the laboratory for testing
Dispose of the vomit and offer her mouth care and a drink
Give an antiemetic and recheck all her observations in 4 hours
Escalate urgently as a possible upper GI bleed and keep a record
12.w: Coffee-ground vomit suggests partly digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal bleed; NSAID use is a risk factor. With a rising pulse and falling blood pressure she needs urgent escalation (P3.12) and accurate recording of the amount and appearance (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: A stool sample does not address an acute bleed with haemodynamic change.
n.1: Disposing of it without escalation ignores a possible bleed; oral fluids may need withholding pending review.
n.2: An antiemetic does not address a possible bleed, and 4-hourly observations are too infrequent.

12.q: Stanley, 80, has end-stage heart and kidney disease and full capacity. The consultant judges that CPR would not succeed and records a DNACPR decision. Stanley tells the nurse he does not accept this and wants 'everything done'. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record that CPR will be attempted because Stanley has requested it
Ask his family to confirm the decision on his behalf at the next visit
Leave the decision unexplained to avoid causing Stanley more distress
Explain the decision sensitively and offer him a second opinion
12.w: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BMA, RCUK, RCN): where CPR would not be successful, clinicians have no obligation to offer it, but the patient should be informed sensitively, and if they do not accept the decision a second opinion should be offered. Tracey [2014]: presumption of involving the patient.

n.0: Clinicians are not obliged to offer CPR that would not succeed; a patient request does not require it (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
n.1: Stanley has capacity, so his family cannot confirm or make the decision for him.
n.2: Stanley must be informed and his concerns heard (Tracey [2014]); avoiding the topic denies him the chance to seek another view.

12.q: Dr Shah, the responsible clinician, wants to place Abi, 38, on a community treatment order on leaving hospital from section 3. Which agreement is legally required before the order can be made?
o: Approval of the proposed order by the First-tier Tribunal
The written agreement of an approved mental health professional
The written consent of Abi's nearest relative to the order
The agreement of Abi's named community mental health nurse
12.w: Section 17A(4) requires the RC's opinion that the criteria are met and an AMHP's written statement agreeing with that opinion and that it is appropriate to make the order.

n.0: Tribunals review CTOs after they are made; they do not approve them in advance.
n.2: The nearest relative's consent is not required for a CTO.
n.3: Care coordinators are consulted, but the statutory agreement is the AMHP's.

12.q: Before a transfer, Rosa checks the mobile hoist on her ward. The examination label shows that its last thorough examination under LOLER was eight months ago, and no examination scheme with different intervals is displayed. What should Rosa do?
o: Use the hoist, because lifting equipment is examined every 12 months
Take the hoist out of use, report it and use another hoist that is in date
Carry out a visual pre-use check and continue if the hoist looks sound
Use the hoist for this transfer and report the overdue date at handover
12.w: Under LOLER 1998, lifting equipment and accessories used for lifting people must be thoroughly examined at least every 6 months (other lifting equipment every 12 months) unless an examination scheme sets other intervals. A hoist overdue for examination should not be used to lift a person and should be reported (HSE, Thorough examinations and inspections of lifting equipment).

n.0: The 12-month interval applies to lifting equipment that is not used to lift people; patient hoists fall under the 6-month interval.
n.2: A pre-use check is good practice but does not replace the thorough examination by a competent person that LOLER requires.
n.3: Knowingly using equipment that is overdue for its statutory examination puts the patient at risk; the problem must be dealt with before the transfer.

12.q: Ms Silva, 30, is 28 weeks pregnant and detained on an acute ward with mania. After de-escalation fails she is given rapid tranquillisation. What is the most appropriate care immediately afterwards?
o: Avoid seclusion and monitor her closely afterwards
Seclude her to reduce stimulation as for other patients
Give a long-acting benzodiazepine to avoid repeat doses
Use the standard restraint position without changes
12.w: CG192 1.8.23: a pregnant woman needing rapid tranquillisation is treated as per NG10 except that she should not be secluded after RT, restraint is adapted to avoid harm to the fetus and short half-life drugs are preferred, with paediatric and anaesthetic input.

n.1: CG192 states she should not be secluded after rapid tranquillisation.
n.2: A short half-life benzodiazepine is preferred because of floppy baby syndrome risk.
n.3: Restraint must be adapted to avoid harm to the fetus.

12.q: Ms Clarke, 38, agrees to have a wound swab taken after the nurse explains why it is needed and what it involves. The swab is taken without problems. According to Code 4.2, what should the nurse also make sure of?
o: That the consent is confirmed again by the doctor
That Ms Clarke signs a consent form for the swab
That the consent obtained is documented in her record
That a second nurse witnesses Ms Clarke's agreement
12.w: Code 4.2: make sure that you get properly informed consent and document it before carrying out any action. Verbal consent is valid for a wound swab; the record should show it was obtained.

n.0: The nurse taking the swab obtains the consent; the doctor does not need to confirm it.
n.1: Written consent is not required for a routine swab; verbal consent is valid if documented.
n.3: There is no requirement for a witness to verbal consent for a routine procedure.

12.q: An approved mental health professional has serious concerns that Doreen, 79, who lives alone with severe self-neglect and possible psychosis, will not allow anyone into her flat. What is the lawful route to gain entry and, if necessary, remove her for assessment?
o: Ask her GP to complete a section 5(2) report
Ask a magistrate for a section 135(2) warrant to retake her
Apply to a magistrate for a section 135(1) warrant
Ask the police to use section 136 at her front door
12.w: Under section 135(1) a justice of the peace may, on information on oath from an AMHP, issue a warrant for a constable to enter premises, by force if needed, and remove the person to a place of safety. The constable must be accompanied by an AMHP and a registered medical practitioner (s135(4)).

n.0: Section 5(2) applies to hospital in-patients and is used by the doctor or approved clinician in charge of their treatment, not a GP at home.
n.1: Section 135(2) is for retaking a patient already liable to be detained; Doreen is not.
n.3: Section 136 cannot be used in a dwelling, including at the door of the person's own flat (s136(1A)).

12.q: Mr Tanaka, 82, has severe hearing loss and lip-reads. The nurse needs to explain his discharge plan. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Stand beside him and speak loudly into his better ear
Face him in good light and speak clearly at a normal pace
Give the information to his daughter to pass on later
Speak very slowly with exaggerated mouth movements
12.w: Annexe A 2.3: recognise and accommodate sensory impairments. Code 7.2-7.3: meet people's communication needs using a range of methods.

n.0: He lip-reads, so he needs to see the speaker's face; shouting distorts lip patterns.
n.2: This excludes him from his own care when he can communicate with adjustments.
n.3: Exaggeration distorts lip shapes and makes lip-reading harder.

12.q: A new wound treatment costs £30,000 more per patient than standard care and produces 1.5 more QALYs per patient. Using NICE's standard threshold in force since April 2026, what is the incremental cost per QALY and how does it compare?
o: £30,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, below the threshold range
£45,000 per QALY, above the threshold range
12.w: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = extra cost / extra QALYs = £30,000 / 1.5 = £20,000 per QALY. This is below the standard range of £25,000-£35,000 per QALY, so the treatment would usually be considered cost-effective (P7.3). Two steps: calculate, then compare with the current threshold.

n.0: This ignores the QALY gain and uses the extra cost alone.
n.1: The calculation is right, but £20,000 is below the current £25,000-£35,000 range, not within it.
n.3: This multiplies cost by QALYs instead of dividing.

12.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
12.q: Ms Fox, 22, in a DBT programme, cut her arm last night. Her wound has been treated and she is now calm. Her care plan uses DBT principles. Which approach is most appropriate now?
o: Start continuous one-to-one observation indefinitely
Avoid discussing it so as not to reinforce it
Do a chain analysis of what led to the self-harm
Stop her leave as a consequence of the incident
12.w: Step 1: deal with physical care and wait for calm. Step 2: behaviour chain analysis maps triggers, thoughts, feelings and actions to identify where skills could be used next time. Punitive responses are not part of DBT or NG225.

n.0: Indefinite observation is restrictive and not based on a current risk assessment.
n.1: Avoidance misses learning; DBT addresses self-harm directly.
n.3: Punitive restrictions damage engagement and are not therapeutic.

12.q: Daniel Morgan, 32, has a learning disability and is very anxious about needles. He missed his last two blood test appointments at a busy GP practice clinic. Which reasonable adjustment is most appropriate for the practice nurse to offer?
o: Offer the first appointment of the day with extra time and easy read information
Ask his support worker to bring him in and stay outside the room during the test
Arrange for the test to be done when he next attends hospital as an inpatient
Book him into the next routine clinic slot and send a standard reminder letter
12.w: Equality Act 2010 s20 places a duty to make reasonable adjustments so that disabled people are not at a substantial disadvantage. A quiet first appointment, extra time and accessible information reduce anxiety and support his access (P3.7 principles of reasonable adjustments; P7.9; Accessible Information Standard).

n.1: A familiar support worker can help, but asking them to wait outside removes the support he may need.
n.2: Waiting for an unplanned admission denies him timely, equitable access to routine care.
n.3: Repeating the arrangement that has failed twice makes no adjustment for his disability.

12.q: Mr Ellis, 55, is under the community mental health team after a suicide attempt. During his psychosocial assessment he mentions that the final hearing in his divorce is next Tuesday. Under NICE NG225, how should this be recorded in his formulation?
o: As a protective factor
As a historic factor
As a fixed static factor
As a future factor
12.w: NG225 1.5.10 asks assessors to explore historic, changeable and current, and future factors, including specific upcoming events or circumstances, plus protective factors. An upcoming court hearing is a future factor that may raise distress and should shape the plan around that date.

n.0: A stressful hearing is not protective; protective factors reduce risk, such as supportive relationships.
n.1: Historic factors are past events, such as a previous suicide attempt.
n.2: Static factors cannot change; a dated upcoming event is a future, time-specific factor.

12.q: A registered nurse on a surgical ward calls in sick. The bed manager suggests replacing her with an extra healthcare assistant because the total number of staff on shift would stay the same. Six patients on the ward have intravenous antibiotics due. What is the best response from the nurse in charge?
o: Accept the healthcare assistant, as total staff numbers meet the ward's planned establishment
Ask the healthcare assistant to give the IV antibiotics under her direct supervision
Accept the healthcare assistant and give all six patients' IV antibiotics herself
Explain that registered nurse tasks cannot be covered and escalate the skill mix gap
12.w: Safety depends on skill mix as well as numbers (P6.2; NICE SG1 Box 1 takes skill mix into account). Registered nurse tasks such as IV medicines and assessment cannot be delegated to a healthcare assistant (Code 11.1), so the gap must be escalated.

n.0: Matching headcount ignores the registered nurse time that patients' needs require.
n.1: IV antibiotic administration is outside a healthcare assistant's role; supervision does not make delegation appropriate.
n.2: Taking on extra IV work on top of her own role risks delayed doses elsewhere and hides the shortfall.

12.q: Bryony, 39, is nil by mouth after surgery. Her observations are stable and her prescription is for 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours via a volumetric infusion pump. The nurse is setting up the infusion and will ask a colleague to check it. At what rate should the pump be set?
o: 166 mL/h on the volumetric pump
125 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.5 mL/h on the volumetric pump
80 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.w: Rate (mL/h) = volume / time = 1,000 mL / 8 h = 125 mL/h. Accurate dosage calculation is a patient safety proficiency (P4.14) and the setting should be checked against the prescription.

n.0: 166 mL/h corresponds to 6 hours, not 8.
n.2: 12.5 mL/h is a decimal place error, a tenfold underinfusion.
n.3: 80 mL/h would deliver 1,000 mL over 12.5 hours.

12.q: Ms Grey, 31, has bipolar disorder and has been well on lithium for 3 years. She is now 6 weeks pregnant and remains well. What does NICE CG192 advise the team to consider?
o: Stopping the lithium today to protect the fetus
Continuing lithium with her usual 6-monthly levels
Stopping the lithium gradually over 4 weeks
Switching from lithium to valproate
12.w: CG192 1.4.35: if a woman taking lithium becomes pregnant and is well, consider stopping it gradually over 4 weeks, explaining that stopping may not remove the risk of fetal heart malformations and that relapse risk is high postnatally.

n.0: Abrupt stopping raises the risk of relapse.
n.1: If lithium continues, levels are monitored more often than usual in pregnancy.
n.3: Valproate must not be offered in pregnancy for a mental health problem.

12.q: A surgical registrar asks Priya, a registered nurse, to obtain Mrs Kaur's signature on a consent form for a laparoscopic procedure tomorrow. Priya has never seen this operation and does not know its specific risks or alternatives. What should Priya do?
o: Read the consent form aloud and witness Mrs Kaur's signature
Decline and ask the registrar to take consent from Mrs Kaur
Ask Mrs Kaur whether she has any questions before she signs
Obtain the signature and ask the registrar to explain risks later
12.w: Valid consent needs the person to be informed of material risks and reasonable alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 13 requires nurses to work within the limits of their competence, asking a suitably qualified professional for anything beyond it (13.3). Priya cannot give that information, so the clinician who can should seek consent.

n.0: Reading the form does not allow Priya to answer questions about risks and alternatives she does not know.
n.2: Priya could not answer Mrs Kaur's questions about this operation's risks, so her consent would not be properly informed.
n.3: A signature obtained before the risks are explained does not show informed consent; the form is evidence, not consent itself.

12.q: Ms Bell, 33, is admitted with psychosis. She says she was well until last week. Her partner, whom she has agreed the team can speak to, describes six months of her withdrawing from friends, sleeping poorly and stopping work. How should the nurse use this information?
o: Set the partner's account aside, as Ms Bell is the person assessed
Ask the partner to complete a depression questionnaire for her
Record the partner's account as collateral history beside her own
Use the partner's account in place of Ms Bell's, as more reliable
12.w: Collateral history from a family member or carer, gathered with consent, adds to the person's own account and can reveal a prodromal period. Both views are recorded and the person remains at the centre of the assessment (NMC P3.4; NICE CG178; Triangle of Care).

n.0: She agreed to the contact, and the partner's information may show a significant prodrome.
n.1: Self-report questionnaires are completed by the person; a proxy score would not be valid.
n.3: Her own account remains central; collateral history adds to it rather than replacing it.

12.q: Mr Clarke, 45, has just been admitted to an acute mental health ward with psychosis and has a diagnosis of high blood pressure. The team plans to start an antipsychotic. Which investigation should be offered before the first dose, in addition to the baseline bloods?
o: An EEG to assess his seizure threshold
A bone density scan for prolactin effects
A chest X-ray to assess his heart size
An ECG, given his admission and hypertension
12.w: NICE CG178 1.3.6.2: offer an ECG before starting antipsychotics if the SPC specifies it, if examination identifies cardiovascular risk such as hypertension, if there is a personal history of cardiovascular disease, or if the person is being admitted as an inpatient. Mr Clarke meets two criteria.

n.0: An EEG is not a routine baseline test before starting an antipsychotic.
n.1: Bone density is not a baseline test; prolactin is measured by blood test at baseline.
n.2: A chest X-ray is not part of the baseline antipsychotic checks and does not assess QT interval.

12.q: Ellen, 77, who had C. difficile infection, has been discharged home from a single room. The domestic team asks the nurse what terminal cleaning is required. Which instruction is most appropriate?
o: Use detergent wipes on surfaces and send the curtains as used linen
Clean with a 10,000 ppm available chlorine solution and leave the curtains in place
Clean with neutral detergent and change the curtains at the next routine change
Remove the curtains as infectious linen and clean with 1,000 ppm available chlorine
12.w: NIPCM ch 2.3 terminal decontamination: bag and remove waste, manage curtains and bedding as infectious linen, decontaminate equipment, then clean with a combined detergent and 1,000 ppm available chlorine solution (or detergent followed by 1,000 ppm), working from high to low and least to most contaminated.

n.0: Curtains from an infectious patient's room are infectious linen, and wipes alone are not a terminal clean.
n.1: 10,000 ppm is the strength for blood spills; terminal cleaning uses 1,000 ppm, and curtains are removed.
n.2: Detergent alone does not meet the terminal clean standard, and curtains from an isolation room are removed as infectious linen.

12.q: Cyril, 82, has not opened his bowels for 6 days despite oral laxatives and is uncomfortable. The doctor has prescribed a phosphate enema, and Cyril has given consent after you explained the procedure. In what position should he be placed for administration?
o: Supine with legs raised
Right lateral with legs straight
Prone with a pillow under the hips
Left lateral with knees flexed
12.w: The left lateral position follows the anatomy of the sigmoid colon and rectum, allowing the enema to flow along the bowel by gravity (Annexe B 6.5).

n.0: Supine makes insertion and retention difficult.
n.1: Right lateral works against the anatomy of the descending and sigmoid colon.
n.2: Prone is uncomfortable and does not aid flow into the sigmoid colon.

12.q: At a retirement celebration on the ward, a nurse takes a team photograph. A patient sitting in a bay is visible in the background. The nurse wants to post it on her public social media account. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Post the photograph after blurring the patient's face
Post the photograph with no names or ward details
Post the photograph using strict privacy settings
Post a version without the patient, who has not consented
12.w: NMC social media guidance: do not post pictures of patients and people receiving care without their consent, regardless of whether you believe they could be identified. Code 5.1 and 20.10.

n.0: NMC guidance requires consent before posting images of patients, whether or not you believe they could be identified.
n.1: Removing names does not remove the need for the patient's consent to the image being shared.
n.2: Privacy settings do not replace consent and content can still be shared onward.

12.q: On a busy surgical ward, a doctor asks Holly, a staff nurse, to get a healthcare assistant to give a prescribed dose of intravenous antibiotic so that it is not late. The healthcare assistant has not been trained in IV administration. What should Holly do?
o: Delay the dose until the evening medicines round, when more nurses are on duty
Give the IV dose herself or arrange for another competent registrant to give it
Delegate the IV dose and supervise the healthcare assistant closely at the bedside
Ask the doctor to give the dose, as the healthcare assistant is not trained
12.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence. An untrained healthcare assistant cannot safely give IV medicines, so the dose must be given by a competent registrant without undue delay (Code 18.1; P5.4 roles and scope of practice of team members).

n.0: Delaying a prescribed antibiotic risks harm when a competent nurse can give it now.
n.2: Supervision does not make delegation appropriate when the person lacks the training and competence for the task.
n.3: The doctor could give it, but medicine administration is within Holly's own role; passing it back adds delay without a reason.

12.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
12.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

12.q: Mrs Ball, 79, started sertraline three weeks ago. Her daughter reports she has become drowsy and muddled over two days. Her blood results show sodium 124 mmol/L (previously 139). What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Possible SSRI-induced hyponatraemia; inform the prescriber urgently
Expected sedation from sertraline; give the dose at night instead
Progression of dementia; continue the sertraline as prescribed
Worsening depression; ask for the sertraline dose to be increased
12.w: Hyponatraemia, usually in older people and possibly due to inappropriate ADH secretion, is associated with all antidepressants and more often with SSRIs. The BNF says to consider it in anyone who develops drowsiness, confusion or convulsions on an antidepressant.

n.1: Drowsiness with low sodium is a serious adverse effect, not expected sedation.
n.2: An acute change over two days with a falling sodium is not dementia progression.
n.3: Increasing the SSRI could worsen hyponatraemia.

12.q: Mr Hart, 47, is seen by a mental health nurse after telling his GP he has thought about ending his life. The nurse completes a psychosocial assessment and writes a risk formulation. Which content best describes a risk formulation as NICE NG225 intends it?
o: A total score from a validated suicide risk scale, placed in a band
His historic, current, future and protective factors, linked to a plan
A list of his diagnoses and the medicines prescribed for each one
A rating of low, medium or high risk with a review date
12.w: NG225 says mental health professionals should undertake a risk formulation in every psychosocial assessment, exploring historic, changeable and current, future and protective factors (1.5.10, 1.6.6), and focusing on the person's needs and safety rather than a prediction.

n.0: NG225 1.6.1 advises against using risk tools and scales to predict suicide.
n.2: Diagnoses and medicines may inform the formulation, but on their own they do not explain his risk or guide a plan.
n.3: Global low, medium or high risk stratification is not recommended for predicting suicide or deciding care (NG225 1.6.3-1.6.4).

12.q: Jade believes her ward manager is altering staffing records to hide unfilled shifts. She does not feel able to raise this with the manager herself. What is the most appropriate step?
o: Raise it with the manager's own staff at the next team meeting
Raise it with the designated person named in the trust's policy
Post her concerns on a professional social media group
Wait until she has more evidence before telling anyone
12.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: if you cannot raise the concern with your line manager, stage 2 is the designated person in your organisation (for example a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian). Code 16.1.

n.0: Discussing it with peers does not escalate it to someone able to act.
n.2: Public posting bypasses proper channels and risks confidentiality; NMC guidance uses internal and regulatory routes.
n.3: Code standard 16 requires her to act without delay; she does not need proof to raise a concern.

12.q: Aisha, a staff nurse in an NHS trust in England, raised concerns with her ward manager about unsafe practice on night shifts. Two weeks later nothing has changed and she feels her concerns were dismissed. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Raise the concern with the trust's Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
Post an anonymised account of the problem on a nursing social media group
Contact the National Guardian's Office to request an independent review
Report the ward manager to the NMC for failing to act on the concern
12.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance sets stages: line manager, then a designated person in the organisation, then a higher level, then a regulator. Local Freedom to Speak Up Guardians remain in place to support staff. The National Guardian's Office closed on 30 June 2026, with some functions moving to NHS England (FACTS S-RC, S-NGO).

n.1: Social media is not a route for raising concerns and risks breaching confidentiality (NMC social media guidance).
n.2: The National Guardian's Office closed on 30 June 2026 and does not review individual cases.
n.3: A referral to the regulator is not the next step when internal routes such as the FTSU Guardian have not been used.

12.q: Mr Day, 77, has type 2 diabetes and an infection. He is drowsy and his glucose meter displays 'HI' instead of a number. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the reading as normal and recheck it before the next meal
Assume the meter is faulty and replace it next week
Repeat the test in 4 hours with a different finger
Inform the doctor and send a venous sample for laboratory glucose
12.w: A 'HI' result means the glucose is above the meter's measurable range. In a drowsy person this needs urgent escalation and a laboratory glucose to establish the true value (Annexe B 2.10 and 2.5: manage and interpret blood glucose monitors).

n.0: 'HI' indicates a very high reading, not a normal one.
n.1: Assuming a fault without confirming the glucose risks missing a hyperglycaemic emergency.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours is unsafe in a drowsy person with a possible very high glucose.

12.q: Miss Patel, 45, has a learning disability and has substantial difficulty understanding the safeguarding process. Her only relative is the person suspected of abusing her. The local authority is starting a section 42 enquiry. What should happen?
o: The local authority arranges an independent advocate for her
Her relative supports her, as her closest family member
The enquiry continues without her views, to avoid distress
The nurse acts as her advocate throughout the enquiry
12.w: Care Act 2014 s68 and statutory guidance para 7.3: the local authority must arrange an independent advocate for a safeguarding enquiry where the adult has substantial difficulty being involved and there is no appropriate person to support them. The suspected abuser cannot be that person.

n.1: A relative suspected of abuse is not an appropriate person to support her.
n.2: Excluding her views contradicts Making Safeguarding Personal and the advocacy duty.
n.3: The nurse is not an independent advocate under the Care Act and has a different role.

12.q: A healthcare assistant has been doing continuous one-to-one observation of Leon, 22, for 2 hours and is starting to lose concentration. According to NICE NG10, what should happen?
o: Leon's observation level should be reduced to intermittent
She should observe from the nurses' station to rest
Another staff member should take over so she can have a break
She should continue to the end of the 12-hour shift
12.w: NICE NG10 1.4.20: no individual should undertake continuous observation above the general level for longer than 2 hours; if needed for longer, ensure regular breaks. Fatigue reduces vigilance and engagement.

n.0: Observation levels are changed on clinical grounds, not because the observer is tired.
n.1: Observing from a distance does not meet continuous observation requirements.
n.3: Continuous observation for a whole shift without breaks breaches NG10 1.4.20 and is unsafe.

12.q: Maya, 19, has made a serious attempt to strangle herself on the ward and remains intent on harming herself. The team decide she needs continuous observation. According to NICE NG10, what does this involve?
o: Being kept in the seclusion room with the door locked
Checks every 15 minutes, recorded on an observation chart
Staying within eyesight or arm's length of a designated nurse
Checks every 5 minutes by whichever staff member is free
12.w: NICE NG10 1.4.11: continuous observation means the person is kept within eyesight or at arm's length of a designated one-to-one nurse, with immediate access to other staff. Seclusion must not be used solely to manage self-harm (COP15 26.108).

n.0: Seclusion should never be used solely to manage self-harm (COP15 26.108).
n.1: Fifteen-minute checks are intermittent, not continuous, observation.
n.3: Frequent checks by any staff member are still intermittent and lack a designated observer.

12.q: Under NICE guidance on violence and aggression (NG10), when may manual restraint be used in a health setting?
o: As the first response whenever a person raises their voice
As a last resort when de-escalation fails and harm is likely
As a routine measure to give medicines a person has refused
As a punishment for breaking ward rules on two occasions
12.w: NICE NG10 and Annexe B 2.17: restrictive interventions are used as a last resort, after de-escalation and other strategies fail, when there is a real risk of harm, and must be proportionate and for the shortest time possible.

n.0: Raised voices call for de-escalation, not restraint.
n.2: Restraint is not a routine method of giving refused medicines; covert or compulsory treatment has its own legal safeguards.
n.3: Restraint is never punitive; this would breach human rights and the Code.

12.q: Mr Okoro, 34, started haloperidol five days ago on an acute mental health ward. He is now confused and sweating, his limbs are stiff throughout, his temperature is 39.2 C, his pulse is 124 and his blood pressure keeps changing between readings. Which complication of his medication is most likely?
o: Serotonin syndrome from interaction
Acute dystonic reaction to haloperidol
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) toxicity
12.w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is hyperthermia, fluctuating consciousness, muscle rigidity and autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia, labile blood pressure, sweating). It is rare but potentially fatal and can occur with any antipsychotic (BNF psychoses treatment summary).

n.0: Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and features clonus and hyperreflexia; he has started an antipsychotic.
n.1: Acute dystonia is a localised muscle spasm; it does not cause fever, confusion or autonomic instability.
n.3: Antimuscarinic toxicity causes dry, flushed skin rather than sweating and does not cause generalised rigidity.

12.q: Ellen, 81, has a NEWS2 of 1. Her son tells you she is 'not right' and much quieter than usual. You find she is newly confused but otherwise unchanged. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Rescore NEWS2 with 3 for new confusion and escalate to a doctor
Wait for her next scheduled observations before deciding
Explain that confusion is common in older people in hospital
Document her son's concern and continue 4-6 hourly observations
12.w: New confusion scores 3 in the consciousness parameter (ACVPU 'C', RCP NEWS2 2017). Her score becomes 4 with a single red parameter, which needs at least hourly monitoring and medical review. Family concerns are a valid trigger under Martha's Rule.

n.1: Waiting delays recognition of a new red-score parameter.
n.2: New confusion is a marker of deterioration, such as sepsis or delirium, and must not be normalised.
n.3: Documenting without rescoring misses a single-parameter 3, which needs hourly observations and medical review.

12.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
12.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

12.q: Gordon, 74, is in a single room with a suspected respiratory infection and needs a chest X-ray. The radiology department cannot bring a portable machine today. He is stable and can tolerate a mask. How should the nurse arrange his transfer?
o: Postpone the X-ray until his infection status has been confirmed
Transfer him without a mask and clean the wheelchair once the journey is complete
Ask him to wear an FFP3 respirator during the transfer and X-ray
Ask him to wear a surgical mask if tolerated and inform radiology of his status
12.w: NIPCM ch 2.1: infectious patients are transferred only when clinically necessary, and should wear a surgical mask in communal areas during transfer if tolerated; the receiving department and transport staff must be made aware of the precautions needed.

n.0: The X-ray is clinically needed, and transfer with precautions is appropriate rather than delaying diagnosis.
n.1: Without a mask he exposes others in corridors and waiting areas; cleaning afterwards does not prevent that exposure.
n.2: FFP3 respirators filter incoming air and must not be worn by infectious patients.

12.q: In a nursing home, the GP reviews Hilda, 88, by video call and decides to reduce her bisoprolol dose from tomorrow. The GP cannot visit to amend the medication administration record (MAR). Under RPS/RCN guidance, how should the change be communicated?
o: By a message passed on by Hilda's daughter after the call
By a secure electronic message from the GP, with records updated
By the nurse amending the MAR from her notes of the call
By a text message from the GP to the nurse's personal mobile phone
12.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20.2: if the prescriber cannot issue a new prescription or amend the chart, the changes are communicated by an appropriately secure electronic method and the patient's records are updated.

n.0: A relayed message from a relative is not a direction from the prescriber.
n.2: Without the prescriber's written or secure electronic confirmation, the nurse would be altering a prescription.
n.3: A personal phone is not a secure, auditable route for prescribing information.

12.q: Ms Ahmed, 36, has worried about everything for eight months and scores 13 on the GAD-7 questionnaire at her first appointment with a mental health nurse. How should the nurse interpret the score?
o: As minimal anxiety, as clinical concern starts at a score of 15
As a confirmed diagnosis of GAD, so an SSRI should be started
As a low suicide risk, as anxiety scores predict suicidal acts
As a probable anxiety disorder, needing a full clinical assessment
12.w: A GAD-7 score of 10 or more suggests a probable anxiety disorder, but rating scales are aids to assessment: they support, and do not replace, a clinical assessment and diagnosis, and they do not predict suicide (NICE CG113; NG225 1.6).

n.0: A score of 13 is above the usual threshold of 10 for a probable anxiety disorder.
n.1: A screening score does not make a diagnosis or decide treatment; CG113 also offers psychological interventions before drugs.
n.2: Scales do not predict suicide; NG225 advises against using tools to predict suicide.

12.q: Ellie has worked 60 hours a week for a month to cover vacancies. She has twice nearly given the wrong dose and feels exhausted. Her manager asks her to do another extra shift. What should Ellie do?
o: Accept the shift and ask colleagues to double-check her work
Decline the shift and tell her manager about the near misses
Accept the shift and rest fully on her next day off
Decline the shift and keep the near misses to herself
12.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need for your role. Code 16.3: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity about problems that may prevent you working within the Code. Proficiency P1.5.

n.0: Working while exhausted keeps patients at risk; she must address her fitness for practice (Code 20.9).
n.2: Planning rest later does not address the current risk she has recognised.
n.3: Declining helps, but Code 16.3 requires her to tell someone in authority about problems affecting safe practice.

12.q: Claire Bennett, 42, who has multiple sclerosis, is due for discharge after a relapse. During discharge planning, Sunil, her nurse, learns that her 14-year-old son provides much of her care at home. What should Sunil do?
o: Ask Claire to arrange more help from other family members before discharge
Plan the discharge around the son's school hours, as he already provides her care
Leave the son out of discussions, as he is under 18 and cannot be a carer
Involve the son appropriately and notify the local authority so it can assess him
12.w: NHS trusts must involve unpaid carers, including young carers, in discharge planning as soon as feasible (Care Act 2014 s74 as amended by the Health and Care Act 2022). Where a young carer is identified, the local authority should be notified so it can carry out a young carer's needs assessment, including whether caring is appropriate or excessive (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Other support may help, but the young carer still needs to be identified and referred for assessment.
n.1: Relying on a child's care without assessment may place excessive responsibility on him and ignores safeguarding considerations.
n.2: Young carers are recognised in law and must be identified and involved appropriately, not excluded.

12.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
12.q: Mr Ahmed, 60, has been on a long-stay ward for a year and has a close working relationship with his named nurse. Discharge is planned in 6 weeks and he has started to become anxious when it is mentioned. What should the nurse do?
o: Promise to visit him at home after discharge
Avoid mentioning discharge so that he stays settled
Hand over his care on the day he is discharged
Discuss the ending early and plan community support
12.w: Step 1: recognise anxiety about ending as part of Peplau's resolution phase. Step 2: plan the ending openly and early, linking him with community staff so the relationship closes safely.

n.0: Personal visits cross professional boundaries.
n.1: Avoidance leaves the anxiety unaddressed and makes the ending abrupt.
n.2: A same-day handover gives no chance to build new relationships.

12.q: During a morning shift, a nurse notices that Omar, 44, who is usually sociable, is sitting alone, clenching his fists, staring at another patient and muttering. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Move the other patient off the ward for the rest of the day
Increase his observation level to continuous and inform security
Approach calmly, say he seems upset and ask what is troubling him
Offer him PRN lorazepam straight away to prevent an incident
12.w: NICE NG10 1.3.13 and 1.3.17: build a close working relationship, sensitively monitor changes in mood or composure that may lead to aggression, and communicate respect and empathy. Early engagement on noticing warning signs is the first step before any restrictive measure.

n.0: Removing another patient disrupts their care and does not address Omar's distress.
n.1: Observation should be used after positive engagement fails (NG10 1.4.12); jumping to continuous observation and security is premature.
n.3: PRN medication is part of de-escalation, but the first step is to engage and understand what is wrong.

12.q: Gordon, 66, dies unexpectedly on a surgical ward on the day after a planned procedure. There are no suspicious circumstances, but his death will be referred to the coroner to investigate the cause. He has a peripheral cannula and a urinary catheter. How should the nurse manage these devices during care after death?
o: Leave the cannula in place and spigot the urinary catheter
Remove both and send them with him in a labelled bag
Remove the cannula and catheter before washing him
Remove the cannula but leave the catheter bag attached
12.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause and there are no suspicious circumstances, leave IV cannulae and lines in situ and catheters spigotted; personal care can then be given. Deaths that may be related to a medical procedure or treatment require coroner referral.

n.1: Removing devices could affect the coroner's investigation of a death that may relate to a procedure.
n.2: Devices are left in situ when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause.
n.3: The cannula must stay in situ; the catheter is spigotted, and the bag contents may be discarded per policy.

12.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
12.q: A student asks how DBT differs from standard CBT. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It relies on medication to stabilise emotions first
It balances change strategies with acceptance and validation
It is a brief therapy delivered over 4 sessions
It focuses on interpreting unconscious childhood conflict
12.w: DBT combines CBT change strategies with acceptance, mindfulness and validation (the 'dialectic' between acceptance and change). Comprehensive DBT includes individual therapy, skills groups and phone coaching over many months.

n.0: DBT is psychological; drugs are not used for BPD itself (CG78).
n.2: Comprehensive DBT runs for months; brief interventions under 3 months are not advised for BPD (CG78).
n.3: Interpreting unconscious conflict is psychodynamic.

12.q: Cyril, 82, has heart failure and is on intravenous furosemide 80 mg twice daily. His morning bloods show potassium 3.1 mmol/L (previously 4.0). He feels weak. What best explains this result, and what should the nurse do?
o: IV furosemide dilutes the blood; increase his oral fluid intake
Loop diuretics cause potassium retention; repeat the bloods tomorrow
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; inform the prescriber now
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; give a banana with lunch
12.w: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that increases urinary sodium and potassium excretion, so hypokalaemia is an expected effect (P4.17, applying pharmacology). A fall to 3.1 mmol/L with weakness needs prompt prescriber review for replacement and dose review; low potassium increases arrhythmia risk in heart failure.

n.0: Dilution is not the mechanism, and extra fluid may worsen heart failure.
n.1: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, not retention, and a day's delay is unsafe.
n.3: Dietary potassium will not correct this promptly and the prescriber still needs to know.

12.q: Harold, 79, has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids. Overnight he becomes breathless with RR 26, SpO2 92% on air, crackles at both lung bases and new ankle swelling. His fluid balance is positive 2,300 mL over 24 hours. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase the infusion rate to correct the dehydration
Give a prescribed diuretic before informing anyone
Stop the infusion, sit him up and escalate urgently
Continue the infusion and recheck in 4 hours
12.w: Breathlessness, crackles, oedema and a large positive balance suggest fluid overload. Stop the infusion, sit him upright, give oxygen to target and escalate urgently: NEWS2 RR 26 = 3 and SpO2 92% = 2 gives at least 5 (RCP 2017). CG174 asks for fluid mismanagement to be reported as an incident.

n.0: More fluid worsens overload.
n.1: Treatment decisions need urgent medical review; giving a diuretic first delays escalation.
n.3: Continuing the infusion worsens overload and 4 hours is too long.

12.q: Mr Ito, 31, completes a PHQ-9 with the nurse at his GP surgery. He scores 18. He has no suicidal thoughts and no psychotic symptoms. How should his depression be classified and managed under NICE NG222?
o: As more severe, discussing combined CBT and an antidepressant
As severe enough to need an urgent referral for ECT assessment
As less severe, with guided self-help offered first
As less severe, with active monitoring for the next 2 weeks
12.w: Step 1: NG222 uses a PHQ-9 cut-off of 16; 16 or more is 'more severe'. Step 2: offer a choice of more severe depression treatments, the first in the table being individual CBT with an antidepressant.

n.1: ECT is for severe life-threatening depression or when other treatments fail, not a PHQ-9 score.
n.2: A score of 18 is above the 16 cut-off, so this is not less severe.
n.3: Active monitoring is for people with less severe depression who do not want treatment.

12.q: Ernest, 81, has Parkinson's disease with a tremor and struggles to get food to his mouth. He is eating less than half his meals. Which intervention should be tried first to help him eat?
o: Provide adapted cutlery, a plate guard and help
Give his meals later, when the ward is quieter
Refer him for insertion of a nasogastric feeding tube
Prescribe oral nutritional supplements three times a day
12.w: Annexe B 5.3: assist with eating and drinking and use feeding and drinking aids. Adapted cutlery, plate guards and non-slip mats, plus assistance (for example via a red tray system or protected mealtimes), address the cause of his poor intake.

n.1: Delaying meals does not address his difficulty and may mean food is cold.
n.2: Enteral feeding is not indicated when oral intake can be improved with help.
n.3: Supplements may follow, but his barrier is a physical one that aids can address first.

12.q: Martha, 58, reads the leaflet for a newly prescribed medicine and finds it describes a different condition from hers. The pharmacist confirms the medicine is licensed in the UK but has been prescribed outside the terms of its licence. Martha asks the nurse whether this is allowed. Which reply is accurate?
o: It is a dispensing error, as the leaflet does not match her condition
It is off-label use, and the prescriber should explain it to her
It is allowed once a second doctor countersigns the prescription
It is unlicensed use, so it cannot legally be given on the ward
12.w: Off-label use means prescribing a licensed medicine outside its marketing authorisation (P4.16). It is lawful, but the prescriber takes on greater responsibility and should give the person enough information to make an informed choice. The nurse should check Martha's understanding and refer questions to the prescriber.

n.0: The pharmacist has confirmed the supply is correct; a mismatched leaflet is expected with off-label use.
n.2: Off-label prescribing does not require a second doctor's countersignature.
n.3: An unlicensed medicine has no UK licence at all; this medicine is licensed but used off-label, which is lawful.

12.q: Ivy, 84, now has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to decide where she lives or how she is cared for. Some years ago, with capacity, she wrote a signed letter saying she would like to be cared for at home and prefers baths to showers. How should staff treat this letter?
o: As having no weight now that she lacks capacity to confirm her wishes
As a legally binding instruction that must be followed in the same way as an ADRT
As a statement of her wishes that must be considered in best interests decisions
As binding once her GP has countersigned it and placed it in her record
12.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6)(a): in deciding best interests, consider so far as reasonably ascertainable the person's past and present wishes and feelings, in particular any relevant written statement made when they had capacity. An advance statement of this kind is considered but is not legally binding, unlike a valid and applicable ADRT (ss24-26).

n.0: MCA s4(6)(a) requires decision makers to consider past wishes, in particular relevant written statements made with capacity.
n.1: A statement of wishes and preferences is not legally binding; only a valid, applicable ADRT binds staff to a refusal of treatment.
n.3: A GP signature does not convert a statement of wishes into a binding document.

12.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
12.q: Ms Lane, 32, notices her moods are much harder to manage when she sleeps badly, skips meals and drinks alcohol. Her DBT therapist works with her on these areas. Which module does this belong to?
o: Emotion regulation
Interpersonal effectiveness
Distress tolerance
Radical acceptance
12.w: Emotion regulation includes reducing vulnerability to strong emotions by looking after physical health, eating, sleep, exercise and avoiding mood-altering substances (PLEASE skills).

n.1: Interpersonal effectiveness concerns relationships and requests.
n.2: Distress tolerance is about surviving crises in the moment.
n.3: Radical acceptance is a distress tolerance skill, not a module.

12.q: During the breakfast round, Norma, 85, says she would like to take her tablets after she has eaten and asks the nurse to leave them on her table. Norma has capacity but no self-administration assessment has been done. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the tablets as refused and offer them at lunchtime
Return after breakfast to give them and record once taken
Leave the tablets and sign the chart as given
Leave the tablets and ask a support worker to check later
12.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-4 and 15-17: unless a self-administration risk assessment allows it, the nurse administering remains accountable and must see the dose taken; the record is completed at the time of administration (NICE SC1: record only after the dose is taken).

n.0: Norma has not refused; she asked to take them later, which can be accommodated.
n.2: Signing before the dose is taken creates an inaccurate record and the tablets may be lost or taken by others.
n.3: Delegating a check does not confirm administration and leaves medicines unattended.

12.q: Laura, a staff nurse, has worried for several weeks that the night skill mix on her ward is unsafe, with frequent missed observations. She has not yet raised it with anyone. According to NMC guidance, who should she raise it with first?
o: The NMC, so that it can investigate the ward's safety
The trust chief executive, as the person accountable for staffing
The Care Quality Commission, as the regulator for the ward
Her line manager, verbally or in writing, keeping a record
12.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: stage 1 line manager (verbally or in writing, keep a record); stage 2 designated person; stage 3 higher level; stage 4 regulator or helpline. Code 16.1.

n.0: The NMC regulates individual professionals; this is a system concern for the line manager first.
n.1: A higher level in the organisation is stage 3, after the line manager and designated person.
n.2: Going to a regulator is stage 4 of the NMC guidance, used if internal routes fail or are unsuitable.

12.q: Aaron, 33, has been detained under section 3 since 2 January and first received antipsychotic medication on 4 January. On 10 April he refuses it, and the approved clinician believes it is still needed. What is required to continue the medication lawfully?
o: The written consent of his nearest relative
Continue under section 63, which covers medication throughout detention
A best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act
A certificate from a second opinion appointed doctor
12.w: Section 58 applies once 3 months have passed since medication for mental disorder was first given in the current detention (4 January to 4 April). After that, a patient who refuses or lacks capacity can be given medication only if a SOAD certifies it is appropriate. Aaron refuses on 10 April, beyond 3 months.

n.0: The nearest relative has no power to consent to treatment under Part 4.
n.1: Section 63 is limited by section 58 after the 3-month period; a SOAD certificate is now required.
n.2: MCA s28 excludes Part 4 treatment for mental disorder from MCA authority.

12.q: You observe Jake, a first-year student nurse, using alcohol-based handrub. He applies a small amount, rubs his palms together for about 10 seconds, misses his thumbs and fingertips, and wipes the residue on his tunic. What feedback is most appropriate?
o: Apply a second dose and rub palms for a further 10 seconds
Cover all surfaces, including thumbs and fingertips, for 20 to 30 seconds until dry
Rinse the handrub off under running water after 15 seconds of firm rubbing
Rub all hand surfaces for 40 to 60 seconds, then dry them with a paper towel
12.w: The WHO handrub technique adopted in NIPCM appendix 2 covers all surfaces of the hands, including thumbs and fingertips, and takes 20 to 30 seconds, with hands left to dry naturally. 40 to 60 seconds is the duration for handwashing with soap and water.

n.0: A second dose rubbed on the palms still misses the thumbs and fingertips that he omitted.
n.2: Handrub is not rinsed off; rinsing removes the product before it has acted.
n.3: 40 to 60 seconds is the handwash duration; handrub is rubbed until dry and is not towel-dried.

12.q: Rajesh, 52, is on day 3 of intravenous antibiotics through a forearm cannula. He reports pain at the site, and you see redness and swelling tracking along the vein. He still needs intravenous antibiotics. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply a warm compress and reassess the site at the end of the shift
Leave the cannula in place and record the findings in the care plan
Flush the cannula with 0.9% sodium chloride and continue if it is patent
Remove the cannula and arrange resiting at a different site
12.w: Pain, erythema and swelling at a cannula site indicate phlebitis on a visual infusion phlebitis assessment, which calls for removal of the device. As IV therapy is still needed, a new cannula is resited elsewhere using ANTT, and the findings are documented.

n.0: A compress may ease symptoms after removal, but delaying removal leaves an infected device in place.
n.1: Documentation is needed, but leaving the cannula in place does not manage the phlebitis.
n.2: Patency does not rule out phlebitis; continuing to use an inflamed site risks thrombophlebitis and bloodstream infection.

12.q: Patricia, 73, lives in England and has had regular breast screening. She asks the practice nurse why she has not received an invitation since she turned 71. Which response is accurate?
o: Invitations stop after 70, but she can refer herself for screening
Women over 70 are invited every 5 years instead of every 3 years
Breast screening ends at 70 because no benefit remains after that age
She needs a GP referral to a breast clinic to be screened
12.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): breast screening is offered to women aged 50 to 70; women over 70 can self-refer.
