n.1: Routine invitations are for women aged 50 to 70; after 70 screening is by self-referral.
n.2: Women over 70 can still self-refer; screening is available to them on request.
n.3: A breast clinic referral is for symptoms; screening after 70 is by self-referral.

12.q: Mr Price, 52, on a mental health ward, is rigid and confused after starting an antipsychotic. His observations are: respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on air, blood pressure 150/92, pulse 118, temperature 39.3 C, and new confusion. What is his NEWS2 score and the response required?
o: 11, needing six-hourly observations
6, needing an urgent ward review
9, needing an emergency response
4, needing hourly observations
12.w: NEWS2: respiratory rate 21-24 = 2, SpO2 96% = 0, air = 0, systolic 150 = 0, pulse 111-130 = 2, new confusion = 3, temperature 39.1 or above = 2; total 9. A score of 7 or more triggers an emergency response, which on a mental health unit usually means emergency transfer to acute care (RCP NEWS2).

n.0: The total is 9, and any score of 7 or more needs an emergency response, not six-hourly observations.
n.1: The total is 9, not 6; new confusion alone scores 3.
n.3: The total is 9; a score of 4 would understate his deterioration.

12.q: Nurse Sara notices she has written the wrong blood pressure value in a patient's paper observation chart. What is the correct way to correct the entry?
o: Write the right value over the top of the wrong one
Cover the entry with correction fluid and rewrite it neatly
Tear out the page and copy the chart onto a new sheet
Strike through once, keep it legible, then sign, date and time
12.w: Code 10.3-10.4: complete records accurately without falsification, attribute entries and date and time them. Annexe A 1.8: write accurate, clear, legible records.

n.0: Overwriting makes both values illegible and unattributed.
n.1: Obscuring the original entry could be seen as falsification and makes the change untraceable (Code 10.3).
n.2: Removing pages destroys part of the record and breaches Code 10.3.

12.q: Agnes, 79, has type 2 diabetes with reduced sensation in her feet. Her toenails are long and thickened, and she asks you to cut them during her bath. What is the most appropriate action?
o: File her nails down after soaking her feet for 20 minutes
Explain the risk and refer her to the podiatry service
Ask a healthcare support worker to cut them carefully
Cut her nails straight across with sterile nail clippers
12.w: People with diabetes and reduced sensation are at high risk of foot ulceration from minor trauma, so thickened nails should be cut by a podiatrist. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during nail care.

n.0: Prolonged soaking softens skin and can cause maceration in a person with diabetes.
n.2: Delegating a task that needs specialist assessment does not reduce the risk.
n.3: Cutting thickened nails in a person with diabetic neuropathy risks injury and ulceration.

12.q: Mr Ince, 40, scores 23 on AUDIT and drinks about 18 units a day. He has no history of seizures or delirium tremens, lives with a supportive partner and wants to stop. What does NICE CG115 suggest considering?
o: Advising him to stop drinking at once
Brief advice and a review in 3 months
Assessment for community-based assisted withdrawal
Inpatient assisted withdrawal as the first option
12.w: Step 1: over 15 units a day and AUDIT 20 or more. Step 2: CG115 1.3.4.1: consider assessment for and delivery of community-based assisted withdrawal, with no inpatient criteria present (under 30 units, no seizures or DTs, support at home).

n.0: Abrupt stopping without support risks dangerous withdrawal.
n.1: Brief advice is for hazardous drinking; he is likely dependent and needs assisted withdrawal.
n.3: He meets none of the inpatient criteria.

12.q: Mr Novak, 34, was in a serious car crash 4 months ago. He has flashbacks, nightmares, avoids driving and is constantly on edge. He is diagnosed with PTSD. Which treatment does NICE NG116 recommend first?
o: Non-directive supportive counselling
Regular lorazepam to reduce hyperarousal
Psychologically-focused debriefing
Individual trauma-focused CBT or EMDR
12.w: NG116 1.6.16 and 1.6.19: offer adults individual trauma-focused CBT (more than 1 month after the trauma), or EMDR for PTSD presenting more than 3 months after a non-combat trauma (1.6.19).

n.0: Non-trauma-focused counselling is not a NICE first-line treatment for PTSD.
n.1: Benzodiazepines are not a PTSD treatment and carry dependence risk.
n.2: NICE advises against debriefing to prevent or treat PTSD.

12.q: A trained healthcare worker is giving CPR to an adult with a pocket mask. What ratio of compressions to rescue breaths should be used?
12.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, each breath just enough to make the chest start to rise.

n.1: 15:2 is the ratio used in paediatric life support by healthcare rescuers.
n.2: 5:1 is an obsolete ratio not used in current guidance.
n.3: 30:1 gives too few breaths for adult BLS.

12.q: Mr Shah, 47, has bipolar disorder and develops moderate depression. He is not currently taking any medicine for bipolar disorder. Which medication option does NICE CG185 recommend?
o: Mirtazapine on its own
Quetiapine on its own
Sertraline with lorazepam
Fluoxetine on its own
12.w: CG185 1.6.3: for moderate or severe bipolar depression in a person not taking a drug for bipolar disorder, offer fluoxetine combined with olanzapine, or quetiapine on its own. A psychological intervention for bipolar depression is also offered (1.6.1).

n.0: Antidepressant monotherapy risks switching into mania and is not recommended.
n.2: Neither drug addresses bipolar depression in line with CG185, and the SSRI is unprotected by an antimanic agent.
n.3: Fluoxetine is recommended combined with olanzapine, not as monotherapy.

12.q: Mrs Kowalska, 74, speaks Polish and little English. She needs to consent to a planned procedure. Her 12-year-old grandson offers to interpret. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a bilingual ward housekeeper to interpret during her break
Accept the grandson's offer as he is a trusted relative
Give her the English consent form to take home overnight
Book a professional interpreter before discussing consent
12.w: NHS England Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services in primary care (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; use of anyone under 16 is not acceptable except when immediate and necessary treatment is required. Code 7.2.

n.0: An untrained staff member is not a registered interpreter; reliance on unqualified interpreters is discouraged.
n.1: NHS England guidance says use of anyone under 16 is not acceptable except for immediate necessary treatment.
n.2: An English form does not meet her language needs and is not informed consent.

12.q: While walking to the nurses' station, Chloe, a staff nurse, notices a large pool of spilled water on the corridor floor outside a bay where several patients walk with frames. Nobody else is nearby. What should Chloe do first?
o: Complete an incident report so the hazard is recorded for the ward manager
Ask the domestic team to mop the floor when they reach the ward this afternoon
Make the area safe straight away with a warning sign and arrange for it to be dried
Tell the patients in the bay at the next ward round to avoid that corridor
12.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 require nurses to act promptly on hazards, and s7 Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires reasonable care for others. Removing an immediate slip hazard comes first; reporting follows (P6.6 respond to potential hazards).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate but should follow making the area safe; the hazard remains while the form is completed.
n.1: Leaving a known slip hazard until the afternoon exposes patients with frames to falls.
n.3: Warning patients later does not remove the hazard now and relies on people remembering.

12.q: A GP practice annual report states that on 1 April 2026, 850 of its 12,000 registered adults were living with diagnosed type 2 diabetes. A student nurse on placement asks what this figure measures. Which term is correct?
o: Prevalence
Relative risk
Life expectancy
Incidence
12.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: prevalence is the total number of existing cases in a population at a point in time (point prevalence) or over a period; incidence counts new cases. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2.

n.1: Relative risk compares the risk of an outcome between an exposed and an unexposed group.
n.2: Life expectancy estimates average years of life remaining and is unrelated to this count.
n.3: Incidence counts new cases over a period; this figure counts everyone currently living with the condition.

12.q: Fred, 72, has crusting around both eyelids after a viral illness. You are asked to clean his eyes. Which technique is correct?
o: Use one swab for each eye, wiping back and forth across the lid
Use one swab for both eyes, wiping from outer to inner corner
Use a fresh swab for each eye, wiping from inner to outer corner
Use a dry cotton bud inside the lower lid to remove crusts
12.w: Eye care principles: use sterile saline and a separate swab for each eye, wiping once from the inner canthus outward, so that debris and infection are not carried into the tear duct or the other eye (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wiping back and forth reintroduces debris to the eye.
n.1: Sharing a swab and wiping inward risks cross-infection and moving debris into the tear duct.
n.3: Inserting a cotton bud inside the lid risks corneal injury.

12.q: Mrs Ellis, 81, has advanced heart failure and full capacity. A doctor completes a DNACPR form overnight and asks the nurse not to mention it to her because 'it will only upset her'. Mrs Ellis has said she wants to be involved in all decisions. Which statement best reflects the legal position?
o: She should be consulted unless this is likely to cause her physical or psychological harm
She should be told once the decision has been reviewed by a second consultant
She need not be told because a DNACPR decision is a clinical decision for the doctor
Her husband should be told instead, as the decision affects the whole family
12.w: In R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014] EWCA Civ 822, the Court of Appeal held that Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions and that there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Possible upset is not enough.

n.1: A second opinion does not replace the duty to consult her before the notice is placed; delaying her involvement is not lawful on these facts.
n.2: Tracey held that although CPR is a clinical decision, the patient must be involved and consulted; the clinical nature of the decision does not remove that duty.
n.3: Mrs Ellis has capacity, so the duty to consult is owed to her; informing her husband in her place breaches her Article 8 rights and confidentiality.

12.q: A charge nurse asks what a basic business case for funding two additional healthcare assistant posts should contain. Which content is most appropriate?
o: Last year's off-duty rotas to show how often extra shifts were filled
A list of the staff who support the request, with their signatures
The problem, the options considered, their costs and the expected benefits
Details of recent incidents including the patients' names and dates of birth
12.w: A business case explains why change is needed, the options (including doing nothing), costs, expected benefits to patients and the organisation, and how success will be measured (P7.12). Evidence should be anonymised to protect confidentiality (Code 5).

n.0: Past rotas may support part of the argument but are not the core content of a business case.
n.1: Support from colleagues does not show need, cost or benefit.
n.3: Identifiable patient information is not needed and would breach confidentiality; anonymised data should be used.

12.q: A school nurse is teaching staff about adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), using the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh ACE study. Which experience is counted as an ACE in that study?
o: Living with a household member who served a prison sentence
Being born early and spending time in a neonatal unit
Moving house and changing school during the primary years
Having a parent who regularly worked night shifts
12.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): the nine ACEs were verbal, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up in a household with parental separation, domestic violence, mental illness, alcohol abuse, drug use or incarceration.

n.1: Prematurity is not one of the nine ACEs measured.
n.2: Moving house is not one of the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh study.
n.3: Parental shift work is not one of the nine ACEs measured.

12.q: A ward nurse is referring Mr Kaur, 70, to the community dietitian after finding he has lost 8% of his body weight in 3 months. Which action best supports a safe referral?
o: Ask his GP to make the referral so that it is from a doctor
Send the referral and let the dietitian explain it when they contact him
Send his entire hospital record so that the dietitian has all details
Explain the referral to him and include the reason, urgency and key findings
12.w: P3.16: know when and how to refer safely. The person should understand and agree to the referral (Code 4.2), and the referral should give the reason, urgency and relevant findings, sharing the minimum necessary information (Caldicott principle 3).

n.0: Nurses can refer directly to a dietitian; routing via the GP adds delay.
n.1: He should know about and agree to the referral before it is sent.
n.2: Sending the whole record exceeds the minimum necessary information for the purpose.
